Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) was a randomized clinical trial that studied the effect of photocoagulation on diabetic macular edema.

The results of the study demonstrated the beneficial effects of focal photocoagulation on diabetic macular edema. The study resulted in the recommendation that all eyes with clinically significant diabetic macular edema should be considered for focal photocoagulation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the structure marked with red arrow
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Outer plexiform layer

The marked structure in the slide is the outer plexiform layer of the retina.

The outer plexiform layer (outer synaptic layer) is present between the outer nuclear layer and the inner nuclear layer. This layer stains lightly. This layer consists of the axons of rods and cones which synapse with dendrites of bipolar neurons and horizontal cells.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The test given below in the image is used for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stereopsis test

The given image is of Titmus stereotest, which is done for the assesment of stereopsis (perception of depth).

• The pictures consist of a housefly for children and circular patterns for adults.
• The picture is held in front of the eyes of the patient at a distance of about 16 inches and the patient is asked to wear polarized glasses.
• If the patient's perception of the depth is normal, the housefly appears to rise above the plane, like a 3D image. If the patient is asked to pinch the wings of the housefly, he/she will try to pinch in the air, above the plane of the image.
• If the patient's perception of depth in either eye is defective, then the image appears just like normal 2D image.

Option A: Tests for ocular deviation include

• Cover tests
• Prism cover test- This will tell the amount of deviation in prism dioptres.
• Maddox rod test
• Hirschberg corneal reflex test

The below given image shows Maddox rod test.

Option C: Test for refractive error includes

• Retinoscopy
• Auto refractometry

The below given image shows the findings of Retinoscopy in different refractive errors.

Option D: Tests for colour blindness include

• Ishihara test: It is frequently used to screen for a red–green colour vision deficit. It consists of a test plate followed by 16 plates, each with a series of dots arranged to show a shape or number that the subject is asked to identify.
• Hardy–Rand–Rittler test: It is similar to ishihara test but is used to detect all three color vision defect.
• Farnsworth–Munsell 100-hue test: Is the most sensitive test for both acquired and congenital colour blindness. It consists of 85 caps of different hue that needs to be rearranged.

The below given image depicts the ishihara test.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the first step in the management of an 18-month-old child with both eyes deviated medially:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Refractive error testing

In children, who present with a convergent squint, the first step is to check the visual acuity and estimate the error of refraction.

Convergent squint also known as Esotrpia is commonly seen in children with hyperopia (also known as hypermetropia) of which the accomdative type of esotropia is more common in the age group below 3 years.

The first line of management in the treatment of esotropia includes refractive error correction with glasses.

If a child with accomdative issues, is unable to use spectacles (such as a child ≤ 2 years) or is non compliant with wearing glasses we can eliminate accommodation by temporarily treating him with miotic drugs such as echothiophate.

Further treatment may include orthoptic training with specific exercises or surgical correction when the angle of squint is 10° or more with correcting lenses and when orthoptic training doesnt help in reasonable correction of the squint.

Mnemonic:

The algorithm for the management of accommodative esotropia is as follows:

• R: Refractive correction: Glasses/Miotics
• O: Orthoptics/Occlusion: for amblyopia
• O: Operative correction: for non-accommodative component
• P: Prism correction: for remaining error

Classification of Accomdative esotropia:

Type
Criteria

Refractive

• Associated with high hypermetropia (+4 to +7 D)
• Typically esotropia is for both near and distance.
• Fully correctable by spectacles

Non-refractive

• Occurs independent of refractive errors
• Abnormal accommodative convergence/accommodation (AC/A) ratio
• Typically esotropia is greater for near than for distance
• Fully corrected by bifocal glasses

The below image shows accomdative esotropia before and after correction.

Option A: Forced Duction Test (FDT) is performed to differentiate between the paralytic and restrictive type of inconcomitant squint.

FDT is positive in restrictive squint where a resistance is encountered during passive rotation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is correct regarding the image given below:
options: It is called Argyl Robertson pupil
The vision is normal in right eye
Seen in optic neuritis, the pupil can paradoxically dilate in the both eyes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Seen in optic neuritis, the pupil can paradoxically dilate in the both eyes

The given image of "swinging flashlight test" shows both pupils constricting when the left eye is stimulated (normal response) followed by both pupils abnormally dilating when the right eye is stimulated (abnormal response).

This finding is suggestive of Marcus Gunn pupil which is also known as Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD).

In this patient the right eye is defective (Option A) and the left eye is normal (rules out option B).

Marcus Gunn pupil refers to the paradoxical response of the pupil to light and it is the earliest sign of optic nerve disease such as optic neuritis or optic nerve damage in glaucoma.It is caused due to a defect in the afferent pathway (optic nerve) of the pupillary light reflex in one eye.

Normal response to stimulation of the eye is constriction of the pupil of the stimulated eye (direct light reflex) and also of the contralateral eye (indirect or consensual light reflex).

Causes of RAPD:

• Optic nerve lesions (e.g.All types of optic neuritis, glaucoma)
• Optic tract lesions (e.g., infarction)
• Severe retinal disease (e.g., central retinal artery occlusion, extensive retinal detachment)
• Maculopathy (macular degeneration )

The below given image depicts the findings seen in Marcus Gunn pupil (RAPD).

Option A:Argyl Robertson pupil is seen in neurosyphilis. In this condition,on light stimulation both the pupils will not constrict, but on accommodation (near target) both the pupils will constrict.

Argyll Robertson pupil is attributed to a dorsal midbrain lesion of neurosyphilis that affects the pupillary light pathway but spares the more ventrally placed pupillary near reflex pathway(Accomdation pathway), thereby causing a light-near dissociation.

Features of Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP) include:

• Bilateral small, irregular pupils in dim light
• Accommodation Reflex Present (ARP)- The eye accomdates by constricting the pupil for a near target.
• Light Reflex absent: pupils do not constrict when exposed to bright light.
• Cocaine eye drops(mydriatics) induced mydriasis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with left-sided head tilt which on straightening leads to right hypotropia. This increases on dextroversion and right head tilt. Paralysis of which of the following muscles is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right superior rectus

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of right superior rectus palsy.

The Park's-Bielschowsky three-step test is employed to diagnose the muscle paralysis responsible for vertical eye deviation. In this clinical scenario:

1.

Identify the hypotropic eye in primary gaze

•

Right eye is hypotrophic.

•

This could be due to either right eye elevator weakness or left eye depressor weakness.

•

Possible muscles: Right superior rectus, right inferior oblique, left inferior rectus, or left superior oblique

2.

Observe if hypotropia worsens in specific gazes

•

Hypotropia worsens in right gaze (dextroversion).

•

Paralyzed muscle is one that elevates the right eye in right gaze or depresses the left eye in right gaze.

•

Possible muscles: Left superior oblique and right superior rectus.

3.

Determine if hypotropia worsens in head tilts

•

Hypotropia worsens during right head tilt.

•

The right superior rectus is the muscle involved.

Mnemonic for superior oblique paralysis:

• Step 2: Vertical deviation (hypertropia/hypotropia) is Worse On Opposite Gaze – WOOG
• Step 3: Vertical deviation (hypertropia/hypotropia) deviation is Better On Opposite Tilt – BOOT

Muscle

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient underwent LASIK for myopia and now is undergoing cataract surgery. What is the formula used for lens power calculation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Haigis L

Among the given options, the Haigis-L regression formula is used for calculating the lens power in a patient who is undergoing cataract surgery with a previous history of refractive surgery.

Haigis formula uses Axial Length (L), Corneal curvature (K), and Anterior Chamber Depth (ACD) for the calculation of IOL power (biometry).

• Keratometry measures the curvature of the anterior corneal surface.
• A-scan ultrasonography is used to determine the axial length.

Standard IOL calculations are unsuitable in any type of corneal refractive surgery as they are likely to result in residual refractive errors even after IOL implantation in these patients. In these patients, several other methods of calculating corneal refractive power are used which are then added to the standard and specific formulas such as the Masket, modified masket, Haigis L formula, and double-K method.

Other options:

Options A and B: SRK 1 and SRK 2 are the basic formulas used for IOL power calculations.

SRK formula: P = A-2.5L-0.9K where P is the power of IOL, A is a constant for the lens, L is the axial length and K is corneal curvature.

Option C: Hoffer Q formula is used for IOL power calculation in short eyes (hypermetropia). It uses only two variables; Axial length (L) and corneal curvature (K).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text:
True regarding POAG:

A. Abnormality of the trabecular meshwork is seen on gonioscopy
B. Family members are likely to develop steroid responsiveness.
C. Dilatation of the pupil is associated with exacerbation of IOP
D. First degree relatives are at 1% increased risk of POAG
E. Visual field defect can exist with normal C:D ratio
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. B and E only

In primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG), family members are likely to develop steroid responsiveness (statement B) and visual field defect can exist with a normal C:D ratio (statement E).

Statement A: Gonioscopy cannot visualize the specific abnormalities that occur in the trabecular meshwork in POAG. Gonioscopy diagnoses POAG because of the visibility of all the structures of the angle of the anterior chamber in contrast to the non-visibility of different structures in angle closure glaucoma.

Statement C: Primary angle-closure glaucoma is associated with exacerbation of IOP with pupillary dilatation and not POAG.

Statement D: There is a 10% increased risk of POAG in siblings and a 4% increased risk in children of patients with POAG.

POAG also known as chronic simple glaucoma of adult-onset is characterized by the presence of any 2 of the following 3 categories of changes:

• Increased intraocular pressure:

• IOP >21mmHg on more than one occasion, and/or
• Circadian variation in IOP of >8 mmHg, or
• Asymmetry in IOP > 5 mmHg between both eyes

• Optic nerve head changes suggestive of glaucomatous damage. These may include one or more of the following changes:

• Vertically oval cup
• Cup-disc (C:D) ratio > 0.6 (average cup: disc ratio 0.3-0.4)
• Asymmetry in C:D ratio > 0.2 between both eyes.
• Narrowing, notching, or pallor of the neuroretinal rim.
• Disc haemorrhages
• Nasal shifting of retinal vessels-Bayonetting sign
• Lamellar dot sign

• Visual field changes - isopter contraction, barring of blind spot, paracentral scotoma, Seidel's scotoma, Bjerrum's scotoma, double arcuate scotoma, and Roenne's central nasal step.

A patient presenting with just raised IOP and visual field defects with normal optic nerve head findings such as a normal C:D ratio can still be diagnosed as POAG (statement E).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the correct order of using eye drops and eye ointment?
options: Eye drops first, ointment 15 min later
Ointment first, eye drops 15 min later
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Eye drops first, ointment 15 min later

Eye drops first followed by ointment 15 minutes later is the correct way of usage.

An ointment is thicker in consistency and needs to stay on the eyes for a longer time for absorption of the medication. Hence, it is generally put in the eyes at bedtime.

Eyedrops are watery thin and can be absorbed faster. Hence eyedrops are put first, and after 10-15 minutes, once they are completely absorbed, eye ointment can be applied.

Eye ointments are usually avoided during the daytime as they cause marked blurring of vision.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following helps to differentiate a fixed dilated pupil? A. Phenylephrine B. 1% Pilocarpine C. 0.1% Pilocarpine D. Cocaine 0.5% E. Epinephrine
options: A, B, C, D and E
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B and C only

Among the given options, 1% pilocarpine and 0.1% pilocarpine can be used to differentiate fixed dilated pupil.

Fixed dilated pupil is seen in conditions such as third nerve palsy, Hutchinson's pupil (increased cranial pressure), Adie's pupil, and due to pharmacological mydriasis.

Pilocarpine acts as an agonist at cholinergic muscuranic receptors and ganglion stimulator to cause miosis of the pupil.

Normal strength pilocarpine (1-2%) constricts the dilated pupil of 3rd nerve palsy, whereas there will be no response if the dilation is due to pharmacological mydriasis (anticholinergic causes) such as accidental application of atropine.

0.1% pilocarpine is used to diagnose Adie's pupil. Adie's pupil constricts with weak concentrations of pilocarpine (0.1%), while the normal pupil does not. This is because the denervated sphincter of the iris is very sensitive to topical parasympathomimetics such as pilocarpine. 0.1% pilocarpine also helps differentiate Adie's pupil from Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP).

Note:

Cocaine test (2 to 4%) is done in Horner’s syndrome. In these patients, the small pupil fails to dilate on instillation of mydriatics such as Cocaine which is in contrast to the normal pupil which dilates on instilling cocaine. Alternatively, the small pupils of Horner's syndrome dilate with 1% apraclonidine.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following procedure is shown in the image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterior ethmoidal nerve block

The procedure shown in the given image is an anterior ethmoidal nerve block.

The anterior ethmoidal nerve supplies the roof of the nasal cavity. It is a branch of the nasociliary nerve which in turn is a branch of the ophthalmic nerve (V1). It is sometimes used in endonasal surgery.

Other options:

Option A: In nasolacrimal duct syringing, the puncta of the nasolacrimal duct near the medial canthus of the eye is probed using a lacrimal cannula. The below image shows lacrimal syringing.

Option C: Infraorbital nerve block causes anesthesia in the distribution of infraorbital nerve which includes lower lid, cheek, side of nose, upper lip, and upper teeth. It is most commonly done for dental procedures.

Option D: Trephination of the frontal sinus is a surgical procedure done for the drainage of pus in acute frontal sinusitis. In this procedure, the incision is made on the floor of the frontal sinus.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following pupillary abnormalities is most likely to be observed in a patient with primary open-angle glaucoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Marcus Gunn pupil

Primary open-angle glaucoma commonly causes bilateral and asymmetric optic nerve damage. Marcus Gunn pupil also known as relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is the earliest sign of optic nerve disease as seen in optic nerve neuritis or primary open-angle glaucoma(POAG).

RAPD is caused due to a defect in the afferent pathway (optic nerve) of the pupillary light reflex in one eye.

It is diagnosed by the swinging flashlight test where the flashlight is swung to and fro, and the pupillary response is observed. Normally, both pupils constrict when any one eye is stimulated (due to direct and consensual light reflex). In the presence of RAPD, both pupils will abnormally dilate when the affected eye is stimulated. This paradoxical response of the pupil to light is called Marcus Gunn pupil.

Causes of RAPD:

• Optic nerve lesions (e.g.All types of optic neuritis, glaucoma)
• Optic tract lesions (e.g., infarction)
• Severe retinal disease (e.g., central retinal artery occlusion, extensive retinal detachment)
• Maculopathy (macular degeneration )

Other options:

Option B: Adie tonic pupil is a unilateral dilated pupil with light-near dissociation due to postganglionic parasympathetic pupillomotor nerve supply damage. In these patients the light reflex is absent and the accomdation (near) reflex is sluggish. It is commonly seen in young females and is associated with absent knee jerk.

Option C: Argyll Robertson pupils are bilateral small pupils with light-near dissociation. It is commonly seen in patients with neurosyphilis. In these patients the pupillary reflex is absent but the accommodation reflex is present (ARP).

Option D: Hutchinson's pupil is a clinical sign where the pupil on the side of an intracranial mass lesion is dilated and unreactive to light, due to compression of the oculomotor nerve on that side.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about corneal epithelium?
options: Regeneration is limited to the limbus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bowman's membrane regenerates

Bowman's membrane is acellular. Hence, it will not regenerate but heals by scarring when damaged.

Corneal stem cells are located at the corneoscleral limbus (Option A), so the regeneration is limited to the limbus.

The cornea comprises distinct layers:

1. Corneal epithelium is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (Option C), with microvilli on the apical layer (Option D) to enhance surface area and tear film attachment. It consists of basal, columnar, wing, and squamous cells.
2. Bowman’s membrane, a superficial stromal layer, is acellular, collagen-based, and incapable of regeneration.
3. The stroma, the thickest layer constituting 90% of corneal thickness, houses collagen fibrils with ground substances such as chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate, maintaining transparency. It cannot regenerate and heals with scarring.
4. Dua’s layer or Pre-Descemet's membrane is the toughest.
5. Descemet’s membrane extends anteriorly to Schwalbe’s line and possesses regenerative potential.
6. Endothelium, a metabolically active monolayer, lacks regenerative ability. It maintains deturgescence through active pumps, ensuring transparency with a usual cell density of approximately 3000 cells/mm² measured by specular microscopy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: 31-year-old woman comes to the office due to transient visual changes that are characterized by "loss of vision for a minute" and commonly precipitated by bending forward or lifting objects. During the last 3 months, she has had persistent headaches that she attributes to migraines. The patient takes over-the-counter analgesics as needed. Blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg and pulse is 72/min and regular. BMI is 32.4 kg/m2. Funduscopic findings of the left eye are shown in the image below, with similar findings in the right eye. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the observed funduscopic findings in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Elevated intracranial pressure

•

This patient has papilledema, suggested by transient visual obscurations precipitated by bending, chronic headache, obesity, and bilateral disc edema. Papilledema is caused by raised intracranial pressure with preserved visual acuity initially.

•

Choroidal inflammation causes choroiditis, not disc edema.

• Elevated intraocular pressure causes glaucomatous cupping, not swelling.
• Optic nerve inflammation (optic neuritis) causes painful vision loss and unilateral disc edema, not bilateral papilledema.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: 62-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to acute eye pain. She has a history of seasonal allergies and developed itchy, watery, red eyes after working outdoors in her garden. The patient used over-the- counter eye drops to treat her allergy symptoms, and several hours later, she began experiencing severe right eye pain and headache. On examination, the right eye appears red with a hazy cornea and dilated pupil that responds poorly to light. Palpation of the globes reveals notable firmness on the right compared to the left. Visual acuity in the affected eye is severely diminished. Which of the following medications was most likely used by this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alpha-adrenergic agonist

•

This patient has acute angle-closure glaucoma precipitated by mydriasis from an α-adrenergic agonist (eg, phenylephrine) used in OTC “red-eye” drops. Mydriasis narrows the angle, causing sudden pain, hazy cornea, fixed dilated pupil, and high IOP.

•

Beta blockers lower IOP.

• Mast cell stabilizers treat allergy without pupil dilation.
• NSAIDs do not affect pupil size or IOP.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: 64-year-old woman is brought to the clinic by her husband due to a fall. She was walking in her living room when she tripped over an electrical cord. The patient has had several other ground-level falls in the last 6 months but has had no significant injuries. She also gave up driving a year ago following a near-miss motor vehicle accident. Ophthalmic examination reveals reduced vision in her peripheral visual fields bilaterally and an elevated intraocular pressure. After discussion of treatment options, the patient is initiated on timolol ophthalmic drops. Which of the following structures is the most likely target of this medication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ciliary epithelium

•

This patient has primary open-angle glaucoma (peripheral field loss, raised IOP). Timolol, a non-selective beta-blocker, lowers IOP by reducing aqueous humor production from the ciliary epithelium.

•

Ciliary muscle is targeted by miotics to increase outflow.

• Pupil sphincter is acted on by parasympathomimetics.
• Trabecular meshwork is mainly affected by prostaglandin analogs and miotics, not beta-blockers.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with itching, watering, and redness in both eyes. On examination, small round yellow nodules are observed near the limbus, and conjunctival congestion is noted. The child has a history of recurrent styes and has a past h/o TB. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of this condition?
options: Type I hypersensitivity reaction caused by environmental allergens
Type IV hypersensitivity reaction to endogenous bacterial antigens
Type II hypersensitivity reaction triggered by viral infections
Autoimmune reaction against corneal epithelial cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type IV hypersensitivity reaction to endogenous bacterial antigens

• This child’s symptoms and yellow limbal nodules (phlyctenules) with recurrent styes point to phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis.
• The condition is caused by a delayed (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction to endogenous bacterial antigens, commonly Staphylococcus proteins, and may be associated with tuberculosis.
• It is not an IgE-mediated allergy or an autoimmune process, but a cell-mediated immune response leading to localized ocular inflammation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with recurrent episodes of itching, watering, photophobia, and redness of both eyes. Examination reveals small, elevated, yellow-white nodules near the limbus with surrounding conjunctival congestion. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of this condition?
options: Type I hypersensitivity reaction to environmental allergens
Type IV hypersensitivity reaction to endogenous bacterial antigens
Type II hypersensitivity reaction triggered by viral infection
Autoimmune destruction of corneal epithelial cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type IV hypersensitivity reaction to endogenous bacterial antigens

The child most likely has phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis, a localized, noninfectious inflammatory reaction of the conjunctiva or cornea.

It occurs due to a delayed Type IV hypersensitivity reaction to microbial antigens, most commonly:

• Staphylococcal antigens from chronic blepharitis or recurrent styes
• Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens, especially in endemic regions

The organism is usually not present within the ocular lesion; the lesion represents an immune response to its antigens.

Clinical features

• Small yellow-white phlycten near the limbus
• Conjunctival congestion
• Watering and photophobia
• Foreign-body sensation
• Recurrent episodes
• Corneal involvement may produce pain and later scarring

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Type I hypersensitivity is seen in allergic conjunctivitis and vernal keratoconjunctivitis, usually with intense itching, papillae, and ropy discharge.
• C. Type II hypersensitivity involves antibody-mediated cellular injury and is not the mechanism here.
• D. Autoimmune attack against corneal epithelial cells is not the typical pathogenesis of phlyctenular disease.

High-yield pearl

• Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis = Type IV hypersensitivity to staphylococcal or tubercular antigens.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the ophthalmology clinic because she has increasing difficulty seeing distant objects at school. She reports that road signs and the classroom projector appear blurry, although she can read books at close range without any problem. Examination reveals normal pupillary reflexes and intact extraocular movements. Visual acuity testing shows impaired distance vision that improves with concave corrective lenses. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of this patient’s visual defect?
options: Degeneration of retinal ganglion cells from elevated intraocular pressure
Failure of binocular visual cortex maturation during childhood
Increased axial length of the globe
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased axial length of the globe

This patient has myopia (nearsightedness), characterized by:

• Blurred distance vision
• Preserved near vision
• Improvement with concave (diverging) lenses

The usual pathophysiology is increased axial length of the globe, causing light rays from distant objects to focus anterior to the retina.

Key concepts:

• Myopia → elongated eyeball; corrected with concave lenses
• Hyperopia → short eyeball; image focuses behind retina; corrected with convex lenses
• Presbyopia → age-related loss of lens elasticity causing impaired near vision
• Amblyopia → abnormal visual cortex development due to impaired binocular vision in childhood
• Glaucoma → retinal ganglion cell damage from elevated intraocular pressure leading to peripheral vision loss.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 14-day-old neonate born at 28 weeks of gestation had developed respiratory distress syndrome at birth. You want to screen for retinopathy of prematurity. How many weeks from now would you schedule the screening?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 weeks

ROP Screening – AIIMS / Indian Guidelines

1. Which babies to screen (Eligibility criteria)

Mandatory screening

• Gestational age (GA) ≤ 34 weeks
• Birth weight (BW) ≤ 2000 g

Also screen (even if >34 weeks or >2000 g) if risk factors present

• Oxygen therapy (especially prolonged/unregulated)
• Mechanical ventilation / CPAP
• Respiratory distress syndrome
• Sepsis
• Blood transfusion / exchange transfusion
• Intraventricular hemorrhage
• Apnea
• Poor postnatal weight gain

2. Timing of first screening

Standard timing

• At 25–30 days of life (\~4 weeks); In our case, baby is already 2 weeks, so the screening is two weeks from now on.

Earlier screening (high-risk babies)

• At 2–3 weeks if:

• GA <28 weeks
• BW <1200 g
• Unstable clinical course

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with progressively blurred vision. Slit-lamp exam reveals superotemporal lens displacement with stretched zonules. He's tall, long-limbed, with arachnodactyly. Which best describes this ocular condition?
options: Lens dislocation due to inflammatory adhesions
Partial lens displacement due to zonular weakness
Posterior displacement of lens into the vitreous
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Partial lens displacement due to zonular weakness

Ectopia lentis refers to partial or complete displacement of the lens from its normal position, resulting from weak or defective zonular fibers (the suspensory ligaments anchoring the lens).

In this vignette, the combination of tall stature, long limbs, arachnodactyly, and superotemporal lens subluxation points strongly toward Marfan syndrome — where a fibrillin-1 defect leads to weakened zonules and characteristic upward-outward lens displacement.

Why the other options don't fit?

• A. Lens dislocation due to inflammatory adhesions: Inflammatory adhesions describe synechiae (iris adhering to lens or cornea), not ectopia lentis
• C. Lens opacification from protein aggregation: Protein aggregation causing lens opacity describes a cataract, a different pathology entirely
• D. Posterior displacement of lens into the vitreous: Posterior displacement into the vitreous describes true lens dislocation (complete separation), not the partial subluxation seen here

High-yield pearl:

Direction of lens displacement can help distinguish causes:

• Marfan syndrome → superotemporal
• Homocystinuria → inferonasal (also has zonular weakness, but opposite direction — a classic paired distractor in exams)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presents with lifelong night blindness since childhood. Fundus examination under normal lighting reveals a golden-yellow metallic sheen. After prolonged dark adaptation, however, the fundus appearance normalizes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Oguchi disease

Oguchi disease is a rare, autosomal recessive form of congenital stationary night blindness (CSNB).

Its hallmark finding is the Mizuo–Nakamura phenomenon:

• In light-adapted state → retina shows an unusual golden or metallic yellow sheen
• After prolonged dark adaptation (several hours) → fundus appearance reverts to normal

This reversible color change is unique to Oguchi disease and is considered pathognomonic.

Why the other options don't fit?

• A. Retinitis pigmentosa: Progressive condition with bone-spicule pigmentation, arteriolar attenuation, and waxy disc pallor; not stationary, and lacks the golden sheen
• C. Fundus albipunctatus: Another CSNB variant, but characterized by discrete white-yellow dots scattered across the fundus, with markedly delayed (not absent) dark adaptation — no metallic sheen or reversibility
• D. Vitamin A deficiency: Causes night blindness with xerophthalmia (Bitot spots, conjunctival/corneal dryness), not a metallic fundus sheen

High-yield pearl:

• Whenever a vignette pairs "night blindness" with a "golden/metallic sheen that normalizes with dark adaptation," think Oguchi disease + Mizuo–Nakamura phenomenon — this is a classic, distinctive buzzword combination in ophthalmology exams.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presents with leukocoria and is diagnosed with persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV). The child subsequently undergoes lens extraction. What is the most common postoperative complication in such cases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinal detachment

PHPV, now more commonly termed persistent fetal vasculature (PFV), results from failed regression of the embryonic hyaloid vascular system. This leaves behind fibrovascular tissue stretching from the optic disc to the posterior lens surface.

This fibrovascular stalk exerts chronic traction on the retina. When surgery removes the lens (and often the associated vitreous/fibrovascular tissue), the support structures are further disrupted, and the pre-existing tractional forces can precipitate retinal detachment — making it the most frequent postoperative complication.

Clarifying the distractor:

• Vitreous hemorrhage can certainly occur, given the vascularity of the fibrous tissue — but in exam contexts, retinal detachment is designated the most common complication due to the underlying tractional pathology.

Why the other options don't fit?

• A. Orbital cellulitis: An infectious complication, not a mechanistic consequence of PHPV surgery
• D. Keratitis: Unrelated to the posterior segment pathology driving PHPV

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presents with leukocoria in the left eye. The CT is shown below. The most likely mutated gene is on the same chromosome as which of the following genes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. BRCA2

•

Leukocoria with CT showing intraocular calcification suggests retinoblastoma, caused by mutation of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 13q14. BRCA2 is also located on chromosome 13, so it’s on the same chromosome as RB1.

•

BRCA1 is on chromosome 17.

•

NF1 is on chromosome 17.

•

APC is on chromosome 5.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 2-year-old child with leukocoria and calcified intraocular masses is found to have tumors 4–10 DD in size behind the equator. According to Reese-Ellsworth classification, to which group does this case belong?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Group 2

| Group | Prognosis for Maintenance of Sight | Features

| ----- | ---------------------------------- | --------

| 1 | Very favourable |  Solitary or multiple tumor < 4 DD, at or behind equator

| 2 | Favourable |  Solitary or multiple tumor 4–10 DD, behind equator

| 3 | Possible | - Any lesion anterior to equator

| | | - Solitary tumor > 10 DD behind equator

| 4 | Unfavourable | - Multiple tumors\, some >10 DD

| | | - Any lesion extending anteriorly to ora serrata

| 5 | Highly unfavourable | - Massive tumors involving > half of retina

| | | - Vitreous seeding

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 21-year-old student presents with ocular redness, foreign body sensation, and excessive tearing, following the use of a contact lens. An interface contrast microscopy from his corneal scraping is shown below. Which of the following is false regarding the treatment of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Topical Steroids

• This is Acanthamoeba keratitis (contact lens use + cysts on microscopy).
• Topical steroids are avoided because they can worsen infection and mask progression; if ever used, it’s only later with adequate anti-amoebic cover
• Oral NSAIDs help pain (often severe).
• Topical PHMB is a first-line anti-amoebic (cysts + trophozoites).
• Epithelial debridement can reduce organism load and improve drug penetration.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 23-year-old medical student presents to the ophthalmology OPD with progressive difficulty in seeing distant objects, particularly while reading signboards and viewing the classroom screen. Near vision is relatively preserved. There is no history of ocular trauma or previous ocular surgery. As part of the evaluation, retinoscopy is performed as demonstrated in the accompanying video. Assume that the examination is being performed at a working distance of 1 metre. Based on the finding demonstrated in the video, which of the following refractive errors is most likely present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Myopia of more than 1 D

The video demonstrates “against” movement of the retinoscopic reflex. At a working distance of 1 metre, against movement indicates myopia >1 D.

With → <1 D myopia / emmetropia / hypermetropia

Neutral → 1 D myopia

Against → >1 D myopia

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 24-year-old patient presents with complaints of ocular deviation noticed by family members. On examination, a cover–uncover test reveals a manifest deviation. To quantify the angle of deviation at distance and near, which of the following tests is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prism bar cover test

The prism bar cover test (more precisely, the prism and alternate cover test, PACT) is the gold standard for objective measurement of ocular deviation.

• Prisms of increasing power are placed base-opposite to the direction of deviation (base-out for esotropia, base-in for exotropia, base-down for hypertropia)
• The examiner performs alternate cover while increasing prism power
• The endpoint is neutralisation — the point at which no refixation movement occurs
•

Result expressed in prism dioptres (Δ)

| Option | What it actually does | Why it fails

| ------ | --------------------- | ------------

| A. Hirschberg | Estimates deviation from corneal light reflex displacement: \~15Δ per mm of decentration | Gross screening only. Crude, ±10Δ error. Reserved for uncooperative patients/infants or dense amblyopia where fixation is unreliable.

| B. Maddox rod | Dissociates using a red streak → patient reports separation | Subjective, and classically measures phorias and cyclodeviations/torsion. In a manifest tropia with possible suppression or ARC, the subjective answer may be absent or misleading.

| D. Synoptophore | Measures objective and subjective angle, assesses grades of binocular single vision, ARC, fusional amplitudes | Its role is sensory evaluation and angle of anomaly

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents after a blunt ocular injury. Vision in the affected eye is hand movements. Slit-lamp examination shows a deep anterior chamber, and fundoscopy reveals a crystalline lens lying in the vitreous cavity. Which of the following findings is least likely in this patient?
options: Reduction in the number of Purkinje images
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Induction of axial hypermetropia

This is posterior dislocation of the lens into the vitreous after blunt trauma. Typical findings include a deep anterior chamber (aphakia), iridodonesis due to loss of lens support, and fewer Purkinje images because the lens surfaces are no longer in their normal position. The refractive error produced is aphakic (high) positional hypermetropia, not axial hypermetropia (which is due to a short eyeball). Hence C is least likely.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis is experiencing double vision. On examination, her eye movements are normal except for her right gaze where her left eye fails to adduct and her right eye shows nystagmus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left internuclear ophthalmoplegia

•

In multiple sclerosis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) is common due to a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). Failure of the left eye to adduct on right gaze with abducting nystagmus of the right eye localizes to the left MLF.

•

Right INO would affect right adduction.

•

Abducens palsy causes impaired abduction, not adduction failure with nystagmus.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 28-year-old male patient presents with a history of progressive vision loss and night blindness. Upon examination, the patient displays characteristic retinal degeneration with peripheral bone spicule pigmentation. Which of the following syndromes is not likely associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Marfan syndrome

The patient has retinitis pigmentosa (RP), characterized by:

• Progressive night blindness
• Peripheral visual field loss (“tunnel vision”)
• Bone spicule pigmentation on fundus examination
• Attenuated retinal vessels and waxy optic disc pallor

Pathophysiology: Progressive degeneration of rod photoreceptors followed by cones

Syndromic associations of RP:

• Usher syndrome → sensorineural hearing loss
• Refsum disease → phytanic acid accumulation, ataxia, neuropathy
• Kearns–Sayre syndrome → mitochondrial disorder with ophthalmoplegia and pigmentary retinopathy

Marfan syndrome is not classically associated with retinitis pigmentosa.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with progressive decrease in central vision. She also has yellowish papular lesions on the neck and axillae with a “plucked-chicken” appearance. Fundus is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pseudoxanthoma elasticum

•

This patient’s progressive central vision loss with yellowish papular skin lesions in flexural areas showing a “plucked-chicken” appearance is classic for pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE).

•

Fundus typically shows angioid streaks due to breaks in Bruch’s membrane, predisposing to choroidal neovascularization.

•

Ehlers–Danlos and Marfan syndromes cause connective tissue laxity but not these skin or retinal findings, while Stargardt disease lacks characteristic skin lesions.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 29-year-old man undergoes surgical repair after a penetrating injury to his left eye caused by a workplace accident. His postoperative recovery is uneventful, with gradual improvement in visual acuity. Eight weeks later, he develops progressive blurring of vision, photophobia, and ocular pain in his previously uninjured right eye. Slit-lamp examination reveals cells and flare in the anterior chamber, vitreous inflammation, and multiple yellow-white choroidal lesions, consistent with bilateral granulomatous panuveitis. Disruption of which of the following physiological immune mechanisms most likely predisposed this patient to his current condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Immune privilege

This patient has sympathetic ophthalmia, a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis that develops weeks to months after penetrating ocular trauma or intraocular surgery.

The underlying mechanism is loss of ocular immune privilege.

Normally, the eye is an immune-privileged site, meaning that ocular antigens—particularly uveal and retinal antigens—are sequestered from the systemic immune system by the blood-retinal barrier and local immunosuppressive mechanisms.

Following penetrating trauma:

• Previously hidden ocular antigens become exposed.
• Antigen-presenting cells activate autoreactive T lymphocytes.
• A Type IV (T-cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction develops.
• Both the injured (exciting eye) and the uninjured (sympathizing eye) become inflamed, producing bilateral granulomatous panuveitis.

Why the other options are incorrect?

A. Complement regulation

• Defects predispose to disorders such as atypical HUS or hereditary angioedema.
• Complement dysregulation is not the mechanism of sympathetic ophthalmia.

C. Immune surveillance

• Refers to immune recognition and elimination of malignant or infected cells.
• Not responsible for autoimmune inflammation following ocular trauma.

D. Positive selection

• Occurs in the thymic cortex, where T cells capable of recognizing self-MHC are selected.
• Unrelated to post-traumatic autoimmune uveitis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 30 year old patient with chief complaint of watering for 1 week after a road traffic accident. The following test was advised after a few initial clinical tests. Which of the following is not true regarding the given test?
options: This test gives an idea about anatomy of lacrimal pathway
It provides information regarding lacrimal pump failure
The increased watering from his right eye can be termed as epiphora
A non-ionic iodinated contrast is injected into canaliculus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It provides information regarding lacrimal pump failure

• The described test is dacryocystography, done for post-traumatic epiphora.
• It evaluates the anatomy of the lacrimal drainage pathway by injecting a non-ionic iodinated contrast into the canaliculus and taking radiographs. Watering of the eye is correctly termed epiphora.
• However, dacryocystography does not assess lacrimal pump function; pump failure is evaluated by functional tests like dye disappearance or Jones tests.
•

Lacrimal pump: The lacrimal pump is the active mechanism that moves tears from the conjunctival sac into the nose during blinking. The pretarsal and preseptal fibres of orbicularis oculi (Horner's muscle / pars lacrimalis) compress the ampullae and canaliculi while simultaneously dilating the lacrimal sac → negative pressure draws tears in; on eye-opening the sac recoils and pushes tears down the NLD.

| Test | What it assesses | Method | Interpretation

| ---- | ---------------- | ------ | --------------

| Fluorescein Dye Disappearance Test (FDDT) | Physiological drainage (screening) | Fluorescein in both fornices; observe under cobalt blue at 5 min | Symmetric clearance = normal. Asymmetric/delayed = drainage or pump dysfunction. Best non-invasive screen, esp. paediatric

| Jones I (Primary dye test) | Functional patency of whole system | Fluorescein in fornix → cotton bud at inferior meatus after 5 min | +ve (dye recovered) = patent + functional pump. −ve = block (anatomical or functional) → do Jones II. \~20% false −ve in normals

| Jones II (Secondary dye test) | Localises the block | After −ve Jones I: wash out residual dye, irrigate with clear saline | Dye-stained fluid from nose = dye had reached sac → partial/functional block distal to sac. Clear fluid from nose = dye never entered sac → upper (punctal/canalicular) problem. No fluid = complete NLD obstruction

| Dacryoscintigraphy | Most physiological functional test | Tc-99m pertechnetate drop, gamma camera tracks flow | Delineates functional/partial blocks that syringing (anatomical) misses

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presents with redness and pain in the eye. Examination revealed an IOP of 38 mm of Hg, aqueous flare and is shown below. Which of the following drugs must be avoided in her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prostaglandin analogs

•

This patient has secondary inflammatory glaucoma (uveitic glaucoma) suggested by high IOP with aqueous flare. Prostaglandin analogs are avoided because they increase intraocular inflammation and can worsen uveitis.

•

Beta blockers reduce aqueous production and are safe.

•

Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors effectively lower IOP in inflammatory glaucoma.

•

Mannitol can be used short-term for acute IOP reduction.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with a dilated right pupil noticed incidentally, along with blurred near vision in that eye. She denies any eye drop use, trauma, or systemic illness. Examination shows the right pupil reacts poorly to direct light but constricts slowly and tonically with sustained near effort (accommodation). Application of 0.1% dilute pilocarpine causes the right pupil to constrict. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is correct?
options: The lesion is most likely at the posterior commissure, and the accommodation reflex is expected to be absent
This finding is due to denervation hypersensitivity following a lesion at the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves, and the accommodation reflex is typically preserved
The pupil's constriction with dilute pilocarpine indicates pharmacological mydriasis from prior atropine exposure
Pupil size would be expected to be equal between the two eyes, since this is a bilateral, symmetric condition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. This finding is due to denervation hypersensitivity following a lesion at the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves, and the accommodation reflex is typically preserved

| | Tonic/Adie's pupil | Pharmacological mydriasis | Argyll Robertson pupil (for contrast)

| --- | ------------------ | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------

| Cause | Lesion at ciliary ganglion/short ciliary nerve | Drugs — atropine | Posterior commissure lesion (neurosyphilis)

| Light reflex | Ipsilateral pupil does not constrict ("tonic" — slow, sustained near constriction instead) | Does not constrict | Absent

| Accommodation reflex | Normal (preserved) | Absent — cycloplegic action relaxes ciliary muscle, causing loss of accommodation | Present

| Response to 0.1% dilute pilocarpine | Constricts — due to denervation hypersensitivity (denervated sphincter pupillae over-expresses receptors, becoming hyper-reactive) | Does not constrict, even with standard 1% pilocarpine | —

| Pupil size | Anisocoria | Anisocoria | Anisocoria

The dilute (0.1%) pilocarpine test is the key bedside differentiator: a denervated iris sphincter in Adie's tonic pupil upregulates its cholinergic receptors, becoming hypersensitive enough to constrict even to a sub-therapeutic (0.1%) pilocarpine concentration that would have no effect on a normal pupil. A pharmacologically dilated (atropinized) pupil, in contrast, has its muscarinic receptors competitively and completely blocked, so it fails to constrict even with a full-strength (1%) pilocarpine concentration.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 31-year-old man presents with painless progressive diminution of vision, floaters, and photophobia in his left eye 4 weeks after undergoing repair of a penetrating corneoscleral injury to the right eye. Examination shows following. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sympathetic ophthalmia

• Sympathetic ophthalmia is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis that develops days to weeks after penetrating ocular trauma or intraocular surgery.
• The injured eye is the exciting eye, while the fellow eye is the sympathizing eye.
• It is caused by a Type IV (T-cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction against previously sequestered uveal antigens.
• Dalen–Fuchs nodules (collections of epithelioid cells between Bruch's membrane and the retinal pigment epithelium) are characteristic histopathological findings.
• The history of ocular trauma distinguishes it from Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada syndrome, which presents with similar granulomatous panuveitis but without preceding trauma and is associated with meningismus, tinnitus, vitiligo, poliosis, and alopecia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents to the ophthalmology OPD with a history of progressive diminution of vision in his left eye for the past few months. There is no history of ocular trauma or previous ocular surgery. On examination, both pupils are equal in size at rest, and the anterior segment examination is unremarkable. Visual acuity is reduced in the left eye compared with the right eye. As part of the neuro-ophthalmological examination, the examiner performs the pupillary light examination demonstrated in the accompanying video, alternately moving a bright light between the two eyes. Based on the pupillary response demonstrated in the video, which of the following is the most likely underlying pathology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left optic nerve lesion

• The video demonstrates a left Marcus Gunn pupil (left relative afferent pupillary defect/RAPD) on the swinging flashlight test.
• When the light is moved from the normal right eye to the affected left eye, both pupils appear to dilate because the afferent light stimulus reaching the brain is reduced.
• Marcus Gunn pupil = RAPD = afferent pathway defect, classically due to an optic nerve lesion (e.g., optic neuritis) or severe asymmetric retinal disease.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman comes to the office due to double vision. The patient first experienced difficulty focusing her eyes while at work yesterday. On awakening this morning, her symptoms had progressed to frank diplopia. A complete physical examination is performed, including a full neurologic assessment. Shining light into the patient's right eye causes constriction of her right pupil, but not the left pupil. Shining light into her left eye causes constriction of only her right pupil. Which of the following additional physical examination findings is likely to be found in this patient?
options: Absence of the left corneal reflex
Inability to close the left eye
Inward deviation of the left eye
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Drooping of the left eyelid

•

Both light tests show only the right pupil constricts, meaning afferent pathways are intact, but the left pupil cannot constrict to direct or consensual light → a left efferent pupillary defect (left CN III parasympathetic involvement).

•

A CN III palsy also causes ptosis from levator palpebrae weakness.

• Absent left corneal reflex = V1/VII lesion.
• Inability to close left eye = CN VII palsy.
• Inward deviation suggests CN VI palsy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman presents to the clinic with recurrent episodes of transient visual dimming lasting a few seconds, triggered by standing up quickly or bending forward. For the past two months, she has also had near-daily morning headaches, for which she has been self-medicating with ibuprofen or aspirin. She is on no other medications, and her medical history is unremarkable apart from an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. She does not use tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drugs. Vitals: temperature 36.4°C (97.6°F), blood pressure 138/88 mmHg, pulse 93/min. BMI is 35 kg/m². Visual field testing reveals bilaterally enlarged blind spots. Which ocular finding is most characteristically associated with this patient's underlying condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Papilledema

• This vignette describes idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) — classically seen in obese women of reproductive age (BMI 35 here), presenting with daily morning headaches, transient visual obscurations triggered by postural changes (standing, bending — which transiently raise intracranial pressure further), and enlarged blind spots on visual field testing.
• The enlarged blind spot is a direct consequence of optic disc swelling (papilledema) from raised intracranial pressure, which enlarges the physiologic blind spot as it compresses/distorts the surrounding retina.

Why the others are wrong?

• A. Amaurosis fugax: Describes embolic transient monocular vision loss, not associated with headache or positional triggers.
• B. Open-angle glaucoma: Causes gradual, peripheral field loss (not enlarged blind spot as the primary finding) and is not linked to postural symptoms or headache.
• C. Optic neuritis: Presents with painful, unilateral vision loss, often with dyschromatopsia, and is associated with demyelinating disease, not fitting this pattern.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with progressively worsening blurry vision, eye pain, and redness in the right eye. Examination reveals restricted eye movement, and fundoscopic evaluation identifies a well-defined cystic lesion in the vitreous humor, accompanied by surrounding inflammation. What is the most probable diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ocular cysticercosis

• The presence of a well-defined cystic lesion in the vitreous with surrounding inflammation is characteristic of ocular cysticercosis caused by Taenia solium larvae.
• Symptoms include progressive blurring of vision, ocular pain, redness, and restricted eye movements due to inflammatory response.

Other options:

• A. Ocular toxoplasmosis usually presents as retinochoroiditis.
• B. Endophthalmitis is a diffuse purulent infection.
• DTubercular posterior uveitis does not produce a discrete vitreous cyst.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with complaints of blurred vision following a minor head injury. On pupillary examination using the swinging flashlight test, illumination of the right eye causes both pupils to constrict, but when the light is quickly moved to the left eye, both pupils paradoxically dilate. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Left optic nerve lesion

• Marcus Gunn pupil = Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD).
• Occurs due to partial or complete lesion of the optic nerve or severe retinal disease.

In the swinging flashlight test:

• Light in normal eye → both pupils constrict
• Light in affected eye → reduced afferent signal → pupils dilate instead of constricting

Since shifting light to the left eye causes dilation, the left optic nerve is affected.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with painful ophthalmoplegia of the right eye. Examination reveals ptosis and complete ophthalmoplegia, loss of corneal reflex with decreased sensation over the forehead, normal visual acuity, and no contralateral eye involvement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Superior orbital fissure syndrome

Orbital/parasellar syndromes are distinguished by which cranial nerves are involved and, critically, whether the optic nerve (vision) is spared or affected — this determines anatomical localization along the orbit-to-cavernous sinus continuum.

Superior orbital fissure syndrome:

• Structures passing through: CN III, IV, VI, and V1 (ophthalmic division of trigeminal)
• Clinical picture: complete ophthalmoplegia (III, IV, VI) + ptosis (III) + corneal reflex loss and forehead hypoesthesia (V1)
• Vision is preserved, since the optic nerve (CN II) passes through the separate optic canal, not the superior orbital fissure

This matches the case exactly: ophthalmoplegia + V1 sensory loss + normal visual acuity.

Why the other options are wrong?

• A. Orbital cellulitis: Presents with lid edema, proptosis, chemosis, and fever from infection, not this clean cranial neuropathy pattern; ophthalmoplegia when present is usually incomplete/mechanical rather than a discrete CN palsy pattern.
• B. Cavernous sinus thrombosis: Typically presents with bilateral involvement (via intercavernous sinus connections), along with proptosis, chemosis, and signs of venous congestion; this patient has strictly unilateral, isolated findings.
• D. Orbital apex syndrome: Same cranial nerve involvement as SOF syndrome, plus CN II (optic nerve) involvement, since the orbital apex encompasses both the superior orbital fissure and the optic canal. This would present with visual loss — absent here, ruling this out.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man develops sudden bilateral visual loss 24 hours after an episode of acute pancreatitis. Fundus examination shows cotton wool spots and polygonal areas of retinal whitening around the optic disc. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Purtscher retinopathy

•

The key clues are sudden bilateral visual loss following acute pancreatitis and fundus findings of cotton wool spots with polygonal areas of retinal whitening (Purtscher flecken) around the optic disc.

•

These are classic for Purtscher retinopathy, a microvascular occlusive retinopathy seen after trauma, acute pancreatitis, and other systemic insults.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man develops sudden, painless loss of vision in his left eye, with a normal fundus on examination. During the swinging flashlight test, shining light into the left eye causes both pupils to dilate, while shining light into the right eye causes both pupils to constrict. Where is the lesion most likely located?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left optic nerve

This describes a Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD), also called a Marcus Gunn pupil.

Step-by-step logic:

• Light in the normal (right) eye → intact afferent signal → both pupils constrict normally.
• Light in the affected (left) eye → reduced afferent input reaches the brain → the brain "perceives" less light than it actually received → both pupils paradoxically dilate relative to their prior constricted state.

This pattern localizes the lesion to the afferent limb of the pupillary pathway — i.e., the left optic nerve — since the efferent pathway (oculomotor nerve, Edinger-Westphal nucleus) is intact bilaterally (confirmed by normal constriction when the good eye is stimulated).

Why the distractors are wrong?

• B. Right optic nerve: It would produce the opposite pattern (defect on light in right eye).
• C. Left oculomotor nerve: A third nerve lesion affects the efferent pathway, causing a fixed/dilated pupil regardless of which eye is illuminated, often with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia.
• D. Edinger-Westphal nucleus: A central efferent lesion would impair constriction bilaterally regardless of which eye is stimulated, not produce a relative afferent defect.

High-yield line: RAPD = swinging flashlight test positive = lesion in optic nerve/anterior visual pathway, NOT the pupillomotor efferent pathway.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient presented with a squint. On examination, the secondary deviation was found to be more than the primary deviation. Forced duction test is positive. Which of the following types of squint is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Restrictive squint

•

In restrictive squint, forced duction test is positive due to mechanical restriction of eye movement, and secondary deviation exceeds primary deviation because the normal eye overacts against restriction.

•

Comitant squint has equal deviations in all gazes.

•

Paralytic squint shows increased secondary deviation but has a negative forced duction test.

•

Apparent squint is a false appearance with normal ocular alignment and movements.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman with inactive thyroid-related orbitopathy presents with proptosis, diplopia due to restrictive myopathy, and upper eyelid retraction. She is planned for surgical rehabilitation. Which of the following represents the most appropriate and recommended sequence of surgical management?
options: Eyelid retraction surgery → Strabismus surgery → Orbital decompression
Orbital decompression → Strabismus surgery → Eyelid retraction surgical repair
Strabismus surgery → Orbital decompression → Eyelid retraction surgical repair
Orbital decompression → Eyelid retraction surgical repair → Strabismus surgery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Orbital decompression → Strabismus surgery → Eyelid retraction surgical repair

• In inactive thyroid eye disease, surgical rehabilitation follows a strict sequence.
•

Orbital decompression is done first to correct proptosis and alters globe position.

•

Strabismus surgery follows, as muscle alignment can change after decompression.

• Eyelid retraction repair is performed last because lid position depends on both globe position and ocular alignment.
• This staged approach ensures stable, predictable outcomes and avoids the need for repeat surgeries.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45 y/o man from a tropical region presents with a painful red eye, significant watering, and sensitivity to light after working in a garden with decaying plant material. The patient is diagnosed with keratomycosis. Which of the following is not an examination finding in keratomycosis?
options: Feathery extensions at the margins of the corneal ulcer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Extensive corneal vascularization

• Keratomycosis typically shows feathery margins of corneal ulcer, a sterile immune (Wessely) ring, and endothelial plaque.
• Extensive corneal vascularization is not an acute examination finding; it develops in chronic or healed corneal disease, not in active fungal keratitis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man suddenly develops a severe headache followed by loss of consciousness. Once stabilized, he reports decreased vision in both eyes. Fundus examination shows vitreous hemorrhage. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

This is classic Terson syndrome — intraocular hemorrhage (vitreous, retinal, and/or subhyaloid) occurring in association with intracranial hemorrhage, most classically subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Pathophysiology:

• A sudden rise in intracranial pressure is transmitted along the optic nerve sheath (which is continuous with the subarachnoid space), obstructing venous outflow from the retina and causing rupture of peripapillary retinal vessels, producing vitreous or subhyaloid hemorrhage — often bilateral.

Why the distractors are wrong?

• A. Central retinal vein occlusion: Produces a unilateral "blood and thunder" fundus with diffuse retinal hemorrhages, not typically vitreous hemorrhage, and has no link to sudden headache/LOC.
• C. Diabetic retinopathy: Vitreous hemorrhage can occur here too, but it develops from chronic proliferative changes (neovascularization), not acutely after a headache/LOC event.
• D. Hypertensive retinopathy: Causes chronic fundus changes (AV nicking, flame hemorrhages, cotton wool spots) but not acute vitreous hemorrhage.

High-yield line: Sudden headache + LOC + bilateral vision loss + vitreous hemorrhage → think Terson syndrome → look for SAH.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with complaints of difficulty reading and delayed visual recovery after exposure to bright sunlight. On examination, visual acuity returns to baseline only after 70 seconds following intense light exposure. Which of the following is the most likely interpretation of this test result?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Macular pathology

This is the Photostress Recovery Test (PSRT).

It evaluates:

• Macular function
• Specifically foveal photoreceptor and RPE recovery

Normal Physiology

After bright light exposure:

• Photopigments (especially in cones) are bleached
• Recovery depends on:

o    Photoreceptor integrity

o    Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function

Normal recovery time:

• ≤ 50 seconds (usually 15–35 seconds)

Recovery time = 70 seconds

→ Prolonged recovery

→ Suggests impaired photoreceptor/RPE function

→ Indicates macular pathology

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 47-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of sudden painless visual loss in his right eye. The patient describes the loss of vision as a veil covering the visual field. He is slightly myopic and had a successful cataract extraction with intraocular lens implantation 3 years ago. The examination finding is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment

• The image finding: Dispersed brown-pigmented granules floating in the anterior vitreous — this is Shafer's sign ("tobacco dust" / pigment in the vitreous). These are retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells liberated into the vitreous through a retinal break. Shafer's sign is \~90% predictive of a retinal tear/RRD.
• Surgery (pseudophakia) strongly suggest rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, caused by a retinal break allowing liquefied vitreous to enter subretinal space.
• Breaks in Descemet membrane cause corneal edema.
• Exudative RD is due to inflammation or tumors without retinal breaks.
• Tractional RD occurs from fibrovascular membranes, typically in diabetic retinopathy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 48-year-old man with primary angle-closure glaucoma undergoes gonioscopy for assessment of the iridocorneal angle. The ophthalmologist uses a four-mirror lens that also allows dynamic indentation gonioscopy. Which of the following statements regarding this instrument is incorrect?
options: It helps localize intraocular foreign bodies in selected situations
It is routinely used to measure the angle of the posterior chamber
It helps assess the extent of peripheral anterior synechiae
It provides a mirror image of the opposite anterior chamber angle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is routinely used to measure the angle of the posterior chamber

• Gonioscopy visualizes the anterior chamber angle, not the posterior chamber.
• It is useful for identifying angle structures, peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS), angle recession, and angle-closure mechanisms.
• Four-mirror lenses provide a mirror image of the opposite angle and permit indentation gonioscopy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-week-old premature infant is undergoing routine ophthalmologic screening in the neonatal intensive care unit. He was delivered at 27 weeks of gestation and required mechanical ventilation with high-flow oxygen therapy for severe respiratory distress syndrome during the first 10 days of life. Funduscopic examination now reveals peripheral retinal neovascularization with fibrovascular proliferation extending toward the vitreous humor. Which of the following is the most important risk factor for this infant’s ocular condition?
options: Maternal use of β2-agonist tocolytic agents
Prophylactic erythromycin eye ointment after delivery
Prolonged supplemental oxygen exposure after birth
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prolonged supplemental oxygen exposure after birth

Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) occurs in premature infants due to abnormal retinal vascular proliferation triggered by hyperoxia-induced retinal ischemia. Major risk factors:

• Prematurity (especially <30 weeks gestation)
• Low birth weight
• Prolonged supplemental oxygen exposure

Pathogenesis:

1. Excess oxygen suppresses VEGF and halts normal retinal vessel development.
2. Subsequent retinal hypoxia stimulates excessive VEGF release.
3. Abnormal neovascularization and fibrovascular proliferation occur.

Funduscopic findings:

• Peripheral retinal neovascularization
• Fibrovascular proliferation extending into vitreous
• Retinal traction/detachment in severe cases

Complications:

• Retinal detachment
• Blindness
• Strabismus and myopia

Careful monitoring and titration of oxygen therapy in premature infants help reduce the risk of ROP.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man dies and his corneas are offered for donation. Which of the following in the donor's history is an absolute contraindication to corneal donation?
options: Death due to an unknown cause
History of pulmonary tuberculosis, treated and cured
History of uncomplicated cataract surgery 5 years ago
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Death due to an unknown cause

Absolute contraindications — donor side:

• Death of unknown cause / unknown medical history
• Ocular malignancy: retinoblastoma, choroidal melanoma, adenocarcinoma of the eye
• Haematological malignancy: leukaemia, disseminated lymphoma
• Active septicaemia (bacteraemia, fungaemia, viraemia); active endocarditis
• Viral: HIV/AIDS or high-risk behaviour, active hepatitis B/C, rabies, CMV encephalitis
• Neurological (prion/slow virus): CJD, SSPE, PML, neuro disease of unknown aetiology
• Congenital rubella
• Active intraocular inflammation
• Prior refractive surgery (for PK), intrinsic corneal disease (keratoconus, Fuchs', scarring)

NOT contraindications (high-yield negatives): age extremes (relative only), diabetes, hypertension, sepsis-free cancer of non-ocular/non-haematological origin (most solid tumours are acceptable), tuberculosis, poor visual acuity from refractive error, previous cataract surgery.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 52-year-old man presents with progressive painless visual loss. Visual field examination shows a central scotoma in the right eye and a superotemporal visual field defect in the left eye. Fundus examination is normal. Which of the following best explains this pattern of visual field loss?
options: Lesion at the optic nerve–chiasm junction
Lesion of the lateral geniculate body
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lesion at the optic nerve–chiasm junction

•

This visual field pattern is classic for a junctional scotoma. A lesion at the optic nerve–chiasm junction compresses the optic nerve on one side, causing a central scotoma in that eye, and simultaneously affects the crossing inferonasal fibers from the opposite eye, producing a superotemporal visual field defect contralaterally.

•

Optic tract or lateral geniculate body lesions cause homonymous defects, while pure chiasmal lesions cause bitemporal hemianopia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old farmer presents with severe eye pain, redness, and watering for 3 days following a minor corneal injury from vegetable matter. Examination reveals the following. Which of the following represents the correct sequence of management for this condition?
options: Start empirical fortified antibiotics immediately, followed by scraping the ulcer base for Gram staining and culture, then add topical steroids to reduce inflammation
Scrape the base of the ulcer using the blunt edge of a No. 15 blade, perform Gram staining and culture, start fortified antibiotics, add topical atropine for cycloplegia, and avoid steroids
Perform a corneal biopsy under general anesthesia before starting any antibiotic therapy
Start topical steroids first to reduce the inflammatory response, followed by antibiotics once the culture report is available
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scrape the base of the ulcer using the blunt edge of a No. 15 blade, perform Gram staining and culture, start fortified antibiotics, add topical atropine for cycloplegia, and avoid steroids

| Feature | Detail

| ------- | ------

| Likely organism | Streptococcus pneumoniae — most common cause of bacterial corneal ulcer in India

| Classic descriptors | Ulcus serpens (snake-shaped, serpiginous, spreading ulcer); hypopyon — mobile, sterile collection of pus in the anterior chamber

| Risk factor | Often follows trivial corneal trauma (e.g., vegetable matter), sometimes associated with chronic dacryocystitis

| Management (mnemonic SS) | Step

| ------------------------ | ----

| S | Scrape base of ulcer using blunt edge of a No. 15 blade

| S | Gram Staining and culture

| S | Start fortified antibiotics

| S | Supportive therapy — atropine for cycloplegia, relieves pain

| S | Avoid Steroids

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old patient presents with features suggestive of glaucoma. On examination, the cornea is densely opacified, making visualization of the anterior segment difficult. You want to measure the intraocular pressure (IOP) accurately. Which of the following tonometers is most appropriate in this situation?
options: [Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. [image not included in this edition]

• A: Schiotz tonometer
• B: Goldmann applanation tonometer
• C: Reichert applanation Tono-Pen
•

D: Perkins Mk3 Hand-Held Tonometer

•

We have been given a suspected glaucoma with densely opacified cornea and poor visualization of anterior segment. Standard applanation methods require a clear, regular corneal surface.

• Reichert Applanation Tono-pen Requires minimal corneal surface area
•

Can measure IOP in:

• Corneal scars
• Edematous cornea
• Post-keratoplasty eyes
• Bedridden patients

•

Does not require slit lamp visualization

• Most appropriate when cornea is opaque.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman has difficulty seeing in bright light and is diagnosed with a cataract. Which cataract type is not typically associated with this symptom?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cuneiform cataract

Cuneiform (cortical) opacities are peripheral spoke- or wedge-shaped opacities radiating inward from the equator. In bright light, pupillary constriction removes them from the visual axis, so vision improves; in dim light or at night, mydriasis brings them into the axis, causing blur and glare from oncoming headlights. All the other options are central/axial opacities lying within the constricted pupillary aperture, so miosis worsens them.

One-line rule: Central opacity → sun is the enemy. Peripheral opacity → sun is the friend.

Cuneiform pearls: long asymptomatic phase (opacities lie outside the axis) · night-driving glare · water clefts and vacuoles precede the spokes · classically the cataract with preserved vision on bright-light examination but poor night vision.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 58-year-old airline captain comes to the OPD after he was found to have abnormal vision testing during a pilot medical certification examination. The patient feels well and has no ocular symptoms. Vision testing shows normal visual acuity but moderate loss of peripheral vision in both eyes. Results of the funduscopic examination are shown in the image below. He is started on latanoprost eyedrops. The medication is most likely to improve this patient's condition through which of the following mechanisms?
options: Decreased bicarbonate formation in ciliary body
Decreased formation of abnormal blood vessels in retina
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased outflow of aqueous humor

This asymptomatic patient with peripheral field loss and glaucomatous fundus changes has primary open-angle glaucoma. Latanoprost, a prostaglandin F2α analog, lowers IOP by increasing uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with diabetic macular edema is being followed up as part of a multicenter clinical trial. His baseline visual acuity was recorded using a standardized chart that allows accurate detection of small changes in vision over serial visits. The chart used has five letters per line, uniform spacing, and visual acuity is expressed in logMAR units. Which of the following charts is being used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ETDRS chart

Key Characteristics of ETDRS Chart

• Developed for the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study
• Logarithmic progression of letter size (0.1 logMAR per line)
• Equal number of letters per line (5)
• Equal spacing between letters and rows
• Standardized luminance

Advantage:
