More reproducible and sensitive than Snellen for:

• Diabetic macular edema
• AMD trials
• Multicenter studies

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with severe pain, marked redness, and profound loss of vision in his right eye for 3 days. Examination reveals diffuse lid edema, conjunctival chemosis, corneal haze, proptosis, and painful restriction of extraocular movements. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrates diffuse inflammation involving the entire globe with extension into the orbital tissues. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is incorrect?
options: Untreated cases may progress to cavernous sinus thrombosis
It involves all three coats of the eyeball
Enucleation is the treatment of choice
Painful restriction of ocular movements is a common presentation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enucleation is the treatment of choice

The patient has panophthalmitis, a fulminant suppurative inflammation involving all layers of the eyeball with extension into the orbital soft tissues. It is an ophthalmic emergency requiring prompt treatment.

Why Option C is incorrect

Enucleation is not the treatment of choice.

• Evisceration (removal of the intraocular contents while preserving the scleral shell) is generally preferred for a blind, painful eye with panophthalmitis after initiating systemic antibiotics.
• Enucleation is contraindicated during active panophthalmitis because severing the optic nerve may increase the risk of spreading infection intracranially, including to the meninges.
• Enucleation may be considered later in selected cases after the acute infection has resolved.

Why the other options are correct?

A. Untreated cases can progress to cavernous sinus thrombosis. ✔️

• Infection can spread through the valveless ophthalmic veins, resulting in orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, or brain abscess.

B. It involves all three coats of the eyeball. ✔️

• Panophthalmitis affects:

• Fibrous coat (cornea and sclera)
• Uveal tract
• Retina

• Inflammation extends beyond the globe into the orbital tissues.

D. Presents with painful limitation of movements. ✔️

• Orbital extension causes:

• Painful restriction of extraocular movements
• Lid edema
• Chemosis
• Proptosis

NEET PG Pearls

| Endophthalmitis | Panophthalmitis

| --------------- | ---------------

| Infection confined to intraocular structures | Infection involves the entire globe and extends into orbital tissues

| Extraocular movements usually preserved | Painful restriction of eye movements

| Intravitreal antibiotics are the mainstay | Requires systemic + intravitreal antibiotics; evisceration if the eye is unsalvageable

| No orbital involvement | Orbital cellulitis and cavernous sinus thrombosis may occur

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant with congenital glaucoma has corneal enlargement, clouding, and Haab’s striae. Medical treatment has failed, and the angle is difficult to visualize due to corneal clouding. Which surgical procedure is most appropriate for this infant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trabeculotomy with Trabeculectomy

In congenital glaucoma with corneal clouding and Haab’s striae, angle visualization is poor, making goniotomy unsuitable.

Trabeculotomy does not require a clear cornea.

Combined trabeculotomy–trabeculectomy offers higher success in advanced cases and is preferred after failure of medical therapy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 6-week-old infant is diagnosed with a dense bilateral congenital cataract. Beyond what age would surgical intervention carry a significantly higher risk of irreversible amblyopia due to failure of fixation reflex development?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2–4 months

Preferred timing

• Unilateral dense congenital cataract: surgery by 4–6 weeks of age (preferably ≤6 weeks).
• Bilateral dense congenital cataracts: surgery by 6–8 weeks, completing both eyes by about 8–10 weeks.

This is because irreversible visual deprivation begins much earlier than 2–4 months, even though fixation continues to mature over the first few months.

Standard pediatric cataract surgery consists of lens aspiration (or pediatric ECCE), primary posterior capsulorhexis, and anterior vitrectomy. Primary IOL implantation depends on age and surgeon preference; many infants younger than 6 months are left aphakic initially and corrected with contact lenses, whereas primary PCIOL implantation is more commonly performed in older infants and children.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old diabetic patient presents with gradual painless decrease in vision. Fundus examination shows macular edema. He is planned for an intravitreal sustained-release steroid implant that is FDA approved for this condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dexamethasone 0.7 mg

Ozurdex (dexamethasone intravitreal implant 0.7 mg) is the biodegradable sustained-release implant (NOVADUR polymer matrix) approved for:

• Diabetic macular edema
• Macular edema following CRVO/BRVO
• Non-infectious posterior uveitis

Why the distractors are wrong?

• A. Betamethasone (0.6%) — not used as an intravitreal implant; irrelevant to posterior segment sustained delivery.
• C./D. Triamcinolone acetonide (0.5%/0.4 mg or 0.7%) — intravitreal triamcinolone is used off-label/approved in some contexts, but it's a suspension/crystalline steroid, not a sustained-release biodegradable implant. There's no FDA-approved "triamcinolone 0.7% implant" — this option is a distractor mixing up drug and implant nomenclature.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because his wife has noticed that his left eye looks smaller than his right. He has had worsening left shoulder and arm pain for 3 months. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 35 years. Examination shows left-sided ptosis. The pupils are unequal but reactive to light; when measured in dim light, the left pupil is 3 mm and the right pupil is 5 mm. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's ophthalmologic symptoms?
options: Aneurysm of the posterior cerebral artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Compression of stellate ganglion

•

This patient has Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis worse in dim light) with shoulder/arm pain and heavy smoking, suggesting a Pancoast tumor compressing the cervicothoracic (stellate) ganglion.

•

Cavernous sinus thrombosis causes ophthalmoplegia and chemosis.

• Posterior cerebral artery aneurysm causes CN III palsy with dilated pupil.
• Hypothalamic infarction is rare and would cause broader neurologic deficits.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient complains of decreased distant vision but he does not use spectacles for near vision. The image of his ocular examination is given below. What is this type of refractive error called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Index myopia

•

Index myopia occurs due to increase in refractive index of the crystalline lens, classically seen in nuclear cataract, causing decreased distance vision with preserved near vision (“second sight”).

•

Axial myopia results from increased axial length of the eyeball.

• Curvatural myopia is due to increased corneal or lenticular curvature.
• Positional myopia occurs when the lens is displaced anteriorly.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 62-year-old diabetic patient presents with severe ocular pain, lid edema, proptosis, chemosis, and complete loss of vision following a penetrating eye injury 5 days ago. Ocular movements are restricted and fundus view is not possible. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Panophthalmitis

Panophthalmitis = Suppurative inflammation involving:

• All coats of the eyeball
• Intraocular contents
• Tenon’s capsule
• Often spreads to orbit

The single discriminating idea:

• Endophthalmitis stops at the sclera. Panophthalmitis breaks through it.
• Both follow penetrating trauma. Both give pain, hypopyon, and vision loss.
• The orbital signs are what separate them:

| Finding in this stem | Meaning

| -------------------- | -------

| Proptosis | Inflammation has escaped the globe into orbital fat

| Restricted ocular movements | Extraocular muscles are now inflamed/oedematous

| Lid oedema + marked chemosis | Trans-scleral spread to Tenon's capsule and orbit

| Complete loss of vision (no PL) | Total intraocular destruction

| Severe boring pain | Scleral and orbital involvement

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 64-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled blood pressure presents with sudden painless blurring of vision in his left eye. He reports noticing a dark curtain partially obscuring his visual field since yesterday. Examination shows patchy visual field defects without ocular pain or photophobia. Funduscopic examination demonstrates flame-shaped retinal hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s retinal findings?
options: Embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery
Chronic systemic hypertension causing retinal vascular damage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chronic systemic hypertension causing retinal vascular damage

Hypertensive retinopathy results from chronic systemic hypertension causing retinal arteriolar narrowing, endothelial damage, and retinal ischemia. Characteristic fundoscopic findings include:

• Flame-shaped hemorrhages
• Cotton-wool spots (nerve fiber layer microinfarcts)
• Arteriovenous nicking
• Copper/silver wiring
• Papilledema in severe malignant hypertension

Patients may present with:

• Blurred vision
• Scotomas/visual field defects
• Painless visual loss

Key differentiating features:

• Central retinal artery occlusion → sudden painless monocular vision loss with “cherry-red spot”
• Acute angle-closure glaucoma → painful red eye, halos, elevated intraocular pressure
• Giant cell arteritis → granulomatous vasculitis with headache, jaw claudication, elevated ESR

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 65-year-old diabetic undergoing fundus evaluation for diabetic retinopathy has numerous small, round, yellow-white refractile opacities in the vitreous that remain fixed in position despite eye movement and do not obscure the fundus view. What is the composition of these opacities?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcium pyrophosphate

| Option | Reasoning

| ------ | ---------

| A) Cholesterol crystals | This is the composition of synchysis scintillans (cholesterolosis bulbi), which follows chronic vitreous hemorrhage and does sediment with gravity

| B) Calcium pyrophosphate/hydroxyapatite | Composition of asteroid hyalosis — a degenerative process classically associated with diabetes; particles do NOT sediment because they're tethered to collagen fibrils

| C) Denatured collagen | Not the characteristic particle; collagen is the vitreous scaffold, not the opacity itself

| D) Hemosiderin-laden macrophages | Seen in ocular siderosis/old vitreous hemorrhage clearance, not this entity

Pearl (high-yield differentiator):

• "Does NOT sediment" = Asteroid hyalosis (calcium soaps, unilateral, usually incidental, diabetes link).
• "DOES sediment inferiorly" = Synchysis scintillans (cholesterol, bilateral, post chronic vitreous hemorrhage, associated with a degenerated/aphakic eye).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 65-year-old female patient presents with gradual, progressive visual field loss in both eyes. Fundus is shown below. Which cell type in the retina is primarily affected in this patient's condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ganglion cells

The fundus image shows optic disc cupping, characteristic of glaucoma, a progressive optic neuropathy causing gradual peripheral visual field loss. Primary retinal cells affected:

• Retinal ganglion cells
• Their axons form the retinal nerve fiber layer and optic nerve

Increased intraocular pressure or impaired optic nerve perfusion leads to:

• Ganglion cell apoptosis
• Optic nerve head cupping
• Progressive visual field defects

Typical visual field defect:

• Nasal step
• Arcuate scotoma
• Tunnel vision in advanced disease

Important retinal cell functions:

• Rods/cones → photoreceptors
• Bipolar cells → relay signals
• Amacrine cells → interneurons modulating retinal processing
• Ganglion cells → transmit visual information through optic nerve

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to worsening eye pain. The patient noticed a rash around the left eye yesterday and, this morning, began experiencing left eye pain, redness, and decreased vision. Physical examination shows scattered vesicles on the left side of the forehead and nose and on the left upper and lower eyelids. Left eye examination shows conjunctival erythema, and fluorescein staining demonstrates linear, branching ulcerations on the cornea. Which of the following pathogens is most likely responsible for this patient's current condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Varicella-zoster virus

•

This presentation is herpes zoster ophthalmicus: elderly patient, vesicular rash in V1 distribution (forehead, nose—Hutchinson sign) with branching corneal lesions. VZV reactivation causes severe pain, keratitis, and vision loss.

•

Adenovirus causes epidemic keratoconjunctivitis without vesicles.

• Candida causes fungal keratitis, not dermatomal rash.
• HSV causes dendritic ulcers but typically without a dermatomal vesicular rash.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis presents with dry eyes and mouth. Rose Bengal staining shows corneal damage, and tear analysis reveals a tear-to-lysozyme ratio of 0.1. Which tear film layer is primarily deficient in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aqueous layer

• This patient has secondary Sjögren syndrome associated with rheumatoid arthritis, characterized by dry eyes and dry mouth.
• The markedly reduced tear-to-lysozyme ratio indicates decreased lacrimal gland secretion.
• Lysozyme is produced by the lacrimal glands and reflects aqueous tear production.
• Deficiency of the aqueous layer leads to keratoconjunctivitis sicca, epithelial damage seen with Rose bengal staining, and symptoms of ocular surface dryness rather than primary lipid or mucin layer dysfunction.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 67-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after an episode of transient vision loss in her right eye. While at a movie theater, she experienced sudden "dimming" of vision in that eye lasting about 10 minutes before fully recovering. She has never had a similar episode before but does report occasional headaches. She denies any focal weakness or numbness. Her past medical history includes coronary artery disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Vitals show blood pressure 130/85 mmHg and pulse 65/min and regular. A right-sided carotid bruit is auscultated; neurologic and funduscopic exams are otherwise normal. What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinal embolism

• This is a classic presentation of amaurosis fugax — transient monocular vision loss described as a "curtain coming down" or, as here, sudden "dimming," lasting minutes and resolving completely.
• The clinical context strongly supports an embolic source: significant atherosclerotic risk factors (CAD, hypertension, diabetes) plus a right-sided carotid bruit, pointing to carotid artery atherosclerosis as the source of retinal emboli (often cholesterol/platelet-fibrin emboli that transiently occlude the retinal or ophthalmic artery circulation and then dislodge).
• Demyelinating disorder (B) (e.g., optic neuritis in MS) usually causes painful, subacute vision loss over days, not sudden transient episodes.
• Elevated intracranial pressure (C) classically causes bilateral, brief "grayouts" (transient visual obscurations) associated with papilledema, not typically monocular.

High-yield point:

• Amaurosis fugax + carotid bruit → urgent carotid duplex ultrasound to evaluate for high-grade stenosis, since this is a TIA-equivalent event carrying stroke risk and may warrant carotid endarterectomy if significant stenosis is found.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 68-year-old woman comes to the physician for evaluation of diminished vision for several months. Twenty-eight years ago, she was diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus, which has been well controlled with hydroxychloroquine. Fundoscopic examination shows concentric rings of hypopigmentation and hyperpigmentation surrounding the fovea bilaterally. Visual field examination of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Paracentral scotoma

Hydroxychloroquine toxicity causes bull’s-eye maculopathy (concentric parafoveal pigment changes), producing paracentral scotomas on visual field testing.

• Bitemporal hemianopia suggests chiasmal lesions.
• Right monocular blindness indicates optic nerve/retinal artery occlusion.
• Hemianopia with macular sparing is typical of occipital cortex lesions.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 68-year-old woman is evaluated for vision impairment. The patient has a decrease in both distant and near vision and has had occasional floaters. She has had no pain or redness in her eyes, headache, focal weakness, or sensory loss. Medical history is notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease. Fundoscopic examination is shown here. Which of the following contributed most to the pathogenesis of this patient's current ocular condition?
options: Age-related degeneration of retinal pigment epithelium
Ganglion cell death due to high intraocular pressure
Retinal arterial occlusion from atherosclerotic disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic hyperglycemia-induced microvascular injury

The fundus findings with gradual bilateral visual impairment and floaters in a patient with long-standing diabetes indicate diabetic retinopathy, caused by chronic hyperglycemia leading to microvascular damage, capillary leakage, and ischemia.

A. Age-related degeneration of retinal pigment epithelium: Describes age-related macular degeneration.

C. Ganglion cell death due to high intraocular pressure: Refers to glaucoma with peripheral field loss from ganglion cell death.

D. Retinal arterial occlusion from atherosclerotic disease: Causes sudden, profound vision loss, not a chronic progressive picture.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 68-year-old woman presents 8 months after uncomplicated cataract surgery with progressively worsening vision. She complains of severe foreign body sensation and watering that is most pronounced immediately after waking up. Slit-lamp examination reveals the following. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis?
options: Corneal endothelial decompensation leading to stromal edema
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Corneal endothelial decompensation leading to stromal edema

• This is a classic presentation of Pseudophakic Bullous Keratopathy (PBK) — occurring months after cataract surgery (intraocular lens implantation), with:

• Progressive vision loss
• Foreign body sensation — from ruptured epithelial bullae
• Symptoms worse on waking — same mechanism as Fuchs dystrophy — during sleep, eyelids are closed, tears don't evaporate, and the cornea absorbs more fluid overnight, worsening edema; symptoms partially improve through the day as evaporation resumes
• Watering — reflex tearing from corneal irritation/bullae rupture

• Pathogenesis: Cataract surgery causes a degree of endothelial cell loss (from surgical trauma, phacoemulsification energy, or pre-existing low endothelial reserve as in undiagnosed Fuchs dystrophy). Since corneal endothelial cells do not regenerate (they compensate by cell spreading/enlargement, not division), if the endothelial cell density falls below the critical threshold (\~500–700 cells/mm²), the endothelial pump fails to keep the stroma deturgesced. This leads to stromal and epithelial edema, culminating in epithelial bullae formation — which are fragile and rupture, causing pain and foreign body sensation.

Why the others are wrong?

• A. Failure of corneal epithelial regeneration: Epithelial cells do regenerate well; the epithelium is not the primary defect here — it's secondarily edematous/bullous due to the underlying endothelial failure.
• C. Autoimmune destruction of Bowman's membrane: It is not relevant to PBK; this would suggest something like Mooren's ulcer or a Bowman's layer dystrophy (e.g., Reis-Bücklers), unrelated to post-cataract surgery pathogenesis.
• D. Lens-induced corneal toxicity: It is not a recognized mechanism; phacoanaphylactic or lens-induced uveitis relates to lens protein leakage causing intraocular inflammation, not direct corneal toxicity from an implanted IOL.

Exam tip: PBK = post-cataract surgery + endothelial cell loss + stromal/epithelial edema + painful bullae + morning worsening — the "morning worsening" clue links both Fuchs dystrophy and PBK since they share the same final common pathway: endothelial pump failure.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 68-year-old woman presents with gradually progressive difficulty reading and recognizing faces over the past year. She reports that straight lines appear distorted and that she now requires brighter light for close work. Funduscopic examination reveals multiple yellow deposits clustered around the macula with retinal pigment epithelial changes. Which of the following visual field abnormalities is most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Central scotoma

This patient has age-related macular degeneration (AMD), suggested by:

• Progressive difficulty reading and recognizing faces
• Metamorphopsia (straight lines appear distorted)
• Drusen (yellow deposits) and retinal pigment epithelial changes around the macula

Macular disease primarily affects central vision, producing a central scotoma while peripheral vision is relatively preserved.

Key visual field defects:

• Central scotoma → macular degeneration, optic neuritis
• Arcuate scotoma → glaucoma
• Bitemporal hemianopia → optic chiasm lesion (eg, pituitary adenoma)
• Homonymous hemianopia → postchiasmal lesion
• Binasal hemianopia → rare; bilateral lateral retinal/optic nerve lesions

Dry AMD is associated with drusen accumulation, whereas wet AMD involves choroidal neovascularization mediated by VEGF.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents with watering, foreign body sensation, and inward turning of the lower eyelid. Examination reveals following. All of the following surgical procedures are used in the management except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lazy-T procedure

• Jones lower lid retractor advancement corrects the underlying lower lid retractor disinsertion, a key mechanism of involutional entropion.
• Wies procedure combines transverse blepharotomy with retractor repair and is commonly used for involutional entropion.
• Lateral tarsal strip procedure corrects horizontal lower lid laxity and is frequently combined with retractor repair.
• Lazy-T procedure is primarily performed for medial involutional ectropion with punctal eversion and medial canthal tendon laxity, not for entropion.

Educational Pearl:

The three major anatomical defects in involutional entropion are:

1. Horizontal lid laxity
2. Lower lid retractor disinsertion/dehiscence
3. Preseptal orbicularis muscle override

Successful surgery is directed at correcting one or more of these underlying abnormalities.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A carpenter develops bilateral eye irritation and vision loss after trauma to the right eye. Fundus exam reveals Dalen-Fuchs nodules. Which type of hypersensitivity is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Type 4

•

This presentation suggests sympathetic ophthalmia, where trauma to one eye leads to bilateral granulomatous uveitis with Dalen–Fuchs nodules. It is mediated by a delayed (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction against ocular antigens.

•

Type I is IgE-mediated allergy.

• Type II involves antibody-mediated cytotoxicity.
• Type III is immune-complex deposition.
• Only Type IV explains T-cell–mediated granulomatous inflammation here.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A child was born at 34 weeks of gestation. A thorough ophthalmology examination was performed. There was a white reflex in one eye. On further evaluation, the doctor observed finding as shown in figure. This could be due to abnormality in which embryonic structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mesoderm

• The white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) in a premature infant with the described fundus finding is most consistent with persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV).
• The primary vitreous and hyaloid vascular system develop from mesoderm.
• Failure of regression leads to a fibrovascular mass behind the lens, causing leukocoria.
• Neural crest and surface ectoderm contribute to other ocular structures, while neuroectoderm forms the retina, not the vitreous.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A construction worker has unilateral facial anhidrosis after a back injury. Examination finding is shown below. Which location is the most likely site of lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. White ramus of T1

•

Unilateral facial anhidrosis with the shown findings indicates Horner syndrome due to a preganglionic sympathetic lesion. Preganglionic fibers supplying the eye and face originate from the ciliospinal center (C8–T2) and pass through the white ramus communicantes of T1.

•

Grey rami carry postganglionic fibers, so lesions there spare sweating.

• C8 white ramus does not contribute significantly to ocular sympathetic supply.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A cover-uncover eye test is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Left Exophoria

The cover-uncover test helps detect latent and manifest ocular misalignment.

• Tropia = manifest deviation present even when both eyes are open
• Phoria = latent deviation seen only when fusion is disrupted by covering one eye

Interpretation:

• In exophoria, the eye drifts outward when covered and moves inward to refixate when uncovered.
• In esophoria, the eye drifts inward when covered and moves outward on uncovering.

In this image:

• The left eye deviates outward when fusion is broken
• On uncovering, it moves inward to regain fixation

Diagnosis: Left exophoria

Phorias are latent deviations controlled by binocular fusion and are usually detected only during cover testing.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A eyelid swelling has persisted for several months in an adult. Histopathology reveals chronic lipogranulomatous inflammation. Which statement regarding this lesion is false?
options: It arises from obstruction of a meibomian gland.
It may be managed with incision and curettage.
Intralesional steroid injection may be used in selected cases.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is painful.

• Chalazion is a PAINLESS chronic lipogranulomatous inflammation of the meibomian gland.
• Recurrent or atypical lesions should raise suspicion for sebaceous gland carcinoma.
• Management includes conservative measures, intralesional triamcinolone, or incision and curettage.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A male patient with a history of hypermature cataract presents with a 2 day history of ciliary congestion, photophobia, blurring of vision and on examination has a deep anterior chamber in the right eye. The left eye is normal. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phacolytic glaucoma

• Phacolytic glaucoma occurs in hypermature cataract due to leakage of high-molecular-weight lens proteins, causing secondary open-angle glaucoma with deep anterior chamber, ciliary congestion, photophobia, and raised IOP.
• Phacomorphic glaucoma has a shallow AC from an intumescent lens.
• Phacotoxic glaucoma is an older term, not commonly used.
• Phacoanaphylactic uveitis is a granulomatous inflammatory reaction following lens capsule rupture, usually post-surgery or trauma.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A middle-aged woman develops slowly progressive unilateral proptosis. MRI orbit demonstrates following. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sphenoid wing meningioma

• Enhancing mass with dural tail sign associated with hyperostosis of the sphenoid wing is highly characteristic of sphenoid wing meningioma.
• Patients present with slowly progressive unilateral proptosis and visual decline.
• Optic nerve glioma enlarges the optic nerve without causing hyperostosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A neonate was found to have the following finding on routine examination of the eye. All of the following may be differentials except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Congenital glaucoma

The image shows leukocoria in the left eye (white-yellow pupillary reflex) against a normal red reflex on the right — picked up exactly the way this classically is, on red reflex testing (Brückner test).

Why D is the exception

Congenital glaucoma does not cause true leukocoria. Its presentation is a different triad entirely:

• Epiphora, photophobia, blepharospasm
• Buphthalmos, corneal enlargement (>12 mm), Haab striae
• The cornea becomes hazy/steamy from oedema — this is a corneal opacity, i.e. at most a pseudoleukocoria. The white you see is anterior to the pupil, not a reflection from a retrolental/retinal lesion.

The distinction that matters: leukocoria = abnormal reflection from a lesion at or behind the lens plane. Corneal disease (glaucoma, sclerocornea, Peters anomaly, birth trauma) is pseudoleukocoria.

Leukocoria differentials

• Cataract (congenital)
• Retinoblastoma (calcification on USG — the one you must never miss)
• ROP stage 5
• Coats disease (unilateral, older male child, no calcification, exudative RD)
• PHPV/PFV
• Toxocariasis (granuloma)
• Coloboma of choroid / Myelinated nerve fibres / Norrie disease / Retinal dysplasia

| Option | Mechanism of leukocoria

| ------ | -----------------------

| Congenital cataract | Opaque lens itself — commonest cause of leukocoria overall

| PHPV/PFV | Retrolental fibrovascular plaque, microphthalmic eye, elongated ciliary processes, unilateral

| ROP (Stage 5) | Total retinal detachment → retrolental fibroplasia; preterm, low birth weight

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient complains of "fluctuating refractory error”. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diabetic cataract

•

Fluctuating refractive error is classically seen in diabetes mellitus due to changes in blood glucose altering the refractive index of the lens via sorbitol accumulation, causing alternating myopic and hypermetropic shifts.

•

Nuclear cataract causes a fixed myopic shift (“second sight”).

•

Cortical cataract mainly causes glare and polyopia.

•

Posterior subcapsular cataract causes glare and near vision difficulty, not refractive fluctuation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient has progressive bilateral corneal guttata with morning blurring of vision due to endothelial pump failure. Which corneal dystrophy is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fuchs corneal dystrophy

Fuchs dystrophy affects the Descemet membrane and corneal endothelium, causing guttata, stromal edema and reduced vision, especially on waking.

• Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy is a primary disorder of the corneal endothelium — progressive loss and dysfunction of endothelial cells leads to corneal guttata (wart-like excrescences on Descemet's membrane, seen as a "beaten metal" appearance on specular reflection).
• As endothelial pump function fails, the cornea can't stay deturgesced, leading to stromal and epithelial edema — classically worse on waking (morning blurring) because eyes are closed overnight, tears aren't evaporating, and stromal hydration peaks; it improves through the day as evaporation resumes. Advanced disease leads to painful bullous keratopathy.

The other three are all stromal dystrophies, not endothelial, so they don't fit the "endothelial pump failure" mechanism:

• A. Lattice dystrophy — amyloid deposits in the stroma, branching linear/lattice pattern (TGFBI gene).
• B. Granular dystrophy — hyaline/"breadcrumb" deposits in the stroma, sparing the periphery early on.
• D. Reis-Bücklers dystrophy — actually a Bowman's layer dystrophy (anterior), causing recurrent erosions and superficial reticular scarring — again not endothelial.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient on worth 4 dot test was interpreted like this:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Crossed diplopia

In the Worth 4 dot test, the patient wears red-green glasses (conventionally red lens over the right eye, green lens over the left eye) and views 4 illuminated dots (1 red, 2 green, 1 white) in a diamond pattern.

• If there's no diplopia and normal fusion, the patient sees 4 dots (the white dot takes on a blended color).
• If there's diplopia, the patient sees 5 dots — as shown in this image (2 red + 3 green).

The key is the relative position of the red vs. green images:

• Here, the red dots (right eye's image) appear on the left, and the green dots (left eye's image) appear on the right.
• Each eye's image is displaced to the opposite side of the eye that produced it — right eye sees to the left, left eye sees to the right. This crossing over is the hallmark of crossed diplopia, which occurs in exodeviation (divergent squint), because the visual axes diverge, causing the image to fall on the nasal retina of each eye, which projects to the temporal (opposite) visual field.

| Diplopia type | Underlying deviation | Image relationship

| ------------- | -------------------- | ------------------

| Crossed | Exodeviation | Right eye image → left side; Left eye image → right side

| Uncrossed | Esodeviation | Right eye image → right side; Left eye image → left side

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presented with foreign body sensation, redness, and excessive watering from the right eye for 15 days after a twig brushed against his eye. Examination is shown below. Which among the following is the appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Amphotericin B drops

•

The history of vegetative trauma (twig) with persistent foreign body sensation and redness suggests fungal keratitis. Amphotericin B is an effective topical antifungal, especially for yeast and some filamentous fungi.

•

Acyclovir is for herpetic keratitis.

• Propamidine isethionate is used in Acanthamoeba keratitis.
• Hydrocortisone is contraindicated as steroids worsen fungal infections by promoting fungal proliferation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presented with painless decrease in vision and metamorphopsia. Fundus examination revealed the lesion shown in the image. What is the expected finding on ultrasonography?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Collar stud appearance

•

Painless visual loss with metamorphopsia and the shown fundus lesion suggest choroidal melanoma. On ultrasonography, melanoma classically shows a collar-stud (mushroom) appearance due to tumor breaking through Bruch’s membrane.

•

Smoke-stack and inkblot patterns are FFA findings of central serous chorioretinopathy, not USG features.

•

Double circulation is an angiographic sign of melanoma, not an ultrasound finding.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with bilateral anterior stromal, breadcrumb-like corneal opacities with clear intervening cornea. Histopathological confirmation is planned. Which stain best demonstrates the deposited material?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Masson's trichrome

Granular corneal dystrophy contains stromal hyaline deposits, which stain positively with Masson's trichrome.

• Congo red → Amyloid (lattice dystrophy)
• Alcian blue → Mucopolysaccharides
• PAS → Basement membrane/glycoproteins

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient receiving long-term therapy for ventricular arrhythmia develops the following on slit-lamp examination. Which other finding is classically associated with this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior subcapsular cataract

Amiodarone:

• Corneal verticillata (vortex keratopathy)
• Anterior subcapsular cataract
• Optic neuropathy (rare)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient scheduled for FLACS is told that the laser achieves precise tissue cutting with minimal collateral damage by delivering ultrashort pulses. What is the approximate duration of each laser pulse?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 10⁻¹⁵ seconds

The term "femtosecond" itself gives away the answer — 1 femtosecond = 10⁻¹⁵ seconds.

These ultrashort pulses work through a mechanism called photodisruption, where high-intensity laser energy creates a rapid, localized plasma that mechanically cleaves tissue — rather than burning or heating it.

Key advantages of this mechanism:

• Minimal thermal spread — the pulse is too brief to conduct significant heat to surrounding tissue
• High spatial precision — cuts can be placed with micron-level accuracy (capsulotomy, lens fragmentation, corneal incisions)
• Reduced collateral damage — compared to conventional phacoemulsification, which relies on ultrasonic energy and generates more heat

Quick reference — order of magnitude recall:

• Millisecond = 10⁻³ s
• Microsecond = 10⁻⁶ s
• Nanosecond = 10⁻⁹ s
• Femtosecond = 10⁻¹⁵ s ← FLACS pulse duration

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient suddenly develops painless monocular vision loss. Perimetry shows the following. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy

• The vignette describes sudden, painless, monocular vision loss with an altitudinal field defect on perimetry (loss of either the superior or inferior half of the visual field, respecting the horizontal midline).
• This altitudinal pattern occurs because the optic nerve head is supplied by the short posterior ciliary arteries, which have a segmental distribution — infarction of one sector (superior or inferior) produces a corresponding altitudinal defect. This is the classic field defect for AION, especially non-arteritic AION in patients with vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension) or arteritic AION (giant cell arteritis) in the elderly.
• Fundoscopy in AION classically shows pale, swollen optic disc with splinter hemorrhages, sometimes with a "disc at risk" (crowded, small cup) in the fellow eye.

Why the others are wrong?

• A. Pituitary adenoma: Causes bitemporal hemianopia due to compression of the decussating fibers at the optic chiasm, and typically progresses gradually, not suddenly, and is binocular, not monocular.
• C. Occipital infarction: Causes homonymous hemianopia (often with macular sparing due to dual blood supply from PCA and MCA), affecting the same half of the visual field in both eyes, not monocular.
• D. Methanol poisoning: Causes bilateral toxic optic neuropathy with central or cecocentral scotomas, not monocular altitudinal defects; typically presents with a history of toxic ingestion, metabolic acidosis.

Key exam point:

• Sudden + painless + monocular + altitudinal field defect = AION.
• Contrast with monocular central scotoma (optic neuritis — usually painful) and arcuate scotoma (glaucoma, chronic).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient undergoes cataract surgery planning. The K required in the SRK formula is measured by which investigation? E = A − 2.5L − 0.9K
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Keratometry

SRK formula:

• L = Axial length → A-scan biometry (or optical biometry in modern practice)
• K = Corneal curvature → Keratometry

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with 1.5D myopia undergoes streak retinoscopy. The patient is seated one meter from the light source and is asked to fixate on a distant object as the retinoscopy is performed. With respect to the movement of the plane mirror in the retinoscope, the red reflex in the eye exhibits:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Movement against the plane

In streak retinoscopy using a plane mirror, a myopic eye (>1 D) shows against movement because the patient’s far point lies in front of the retinoscope (working distance 1 m = 1 D).

Other options:

• A. With plane movement is seen in emmetropia, hypermetropia, or myopia <1 D.
• C. No movement occurs when refractive error equals working distance.
• D. Oblique movement suggests irregular astigmatism, not simple myopia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with a history of diabetes and hypertension underwent fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) to evaluate his decreasing vision. The FFA yields an image as shown below. The given FFA is characteristic of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Macular ischemia

• The FFA is showing enlarged fovea avascular zone arrow (white arrow), and capillary non-perfused areas (blue arrow).
• Both of which are suggestive of macular ischemia which when combined with the history of diabetes in this patient points towards diabetic macular ischemia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A student with myopia wishes to undergo surgery. Which option is not suitable for correcting her refractive error?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Conductive keratoplasty

• Conductive keratoplasty is used to treat hypermetropia and presbyopia, not myopia, making it unsuitable.
• SMILE corrects myopia by removing a stromal lenticule.
• Radial keratotomy was historically used for myopia, though now obsolete.
• Intracorneal ring segments flatten the cornea and can reduce low-to-moderate myopia or irregular astigmatism.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: According to the grading of trachoma, what defines the follicular stage?
options: 5 or more follicles in the upper tarsal conjunctiva
3 or more follicles in the lower tarsal conjunctiva
5 or more follicles in the lower tarsal conjunctiva
3 or more follicles in the upper tarsal conjunctiva
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 5 or more follicles in the upper tarsal conjunctiva

The follicular stage of trachoma (TF) is defined by the presence of ≥5 follicles, each ≥0.5 mm, on the upper tarsal conjunctiva.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All are true about corneal dystrophies and stains used except:
options: Macular dystrophy stains with Alcian blue
Schnyder's dystrophy shows mucopolysaccharides with Congo red
Granular dystrophy is stained by Masson trichome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Schnyder's dystrophy shows mucopolysaccharides with Congo red

• Schnyder’s corneal dystrophy shows cholesterol and lipid deposition, not mucopolysaccharides;
• Congo red stains amyloid, not lipids.
• Macular dystrophy stains with Alcian blue due to mucopolysaccharides (true).
• Granular dystrophy stains with Masson trichrome (true).
• Lattice dystrophy has amyloid deposition, Congo red positive (true).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All are true about diabetic retinopathy features except:
options: NVD of any disc area with VH is high-risk
Vitreous hemorrhage with NVE is a high-risk feature
Clinically significant macular edema includes thickening within 500 µm of fovea
Tractional retinal detachment is a sign of NPDR
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tractional retinal detachment is a sign of NPDR

Tractional retinal detachment (TRD) is a feature of proliferative, not non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

Clinically Significant Macular Edema (CSME)

(Any 1 of the 3 criteria):

• Thickening of retina within 500 microns of foveal center
• Hard exudates within 500 microns of center
• Zone of retinal thickening ≥ 1 DD

Advanced Diabetic Eye Disease:

• Persistent vitreous hemorrhage
• Tractional retinal detachment
• Neovascular glaucoma

Early PDR (without high-risk characteristics):

• Neovascularization at optic disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE)

High-risk PDR:

• NVD < 1/4 disc area + VH or PRH
• NVD 1/4–1/3 disc area ± VH or PRH
• NVE > 1/2 disc area + VH or PRH

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All are true about Foster–Kennedy syndrome except:
options: Can be seen in occipital lobe neoplasms
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Can be seen in occipital lobe neoplasms

•

Foster–Kennedy syndrome classically shows ipsilateral optic atrophy due to direct optic nerve compression and contralateral papilledema from raised intracranial pressure. It is most commonly caused by frontal lobe or olfactory groove meningiomas.

•

Occipital lobe tumors produce visual field defects (homonymous hemianopia) and do not cause Foster–Kennedy syndrome, making option C incorrect.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All are true about the oculocardiac reflex except:
options: Most commonly due to inferior rectus stimulation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Most commonly due to inferior rectus stimulation

•

The oculocardiac reflex is mediated by trigeminal (V1) afferents and vagal efferents, and is commonly triggered during strabismus surgery, especially on extraocular muscle traction. It is most commonly elicited by medial rectus stimulation, not inferior rectus, making option C incorrect.

•

Initial management is immediate cessation of surgical stimulation, which usually reverses bradycardia; anticholinergics may be used if persistent.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All of the following correctly describe the organization of NPCBVI except:
options: Vision centers are at primary level staffed by optometrists with 20,000 centers nationally
Service centers perform minor eye surgeries including cataract and lid surgeries
Training centers at tertiary level perform corneal transplantation, retinal and glaucoma surgeries
Centers of excellence make guidelines, conduct research and perform major surgeries at apex level with 200 centers
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Centers of excellence make guidelines, conduct research and perform major surgeries at apex level with 200 centers

NPCBVI organization revision table:

| Level | Type | Staff | Number | Function

| ----- | ---- | ----- | ------ | --------

| Primary | Vision centers (CoE) | Optometrists | 20,000 | Basic eye care, school health monitoring

| Secondary | Service centers | Ophthalmologists | 2,000 | Minor surgeries: cataract + lid

| Tertiary | Training centers | Senior ophthalmologists | 200 | Training + major surgeries (corneal transplant, retinal, tumor, glaucoma)

| Apex | Centers of excellence | Senior ophthalmologists + program managers | 20 | Guidelines + research only (NOT major surgeries)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All of the following statements about degenerative (pathologic) myopia are true except:
options: It is typically associated with a refractive error greater than -6 diopters
It shows a higher prevalence in females
Posterior staphyloma is a characteristic fundus finding
Progression halts after adolescence, with the condition remaining stable thereafter
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Progression halts after adolescence, with the condition remaining stable thereafter

Degenerative (pathologic) myopia is distinct from simple myopia in that it is progressive throughout life, not just during the school-age/adolescent growth years. This continued axial elongation is what drives its characteristic complications.

Why the other options are correct (and not the exception)?

• A. It is typically associated with a refractive error greater than -6 diopters: Degenerative myopia is defined by high myopia, conventionally > -6 D (some texts use -8 D), along with significant axial elongation (often >26 mm).
• B. It shows a higher prevalence in females: It shows a well-documented female preponderance, unlike simple myopia which has a more even sex distribution.
• C. Posterior staphyloma is a characteristic fundus finding: Posterior staphyloma (a outward bulging of the sclera, choroid, and retina) is a hallmark structural finding, along with lacquer cracks, Fuchs spot, and chorioretinal atrophy.

Why D is the exception?

• Unlike simple/school myopia, which typically stabilizes by the late teens/early twenties, degenerative myopia continues to progress with age due to ongoing scleral thinning and axial elongation, predisposing to complications like choroidal neovascularization, retinal detachment, and staphyloma enlargement even in adulthood.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All of the following statements regarding the condition shown in given image are correct except?
options: It is the most common juvenile macular dystrophy
Vitamin A supplement improve this condition
Fundus fluorescein angiography shows a dark choroid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin A supplement improve this condition

The fundus photograph shows:

• Beaten-bronze appearance at macula
• FFA image showing dark (silent) choroid

This is classic for Stargardt disease.

• Most common juvenile macular dystrophy
• Caused by mutation in ABCA4
• Lipofuscin accumulation in RPE
• FFA → Dark choroid
• Central vision loss
• Peripheral vision relatively preserved

Vitamin A does not improve Stargardt — it is actively contraindicated.

This is one of the few genuinely dangerous misconceptions in retinal disease, and it's a beautiful "except" answer because it inverts a rule students over-generalise from retinitis pigmentosa (where high-dose vitamin A palmitate 15,000 IU/day was suggested by the Berson trial).

• ABCA4 encodes the rim protein (ATP-binding cassette transporter) in photoreceptor outer segment discs
• Its job: flip all-trans-retinal (and its Schiff base, N-retinylidene-PE) from the intradiscal to the cytoplasmic face for recycling
• ABCA4 mutation → all-trans-retinal accumulates inside the disc → condenses with a second retinal molecule → forms A2E
• A2E is the toxic bisretinoid core of lipofuscin → accumulates in RPE → RPE death → photoreceptor loss

Therefore: giving more vitamin A supplies more substrate → more A2E → accelerated RPE toxicity. Vitamin A supplementation is explicitly avoided in ABCA4-related disease.

| | Stargardt | RP

| --- | --------- | ---

| Vision lost first | Central | Peripheral (night blindness first)

| Vitamin A | Contraindicated | Historically supplemented

| FFA | Dark choroid | Window defects, no dark choroid

| ERG | Normal early (photopic ↓ late) | Scotopic ↓↓ early

| Gene | ABCA4 | RHO, RPGR, USH2A

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An 18-year-old with rapidly progressing myopia has the following appearance on downward gaze. Which of the following systemic conditions is not associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alport syndrome

The image demonstrates Munson's sign, a V-shaped bulging of the lower eyelid on downgaze, which occurs due to protrusion of the conical cornea in advanced keratoconus.

Clinical features of keratoconus

• Progressive myopia
• Irregular astigmatism
• Corneal thinning
• Conical protrusion of the cornea
• Munson's sign (advanced disease)
• Fleischer ring (iron deposition)
• Vogt's striae

Systemic associations of keratoconus

✔ Ehlers–Danlos syndrome

• Connective tissue disorder with abnormal collagen
• Well-recognized association

✔ Marfan syndrome

• Fibrillin defect
• Increased incidence of keratoconus has been reported

✔ Osteogenesis imperfecta

• Type I collagen disorder
• Corneal thinning and keratoconus may occur

❌ Alport syndrome

• Characteristically associated with anterior lenticonus, not keratoconus.

Why Alport syndrome is incorrect

Alport syndrome (Type IV collagen defect) classically causes:

• Anterior lenticonus ⭐ (pathognomonic)
• Dot-and-fleck retinopathy
• Posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy (occasionally)

It is not a recognized association of keratoconus.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An elderly patient with a sclerotic type of hypermature cataract presents with sudden rise in intraocular pressure and iridocorneal touch. Slit-lamp examination shows lens subluxation. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phacotopic glaucoma

•

In this elderly patient, a sclerotic hypermature cataract with lens subluxation, sudden rise in IOP, and iridocorneal touch points to phacotopic glaucoma. This occurs due to dislocation or subluxation of the lens, which mechanically blocks aqueous outflow or causes pupillary block.

•

Phacomorphic glaucoma is due to an intumescent lens, phacolytic glaucoma results from protein leakage without subluxation, and phacoanaphylactic glaucoma is an inflammatory response after lens protein exposure.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An ophthalmologist conducting blindness surveillance under the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI) classifies a patient as blind based on presenting visual acuity. Which of the following fulfills the programme definition of blindness?
options: Presenting visual acuity <6/60 in the better eye
Presenting visual acuity <3/60 in the better eye
Best corrected visual acuity <6/18 in the better eye
Best corrected visual acuity <1/60 in the better eye
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Presenting visual acuity <3/60 in the better eye

NPCBVI defines blindness as:

• Presenting distance visual acuity <3/60 in the better eye, or
• Visual field restricted to <10° around fixation.

NPCBVI uses presenting visual acuity, not best-corrected acuity, for its operational/surveillance definition. This is deliberate — the programme is tracking the burden of avoidable blindness (uncorrected refractive error, cataract, etc.) in the population, not just uncorrectable/best-corrected blindness. This is why C and D (which specify "best corrected") are wrong — they don't match the programme's operational definition, even though they sound like standard clinical descriptions of blindness.

The cutoff is <3/60, not <6/60. This trips people up because the WHO's older definitions and some contexts use <6/60 as a "visual impairment" or "low vision" threshold, while <3/60 is the blindness threshold. Remember the tiered WHO/NPCBVI categories roughly as:

• Normal/mild: 6/6 to 6/18
• Moderate visual impairment (low vision): <6/18 to 6/60
• Severe visual impairment: <6/60 to 3/60
• Blindness: <3/60 (down to no light perception), or visual field <10° around fixation in the better eye

The field criterion (<10° around fixation) is the second, independent criterion — useful for conditions like advanced glaucoma or retinitis pigmentosa where central acuity may be preserved but the field is severely constricted.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Assertion (A): With 10% cocaine, a normal pupil dilates, but a Horner pupil does not dilate. Reason (R): Cocaine blocks the reuptake of noradrenaline released at the postganglionic sympathetic nerve endings.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

Sympathetic pathway to the pupil:

• Hypothalamus
• Ciliospinal center (C8–T2)
• Superior cervical ganglion
• Postganglionic fibers → dilator pupillae

Cocaine:

• Blocks reuptake of noradrenaline
• Increases synaptic NA concentration
• Enhances sympathetic effect → mydriasis

Normal Eye

• NA is released normally.
• Cocaine blocks reuptake.
• NA accumulates.
• Pupil dilates.

Horner Pupil

• Sympathetic denervation → little or no NA released.
• Cocaine blocks reuptake, but there is no NA to accumulate.
• No dilation occurs.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Depending on the location of the staphyloma in the eye which among the following options is matched correctly with its cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Equatorial staphyloma - scleritis

Staphyloma = Ectasia of uveal tissue through a thinned sclera

• Anterior staphyloma involves the cornea, usually after central corneal ulcer.
• Intercalary staphyloma occurs at the limbus, due to Scleritis or Secondary glaucoma.
• Equatorial staphyloma occurs at the equator of the globe due to Scleritis

| # | Staphyloma | Location | Lining tissue | Principal causes

| --- | ---------- | -------- | ------------- | ----------------

| 1 | Corneal (anterior) staphyloma | Cornea | Iris (pseudocornea) | Healed sloughing/perforated corneal ulcer (bacterial keratitis, gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum), keratomalacia, trauma/perforation, corneal melts — the ectatic corneal scar becomes lined by adherent iris

| 2 | Ciliary (intercalary is nearby) — ciliary staphyloma | Over the ciliary body (\~2–3 mm behind limbus) | Ciliary body | Scleritis (esp. necrotising), chronic/absolute glaucoma, trauma over the ciliary zone, ciliary body inflammation → weakened sclera bulges

| 3 | Intercalary staphyloma | At the limbus — over the root of iris / anterior ciliary region | Root of iris + anterior ciliary body | Peripheral corneal ulcer / marginal keratitis, anterior scleritis, trauma, or raised IOP (secondary glaucoma) at the limbal zone

| 4 | Equatorial staphyloma | At the equator of the globe | Choroid | Scleritis (especially at the exits of vortex veins where sclera is thin), chronically raised IOP, degenerative myopia — bulge at the equatorial thin zone

| 5 | Posterior staphyloma | Posterior pole, around/near optic disc & macula | Choroid | Pathological (degenerative/high) myopia — the classic cause; progressive axial elongation stretches and thins the posterior sclera. Also posterior scleritis

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During administration of an anesthetic block for ophthalmic surgery, which of the following extraocular muscles is least likely to be affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Superior oblique (SO)

Retrobulbar and peribulbar anaesthesia work by depositing local anaesthetic into the intraconal space — the cone bounded by the four recti and their intermuscular septa, with its apex at the annulus of Zinn. Akinesia therefore follows a simple rule:

A muscle is blocked if its nerve enters the orbit through the annulus of Zinn.

The muscle's own position is largely irrelevant. What matters is whether its motor nerve is bathed in the drug.

Applying the rule

| Nerve | Passes through annulus of Zinn? | Muscles supplied | Effect of block

| ----- | ------------------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------

| CN III (superior division) | Inside | SR, LPS | Akinetic + ptosis

| CN III (inferior division) | Inside | MR, IR, IO, sphincter pupillae | Akinetic + mydriasis

| CN VI | Inside (lies deepest in cone, on LR's ocular surface) | LR | Akinetic — earliest and most reliable

| CN IV | OUTSIDE — enters via the widest, most superolateral part of the SOF, then runs medially along the orbital roof, extraconally, to reach SO from above | SO | Spared longest ✔

CN IV is also the most slender cranial nerve and the only one that reaches its muscle without ever entering the cone. The anaesthetic simply never meets it in adequate concentration.

The bedside proof

This isn't theoretical — it produces a specific, observable sign:

In an eye with an otherwise complete retrobulbar block, ask the patient to look down-and-in, or watch the conjunctival vessels: intorsion persists while all other movement is abolished.

That residual intorsion is the superior oblique announcing that CN IV was missed. It is the single most testable correlate of this question.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During an ophthalmic physiology discussion, a resident is asked about the biochemical composition of the vitreous humour. Which of the following substances is present in higher concentration in the vitreous humour compared to blood?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ascorbate

Ascorbate (Vitamin C) is actively transported into the vitreous and aqueous via the ciliary epithelium, reaching concentrations several-fold higher than plasma. It functions as a key antioxidant, scavenging free radicals generated by light exposure and protecting the retina and lens from oxidative damage (this is also why ascorbate depletion is linked to cataractogenesis).

Why the distractors are wrong?

• A. Sodium: Vitreous is essentially an extracellular gel; Na⁺ concentration closely parallels plasma, since it equilibrates freely with surrounding fluids.
• B. Potassium: Roughly similar to or only marginally different from plasma; not a distinguishing feature.
• C. Glucose: Present at a lower concentration than blood (about two-thirds of plasma levels), since it's consumed by the lens and retina and diffusion from blood is limited by the blood-retinal/blood-aqueous barriers.

High-yield one-liner for recall:

• "Vitreous is Ascorbate-rich, Glucose-poor, and Na⁺/K⁺ ≈ plasma."

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During fundus examination of a 58-year-old patient with long-standing systemic hypertension, the ophthalmologist notes that at the sites where retinal arterioles cross retinal veins, the venous segment appears narrowed on either side of the crossing. This fundus finding is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gunn sign

• Gunn sign refers to venous narrowing on either side of an arteriovenous crossing, caused by arteriolar sclerosis compressing the vein in long-standing hypertension
• Salus sign is deflection of the vein at the AV crossing.
• Bonnet sign describes venous banking distal to the crossing.
• Elschnig sign refers to choroidal infarcts seen in malignant hypertension, not AV crossing changes.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During routine ocular examination, a patient is found to have anisocoria. Slit-lamp evaluation shows a well-formed iris with normal architecture and a round pupil. On pharmacological testing, the larger pupil fails to constrict with instillation of dilute pilocarpine, and also shows no response to 1% pilocarpine. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the pupillary abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Atropine use

• The larger pupil failing to constrict with both dilute and 1% pilocarpine indicates pharmacologic mydriasis.
• Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors of the iris sphincter, making the pupil unresponsive to cholinergic agents.
• In Adie pupil, constriction occurs with dilute pilocarpine due to denervation hypersensitivity.
• Oculomotor nerve palsy and sphincter trauma usually show some response to strong pilocarpine, unlike atropine-induced blockade.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During treatment planning for ocular radiotherapy, clinicians must account for the differing radiosensitivity of various retinal cell layers. Which retinal cell type is the most radioresistant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Retinal pigment epithelium

Radiosensitivity generally correlates with a cell's mitotic activity and degree of differentiation — rapidly dividing, poorly differentiated cells are more radiosensitive, while quiescent, terminally differentiated cells resist radiation damage better.

Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) fits the radioresistant profile because it is:

• Highly differentiated — a specialized, mature cell type
• Post-mitotic / low turnover — minimal ongoing cell division means fewer cells caught in radiosensitive phases of the cell cycle

This same principle explains why the RPE tends to survive radiation doses that damage the neurosensory retina (photoreceptors, bipolar cells, ganglion cells) — a fact relevant to complications like radiation retinopathy, where the vascular endothelium and neural retina are affected more than the RPE.

Underlying concept (Law of Bergonié and Tribondeau): Cells that are rapidly dividing and undifferentiated are the most radiosensitive; cells that are non-dividing and well-differentiated are the most radioresistant.

High-yield pearl:

• This same logic applies broadly across radiobiology — e.g., germ cells and bone marrow are highly radiosensitive, while neurons and muscle cells are radioresistant, due to their differentiation and mitotic status.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During your first ophthalmology OPD posting, you notice that the instrument demonstrated in the accompanying video is being used repeatedly for examination of patients. Under supervision, you use the same instrument to examine a patient and obtain a magnified, stereoscopic view of the ocular structures. Which of the following structures can be best evaluated using this instrument without any additional accessory lens?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterior chamber and cornea

The instrument demonstrated is a slit-lamp biomicroscope. It provides a magnified, stereoscopic examination of the anterior segment, including the eyelids, conjunctiva, cornea, anterior chamber, iris, and lens.

The fundus (optic disc, macula and retina) requires an additional condensing/fundus lens, such as a +78 D or +90 D lens, for slit-lamp fundus examination.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Following failure of balloon catheter dilatation in congenital dacryocystitis, the next step is usually:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Silicone tube intubation

Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (congenital dacryocystitis) is usually due to failure of canalization at the valve of Hasner, leading to epiphora and recurrent discharge in infants.

Stepwise management:

1. Conservative treatment:

• Crigler lacrimal sac massage
• Topical antibiotics if infected

2. Persistent obstruction:

• Probing of nasolacrimal duct

3. Failure of probing/balloon catheter dilatation:

• Silicone tube intubation (next preferred step)

4. Refractory cases:

• Dacryocystorhinostomy (rare in children)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Given below are statements regarding panophthalmitis. All are true except:
options: Untreated cases can progress to cavernous sinus thrombosis
It involves all three coats of the eyeball.
Enucleation is the treatment of choice.
Presents with painful limitation of movements.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enucleation is the treatment of choice.

Panophthalmitis is a severe, suppurative inflammation involving all layers of the eyeball (sclera, choroid, retina) along with intraocular contents and surrounding orbital tissues. It usually results from severe ocular infection following trauma, surgery, corneal ulcer, or endogenous spread.

Clinical features include:

• Severe ocular pain
• Marked redness and swelling
• Proptosis
• Painful restriction of extraocular movements
• Loss of vision

Complications:

• Orbital cellulitis
• Cavernous sinus thrombosis
• Intracranial spread of infection

Management:

• Intensive systemic and intravitreal antibiotics
• Evisceration is generally preferred in severe uncontrolled infection
• Enucleation is usually avoided initially because it may increase the risk of spread through the optic nerve sheath.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the correct pair:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Foster Fuch spots - Myopia

• Foster–Fuchs spots are areas of chorioretinal atrophy or hemorrhage seen in pathologic (high) myopia, making this pair correct.
• Vogt triad is seen in angle closure glaucoma.
• Vogt striae occur in keratoconus.
• Shield ulcer is classically associated with vernal keratoconjunctivitis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the correct statements: 1. Direct invasion is the primary method of spread for retinoblastoma 2. The appearance of punched-out lesions in the retina is crucial for diagnosing toxoplasmosis. 3. The optimal sequence of dyes for ocular surface examination is as follows: Rose Bengal --> Lisssamine green --> Fluorescein 4. Interstitial Nucleus of Cajal is the center for vertical gaze.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 4

• Retinoblastoma most commonly spreads by direct invasion along the optic nerve and adjacent tissues.
• Toxoplasmosis shows characteristic punched-out chorioretinal lesions (true).
• The dye sequence is incorrect—fluorescein should be instilled first, not last (false).
• The interstitial nucleus of Cajal is a key center for vertical gaze holding (true).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the correct statements: 1. Microaneurysms appear as hyperfluorescent branching pattern on FFA 2. Hard exudates are found in outer plexiform layer 3. Normal A:V ratio is 3:2 at the fundus 4. IOC for best disease is EOG
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2, 4

• Hard exudates are lipid deposits located in the outer plexiform layer (true).
• EOG is the investigation of choice for Best disease (true).
• Microaneurysms show punctate hyperfluorescence.
• The normal artery:vein ratio is 2:3.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the device:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ex-Press implant

• The Ex-Press implant is a small stainless-steel microshunt placed under a scleral flap to drain aqueous humor from the anterior chamber, functioning like a modified trabeculectomy without a plate or valve.
•

Key advantage: eliminates punch sclerostomy + peripheral iridectomy → less hyphema, less hypotony, more predictable flow (fixed 50 µm lumen), faster AC re-formation.

| Option | Key features | Why it's wrong here

| ------ | ------------ | -------------------

| A. Ex-PRESS ✓ | 400-series stainless steel, \~2.6–3 mm, 50 µm lumen, spur + back plate, non-valved, plateless | Matches figure exactly

| B. Ahmed | Valved (Venturi/silicone elastomer membrane), polypropylene/silicone plate \~184 mm², tube to AC | Figure shows no tube–plate assembly or valve chamber

| C. Molteno | Non-valved, first GDD (1969), plate 133 mm² (single) / 265 mm² (double) | No end plate in figure

| D. Baerveldt | Non-valved, largest plate (250/350/425 mm²), barium-impregnated silicone, wings tucked under recti | No plate; Baerveldt requires a long tube

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the visual field defect:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Blind spot enlargement

• Blind spot enlargement refers to an increase in the physiological scotoma corresponding to the optic disc.
• It commonly occurs due to papilledema, where raised intracranial pressure causes swelling of the optic nerve head.
• Other causes include optic neuritis, peripapillary inflammation, and high myopia.
• Visual acuity is usually preserved initially, but perimetry shows enlargement of the blind spot.
• It is an important early visual field sign in intracranial space-occupying lesions.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In Hirschberg test, each 1 mm of corneal reflex displacement corresponds to approximately:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 15 prism diopters

• In the Hirschberg test, the position of the corneal light reflex is used to estimate ocular deviation. Each 1 mm displacement of the corneal reflex from the center of the pupil corresponds to approximately 15 prism diopters of deviation.
• This makes Hirschberg a quick screening test, giving only a rough estimate compared to prism bar cover testing.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In Keratoconus all are seen except:
options: Distortion of corneal reflex at center
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypermetropic refractive error found

Keratoconus is a corneal ectasia causing progressive myopia and irregular astigmatism, not hypermetropia.

• Munson’s sign is a classic bulging of the lower lid on downgaze.
• Central or paracentral corneal thinning is a hallmark feature.
• Distortion of the corneal reflex occurs due to irregular corneal curvature.

Thus, hypermetropic refractive error is not seen in keratoconus.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In which of the following situations is retrobulbar block considered safe?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Enucleation

• Retrobulbar block is safe in enucleation, as the globe is being removed and risk of perforation is irrelevant.
• Penetrating eye trauma is a contraindication due to risk of globe rupture.
• High myopia increases the risk of scleral perforation from elongated globe.
• Coagulopathy raises the risk of retrobulbar hemorrhage.
• Hence, enucleation is the situation where retrobulbar anesthesia is considered safe.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Local anesthesia used in cataract surgery is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lignocaine 2%

• Lignocaine 2% is the most commonly used local anesthetic in cataract surgery, given via peribulbar, retrobulbar, or sub-Tenon’s block
• Proparacaine is a topical anesthetic used for diagnostic procedures, not surgery.
• Prilocaine is rarely used in ophthalmic blocks.
• Ropivacaine can be used in regional anesthesia but not at 0.05% and is uncommon for routine cataract surgery.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Match the corneal examination technique with what it measures/detects:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. a–2, b–1, c–3, d–4

| Technique | Measures/detects | Additional details

| --------- | ---------------- | ------------------

| Pachymetry | Corneal thickness (normal \~540 microns/0.5–0.6 mm) | IOP is directly proportional to CT; a post-LASIK thinned cornea gives a falsely low IOP reading

| Keratometry | Corneal curvature | Used in astigmatism (vertical ≠ horizontal curvature), keratoconus, and IOL power calculation; uses keratometric mires

| Fluorescein dye | Areas of broken epithelium (ulcer base); orange dye, viewed under cobalt blue filter → green fluorescence; dendritic pattern in HSV keratitis | Also used in: Goldmann applanation tonometry, Seidel's test (locating perforation site), tear film breakup test (>3 sec normal), fundus fluorescein angiography

| Topography | Detailed map of corneal surface contour | Uses a Placido disc — projects concentric rings onto the cornea; irregular ring spacing/distortion detects subtle curvature changes (e.g., early keratoconus) not picked up by keratometry alone

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Match the corneal layer with its characteristic feature:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. a–2, b–1, c–3, d–4

| Layer | Key feature

| ----- | -----------

| 1. Epithelium | Non-keratinized stratified squamous; superficial cells have microvilli (adhere to the mucin layer of the tear film), basal columnar cells are mitotically active (regeneration)

| 2. Bowman's layer | False basement membrane (PAS-negative), acellular; no regeneration — heals only by scarring → corneal opacity → loss of vision

| 3. Stroma | Collagen (m/c Type I) + GAGs (m/c keratan sulphate — responsible for corneal transparency)

| 4. Dua's layer | Strongest layer of the cornea

| 5. Descemet's membrane | Secreted by the underlying endothelium; regenerates; Schwalbe's line = its peripheral termination

| 6. Endothelium | Metabolically most active layer; maintains corneal transparency (via pump function regulating stromal hydration)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Match the following corneal dystrophies with the primary layer involved: 1. Meesmann dystrophy 2. Reis-Bücklers dystrophy 3. Granular dystrophy 4. Fuchs dystrophy a. Bowman membrane b. Endothelium/Descemet membrane c. Corneal epithelium d. Corneal stroma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b

• 1. Meesmann dystrophy → c. Epithelium
• 2. Reis-Bücklers dystrophy → a. Bowman membrane
• 3. Granular dystrophy → d. Stroma
• 4. Fuchs dystrophy → b. Endothelium/Descemet membrane

| Layer | Dystrophy | Key Feature

| ----- | --------- | -----------

| Epithelium | Meesmann dystrophy | Intraepithelial microcysts, autosomal dominant, onset in early childhood, usually asymptomatic or mild irritation

| Bowman membrane | Reis-Bücklers dystrophy | Recurrent corneal erosions, superficial reticular/honeycomb scarring, reduced vision over time

| Stroma | Granular dystrophy | Discrete, "breadcrumb"-like hyaline deposits (TGFBI gene), clear intervening stroma, spares periphery early

| Endothelium/Descemet | Fuchs endothelial dystrophy | Corneal guttata, morning blurring from endothelial pump failure (as in your earlier question)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: MK medium used for corneal preservation is effective for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 48 to 72 hours

• McCarey–Kaufman (MK) medium is a short-term corneal preservation medium, effective for 48–72 hours at 4°C. It is commonly used in developing settings due to low cost and simplicity.
• 7–14 days and 30 days correspond to intermediate/long-term media like Optisol-GS or organ culture.
• 1 year storage is not possible for donor corneas.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: On slit-lamp examination, a patient with acute anterior uveitis shows a visible beam of light in the anterior chamber due to light scattering by protein. This optical phenomenon is best explained by which physical principle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tyndall effect

| Option | Status | Reasoning

| ------ | ------ | ---------

| A) Tyndall effect | Correct | Scattering of light by colloidal-sized protein particles suspended in the aqueous — the basis of "flare"

| B) Purkinje shift | Distractor | Relates to shift in peak spectral sensitivity of the eye from photopic to scotopic vision, unrelated

| C) Doppler effect | Distractor | Relates to frequency shift with relative motion; used in retinal/vascular flow studies, not flare

| D) Stokes' law | Distractor | Relates to particle settling velocity in a fluid (physics), not light scattering

Pearl:

• Flare = protein leak (marked in non-granulomatous uveitis).
• Cells = active inflammatory cells (denotes disease activity, guides steroid tapering).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Regarding development of ocular structures, consider the following statements: 1. The eye begins to develop by the third week of intrauterine life. 2. The macula develops fully by around 4 years of postnatal life. 3. The cornea attains adult diameter by approximately 2 years of age. 4. The lens continues to grow throughout life. Which of the above statements are true?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3 and 4

• The eye starts developing in the 3rd week of intrauterine life with formation of the optic pit.
