• The cornea reaches near-adult diameter by about 2 years, earlier than many other ocular structures.
• The lens continues to grow throughout life due to continuous addition of lens fibers.
• The macula is not fully developed at birth. Foveal differentiation — centrifugal displacement of the inner retinal layers away from the foveola and centripetal migration/elongation of cones — completes by roughly 4 months of postnatal life. This is why:

• Fixation and following become steady by \~3 months
• Visual acuity is only \~6/200 at birth, reaching near-adult levels only after foveal maturation

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Regarding the embryological development of the eye, which of the following statements is correct?
options: Lens develops from neural crest cells
Corneal endothelium develops from neural crest cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Corneal endothelium develops from neural crest cells

• A. Retina develops from surface ectoderm: Incorrect. Retina develops from neuroectoderm, not surface ectoderm
• B. Lens develops from neural crest cells: Incorrect. Lens develops from surface ectoderm, not neural crest
• C. Corneal endothelium develops from neural crest cells: Correct. Corneal endothelium (and stroma) arise from neural crest cells
• D. Sclera develops from neuroectoderm: Incorrect. Sclera develops from mesoderm and neural crest, not neuroectoderm

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Regarding the hyaloid vascular system and its persistence, consider the following statements: 1. The hyaloid artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery that supplies the developing crystalline lens during fetal life. 2. Physiological regression of the hyaloid artery begins around the third trimester and is usually complete by birth. 3. Persistence of the hyaloid artery may present clinically as persistent fetal vasculature (PFV). 4. Mittendorf dot represents a remnant of the posterior tunica vasculosa lentis on the posterior lens capsule. 5. Bergmeister papilla is a glial remnant seen on the optic disc due to incomplete regression of the hyaloid artery. 6. Persistent fetal vasculature is commonly associated with bilateral disease and normal axial length. Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, 4 and 5

| # | Statement | Verdict | Reasoning

| --- | --------- | ------- | ---------

| 1 | Hyaloid artery = branch of ophthalmic artery, supplies developing lens | TRUE | It is the terminal continuation of the primitive dorsal ophthalmic artery, entering via the embryonic (optic/choroidal) fissure at \~4–5 weeks. It supplies the lens via the posterior tunica vasculosa lentis, which anastomoses anteriorly with the annular vessel to complete the capsulopupillary portion + pupillary membrane.

| 2 | Regression begins in the third trimester, complete by birth | FALSE | Regression begins at \~4 months (start of 2nd half of gestation) and is essentially complete by \~8–8½ months — i.e. it starts in the second trimester and finishes before term, not "by birth." The second half of the claim is nearly right; the onset is wrong.

| 3 | Persistence → PFV | TRUE | PFV (old term: PHPV, Reese 1955; renamed by Goldberg, 1997).

| 4 | Mittendorf dot = remnant of posterior tunica vasculosa lentis on posterior lens capsule | TRUE | Small white opacity at the anterior attachment of the hyaloid artery, characteristically inferonasal to the posterior pole of the lens. Visually insignificant, \~2% of population.

| 5 | Bergmeister papilla = glial remnant on disc | TRUE | Failure of regression of the posterior/glial sheath of the hyaloid artery → small tuft of fibroglial tissue on the disc, usually nasal. Benign.

| 6 | PFV = bilateral, normal axial length | FALSE | PFV is classically UNILATERAL (\~90%) and the eye is MICROPHTHALMIC (short axial length). Bilateral PFV should make you think systemic syndrome (Norrie disease, Warburg, trisomy 13).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Regarding the parvocellular and magnocellular visual pathways, consider the following statements: 1. The parvocellular pathway is primarily involved in color vision and fine spatial resolution. 2. The magnocellular pathway is more sensitive to motion and temporal changes in visual stimuli. 3. Parvocellular fibers predominantly terminate in layers 3–6 of the lateral geniculate nucleus. 4. Magnocellular fibers project mainly to layers 1 and 2 of the lateral geniculate nucleus. 5. Lesions affecting the magnocellular pathway preferentially impair red–green color discrimination. 6. Parvocellular ganglion cells have smaller receptive fields and slower conduction velocity compared to magnocellular cells. Which of the above statements are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6

There are two major parallel visual pathways from retina → LGN → visual cortex:

• Parvocellular (P pathway) → detail & color
• Magnocellular (M pathway) → motion & luminance contrast

Both terminate in the Lateral geniculate nucleus.

| Feature | Parvocellular (P pathway) | Magnocellular (M pathway)

| ------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------

| Cell size | Small | Large

| Receptive field | Small | Large

| Conduction speed | Slower | Faster

| Function | Color & detail | Motion

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Salt-and-pepper retinopathy may be encountered in all of the following conditions except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ocular tuberculosis

Salt-and-pepper fundus (pseudo-retinitis pigmentosa) occurs in:

• Congenital rubella
• Congenital syphilis
• Refsum disease
• Leber congenital amaurosis
• Carriers of albinism

Tuberculosis is not a recognized cause.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Steroids are used in all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute dacryocystitis

• Steroids are contraindicated in acute dacryocystitis because it is an active bacterial infection, and steroids can worsen infection and delay healing.
• Vernal conjunctivitis benefits from topical steroids to control severe allergic inflammation.
• Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction where steroids reduce inflammation.
• Acute iridocyclitis requires steroids to suppress intraocular inflammation and prevent synechiae.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The distance of the fovea from the temporal margin of the optic disc is approximately:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 disc diameters

The fovea lies temporal to the optic disc and is responsible for the sharpest central vision due to its high cone density.

Normal anatomical relationship:

• The fovea is located approximately 2 disc diameters temporal to the optic disc
• It lies slightly below the horizontal meridian

Important retinal landmarks:

• Optic disc → site of optic nerve exit; no photoreceptors (physiologic blind spot)
• Macula → central retinal area for detailed vision
• Fovea centralis → center of macula with maximal visual acuity

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The following device is used for all of the following indications except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Corneal tattooing

• The device referred to is the stenopaic slit. It is used in the Fincham test to differentiate aphakia from pseudophakia, to determine the axis of astigmatism by narrowing the effective pupil, and for planning optical iridectomy by allowing vision through a small aperture.
• Corneal tattooing is a cosmetic/therapeutic procedure performed with needles or trephines and does not use a stenopaic slit, making it the incorrect option.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The instrument shown in the image is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lister’s perimeter

Lister’s perimeter is a manual instrument used for assessing the visual field by kinetic perimetry.

• A moving target is brought from the peripheral field toward the center
• The point at which the patient first detects the target is plotted
• Used to map boundaries of the visual field

Clinical uses:

• Detection of visual field defects
• Evaluation of glaucoma
• Neuro-ophthalmic lesion assessment
• Retinal disease evaluation

Comparison with other perimeters:

• Humphrey Field Analyzer → automated static perimetry
• Goldmann perimeter → manual kinetic perimetry using a hemispherical bowl
• Octopus perimeter → automated computerized perimeter
• Lister’s perimeter → older arc perimeter/manual kinetic device

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The painful acute lesion shown in the image is most consistent with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Internal hordeolum

An internal hordeolum is an acute, painful, purulent infection of the meibomian gland, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Clinical features:

• Painful, tender eyelid swelling
• Redness and localized edema
• Lesion points toward the conjunctival surface (inside of eyelid)

Important distinctions:

• Internal hordeolum → meibomian gland infection
• External hordeolum (stye) → infection of gland of Zeis or Moll at eyelash follicle
• Chalazion → chronic painless granulomatous inflammation of meibomian gland
• Dacryocystitis → infection of lacrimal sac near medial canthus

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The physician noticed the following finding in a patient that came to the OPD for an eye exam. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Horner syndrome

• Horner syndrome presents with mild ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis due to sympathetic pathway disruption, producing a characteristic appearance often noticed on routine exam.
• Myasthenia gravis causes variable, fatigable ptosis without pupillary involvement.
• 3rd cranial nerve palsy typically shows ptosis with dilated pupil and ophthalmoplegia.
• LPS over-function causes lid retraction rather than ptosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What can be the reason for following condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitreomacular adhesion

• Vitreomacular adhesion occurs due to incomplete posterior vitreous detachment, where the vitreous remains adherent to the macula without causing traction or retinal distortion.
• Vitreomacular traction causes macular distortion and symptoms, not simple adhesion.
•

| Feature | VMA (B) ✔ | VMT (A) ✘

| ------- | --------- | ---------

| Posterior hyaloid | Attached at fovea | Attached at fovea

| Foveal contour | Normal/preserved | Distorted, elevated, blunted

| Intraretinal changes | Absent | Pseudocysts, schisis, IS/OS disruption

| Subretinal fluid | Absent | May be present

| Symptoms | Usually asymptomatic | Metamorphopsia, ↓VA

| Definition (IVTS) | Perifoveal PVD + persistent foveal attachment, unchanged foveal morphology | Same attachment + distortion of retinal architecture

* Central serous retinopathy results from choroidal hyperpermeability with subretinal fluid.

* Cystoid macular edema is due to breakdown of the blood–retinal barrier causing intraretinal cysts, not vitreous attachment.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most likely explanation for this specific disc appearance?
options: The pathology lies anterior to the lamina cribrosa
The pathology lies posterior to the lamina cribrosa
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The pathology lies posterior to the lamina cribrosa

The fundus photograph shows optic disc pallor with sharply defined disc margins, consistent with primary optic atrophy rather than secondary optic atrophy.

• Primary optic atrophy results from damage posterior to the lamina cribrosa (e.g., optic neuritis, compressive optic neuropathy, traumatic optic neuropathy).
• The optic disc appears:

• Chalky white or pale
• Well-defined disc margins
• Normal retinal vessels or mild attenuation
• No preceding disc edema

Why not the other options?

• A. The atrophy followed papilledema❌: This describes secondary optic atrophy, which shows blurred disc margins due to previous swelling.
• B. The pathology lies anterior to the lamina cribrosa❌: Lesions anterior to the lamina (e.g., ischemic optic neuropathy, papilledema) typically produce disc swelling initially, followed by secondary optic atrophy, not the sharply demarcated pallor seen here.
• D. Concurrent vitreous hemorrhage is present❌: There is no evidence of vitreous hemorrhage. The retinal vessels are clearly visible without obscuration.

High-yield NEET PG Pearl:

| Type of optic atrophy | Disc margins | Cause

| --------------------- | ------------ | -----

| Primary optic atrophy | Sharp | Lesion posterior to lamina cribrosa

| Secondary optic atrophy | Blurred | Follows papilledema or papillitis

| Consecutive optic atrophy | Waxy pale | Retinal disease (e.g., retinitis pigmentosa)

| Glaucomatous optic atrophy | Increased cupping | Glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the primary material used in manufacturing soft contact lenses?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hydroxyethyl methyl acrylate

• Soft contact lenses are made from hydrophilic hydrogel polymers, primarily hydroxyethyl methyl acrylate (HEMA), which allows high water content and flexibility for comfort.
• Cellulose acetate butyrate and polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) are rigid lens materials.
• Silicone alone is not used; silicone hydrogel lenses combine silicone with hydrophilic polymers, not pure silicone.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What would you expect to see on the instillation of 1% hydroxyamphetamine into both the eyes of a patient with right-sided postganglionic Horner syndrome?
options: No change observed in both eyes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Only left eye dilates

Hydroxyamphetamine test is used to localize Horner syndrome.

It helps differentiate:

• Preganglionic (1st or 2nd order) lesion
• Postganglionic (3rd order) lesion

Hydroxyamphetamine:

• Causes release of norepinephrine (NA) from intact postganglionic sympathetic nerve terminals.
• Does not act directly on the iris dilator.
• Requires functioning postganglionic neurons.

| Eye | Postganglionic status | Response to hydroxyamphetamine

| --- | --------------------- | ------------------------------

| Right | Damaged | No dilation

| Left | Normal | Dilates

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following can occur in a patient with prolactinoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superior quadrantanopia

• A prolactinoma can compress the inferior fibers of the optic chiasm, which carry information from the superior temporal visual fields, leading to superior quadrantanopia.
• Inferior quadrantanopia occurs with superior chiasmal or temporal lobe lesions.
• Priapism is unrelated and seen with spinal or autonomic disorders.
• Failure of lactation is incorrect—prolactinoma causes galactorrhea, not failure of lactation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following correctly lists the layers of the sclera from outermost to innermost?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Episclera > Sclera proper > Lamina fusca

• The sclera is composed of three distinct layers arranged from outside to inside.
• The episclera is the outermost, loose, vascular connective tissue layer that allows movement of the globe and supplies blood.
• The sclera proper forms the thick, dense, collagenous middle layer providing rigidity and protection to the eyeball.
• The lamina fusca is the thin, pigmented innermost layer, lying adjacent to the choroid.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following has familial inheritance? 1. Retinoblastoma 2. Retinitis pigmentosa 3. Муоріа 4. Primary open angle glaucoma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4

Retinoblastoma

• Caused by mutation in RB1
• Inherited form: autosomal dominant with high penetrance
• Bilateral cases usually familial

Retinitis pigmentosa

• Modes of inheritance:
• Autosomal dominant/ Autosomal recessive/ X-linked

Myopia

• Multifactorial inheritance
• Strong familial clustering
• High myopia has identifiable genetic loci

Primary open-angle glaucoma

• Polygenic inheritance
• Associated genes: MYOC, OPTN etc.
• Positive family history is a major risk factor

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is false?
options: External hordeolum is an acute inflammation of the Zeis gland
Meibomian gland is a modified apocrine gland
Internal hordeolum is an acute suppurative inflammation of meibomian gland
Chalazion is a chronic granulomatous inflammation of the meibornian gland
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Meibomian gland is a modified apocrine gland

• The Meibomian gland is a modified sebaceous gland, not apocrine.
• External hordeolum is an acute suppurative infection of Zeis (or Moll) glands (true).
• Internal hordeolum is an acute suppurative inflammation of the Meibomian gland (true).
• Chalazion is a chronic granulomatous inflammation of the Meibomian gland due to lipid retention (true).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a feature of optic neuritis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Improved dark adaptation

Optic neuritis is an inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the optic nerve, commonly associated with multiple sclerosis.

Typical features:

• Acute/subacute monocular visual loss
• Pain with eye movement
• Reduced color vision (especially red desaturation)
• Central scotoma
• Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)
• Phosphenes (flashes of light with eye movement)

Dark adaptation is typically impaired, not improved.

Patients with optic neuritis may have decreased visual function in dim light due to optic nerve dysfunction. “Improved dark adaptation” is not a feature

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct order of development?
options: Optic pit → optic vesicle → optic cup
Optic vesicle → optic pit → optic cup
Optic pit → optic cup → optic vesicle
Optic cup → optic pit → optic vesicle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Optic pit → optic vesicle → optic cup

Eye development begins with formation of the optic pit in the forebrain neuroectoderm, which then evaginates to form the optic vesicle. Subsequent invagination of the optic vesicle results in the double-walled optic cup, giving rise to the retina and optic nerve structures.

| Step | Structure | What happens | Timing

| ---- | --------- | ------------ | ------

| 1 | Optic pit / optic sulcus (optic groove) | Paired grooves appear in the neuroectoderm of the forebrain (diencephalon) neural folds | \~Day 22

| 2 | Optic vesicle | As the neural tube closes, the optic pits evaginate (out-pouch) laterally toward the surface ectoderm | \~Day 24–25

| 3 | Optic cup | The optic vesicle invaginates (in-folds) → double-walled optic cup | \~Day 27–32

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following options is incorrect about Eale's disease?
options: Causes gradual painful loss of vision
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Causes gradual painful loss of vision

Eales disease is an idiopathic obliterative retinal vasculopathy seen commonly in young adults and is strongly associated with hypersensitivity to tuberculoprotein.

• Peripheral retinal vasculitis
• Retinal ischemia with neovascularization
• Recurrent vitreous hemorrhages causing sudden painless visual loss
• More common in young males

Clinical presentation:

• Floaters
• Blurred vision
• Recurrent painless diminution of vision due to vitreous hemorrhage

Treatment:

• Corticosteroids for active vasculitis
• Laser photocoagulation for retinal ischemia/neovascularization
• Anti-tubercular therapy if tuberculosis is associated
• Vitrectomy for nonresolving vitreous hemorrhage

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statement is incorrect about Retinitis Pigmentosa?
options: ERG shows decreased amplitude of a and b wave
Late presentation is loss of peripheral vision
Night blindness is a late feature
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Night blindness is a late feature

• Retinitis pigmentosa is a rod–cone dystrophy, so rod involvement predominates early, causing early night blindness (nyctalopia), not late.
• ERG characteristically shows reduced a- and b-wave amplitudes due to photoreceptor dysfunction.
• Patients initially develop peripheral visual field loss (tunnel vision), with central vision affected later as cones degenerate. Hence, calling night blindness a late feature is incorrect.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements best describes the Fincham’s test result in a patient with lenticular halo?
options: Halos remain intact but brightness is reduced
Halos are broken and revolve as the slit moves
No halos are visible through the stenopaic slit
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Halos are broken and revolve as the slit moves

In lenticular halo (e.g., early cataract), Fincham’s test with a stenopaic slit breaks the halo into segments that move with the slit, confirming a lenticular origin.

A fits corneal edema where halos persist.

B is incorrect—lenticular halos don’t disappear.

D suggests absence of halos, not diagnostic.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the correct treatment of this condition is correct?
options: Topical steroids remain the mainstay of treatment once the epithelium re-epithelializes, similar to herpetic stromal keratitis
Topical PHMB (polyhexamethylene biguanide) 0.02% is the drug of choice, with chlorhexidine 0.02% and propamidine 0.1% also used clinically
A ring abscess on examination indicates a poor prognosis and is an indication for immediate penetrating keratoplasty rather than medical therapy
Diagnosis is best made using Gram staining alone, as culture techniques have no role in confirming this condition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Topical PHMB (polyhexamethylene biguanide) 0.02% is the drug of choice, with chlorhexidine 0.02% and propamidine 0.1% also used clinically

| Feature | Acanthamoeba keratitis

| ------- | ----------------------

| Etiology | Contact lens use + exposure to dirty water (tap water/swimming pool)

| Symptoms | Severe pain, often disproportionate to clinical signs

| Signs | Pseudodendrites, radial keratoneuritis, ring abscess (pathognomonic)

| Investigations | PCR; culture on non-nutrient agar enriched with E. coli (pseudopods positive); in-vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM); staining — Gram stain and calcofluor white (shows double-walled acanthamoeba cyst)

| Treatment (DOC) | PHMB 0.02%

| Other clinically used agents | Chlorhexidine 0.02%, Propamidine 0.1%

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the innervation of extraocular muscles is false?
options: Medial rectus muscle is innervated by the ipsilateral occulomotor nerve
Superior rectus muscle is supplied by the contralateral oculomotor nuclear complex
Levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by a single midline (central caudal) nucleus
Inferior oblique muscle is supplied by the contralateral oculomotor nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inferior oblique muscle is supplied by the contralateral oculomotor nerve

• Medial rectus receives ipsilateral oculomotor supply (true).
• Superior rectus is innervated by the contralateral oculomotor nuclear complex (true).
• Levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by the single midline central caudal nucleus (true).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the proteins and metabolism of the crystalline lens is false?
options: α-crystallins are the largest molecular weight crystallins
β-crystallins are the most abundant crystallins in the lens
Maximum nutrition of the lens occurs by aerobic glycolysis
Albuminoid proteins are increased in cataract
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Maximum nutrition of the lens occurs by aerobic glycolysis

The crystalline lens is avascular and derives most of its energy from anaerobic glycolysis, not aerobic metabolism.

• α-crystallins have the largest molecular weight and  act as chaperone proteins
• β-crystallins are the most abundant lens proteins
• Albuminoid (insoluble) proteins increase in cataract due to protein denaturation

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding this condition is incorrect about Eales disease?
options: Causes gradual painful loss of vision
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Causes gradual painful loss of vision

• Eales disease is an idiopathic obliterative retinal periphlebitis, most commonly affecting young healthy males (20–40 years). It is strongly associated with hypersensitivity to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens.
• The disease classically presents with recurrent, painless episodes of sudden visual loss due to vitreous hemorrhage.

Why Option A is incorrect?

• Vision loss in Eales disease is typically painless, not painful.
• The decrease in vision is usually sudden, resulting from recurrent vitreous hemorrhages due to retinal neovascularization.

Why the other options are correct?

B. Tubercular etiology is implicated ✔️

• Although the exact cause is unknown, hypersensitivity to tuberculoprotein is strongly implicated.
• Patients are often evaluated for latent or active tuberculosis.

C. Recurrent vitreous hemorrhages occur ✔️

• Retinal ischemia leads to neovascularization.
• Fragile new vessels bleed repeatedly, causing recurrent vitreous hemorrhage.

D. Treatment includes corticosteroids ✔️

• Systemic or periocular corticosteroids are used during the active inflammatory (periphlebitis) stage.
• Additional treatment includes:

• Laser photocoagulation for ischemic retina/neovascularization
• Anti-VEGF in selected cases
• Pars plana vitrectomy for non-resolving vitreous hemorrhage

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding this is correct?
options: Topical steroids are an essential part of first-line therapy for a dendritic corneal ulcer, to reduce viral-induced inflammation
Necrotising stromal keratitis and disciform keratitis, both occurring with an intact corneal epithelium, are treated with topical acyclovir combined with topical steroids
A neurotrophic (metaherpetic) ulcer results from CN VII palsy causing lagophthalmos and exposure of the cornea
Lagophthalmos is exclusively a consequence of herpetic corneal disease and is not seen in any other condition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Necrotising stromal keratitis and disciform keratitis, both occurring with an intact corneal epithelium, are treated with topical acyclovir combined with topical steroids

| Stage/entity | Epithelium | Treatment

| ------------ | ---------- | ---------

| Superficial punctate keratitis → Dendritic ulcer → Geographic ulcer (if untreated) | Broken/eroded | Acyclovir 3% / Ganciclovir eye ointment; Steroids contraindicated

| Necrotising stromal keratitis | Intact | 3% Acyclovir eye ointment + Topical steroids

| Disciform keratitis / endotheliitis | Intact | 3% Acyclovir eye ointment + Topical steroids

| Metaherpetic keratitis / neurotrophic ulcer | — | Due to CN V atrophy/palsy → corneal anesthesia

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of these is a true statement? 1. Ferry’s Line: corneal epithelial iron line at the edge of filtering blebs 2. Stockers Line: Corneal epithelial iron line at the edge of pterygium 3. Hudson-Stahli line: visible all around the base of cone in Keratoconus 4. Fleischer’s ring: Horizontal corneal epithelial iron line at the inferior one third of cornea due to aging 5. Coat’s white ring: A form of iron deposit at the level of Bowman’s layer of cornea
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 5

• Stocker’s line is an iron line at the head of a pterygium (true).
• Hudson–Stähli line is an age-related horizontal iron line, not seen around the cone in keratoconus (false).
• Fleischer’s ring is seen in keratoconus, not due to aging (false).
• Coats’ white ring is an iron-containing scar at Bowman’s layer after foreign body injury (true).
• Ferry’s line: Corneal epithelial iron line at the edge of filtering blebs (true)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of these statements is true regarding perimetry?
options: Kinetic perimetry is used in quantification and tracking of visual changes in established glaucoma
In Static perimetry, stimulus intensity is held constant and moved centrally with detection
Visual field defect to be classified as glaucoma, it should have the corresponding optic nerve head abnormalities
Early signs include generalised constriction of isopters and barring of blind spot
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Early signs include generalised constriction of isopters and barring of blind spot

•

Initial indications of glaucoma in perimetry involve a widespread narrowing of isopters and the appearance of a blockage within the blind spot.

•

Perimetry is a diagnostic test used to assess a person's visual field.

•

Static Perimetry: Traditional method involving fixed stimulus points presented on a static grid. Goldmann perimetry and Humphrey Visual Field Analyzer are common devices for static perimetry.

•

Kinetic Perimetry: Moving stimuli are used to determine the boundaries of the visual field. Useful for mapping the extent of peripheral vision.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which tonometer is specifically useful for post-LASIK IOP measurement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pascals tonometer (Dynamic Contour Tonometer)

After LASIK surgery, corneal thickness and biomechanics are altered, causing conventional applanation tonometry to underestimate intraocular pressure (IOP). The Pascal Dynamic Contour Tonometer (DCT) is particularly useful post-LASIK because:

• It is less affected by corneal thickness and corneal rigidity
• Provides more accurate IOP measurements after refractive surgery

Why Goldmann tonometry is less reliable post-LASIK:

• Goldmann applanation tonometry assumes normal corneal thickness and biomechanics
• LASIK thins and reshapes the cornea, leading to falsely low readings

High-yield ophthalmology pearls:

• Goldmann applanation tonometry = gold standard in normal corneas
• Pascal DCT = preferred in post-LASIK eyes
• Thin cornea → falsely low IOP readings
• Thick cornea → falsely high IOP readings

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: While administering intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy, the ophthalmologist inserts the needle through a relatively avascular portion of the ciliary body located posterior to the limbus. Which structure is traversed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pars plana

Intravitreal injections are given through the pars plana (3.5–4 mm posterior to the limbus), avoiding injury to the lens anteriorly and retina posteriorly.

• The pars plana is the posterior, flatter part of the ciliary body — it is relatively avascular and lacks major structures like ciliary processes, making it the safest entry point for intravitreal injections and vitrectomy sclerotomies.
• The standard injection site is 3.5 mm posterior to the limbus in pseudophakic/aphakic eyes and 4.0 mm posterior to the limbus in phakic eyes — this distance ensures the needle:

• Avoids the lens (which lies anteriorly, and could be injured if the injection is too anterior)
• Avoids the retina (which could be injured if the injection is too posterior, especially since the retina thins out but the pars plana corresponds roughly to the area overlying the peripheral retina/ora serrata region)

Why the others are wrong?

• A. Pars plicata: The anterior, folded part of the ciliary body containing the ciliary processes (site of aqueous humor production) — highly vascular, so injections here risk hemorrhage and are never used as an entry site.
• C. Ora serrata: The serrated junction between the retina and the pars plana (peripheral limit of the retina) — a landmark, not an entry zone itself; it's more posterior than the standard injection site and marks the retinal periphery.
• D. Ciliary processes: Part of the pars plicata, vascular structures responsible for aqueous production — definitely not the injection site.

Exam tip:

• "Avascular ciliary body zone, 3.5–4 mm posterior to limbus, safe entry for intravitreal injection/vitrectomy" = pars plana, every time.
• Contrast with pars plicata (vascular, aqueous-producing, anterior).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 10-year-old male child presented with the following finding. What’s your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Limbal dermoid

Limbal dermoid is a congenital choristoma (normal tissue in an abnormal location) typically seen at the inferotemporal limbus.

• Present since childhood
• Painless, well-defined, whitish/yellow mass at the limbus
• May contain hair follicles, sebaceous glands
• Can cause astigmatism or amblyopia if large

Pathogenesis:

• Developmental anomaly with ectodermal tissue (skin-like elements) in the cornea/conjunctiva

Why not others:

• Papilloma: Pedunculated, vascular lesion (HPV-related)
• Pyogenic granuloma: Red, vascular, rapidly growing lesion
• Pinguecula: Degenerative yellow lesion in adults, not congenital

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl presents with a painless, slowly enlarging mass situated lateral to the lateral canthus, which has been present for the past 10 years. On examination, the swelling is non-tender and gradually progressive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dermoid cyst

A dermoid cyst is the most common congenital orbital tumor in children, typically presenting as a painless, slow-growing mass near the lateral canthus (superotemporal orbit).

Key clinical features:

• Present since childhood
• Gradually enlarging, non-tender swelling
• Commonly located at zygomaticofrontal suture (lateral eyebrow region)
• Firm, well-defined, mobile mass

Developmental inclusion cyst containing ectodermal elements (hair follicles, sebaceous glands)

Why not others:

• Capillary hemangioma: Appears in infancy, rapidly grows, may regress
• Lacrimal gland tumor: Usually presents later, may cause globe displacement
• Epidermoid cyst: Similar but deeper, less common in this location

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 20-year-old male presents with golden-brown ring over iris on examination. What next is done to diagnose the condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Serum ceruloplasmin

A golden-brown ring at the corneal periphery (Kayser–Fleischer ring) is characteristic of Wilson’s disease due to copper deposition in Descemet’s membrane.

Next best diagnostic step: Serum ceruloplasmin ↓ (initial screening test)

Supporting investigations:

• ↑ 24-hour urinary copper excretion
• ↑ hepatic copper (gold standard confirmation)
• Slit-lamp exam for KF ring

Why not others:

• Serum iron: Hemochromatosis
• Alpha-1 antitrypsin: AAT deficiency (liver/lung disease)
• Alpha-fetoprotein: Hepatocellular carcinoma marker

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-month-old child presents with photophobia and watering. Which of the following cannot be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction

In infants, photophobia + watering (epiphora) suggests corneal irritation or raised intraocular pressure, not just a drainage problem.

• Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (CNLDO) causes:

• Watering and discharge
• NO photophobia
• Cornea remains clear → hence not a cause here

Conditions that DO cause photophobia + watering:

• Congenital glaucoma:

• Triad: Epiphora + Photophobia + Blepharospasm
• Due to corneal edema and raised IOP

• Congenital entropion / distichiasis:

• Misdirected lashes rub cornea → corneal irritation
• Leads to photophobia and tearing

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male with a history of recurrent sinusitis presents with decreased vision, eye protrusion, and fever. A computed tomography (CT) scan was done. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Orbital cellulitis with sinusitis

Orbital cellulitis is a postseptal orbital infection, most commonly due to spread from paranasal sinusitis (especially ethmoid sinus). Key distinguishing features (vs preseptal cellulitis):

• Proptosis
• Painful/restricted eye movements
• Decreased vision
• Fever and systemic toxicity

Imaging (CT scan):

• Orbital soft tissue inflammation behind the orbital septum
• Associated sinus opacification
• Helps detect complications (abscess, intracranial spread)

Why not others:

• A. Preseptal cellulitis with sinusitis: No proptosis, no vision loss, no ophthalmoplegia
• C. Subperiosteal abscess: Localized collection; would show a well-defined lenticular collection on CT
• D. Cellulitis (nonspecific): Does not localize to orbit

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old male presents with drooping of the right upper eyelid and constricted pupil following a neck injury. On examination, there is mild ptosis with preserved ocular movements. Which muscle is primarily responsible for the ptosis in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Muller's muscle

In Horner syndrome, ptosis occurs due to paralysis of Müller’s muscle (superior tarsal muscle), which is supplied by the sympathetic nervous system.

• Müller’s muscle provides minor eyelid elevation (\~1–2 mm)
• Loss of sympathetic supply → mild ptosis

Associated features of Horner syndrome:

• Ptosis (mild)
• Miosis (constricted pupil)
• Anhidrosis (loss of sweating)
• ± Apparent enophthalmos

Why not others:

• Levator palpebrae superioris (LPS):

• Supplied by oculomotor nerve (CN III)
• Causes severe ptosis in 3rd nerve palsy

• Orbicularis oculi:

• Closes eyelids (CN VII), not involved in ptosis

• “Horner muscle”: Not a standard anatomical term

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is brought with complaints of poor vision in one eye. On examination, there is no obvious squint. Visual acuity is 6/6 in the right eye and 6/24 in the left eye. Cycloplegic refraction reveals +1.00 D in the right eye and +5.50 D in the left eye. Fundus examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anisometropic amblyopia

Anisometropia is defined as a difference in refractive error between the two eyes, leading to unequal image clarity.

Difference in myopia, hypermetropia, or astigmatism between eyes.

Clinical significance:

• Can cause anisometropic amblyopia (lazy eye) in children
• Due to unequal image size/clarity (aniseikonia) → brain suppresses one eye
• Important cause of unilateral amblyopia

Types of Amblyopia (Lazy Eye)

A. Isoametropic Amblyopia

Occurs when both eyes have high but equal refractive error.

• Brain receives blurred images from both eyes.
• Usually due to high:

• hypermetropia,
• myopia,
• or astigmatism in both eyes equally.

Example:

Both eyes have +7D hypermetropia → bilateral blurred vision → amblyopia develops in both eyes.

B. Strabismic Amblyopia

Occurs due to squint (strabismus).

• Brain suppresses image from deviated eye to avoid diplopia.
• Suppressed eye becomes amblyopic.

Example:

Child with esotropia suppresses input from one eye → reduced vision in that eye.

C. Anisometropic Amblyopia

Occurs when there is unequal refractive error between the two eyes.

• Brain prefers clearer image from better eye.
• Blurred eye gets suppressed and becomes amblyopic.

Example:

One eye +1D, other eye +6D hypermetropia → poorer eye develops amblyopia.

D. Deprivation Amblyopia

Occurs when visual stimulus is blocked during visual development.

• Most severe form.
• Due to obstruction of visual axis.

Causes:

• Congenital cataract
• Ptosis
• Corneal opacity

Example:

Unilateral congenital cataract prevents image formation → amblyopia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a foreign body (chuna) in his eyes and complains of irritability and lacrimation. What is the first step of management in this patient?
options: Irrigation of eye with normal saline
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Irrigation of eye with normal saline

Chemical injury to the eye (e.g., chuna/lime = alkali burn) is an ocular emergency, and the first and most important step is immediate copious irrigation.

• Alkali substances penetrate rapidly and cause liquefactive necrosis
• Immediate dilution/removal of the chemical limits depth of damage and improves prognosis

Management priority:

• Start irrigation immediately (do not wait for history or examination)
• Use normal saline, Ringer lactate, or even clean water if saline unavailable
• Continue until ocular pH normalizes (\~7–7.4)
• Evert eyelids to remove retained particles

Why not others:

• Antibiotic drops: Given later to prevent infection
• Tarsorrhaphy: For healing in severe cases, not initial step
• Scraping: Not indicated initially and may worsen injury

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with complaints of dryness, foreign body sensation, and burning in both eyes. Which of the following test is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Schirmer test

The image demonstrates the Schirmer test, which measures aqueous tear production and is used to diagnose dry eye disease (keratoconjunctivitis sicca), including Sjögren syndrome.

A standardized filter paper strip is placed in the lower conjunctival fornix at the junction of the middle and lateral third of the lower eyelid. After 5 minutes, the length of the wetted paper is measured.

Interpretation of Schirmer Test

• >10 mm wetting in 5 minutes: Normal
• 5–10 mm: Borderline
• <5 mm: Severe aqueous tear deficiency (positive test) ⭐

Why not the other options?

• B. Fluorescein staining test: Detects corneal epithelial defects and is also used to assess tear break-up time (TBUT).
• C. Rose Bengal staining: Stains devitalized conjunctival and corneal epithelial cells in dry eye.
• D. Tear break-up time (TBUT): Measures tear film stability after fluorescein instillation; abnormal if <10 seconds.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with painful swelling on the eyelid and a lesion with pus at the base of the eyelash. Which of the following glands is involved in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Zeis gland

External hordeolum (stye) is an acute, painful infection of the glands of Zeis (sebaceous glands of eyelash follicles).

• Painful, tender swelling at eyelid margin
• Pus point at base of eyelash
• Usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus

Differentiation:

• Meibomian (tarsal) gland → internal hordeolum/chalazion (deeper, less pointed)
• Lacrimal gland → superolateral swelling, not at lash base

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with a history of blunt ocular trauma undergoes CT imaging as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Blowout fracture

Blowout fracture is a fracture of the orbital floor (most common) or medial wall due to blunt trauma, causing herniation of orbital contents into the maxillary sinus.

• Diplopia (especially on upward gaze)
• Enophthalmos (sunken eye)
• Infraorbital nerve anesthesia (cheek, upper lip numbness)

CT findings:

• Discontinuity of orbital floor
• Herniation of fat/inferior rectus into maxillary sinus (“teardrop sign”)

Pathophysiology:

• Sudden increase in orbital pressure → weakest wall (floor) fractures

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with suspected proptosis is evaluated in the ophthalmology clinic. Which of the following instruments is being used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hertel’s exophthalmometer

The instrument shown is a Hertel’s exophthalmometer, which is used to measure the degree of proptosis (exophthalmos) by determining the distance from the lateral orbital rim to the apex of the cornea.

Normal Values

• Normal protrusion: 12–21 mm
• Difference between the two eyes: ≤2 mm
• Values >21 mm or an inter-eye difference >2 mm suggest proptosis.

Why not the other options?

• B. Tonometer: Measures intraocular pressure (IOP); used in glaucoma.
• C. Keratometer: Measures corneal curvature; used in astigmatism and contact lens fitting.
• D. Retinoscope: Used for objective refraction to determine refractive errors.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All the following are functions of the superior oblique muscle except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adduction

The superior oblique muscle has three primary actions:

• Intorsion (primary action)
• Depression (especially in adducted eye)
• Abduction

Why A is correct (NOT a function):

• Adduction is NOT a function of the superior oblique
• Adduction is mainly performed by the medial rectus

Superior oblique passes through the trochlea, giving it a unique action:

• Pulls the eye downward and outward
• Rotates the top of the eye inward (intorsion)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An elderly patient presents with watering, irritation, and foreign body sensation in the eye. On examination, the eyelid is as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Entropion

The lower eyelid is turned inward (inverted), causing the eyelashes to rub against the cornea and bulbar conjunctiva (trichiasis). The eye appears watery (epiphora) with conjunctival congestion due to chronic irritation. Long-standing entropion may produce corneal epithelial defects, abrasions, ulceration, vascularization, and corneal scarring, leading to visual impairment if untreated.

Key image findings

• Inward rolling (inversion) of the eyelid margin
• Eyelashes directed toward the globe
• Lashes touching the cornea/conjunctiva
• Excessive tearing (epiphora)
• Conjunctival hyperemia
• May show corneal haze, abrasion, ulcer, or scar in advanced cases

Clinical symptoms

• Foreign body sensation
• Watering
• Pain or irritation
• Photophobia
• Blurred vision (if cornea involved)

High-yield causes

• Involutional (senile) – most common; due to lid laxity
• Cicatricial – trachoma, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, chemical burns
• Congenital
• Spastic – secondary to blepharospasm

NEET PG Pearl

Differentiate entropion from ectropion:

| Entropion | Ectropion

| --------- | ---------

| Eyelid turns inward | Eyelid turns outward

| Lashes rub the cornea | Lashes point away from the eye

| Corneal irritation and ulceration are common | Exposure keratopathy and epiphora are common

| Trichiasis may be present | Punctum is everted, impairing tear drainage

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Diagnose the image seen in a 10-year-old child.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Herbert pits

Herbert pits are depressed scars at the limbus resulting from healed follicles in trachoma.

• Seen in chronic trachoma (Chlamydia trachomatis infection)
• Represent healed limbal follicles
• Typically located at the superior limbus
• Associated with other sequelae:

• Pannus formation (superior corneal vascularization)
• Trichiasis
• Entropion

Why not others:

• Horner-Trantas spots: White limbal dots in vernal keratoconjunctivitis
• Pannus: Superficial vascularization, not pits
• Corneal dystrophy: Bilateral, hereditary, non-inflammatory

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Examine the image provided. The ocular finding demonstrated is characteristic of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Herbert's pits

Herbert’s pits are small, shallow depressions at the limbus, seen as healed lesions of trachoma.

• Result from healing of limbal follicles
• Indicative of chronic trachoma (Chlamydia trachomatis)
• Often associated with other signs like pannus and Arlt’s line

Differentiation:

• Horner–Trantas spots → allergic (VKC), limbal white dots
• Pannus → superficial corneal vascularization
• Arlt’s line → conjunctival scarring

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Following instrument is used to measure:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Proptosis

The instrument shown is a Hertel exophthalmometer, used to measure proptosis (forward protrusion of the eyeball).

• Measures the distance between the lateral orbital rim and the corneal apex
• Allows quantification and comparison between both eyes
• Detects and monitors proptosis in conditions such as:

• Thyroid eye disease
• Orbital tumors
• Orbital cellulitis

Why not others:

• Squint: Assessed by cover test, prism bar
• Ptosis: Measured by MRD (margin reflex distance)
• Diplopia: Evaluated by Hess chart, diplopia charting

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In case of a chemical injury to the eye, what is the immediate first step in the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Copious irrigation with saline

Chemical injury to the eye is an absolute ocular emergency, and the immediate first step is copious irrigation with saline (or any clean fluid available).

• Chemicals (especially alkali) penetrate rapidly and cause ongoing tissue damage
• Immediate dilution and removal of the chemical limits severity of injury and improves prognosis

Key management principles:

• Start irrigation immediately (do NOT delay for history or examination)
• Use normal saline, Ringer lactate, or even clean water if nothing else is available
• Continue until ocular surface pH normalizes (≈ 7–7.4)
• Evert eyelids to remove retained particles

Why not others:

• Visual acuity, history, IOP measurement → important but only after irrigation
• Any delay worsens corneal and limbal damage

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The pathological finding shown in the image is typically associated with which of the following diseases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wilson's disease

Kayser–Fleischer ring is a golden-brown ring at the corneal periphery due to copper deposition in Descemet’s membrane, classically seen in Wilson’s disease.

• Seen on slit lamp examination
• Begins superiorly and inferiorly → becomes circumferential
• Associated with hepatic + neurological symptoms

Pathophysiology:

• Defect in copper metabolism (ATP7B mutation) → copper accumulation

Differentiation:

• Siderosis → iron deposition (rusty discoloration)
• Chalcosis → sunflower cataract
• Primary biliary cirrhosis → no KF ring typically

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the best step to establish a diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hepatic copper estimation

Wilson’s disease is a disorder of copper metabolism characterized by impaired biliary excretion of copper → accumulation in liver, brain, and cornea (Kayser–Fleischer ring).

Best diagnostic test: Hepatic copper estimation (liver biopsy) = gold standard

• Shows markedly increased hepatic copper (>250 µg/g dry weight)

Supporting findings:

• ↓ Serum ceruloplasmin
• ↑ 24-hour urinary copper excretion
• Kayser–Fleischer ring on slit-lamp (as shown)

Why not others:

• Serum ceruloplasmin: Low but not specific (can be low in other conditions)
• Urinary copper: Sensitive but not definitive
• Serum copper: Variable and unreliable

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of proptosis in a middle-aged person?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thyroid eye disease

The most common cause of proptosis in a middle-aged adult is thyroid eye disease (Graves’ orbitopathy).

• Autoimmune process associated with Graves disease
• Inflammation and deposition of glycosaminoglycans in:

• Extraocular muscles (muscle belly enlargement)
• Orbital fat

• Leads to increased orbital volume → proptosis

Key clinical features:

• Bilateral (often asymmetric) proptosis
• Lid retraction, lid lag
• Restrictive ophthalmoplegia (especially impaired upgaze)
• Exposure keratopathy

Why not others:

• Orbital varix: Intermittent proptosis (worse on Valsalva), rare
• Retinoblastoma: Pediatric tumor
• Cavernous hemangioma: Common benign orbital tumor in adults but not the most common cause overall

| Category | Adults – Most Common | Children – Most Common

| -------- | -------------------- | ----------------------

| Intraocular Tumors | Melanoma | Retinoblastoma

| Intraorbital Tumors | Hemangioma | Rhabdomyosarcoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in the image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dermoid

Limbal dermoid is a congenital choristoma presenting as a well-circumscribed, whitish/yellowish mass at the limbus, often seen in childhood.

• Present since birth or early childhood
• Firm, elevated lesion at inferotemporal limbus
• May contain hair follicles, sebaceous glands
• Can induce astigmatism → amblyopia

Associations: Goldenhar syndrome (oculoauriculovertebral dysplasia)

Differentiation:

• Pterygium: Triangular fibrovascular growth encroaching onto cornea (acquired)
• Pinguecula: Yellow conjunctival degeneration, does not involve cornea
• Dermolipoma: Soft, yellow mass in superotemporal conjunctiva

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms are associated with acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis? I. Coxsackie B II. Coxsackie A III. Enterovirus 70 IV. Polio virus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I, II and III

Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis is a contagious viral conjunctivitis characterized by sudden onset redness, subconjunctival hemorrhage, pain, and watering.

Causative organisms:

• Enterovirus 70 → classic and most common cause in epidemics
• Coxsackie A (especially A24 variant)
• Coxsackie B (less common but associated)

Why not Poliovirus:

• Poliovirus primarily affects the central nervous system → causes poliomyelitis
• Not associated with hemorrhagic conjunctivitis

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statement is true about orbital cellulitis?
options: It is present anterior to the orbital septum
Presents with proptosis, orbital swelling, normal pupil, and extraocular movements
Ethmoid sinusitis is the most common etiology
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ethmoid sinusitis is the most common etiology

Orbital cellulitis is a postseptal infection of the orbit, most commonly arising from ethmoid sinusitis due to the thin lamina papyracea.

Key clinical features:

• Proptosis
• Painful and restricted extraocular movements
• Decreased vision ± afferent pupillary defect
• Eyelid edema, fever

Ethmoid sinusitis is the most common source of orbital cellulitis spread.

Why other options are incorrect:

• A) Anterior to septum = preseptal cellulitis, not orbital
• B) Requires IV antibiotics, not just topical
• C) EOM are restricted and painful, not normal

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is NOT true about the given image?
options: Improves on treatment of thyroid status
Vision loss may be seen in some cases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Improves on treatment of thyroid status

The image depicts thyroid eye disease (Graves’ orbitopathy) characterized by proptosis, lid retraction, and conjunctival congestion.

Ophthalmopathy does NOT reliably improve with correction of thyroid status

→ It follows an independent autoimmune course

Important facts:

• Can occur in hyperthyroid, hypothyroid, or euthyroid patients (\~10% euthyroid)
• May cause vision loss due to:

• Optic nerve compression
• Exposure keratopathy

•

Severity is graded using NOSPECS classification

•

Treating thyroid dysfunction does not necessarily reverse eye disease

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 24-year-old student presents with redness, watering, foreign body sensation, and mild photophobia for 3 days. It started in one eye and then involved the other eye. There is tender preauricular lymph node enlargement. Examination of the eye is as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis

Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) is an adenoviral conjunctivitis characterized by acute follicular conjunctivitis, preauricular lymphadenopathy, and subsequent corneal involvement (keratitis). It is highly contagious and often begins in one eye before involving the other.

• Etiology: Adenovirus (serotypes 8, 19, 37 are common)
• Symptoms: Red eye, watering, irritation, photophobia, blurred vision
• Signs:

• Follicular conjunctivitis
• Tender preauricular lymphadenopathy
• Pseudomembranes (may occur)
• Subepithelial corneal infiltrates appear after 1–2 weeks and may reduce vision

• Transmission: Highly contagious by direct contact, contaminated instruments, swimming pools
• Treatment: Supportive—cold compresses, lubricants, hygiene measures. Topical steroids are reserved for severe corneal infiltrates under ophthalmologist supervision.

Differentiating from Other Options

• A. Allergic conjunctivitis: Severe itching, bilateral from onset, papillae, no preauricular lymphadenopathy.
• B. Bacterial conjunctivitis: Purulent discharge, eyelids stuck together, no significant preauricular lymphadenopathy.
• D. Herpes simplex keratitis: Usually unilateral with dendritic corneal ulcer on fluorescein staining.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 26-year-old female patient complains of a nodular lesion near the limbus as shown, with mild discomfort that resolves after treatment with the use of a topical drug. What can be the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Episcleritis with Rheumatoid Arthritis

Episcleritis is a benign, self-limiting inflammation of the episclera presenting with a localized nodular redness near the limbus, mild discomfort, and rapid response to topical therapy.

• Sectoral or nodular redness near limbus
• Mild pain or discomfort (not severe)
• No significant vision loss
• Vessels are superficial and mobile
• Blanch with phenylephrine

Association: Can be associated with systemic diseases, especially rheumatoid arthritis, but often idiopathic

Why not others:

• Scleritis: Severe pain, deep violaceous redness, does not blanch, vision-threatening
• Pinguecula: Yellowish degenerative lesion, non-inflammatory
• Pterygium: Fibrovascular growth crossing cornea

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 27-year-old male presents with myopic astigmatism comes with acute onset pain, lowering of visual acuity. He has a history of frequent change of glasses and eye rubbing. An image of the eye just after a procedure is shown below. Which procedure has been done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intracameral C3F8 injection

Acute hydrops in keratoconus (suggested by history of progressive myopic astigmatism, frequent change of glasses, and eye rubbing) results from a tear in Descemet’s membrane, leading to stromal edema and sudden vision loss.

Management principle:

Intracameral injection of long-acting gas (e.g., C3F8 or SF6) is used to:

• Tamponade Descemet’s membrane tear
• Reduce aqueous influx into stroma
• Accelerate resolution of corneal edema
• Improve visual recovery

Why not other options:

• DSEAK: Endothelial keratoplasty for endothelial failure
• DALK: For stromal diseases, not acute hydrops
• Collagen cross-linking: Used to halt progression, not treat hydrops

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with pain, redness and photophobia. He has a history of contact lens usage. An eye examination is shown below. Which of the following stains is used to stain the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Calcofluor white stain

A contact lens user presenting with pain, redness, photophobia, and ring-shaped corneal infiltrate suggests Acanthamoeba keratitis.

• The causative organism (Acanthamoeba, a free-living protozoa) is best demonstrated using Calcofluor white stain, which binds to cyst walls and fluoresces under UV light.

Supporting clinical clues:

• Severe pain out of proportion to clinical findings
• History of contact lens use / exposure to contaminated water
• Ring-shaped stromal infiltrate (classic but late sign)

Why not others:

• Gram stain: Bacterial keratitis
• Ziehl-Neelsen stain: Mycobacteria / Nocardia
• Gomori methenamine silver stain: Fungi

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman is diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. What associated complication is shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Scleromalacia perforans

Scleromalacia perforans is a severe ocular complication of rheumatoid arthritis, characterized by painless, progressive thinning of the sclera.

• Painless scleral thinning (important differentiating point)
• Bluish/black discoloration due to underlying uveal show
• Minimal or no inflammation
• Risk of globe perforation
• Autoimmune-mediated necrotizing scleritis without inflammation
• Associated with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis

Why not others:

• Ciliary staphyloma: Outpouching due to raised IOP
• Coloboma: Congenital defect
• Malignant melanoma: Pigmented tumor, not scleral thinning

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 56-year-old female with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis presents with painless, gradual blurring of vision in the left eye. On examination, the sclera is as shown in the image. There is no ciliary congestion or significant redness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Scleromalacia perforans

Scleromalacia perforans is a necrotizing anterior scleritis without inflammation, classically associated with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. It presents with painless progressive scleral thinning and minimal or no redness, with the underlying dark uveal tissue becoming visible through the thinned sclera.

• Most common association: Rheumatoid arthritis
• Symptoms: Usually painless, unlike typical scleritis
• Signs: White, avascular scleral thinning with bluish-black hue due to exposed uvea
• Complication: Risk of globe rupture/perforation despite the name “perforans” (actual perforation is uncommon)

Differentiate from Other Options:

• A. Scleritis: Severe boring eye pain, deep violaceous congestion, tenderness.
• B. Episcleritis: Mild discomfort, sectoral redness, self-limiting, no scleral thinning.
• D. Anterior uveitis: Pain, photophobia, ciliary congestion, cells and flare in the anterior chamber.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 68-year-old patient presents with complaints of painful watering, reduced vision, and worsened symptoms on waking in the morning. There is a history of previous cataract surgery 2 years back. Slit-lamp examination of the cornea is shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bullous keratopathy

Bullous keratopathy is caused by corneal endothelial decompensation, leading to stromal and epithelial edema with formation of painful epithelial bullae. It is a well-known late complication of cataract surgery (pseudophakic/aphakic bullous keratopathy).

• Cause: Loss of corneal endothelial cells → endothelial pump failure → corneal edema.
• Symptoms: Blurred vision (worse in the morning), pain, foreign body sensation, watering, photophobia.
• Signs: Stromal edema, Descemet folds, epithelial bullae, decreased corneal transparency.
• Common causes: Fuchs endothelial dystrophy, postoperative endothelial damage (especially after cataract surgery), trauma.

Management

• Hypertonic saline (5%) drops/ointment
• Lubricants and bandage contact lens for painful bullae
• Control raised IOP if present
• Definitive treatment: Endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK/DSEK) or penetrating keratoplasty when indicated

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Fuchs endothelial dystrophy: Causes guttae and morning blur but is usually bilateral and not classically associated with prior cataract surgery.
• C. Acute angle-closure glaucoma: Severe ocular pain, red eye, mid-dilated fixed pupil, markedly elevated IOP.
• D. Herpes simplex keratitis: Characteristic dendritic corneal ulcer staining with fluorescein, not bullous edema after cataract surgery.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A girl with a history of contact lens use presents with eye pain and decreased vision. She does not follow proper lens hygiene. Which of the following organisms is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acanthamoeba

Acanthamoeba keratitis is a severe corneal infection classically associated with contact lens use and poor hygiene.

• Severe pain disproportionate to findings
• Redness, photophobia, decreased vision
• Ring-shaped corneal infiltrate (late finding)

Risk factors:

• Improper lens cleaning
• Exposure to contaminated water (tap water, swimming)

Clinical importance: Often misdiagnosed early → can lead to vision loss

Why not others:

B. Herpes simplex → dendritic ulcer, ↓ corneal sensation

C. Fungal → vegetative trauma, feathery margins

D. Pneumococcus → bacterial ulcer, not linked to lenses

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presented with redness and extreme pain in the eye. There is also diminution of vision and discharge after the use of contact lenses. Which organism can be the causative agent here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acanthamoeba

Acanthamoeba keratitis is a severe, vision-threatening corneal infection classically associated with contact lens use, especially with poor hygiene or exposure to contaminated water.

• Severe pain disproportionate to clinical findings (hallmark)
• Redness, photophobia, ↓ vision
• Ring-shaped corneal infiltrate (late sign)
• History of contact lens use / water exposure

Pathogenesis:

• Free-living protozoa (Acanthamoeba) invade cornea
• Often introduced via contaminated lens solutions or water

Why not others:

• Staphylococcus / Streptococcus: Cause bacterial keratitis but pain is not disproportionately severe
• Listeria: Rare ocular infection, not typical in contact lens users

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a linear, branching corneal ulcer as shown in the image, decreased corneal sensation, along with loss of corneal sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Viral Keratitis

Herpes simplex viral keratitis presents with a dendritic (branching) corneal ulcer and reduced corneal sensation.

• Linear, branching ulcer with terminal bulbs (seen on fluorescein staining)
• Decreased corneal sensation (important clue)
• Pain, redness, photophobia

Pathophysiology:

• HSV infects corneal epithelium → dendritic epithelial ulcer

Why not others:

• Pseudomonas → rapidly progressive suppurative ulcer
• Acanthamoeba → severe pain, ring infiltrate
• Fungal → feathery margins, satellite lesions

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with guttate lesions in one eye and bullous keratopathy in the other eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fuchs endothelial dystrophy

Fuchs endothelial dystrophy is a progressive disorder of the corneal endothelium characterized by guttata formation and eventual stromal and epithelial edema leading to bullous keratopathy.

Key clinical progression:

• Early stage:

• Guttate lesions (corneal guttata) on Descemet’s membrane

• Late stage:

• Endothelial failure → corneal edema
• Formation of bullae (bullous keratopathy) → pain, decreased vision

Pathophysiology:

• Loss of endothelial cells → impaired corneal deturgescence (fluid pump function)
• Leads to fluid accumulation in cornea

Why not others:

• Interstitial keratitis: Stromal inflammation, not endothelial dystrophy
• Viral corneal ulcer: Epithelial defect, dendritic pattern
• Keratoconjunctivitis: Surface inflammation, no guttata

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In the case of macular corneal opacity, which of the following is true?
options: Both iris details and pupil margins are seen.
Both iris details and pupil margins are not seen.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pupil margins are seen.

Macular corneal opacity is a moderate-grade corneal opacity in which:

• Pupil margins are visible
• Iris details are NOT clearly visible

Grading of corneal opacities :

• Nebular opacity (mild):

• Iris details clearly visible

• Macular opacity (moderate):

• Pupil margin visible, but iris details blurred

• Leucomatous opacity (dense):

• Neither iris nor pupil details visible

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: On indirect ophthalmoscopy the examiner noticed a concave shaped out bulging of the outer layer in the posterior part of the eye. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Posterior Staphyloma

Posterior staphyloma is a localized outpouching of the posterior sclera, commonly seen in pathological (high) myopia.

• Concave bulging of posterior segment on ophthalmoscopy
• Associated with axial elongation of eyeball
• Leads to progressive visual deterioration

Pathophysiology:

• Thinning and stretching of sclera → outward bulging of posterior pole
• Predisposes to retinal degeneration, maculopathy, and retinal detachment

Why not other options:

B. Hypermetropia

• Short eyeball → no posterior bulging
• Retina lies anterior, not outpouched

C. Astigmatism

• Due to unequal corneal curvature
• No posterior segment abnormality

D. Corneal ulcer

• Anterior segment pathology
• Seen on cornea, not on fundus/ophthalmoscopy

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Pterygium can lead to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Astigmatism

Pterygium is a fibrovascular growth of conjunctiva extending onto the cornea that can distort corneal curvature, leading to astigmatism.

Mechanism:

• Progressive growth over cornea → mechanical traction and flattening (especially horizontal meridian)
• Causes irregular or with-the-rule astigmatism → decreased visual acuity

Why not others:

• Eye pain: Usually asymptomatic or mild irritation, not significant pain
• Macular edema: Posterior segment pathology, unrelated to pterygium
• Purulent discharge: Seen in bacterial conjunctivitis, not pterygium

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the dye and filter used as seen in the image?
options: Fluorescein dye - visualised under cobalt blue filter
Fluorescein dye - visualised under green filter
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fluorescein dye - visualised under cobalt blue filter

Fluorescein staining is used to detect corneal epithelial defects and is best visualized under a cobalt blue filter.

• Fluorescein dye accumulates in areas of epithelial loss
• Under cobalt blue light, it appears bright green (fluorescent)
• Commonly used in corneal ulcer, abrasion, dendritic ulcers (HSV), and tear film evaluation

Clinical relevance:

•

Helps identify pattern of lesions (e.g., dendritic pattern in herpes keratitis)

•

Used in Seidel test to detect aqueous leak

Why not others:

• Lissamine green: Stains devitalized cells, viewed in white light
• Green filter: Not used for excitation of fluorescein

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the indication of this procedure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratoconus

The image shows intrastromal corneal ring segments (ICRS), which are used in the management of keratoconus.

• Keratoconus is a progressive ectatic disorder causing corneal thinning and conical protrusion, leading to irregular astigmatism and visual distortion.

Indication of the procedure:

• To flatten the cornea and improve refractive error in moderate keratoconus
• Used when spectacles/contact lenses are not tolerated
• Helps delay or avoid corneal transplantation

Mechanism: Ring segments inserted in corneal stroma → arc-shortening effect → central corneal flattening

Not used for:

• Vogt’s limbal girdle (degenerative peripheral opacity)
• Keratoglobus (diffuse thinning)
• Corneal dystrophies (genetic, require different management)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which ocular condition is treated as shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratoconus

Intracorneal ring segments (Intacs) are used in the management of keratoconus, a progressive corneal ectasia.

• Intacs are placed in the corneal stroma
• They flatten and regularize the corneal curvature
• Improve irregular astigmatism and visual acuity

Indications:

• Mild to moderate keratoconus
• Contact lens intolerance
• Alternative to delay or avoid keratoplasty

Often combined with corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL) for stabilization

Why not others:

• Cataract: Treated with lens extraction
• Corneal ulcer: Treated medically (antibiotics/antifungals)
• Glaucoma: Managed with medications/surgery affecting aqueous outflow

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following accurately pairs the diagnostic stain with the corneal condition it indicates?
options: Cobalt blue with trypan blue for corneal ulcer
Cobalt green with Rose Bengal stain for corneal opacity
Cobalt blue with fluorescein stain for corneal ulcer
Cobalt blue with lissamine green for corneal abrasion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cobalt blue with fluorescein stain for corneal ulcer

Fluorescein staining viewed under cobalt blue light is the standard method to detect corneal epithelial defects, such as corneal ulcers and abrasions.

• Fluorescein dye stains areas where corneal epithelium is absent
• Under cobalt blue light, these areas appear bright green

Clinical applications:

• Corneal ulcer
• Corneal abrasion
• Dendritic ulcers (herpes simplex)
• Detection of foreign body tracks

Why other options are incorrect:

• Trypan blue: Used in cataract surgery (capsule staining), not cornea
• Rose Bengal / Lissamine green: Stain devitalized or damaged epithelial cells, mainly used in dry eye, not primary for ulcers
• Cobalt green light: Not the standard filter (cobalt blue is used)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following correctly identifies the storage medium used for preserving a corneal graft and the type of suture material shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. McCarey Kaufman medium; Nylon

Successful corneal transplantation (keratoplasty) requires proper donor cornea preservation and appropriate suture material for graft fixation.

Corneal preservation media: McCarey–Kaufman (MK) medium

• Short-term storage (≈ 48–96 hours) at 4°C
• Commonly used in eye banks (especially in resource-limited settings)

Suture material in keratoplasty: Nylon (10-0 monofilament)

• Non-absorbable
• Minimal tissue reaction
• Provides long-term tensile strength → ideal for corneal graft suturing

Why other options are incorrect:

• Vicryl: Absorbable → loses strength → not suitable for cornea
• Prolene: Non-absorbable but less commonly used than nylon in cornea
• Silk: Causes more tissue reaction → avoided in ocular surgery

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which surgical procedure should a 21-year-old boxer avoid to maintain optimal visual health?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. RK

Radial keratotomy (RK) should be avoided in individuals prone to ocular trauma (e.g., boxers), as it causes permanent structural weakening of the cornea.

Why RK is contraindicated:

• Involves deep radial incisions in the cornea
• These incisions never regain full strength
• High risk of corneal rupture even with minor trauma

Why other options are relatively safer:

• PRK, LASIK, SMILE:

• Do not involve full-thickness radial cuts
• Better structural integrity compared to RK
• Though trauma precautions still apply, they are safer than RK

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient presented with a penetrating injury to his left eye for which he was treated with corneoscleral suturing and discharged a week later. He returns 2 months later complaining of diminished vision, associated with redness, pain, and photophobia in the right eye. Direct ophthalmoscopy revealed discrete yellow-white nodules in the fundus. What part of the eye is most commonly affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Uvea

The clinical case is suggestive of sympathetic ophthalmitis, which is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis and hence the affected part is the uvea.

Dalen–Fuchs nodules are seen below the retinal pigment epithelium on ophtalmoscopy.

Sympathetic Ophthalmitis (SO) is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis occurring after penetrating trauma which usually begins 4–8 weeks after the injury to the eye (the exciting eye). It can also develop after surgeries, proton beam irradiation, Nd: YAG photocoagulation, and cryotherapy. It is an delayed hypersensitivity reaction mediated by T cells.

The exciting eye is often red and irritable, and the sympathizing eye may develop irritation, blurred vision, photophobia, and loss of accommodation.

Fundoscopy:

* Multifocal choroidal infiltrates

* Infiltrates corresponding to Dalen–Fuchs nodules are seen below the retinal pigment epithelium

* Exudative retinal detachment, vasculitis, and optic disc swelling

* Residual chorioretinal scarring gives a sunset glow appearance when the inflammation settles

Treatment :

* Steroids are the basis of treatment.

* High-dose oral prednisolone is given for several months.

* Supplementary topical steroids and cycloplegics for anterior uveitis

* Periocular and intraocular steroids, slow-release intravitreal implants may also be used

* Immunosuppressives such as azathioprine, ciclosporin, and methotrexate are used in resistant cases or as steroid-sparing agents.

* Enucleation of an eye with no visual potential within 2 weeks of injury prevents the occurrence of sympathetic ophthalmitis.
