questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy has been observed by his parents to be increasingly clumsy for the past 6 months. On physical examination, there is leukocoria with an absence of the red reflex in the left eye. A diagnosis was made and enucleation was done. The specimen is shown below. The microscopic appearance shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinoblastoma

The histology, clinical history, and gross specimen point toward a diagnosis of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14.

It most commonly presents with leukocoria followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision.

Signs:

* An intraretinal tumor is a homogeneous, dome-shaped white lesion that becomes irregular, often with white flecks of calcification.

* An endophytic tumor projects into the vitreous as a white mass that may "seed" into the gel.

* An exophytic tumor forms multilobular subretinal white masses and causes an overlying retinal detachment.

Investigations:

* Red reflex testing with a direct ophthalmoscope is a simple screening test for leukocoria.

* Dilated fundus examination using indirect ophthalmoscope

* MRI of the orbit + brain is the investigation of choice.

Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features of a well-differentiated tumor include Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen.

Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy.Vincristine, Carboplatin, Etoposide are the choice of drugs for chemotherapy. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy.

Enucleation is done when the tumor involves more than half of the retina, optic nerve involvement, glaucoma, and anterior chamber involvement.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 37-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes presented with blurred vision, photophobia, and increasing pain in his right eye. He has been using contact lenses for the past 2 years. He gave a history of swimming with his cousins, 2 weeks back, in a local pond. What is the most important risk factor for his diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Contact lenses

The above clinical scenario of a patient presenting with eye pain, photophobia, with a history of swimming in a local pond, followed by the characteristic ring lesion given in the image, is suggestive of Acanthamoeba keratitis, and the most common risk factor is wearing contact lenses.

Acanthamoeba keratitis is an infection of the eyes that typically develops from the entry of the amebic cyst through abrasions on the cornea. Most of the cases are associated with the use of contact lenses and individuals who swim or bathe in contaminated water.

Patients usually present with photophobia, excessive tearing, redness, and foreign body sensation, which can be bilateral in contact lens users. Pain is disproportionate to the degree of keratitis due to perineural invasion. It presents as a ring lesion or ring stromal infiltrate.

Diagnosis of amoebic keratitis is made by the demonstration of the cyst in corneal scrapings by wet mount, histology, and culture. The cysts are smaller (12-25 micrometers) and polygonal or star-shaped, as shown below.

Topical administration of biguanides or chlorhexidine with or without diamidine agents can be used for the management of acanthamoeba keratitis. In severe cases penetrating keratoplasty can be done.

Pearl PF1375: Clinical differential diagnosis of corneal ulcer

Fungal

Parasitic

Risk factors

Contact lens wear

Trauma

Chronic steroid use

Trauma with vegetable matter

Exposure to contaminated water (acanthamoeba)

Clinical features

Hypopyon is fluid and mobile

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is likely to have a rapid course, with deep corneal necrosis.

Less pain and watering compared to the extent of vision loss and signs.

Tend to be indolent but progressive

Hypopyon is thick, immobile.

Relatively more pain and watering compared to the extent of vision loss and signs.

Recurrences are characteristic.

Disproportionately severe pain is a characteristic feature.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old female patient with h/o chicken pox comes to the clinic with the findings shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Herpes Zoster Ophtalmicus

The given image along with the past history of chicken pox is suggestive of a case of herpes zoster ophtalmicus which involves the face and the eyes.

Herpes zoster Opthlamicus:

It is the term used for shingles  involving the dermatome supplied by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve

Pathogenesis: Varicella zoster causes both chicken pox and shingles. Usually after chicken pox, the organism travels in a retrograde fashion to the dorsal root and cranial sensory nerve ganglia and remains dormant until it is activated again. During this time, it travels in an antegrade fashion to the skin and eyes to cause the typical manifestations

Mechanisms of ocular involvement:

* Direct viral inflammation leads to conjunctivitis and epithelial keratitis.

* Secondary and occlusive vasculitis may cause uveitis, keratitis, epicleritis and scleritis. Optic neuritis and cranial nerve palsies may also be seen.

* Cicatrizing processes may occur following severe eyelid, particular skin and conjunctival involvement. Reactivation causes necrosis and inflammation the sensory ganglia causes corneal anaesthesia and neurotrophic keratopathy.

The spread is airborne and through fomites and the lesions cease to be infectious when they crust.

Age and immunocompromised status are the two most important predisposing factors for this condition because of the diminishing T-cell immunity.

Ocular manifestations:

Hutchinson’s rule is related to herpes zoster ophthalmicus. It states that if the tip of the nose is involved, there will be a significant risk of ocular involvement. This is due to the involvement of the nasociliary nerve.

Corneal lesions in herpes zoster ophthalmicus: zoster keratitis

Epithelium

* Superficial punctate keratitis

* Pseudo-dendritic/micro-dendritic ulcer

Stroma:

* Nummular keratitis

* Disciform keratitis (Associated with endothelitis)

Other ocular lesions in herpes zoster:

Uveitis

Episcleritis and scleritis

* Conjunctivitis

* Acute retinal necrosis

* Secondary glaucoma

* Anterior segment necrosis and phthisis bulbi

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 50-year-old female presents with an acute painful red-eye. An image of her eye is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute angle-closure glaucoma

The clinical scenario and a red eye showing corneal edema and a mid-dilated and vertically oval pupil are suggestive of acute angle-closure glaucoma. The pupil is non-reactive to both light and accommodation.

Acute primary angle-closure glaucoma refers to the occlusion of the trabecular meshwork by the peripheral iris (iridotrabecular contact [ITC]), obstructing aqueous outflow. It can be primary when it occurs in an anatomically predisposed eye or secondary to another ocular or systemic factor.

Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ocular emergency that causes acute red-eye and is associated with at least two of the following symptoms:

* Acute onset ocular pain with nausea or vomiting

* Intermittent blurring of vision with halos

* Photophobia or

* Loss of vision.

It is also associated with at least three of the following signs:

* Ciliary congestion

* Corneal edema and subsequent haziness

* Fixed and mid-dilated, usually oval pupil

* Shallow anterior chamber

* Intraocular pressure elevated above 40 mmHg.

Immediate medical management mainly aims at lowering IOP using drugs such as oral acetazolamide or intravenous mannitol. The definitive treatment is laser peripheral iridotomy. This must be followed by prophylaxis of the fellow eye, long-term glaucoma surveillance and management of intraocular pressure in both eyes.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presented to OPD with complaints of fever, left eye lid swelling for the past two days, as shown below. He had a mild flu-like illness a week ago, but no history of trauma. There is no chemosis or any protrusion of the eyeball. Visual acuity, IOP, ocular motility, and pupils were all normal. Slit-lamp examination was unremarkable. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Preseptal cellulitis

The given clinical vignette with eyelid swelling and fever following an infection without proptosis, loss of visual acuity, and ophthalmoplegia are suggestive of preseptal cellulitis/ Periorbital cellulitis.

Preseptal cellulitis is an infection of the subcutaneous tissues anterior to the orbital septum.

Etiological agents: Staph. aureus, Strep. pyogens

Mode of spread: Skin trauma, insect bites, acute hordeolum, dacryocystitis, conjunctivitis, sinusitis, Upper respiratory tract infection, and middle ear infection.

Presentation:

* Tender, firm, erythematous eye lid swelling

* Conjunctiva - usually no chemosis

* Proptosis - absent

* Ocular movements - normal

* Visual acuity - normal

* Systemic symptoms: fever, leucocytosis

Treatment: Antibiotics with systemic analgesics and warm compresses.

Complications: May spread and develop into orbital cellulitis, abscess formation, meningitis, and cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Other options:

Option A:  Panophthalmitis would have an intense purulent inflammation of the whole eyeball that could be seen on a slit-lamp.

Option B: Orbital cellulitis refers to the acute infection of the contents of the orbit behind the orbital septum.It  presents with pain, lid edema, erythema, chemosis, and axial proptosis. Increased pain with movement of eyes and ophthalmoplegia (decreased ocular motility) are the classic symptoms. There is a rapid loss of vision due to the involvement of the optic nerve.

Option D: Endophthalmitis is defined as the inflammation of the inner structures of the eyeball, i.e., uveal tissue and retina, associated with the pouring of exudates into the vitreous cavity, anterior chamber, and posterior chamber.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with photophobia and blurring of vision. After examination a diagnosis of acute uveitis was made. Which of the drugs can be used in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atropine

Among the following atropine can be used in acute uveitis.

Cycloplegics like 1% atropine, relieve spasm of the iris sphincter and ciliary muscles. They prevent the formation of synechiae and reduce exudation.

Steroids and cycloplegics are the mainstays of the treatment of uveitis.

Steroids are the drug of choice in anterior uveitis. They reduce inflammation by their anti-inflammatory effect.

Systemic therapy includes steroids, NSAIDs, and immunosuppressants.

Immunosuppressants like voclosporin (calcineurin inhibitor), are used in severe cases. They are being studied under a program called LUMINATE.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with a history of contact with COVID 19 comes to the opthalmology clinic with complaints of redness,photophobia, epiphora and malaise.Examination under strict precautions was done , however there was no blurring of vision or increase in IOP and fundus was normal. Which part of the eye can be most likely to be affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Conjunctiva

This is a probable case of COVID conjunctivitis and the affected part is conjunctiva.

Conjunctivitis and keratitis are the only reported ocular signs of COVID-19 to date but research and studies are going on.

Covid Conjunctivitis:

* The pathophysiology of SARS-CoV-2 associated conjunctivitis is not completely understood.

* The disease occurs in three stages- viral replication, immune hyperactivity, and then tissue destruction.

* It may also be an inflammatory response to the systemic disease in a form of conjunctival injection and tearing.

* Starts as redness of the eye with a follicular reaction like any other viral conjunctivitis.

* It may resolve by itself or progress to involve coarse epithelial keratitis, pseudomembranous conjunctivitis and bilateral hemorrhagic, pseudomembranous conjunctivitis, or pseudodendritic keratitis.

* Tender lymphadenopathy can be seen.

* Cells in conjunctiva die either by viral-mediated lysis or by immune reactions and resulting in the release of the virus into tears.

* Diagnosis is by RT-PCR confirmation of COVID 19 infection.

* Treatment is supportive as it subsides after the COVID infection.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient's eye was hit by a tennis ball and developed Hyphema. What is the likely source of bleeding ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Circulus arteriosus major

Circulus arteriosus major is responsible for Hyphaema (blood in the anterior chamber).

Hyphaema:

Causes of Hyphaema:

* Ocular injuries

* Postoperative

* Herpes zoster iritis

* Gonococcal iritis

* Intraocular tumor

* Spontaneous (from rubeosis iridis)

Two-way irrigation and aspiration cannula can be used for aspirating hyphaema.

Blood Supply of Eye:

Cornea: Avascular

Uvea: 3 arteries are important.

* Short post ciliary artery- Choroid

* Long post ciliary artery-2 in number join each other near ciliary muscle with anterior ciliary arteries to form circulus arteriolar major (C A major).

* Short anterior ciliary arteries join long posterior ciliary arteries to form C A major.

* Branches from circulus arteriolar major go to the pupillary border to form circulus arteriosus minor(C A minor).

Retina:

* Outer four layers-choriocapillaries (RPE, rods and cones, ELM, outer nuclear layer)

* Inner layers- Central retinal artery

* Macula- Branches of central retinal artery + Choriocapillaries.

* Foveola- Avascular

Optic Nerve Head:

* Surface nerve fibre layer- From retinal arteriole.

* Lamina cribrosa- From ciliary vessels derived from posterior ciliary artery and arterial circle of Zinn and Haller.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All of the following are true about the instrument shown in the image given below except-
options: It is used for the localization of a foreign body.
It is used for the measurement of the angle of the posterior chamber.
It is used for the demonstration of the extent of peripheral anterior synechiae.
It provides a mirror image of the opposite angle.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is used for the measurement of the angle of the posterior chamber.

The given instrument is an indirect gonioscope, which is used to visualize the angle of the anterior chamber, i.e., for gonioscopy, and not the angle of the posterior chamber.

Types:

* Indirect gonioprism- provides mirror image of the opposite angle.

* Direct goniolens- provides a direct view of the angle

Application:

* To view the angle of the anterior chamber

* Localization of the foreign body, abnormal blood vessels, or tumors in the angle

* Demonstration of the extent of peripheral anterior synechiae

* Direct goniolens can be used during goniotomy

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An ophthalmology resident is evaluating an elderly patient with Bell's palsy who complained of dry eye, redness, and irritation. Slit-lamp shows multiple punctate epithelial erosions in the cornea. Which of the following is used to manage this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tarsorrhaphy

The given clinical scenario with corneal punctate epithelial erosions in a Bell's palsy is suggestive of exposure keratitis. Temporary tarsorrhaphy is the surgical management of choice.

It occurs in Bell's palsy due to the inability to close eyes and the drying up of tear film.

Treatment is with artificial tears and eye ointment and taping of eyes during the night. If the recovery is prolonged, temporary tarsorrhaphy is indicated with heavy implants.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Arlt’s line is seen in
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trachoma

Arlt’s line is a conjunctival sign seen in trachoma.

It is a characteristic white conjunctival scar usually formed at the junction between the lower third and upper two-third of the superior tarsus.

Clinical signs in trachoma:

Corneal signs of trachoma include:

* Superficial keratitis

* Herbert’s follicles – Limbal area

* Pannus – superior limbus

* Corneal ulcer

* Herberts pits – Limbal area

* Corneal opacity

Conjunctival signs of trachoma include:

* Congestion – On upper tarsal, fornix

* Follicles (Containing Leber cells on histopathology) – On upper tarsal, fornix

* Papillary hyperplasia

* Arlt’s line – Linear scarring in sulcus subtarsalis

* Concretions – Inspissated mucus, dead epithelial cells in Glands of Henle

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the test shown below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Schirmer test

The image shows a tear strip placed in the lower lid of the eye. This is the Schirmer test which is used to check for dry eye.

Treatment of dry eye include medical treatment (lubricating eyedrops, most commonly methylcellulose derivatives) or surgical treatment (lacrimal punctum occlusion using silicone plugs)

Option B: To measure tear film break-up time(TBUT), fluorescein is instilled into the patient's tear film and the patient is asked not to blink while the tear film is observed under a broad beam of cobalt blue illumination. The TBUT is recorded as the number of seconds that elapse between the last blink and the appearance of the first dry spot in the tear film.

Option C: In rose Bengal staining, the eye is stained using the rose Bengal stain.

Option D: A tear osmolarity test is performed using a handheld sampler that collects a very small sample of tear fluid.

Pearl PF1389: Tear film tests used for the diagnosis of dry eye

Schirmer test

Inference

* 15 mm: Normal

* 5-10 mm: Moderate keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS)

* < 5 mm: Severe KCS

Tear film break up test (TBUT)

Inference

* 15-35 seconds: Normal

* < 10 seconds: Unstable tear film

Rose Bengal staining

Inference

* A pattern: Confluent staining → Severe KCS

* B pattern: Extensive staining → Moderate KCS

* C pattern: Fine punctate stains → Mild KCS

Tear osmolarity test

Abnormal osmolarity is defined by

* An elevated reading, >300 mOsm/L, indicating loss of homeostasis, or

* When the inter-eye difference is >8 mOsm/L, indicating instability of the tear film.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In which of the following diseases is collagen cross linking treatment used for ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratoconus

Collagen cross-linking therapy is used for keratoconus.

Riboflavin eye drops are used in collagen cross-linking therapy for keratoconus. The corneal epithelium is removed and riboflavin eye drops are instilled until the cornea is saturated with riboflavin. The cornea is then exposed to UVA and covered using a soft bandage lens. Riboflavin acts as a photo sensitizing agent and promotes cross-linking of collagen fibers. This stabilizes the corneal stroma and delays the progression of the disease.

Keratoconus:

Clinical Presentation:

* Young male with constantly changing power of glasses with myopia & high cylinder due to myopic astigmatism.

* Corneal topography shows an asymmetric bow tie pattern with the skewed radial axis.

Morphological pattern (3 types):

* Nipple cone (<5mm)

* Oval cone (5-6mm)

* Globus cone (>6mm)

Signs:

* Munson sign

* Enlarged corneal nerves

* Oil droplet reflex

* Rizutti sign (conical reflection on nasal cornea when a penlight is shone from the temporal side)

* Acute Hydrops (percolation of aqueous into stroma through breaks in DM)

* Fleischer ring (at keratoconus base, a brownish ring, probably due to haemosiderin, may form in the epithelium encircling the cone)

* Scissor reflex on retinoscopy

* Vogt striae in slit lamp

Important associations:

* Marfans, Down’s, EDS syndrome

* Osteogenesis imperfecta, MVP

* RP, Leber congenital amurosis

* VKC, aniridia, ectopia lentis

Investigations:

* Corneal topography

* Pachymetry

* Keratometry:

* Steep cornea

* Bow tie pattern

* Paracentral thinning of the cornea (thinnest point)

KISA index is used to classify Keratoconus.

Treatment:

* Spectacle correction

* Contact lens can be used include:

* Rigid Gas Permeable

* Rose K lenses

* Soper lenses

* Corneal collagen cross-linking with Riboflavin

* Intacs

* Surgery

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Microanuerysms are seen in which of the following diseases?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diabetic retinopathy

Among the following microaneurysms are seen in diabetic retinopathy.

Microaneurysms are localized, saccular outpouchings of the capillary wall that are formed either by focal dilatation of the capillary wall where pericytes are absent or by fusion of two arms of a capillary loop.

* Most develop in the inner capillary plexus (inner nuclear layer), frequently adjacent to areas of capillary non-perfusion.

* Loss of pericytes may also lead to endothelial cell proliferation with the formation of ‘cellular’ microaneurysms.

* Microaneurysms may leak plasma constituents into the retina as a result of a breakdown in the blood-retinal barrier or may thrombose.

* They tend to be the earliest sign of DR.

Stages and fundus picture in diabetic retinopathy:

Non-proliferative/ Background Diabetic Retinopathy:

* Microaneurysms

* Dot and Blot hemorrhages

* Exudates

Preproliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (indicates progressive retinal ischemia):

* Intra-retinal microvascular abnormalities

* Venous changes (such as beading)

* Cotton wool spots

* Deep retinal hemorrhages

Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy:

* NeoVascularization of the Optic Disc (NVD)

* NeoVascularization Elsewhere in the periphery of the fundus (NVE)

Advanced Diabetic Eye Disease:

* Tractional retinal detachment

* Vitreous hemorrhage

* Neovascular glaucoma

Pearl PF1636: Early treatment diabetic retinopathy study (ETDRS) classification

Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR):

* Mild NPDR

* At least one microaneurysm must be present

* Moderate NPDR

* Microaneurysms/intraretinal hemorrhage in 2 or 3 quadrants

* Early mild intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA)

* Hard exudates and cotton-wool spots may or may not be present

* Severe NPDR - any one of the following (4-2-1 rule)

* 4 quadrants of microaneurysms and extensive intraretinal hemorrhages

* 2 quadrants of venous beading

* 1 quadrant of IRMA changes

* Very severe NPDR - any two of the following (4-2-1)

* 4 quadrants of microaneurysms and extensive intraretinal hemorrhages

* 2 quadrants of venous beading

* 1 quadrant of IRMA changes

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR):

* PDR without high-risk characteristics (Early PDR)

* Early neovascularization at the optic disc (NVD) or neovascularization elsewhere (NVE)

* PDR with high-risk characteristics as follows

* NVD < 1/4 disc area with vitreous hemorrhage (VH) or preretinal hemorrhage (PRH)

* NVD 1/4 to 1/3 of disc area with or without VH or PRH

* NVE > 1/2 disc area with VH or PRH

Clinically significant macular edema: 1 of the following 3 criteria are present on slit-lamp examination with 90D lens

* Thickening of the retina at or within 500 micron of the center of the fovea.

* Hard exudates at or within 500 micron of the centre of fovea associated with adjacent retinal thickening.

* Development of a zone of retinal thickening one disc diameter or larger in size. At least a part of this should be within one disc diameter of the foveal center.

Advanced diabetic eye disease:

* Persistent vitreous hemorrhage

* Tractional retinal detachment

* Neovascular glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Riya was found to have a height of more than 95 percentile for his age and an arm-span to height ratio of more than 1.05. On further examination, she had flat feet, mild scoliosis, and long slender fingers. An image of her hand showing two characteristic signs is provided below. What is the most common ocular complication expected in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Subluxation of lens

The given features are suggestive of a diagnosis of Marfan's syndrome. Subluxation of the lens is the most common ocular complication.

Image (a) shows Walker-Murdoch (wrist) sign - the ability to join the thumb and fifth finger around the wrist.

Image (b) shows Steinberg (thumb) sign - thumb tip extends from the palm of the hand in a closed fist

Marfan’s syndrome is most commonly associated with superotemporal subluxation of lens.

Congenital subluxation of the lens is called ectopia lentis.

Features of Marfan's syndrome (Mnemonic: MARFAN’S)

* Mitral valve prolapse

* Myopia due to upward dislocation of the lens (bilateral ectopic lentis)

* Aortic root dilatation, Aortic regurgitation

* Retinal detachment

* Fibrillin 1 gene defect: Reduced fibrillin 1 production causing joint laxity

* Fifteen (Chromosome 15 is involved)

* Flat feet

* Arachnodactyly, Astigmatism, Air in lungs (Pneumothorax)

* Nearsightedness

* Subluxation of lens, Scoliosis, Speech disorders, Sleep apnea

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The cherry red spot seen in the image below is seen in _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)

The image shows a cherry-red spot, which is a feature of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO).

Pathophysiology of the cherry-red spot:

A cherry-red spot of the macula is typical and arises in this area because of the absence of ganglion cells at the foveola resulting in the transmission of the normal choroidal color. This is in contrast to the surrounding area where intense retinal whitening blocks the transmission of the normal choroidal color.

Risk factors of CRAO:

* Heart disease

* Carotid artery disease

* Mucormycosis

* Trauma

Clinical features of CRAO:

* Sudden painless loss of vision

* Severe edema: The whole retina looks white in color.

* Marked attenuation of arteries: thread-like arteries

* Interrupted blood flow in the artery and veins: cattle-track appearance

* Cherry-red spot

Treatment is to dislodge the emboli is by suddenly decreasing the intraocular pressure (IOP) by intravenous mannitol or ocular massage. The time limit is only 4 to 6 hours.

Pearl PF1384: Important causes of cherry-red spots

* Commotio retinae

* Central retinal and cilioretinal artery occlusion

* Metabolic storage diseases

* GM1 gangliosidosis

* Mucolipidosis type I (sialidosis)

* GM2 gangliosidosis (Tay-Sachs disease and Sandhoff disease)

* Farber disease

* Niemann–Pick disease

* Retinotoxicity due to specific agents, including quinine, dapsone, gentamicin, carbon monoxide, and methanol

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The following image depicts a particular type of cataract. What history should be elicited from the patient to come to a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Blunt trauma

The above image characteristically depicts a rosette cataract. It typically follows closed globe injuries (blunt trauma), and hence is also known as the concussion cataract.

Concussion cataract

* Early rosette cataract - either in posterior or anterior cortex; feathery lines of opacities along the star-shaped suture lines.

* Late rosette cataract - in posterior cortex; 1-2 years after trauma; smaller and compact than early rosette.

Other options:

Option A: Penetrating trauma is associated with sunflower cataract.

Option B: Steroid use is linked with posterior subcapsular cataract.

Option C: Diabetes is associated with snowflake/ snowstorm cataract.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the investigation shown in the picture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fundus fluorescein angiography

The investigation done in the picture is of fundus fluorescein angiography.

The image depicts a smoke stack pattern in FFA. This is characteristically seen in central serous retinopathy (CSR).

In FFA, sodium fluorescein dye is injected into the antecubital vein. A fundus camera is then used to take photographs.

Indications for fundus fluorescein angiography:

* Diabetic retinopathy

* Vascular occlusion

* Eale’s disease

* Central serous retinopathy

* Cystoid macular edema

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which laser is the most suitable for cataract surgery presently?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Femtosecond laser

Femtosecond laser-assisted cataract surgery (FLACS) is the best available procedure presently for cataract surgery. It is a microincision cataract surgery or a micro-phacoemulsification where a femtosecond laser is used.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: You are studying the optics of a patient with regular astigmatism. Identify the point at which the clearest image is formed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. D

The given figure is a Sturm's conoid. It represents a bundle of light rays formed by a regularly astigmatic surface. The image is clearest or least confusing as point D, the circle of least confusion.

When light passes through a regularly astigmatic surface(surface with toric curvature), vertical and horizontal rays converge at different points.

The distance between the points of convergence (focus) of the vertical and horizontal rays is called the focal interval of strum. (distance between points B and F). The circle of least confusion/ circle of diffusion lies at the mid-point of this interval.

For the given Sturm's conoid,

* At point A, a horizontal oval is formed because vertical rays converge more rapidly than horizontal rays.

* At point B, vertical rays come to a focus, while horizontal rays are still converging; so, it will be a horizontal straight line.

* At points C, D, and E, the vertical rays are diverging and horizontal rays are still converging.

* At point D, the vertical rays have diverged as much as the horizontal rays have converged; so, we get a perfect circle called the circle of least confusion.

* At point E, a vertical oval is formed.

* At point F, a vertical straight line is formed

* At point G and beyond, both rays are diverging, and we always get a vertical oval/prolate ellipse.

Astigmatism is a type of refractive error in which the eye does not focus light evenly on the retina. This results in a distorted or blurred vision. Other symptoms include eyestrain or asthenopia with headaches.

Types:

* Regular astigmatism: In this refractive power changes uniformly from one meridian to another resulting in 2 principal meridians

* Iregular astigmatism: It is characterized by an irregular change of refractive power in different meridians and hence it has multiple meridians.

Types of regular astigmatism:

With the rule astigmatism: The vertical meridian is more curved than the horizontal meridian but they are placed at right angles to one another

Against-the-rule astigmatism: Here Horizontal meridians is more curved than the vertical meridian

Oblique astigmatism: Here, the two principal meridians are not the horizontal and vertical meridians although they are at right angles to each other. It is a type of regular astigmatism. eg : one may be at 45 degrees and the other at 135 degrees.

Bioblique astigmatism: Here, the two principal meridians are not at right angles to each other; for example, one may be at 40 degrees and the other, at 100 degrees. It is also a type of regular astigmatism.

Note: Refractive types of regular astigmatism:

* Simple astigmatism: rays are focused on the retina in one meridian: either in front (simple myopic as shown in the above image) of the retina or behind the retina (simple hyperopic)

* Compound astigmatism: rays in both the meridia are focused in front or behind the retina

* Mixed astigmatism: Light rays in one meridian are focused in front of the retina and those in the other meridian are focused behind the retina

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 26-year-old patient came with complaints of blurring of vision, photophobia, and pain in the eye. He also has congestion of the eyes and joint pain. All ocular complaints are unilateral. Which of the following major histocompatibility complexes (MHC) can be associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HLA B27

The clinical diagnosis here is anterior uveitis seen in ankylosing spondylitis and the major histocompatibility complex associated with this condition is  HLA B27.

HLA B27 is positive in the following conditions:

* Psoriatic spondylitis

* Reactive arthritis due to Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Chlamydia

* Acute anterior uveitis

* Ankylosing spondylitis

Anterior uveitis: Involvement of Iris

* Most common symptom: Photophobia

* Most common sign: Cells in Anterior Chamber

Intermediate Uveitis: Involvement of Pars plana and peripheral part of the retina and the underlying choroid.

* Most common symptom: Floaters

* Sign: Snowball opacities & snow banking. Seen in pars plana > ora serrata (q)

* Most Common complication of Pars planitis

* Posterior Subcapsular Cataract.

Posterior uveitis: Involvement of Choroid

* Most Common Symptom: Floaters

* Most Common cause of visual loss: Cystoid Macular edema

Other options:

HLA B51- Behcet disease

HLA B47- Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

HLA B57- Abacavir Hypersensitivity

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man with a history of using contact lenses, presented with pain, redness and purulent discharge from his right eye. A greyish-white serpiginous ulcer was noted over the lower third of the cornea. The anterior chamber showed a 4 mm hypopyon and a moderate flare reaction. What is the most likely diagnosis ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bacterial corneal ulcer

Hypopyon corneal ulcer with a characteristic serpiginous description (ulcus serpens) is typically caused by Pneumococcus. The bacterial hypopyon is sterile.

Ulcus serpens is a greyish-white or yellowish disc-shaped ulcer occurring near the centre of the cornea. The ulcer has a tendency to creep over the cornea in a serpiginous fashion.

Risk factors include both surgical and non-surgical ocular trauma, dry eye, chronic corneal disease, immune alterations and contact lenses.

An examination may reveal the following signs:

* Swelling of lids and blepharospasm

* Conjunctival hyperemia

* Ciliary congestion, hypopyon and anterior chamber flare reaction

* Iridocyclitis

Image given below shows ulcus serpens.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman is being counseled for surgery for her long-standing dacryocystitis. Which of the following is the surgery of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dacryocystorhinostomy

The treatment of choice for chronic dacryocystitis is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) as it re-establishes the lacrimal drainage.

One of the sequelae of chronic dacryocystitis is mucocele formation, which when infected, leads to pyocele formation and finally lacrimal fibrosis. Treatment of lacrimal sac fibrosis is dacryocystectomy.

Streptococcus hemolyticus and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common etiological agents for acute and chronic dacryocystitis

Initially, the inflammation is controlled with antibiotics and anti-inflammatory agents. Sequelae of acute dacryocystitis is a lacrimal fistula, which is treated with is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 64-year-old woman was brought by her son, during a cataract outreach camp. She gives a history of trauma to her left eye, one year back and a complete loss of vision in that eye since then. Her left eye image is given below. What is the next line of management ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratoplasty

The above image shows a dense white opacity which results due to the scarring of more than half of the stroma. It is characteristic of Leucomatous corneal opacity  and the treatment of choice is keratoplasty.

Depending on the density, corneal opacities are graded as nebula, macula and leucoma.

* Nebular corneal opacity (fog or mist):

* Hard-to-see corneal scar, due to superficial scars involving Bowman's layer and superficial stroma.

* Slit-lamp detection is required.

* A thin, diffuse nebula covering the pupillary area interferes more with vision than the localised leucoma away from the pupillary area. Nebula produces more discomfort due to blurred image (irregular astigmatism).

* Macular corneal opacity:

* Semi-dense opacity that can be seen with proper illumination.

* Due to scarring involving about half the corneal stroma.

* Leucomatous corneal opacity (leucoma simplex):

* White scar that is easily seen just by looking at the eye.

* Due to scarring of more than half of the stroma

* Adherent leucoma:

* It results when healing occurs after perforation of the cornea with incarceration of iris

Secondary changes in corneal opacity which may be seen in long-standing cases include hyaline degeneration, calcareous degeneration, pigmentation and atheromatous ulceration.

Treatment:

* Keratoplasty is the treatment of choice in leucomatous corneal opacities.

* Optical iridectomy may be performed in cases with central adherent leucomas

* Phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) performed with excimer laser is useful only in superficial (nebular) corneal opacities.

* Corneal tattooing is a treatment option in patients with corneal opacities, who have lost their vision or who do not expect to recover it. It improves cosmetic appearance by altering the white colour of the opacity and blending it to normal eye colour.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A tumor in the anterior pituitary pressing on the optic chiasma will present as a case of ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bitemporal hemianopia

A lesion in the optic chiasma will present as bitemporal hemianopia, due to the decussation of nasal fibres which are affected.

Other notable defects:

* Pie in the sky defects

* Superior quadrantic hemianopia

* Involvement of Meyer’s loop - inferior fibers of optic radiations

* Contralateral temporal lobe

* Pie in the floor defects

* Inferior quadrantic hemianopia

* Involvement of Baum’s loop - superior fibers of optic radiations

* Contralateral parietal lobe

* Homonymous hemianopia

* Involvement of retrochiasmal regions such as optic tract, geniculate body, optic radiations.

* Sparing of the macula and more congruous field defect (both sides have the same extent of field loss) when the occipital cortex is involved.

Pearl PF0246: Lesions in the optic pathway

Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above.

* The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other.

* A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye.

* Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia.

* A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness).

* Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the instrument.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chalazion clamp

The given image is of chalazion clamp.

Chalazion clamp which consists of two limbs like forceps, which can be clamped with the help of a screw. The tip of one limb is flattened in the form of a round disc while the tip of the other arm has a small circular ring. It is used to fix the chalazion and achieve hemostasis during the incision and curettage operation.

Other options

Option A- Evisceration spatula consists of a small but stout rectangular blade with a slightly convex surface and blunt edges attached to a handle. It is used to separate out the uveal tissue from the sclera during evisceration operation.

Option C- Enucleation spoon. This is identified by the central cleavage that engages the optic nerve in enucleation.

Option D- Bone punch consists of a stout spring handle and two blades attached at a right angle. It is used to enlarge the bony opening during
dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) operation by punching the bone from the margins of the opening.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The glycosaminoglycan present in the cornea responsible for transparency is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratan sulfate

Keratan sulfate is present between the collagen fibrils in the cornea and plays a major role in corneal transparency.

Note:

Keratan sulfate is made of repeating units of N-acetyl glucosamine and galactose. 2 types of keratan sulfate are seen:

* Keratan sulfate I is present in the cornea.

* Keratan sulfate II is mainly present in the cartilage.

Both keratan sulfate I and dermatan sulfate (KS I and DS) play roles in corneal transparency. However, DS is widely distributed in the body, mainly in the skin. Hence, KS I is the single best choice for this question.

Other factors contributing to transparency of cornea are:

* Peculiar arrangement of corneal lamellae (Maurice theory)

* Peculiar refractive index of corneal lamellae (Goldmann theory)

* Avascularity of cornea

* Corneal crystallins

* Balance between intraocular pressure and swelling pressure

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The patient presents with miosis,anhidrosis and mild drooping of eyelids and a small pupil that remains small even in darkness. The likely diagnosis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Horner syndrome

The clinical scenario with a small sized pupil which does not dilate in response to darkness is due to sympathetic palsy  seen in Horner syndrome (miosis, anhydrosis, ptosis).

In a normal eye, the pupil dilates in response to dim light and constricts in response to bright light. Pupillary dilation is brought about by the contraction of dilator pupillae mediated by sympathetic innervation. Pupillary constriction is due to the contraction of sphincter pupillae mediated by parasympathetic innervation.

The difference in pupillary diameter is called anisocoria. A difference of up to 0.5 mm is common even in normal individuals.

Pearl PF0622: Horner's syndrome

Horner's Syndrome:

Horner's syndrome occurring due to occulo-sympathetic paresis is characterized by the classic triad of:

* Mild ptosis (due to paralysis of Muller's muscle).

* Miosis (due to paralysis of dilator pupillae).

* Reduced ipsilateral sweating (anhydrosis).

Other features include:

* Mild enophthalmos,

* Loss of cilio-spinal reflex,

* Heterochromia, i.e., the ipsilateral iris is lighter in colour,

* Pupil is slow to dilate, and there occurs slight elevation of lower eyelid.

Cocaine test (2% to 4%): Small pupils fail to dilate in Horner's syndrome.

In congenital Horner's syndrome, the additional features seen are heterochromia iridis and unilateral straight hair.

Pearl PF1404: Causes of small and dilated pupils

Causes of small pupils include

* Pontine hemorrhage

* Horner's syndrome

* Old age

* Argyll Robertson pupil

* Drugs and poisons (opiates, organophosphates)

Causes of dilated pupils include

* Holmes–Adie (myotonic) pupil

* Third nerve palsy

* Atropine

* Carbon monoxide

* Ethylene glycol

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not characteristic of the clinical condition given below?
options: Abnormal activity of p53 is seen in the pterygium tissue.
Decreased activity of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases is seen.
Destruction of Bowman's layer occurs when the pterygium invades the cornea.
Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the connective tissue of the conjunctiva occur.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the connective tissue of the conjunctiva occur.

Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the conjunctival connective tissue occurs in pinguecula (and not pterygium).

In pterygium, there is elastotic degeneration of collagen with fibrovascular proliferation.

It is important to distinguish a pterygium from a pinguecula. A pterygium, while histologically similar to a pinguecula, is distinguished by fibrovascular tissue that grows onto the cornea. Pingueculae do not have vascularized tissue and do not cross the limbus.

Pterygium is a subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea. It is a degenerative condition of the sub-conjunctival tissue and is never inflammatory. It occurs due to exposure to UV-B radiation and the most common site is the nasal.

It is made up of three parts-a "cap" (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge), a head, and a body.

Clinical features:

* Astigmatism with the rule - most common finding

* Stocker's line - deposition of iron on the advancing edge

* Fuchs islets - small, discrete, whitish flecks consisting of clusters of pterygial epithelial cells, often present at the advancing edge.

The differential diagnosis is pseudo pterygium.

Pterygium
Pseudo-pterygium

Degenerative process
Inflammatory process

Occurs in elderly
Can occur at any age

Situated at the palpebral aperture
Can occur at any site

Either progressive, regressive, or stationary
Always stationary

A probe cannot be passed underneath
A probe can be passed under the neck

The treatment for pterygium is usually excision. To prevent a recurrence, mitomycin C or 5 fluorouracil is used. Other methods:

* Auto-grafting- Conjunctival limbal autograft (CLAG) from the superior limbal conjunctiva is the best method.

* Bare sclera technique- high recurrence rate of 30 to 80%.

* PERFECT surgery- zero rates of recurrence. (PERFECT stands for Pterygium Extended Removal Followed by Extended Conjunctival Transplant)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old female patient presented for her first complete eye examination after a school vision screening found unequal visual acuity. Her parents have not noted any eye problems. Visual acuity in the right eye was 20/20 and the left eye is 20/80. The rest of the examination including Fundus exam was unremarkable, What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Amblyopia

The most probable diagnosis from the given scenario is Amblyopia.

Amblyopia is an uncorrectable decrease in vision in one or both eyes with no apparent structural abnormality seen to explain it. It is a diagnosis of exclusion. Generally, a difference of two lines or more on an eye chart test of visual acuity between the two eyes or a best-corrected vision of 20/30 or worse would be defined as amblyopia. For example, our patient has 20/20 vision with the right eye and only 20/80 with the left and the left eye even after best-corrected vision couldn't achieve <20/30 vision, the left eye is said to be amblyopic.

Clinical features:

* Decreased contrast sensitivity

* Diminution of vision

* Sunglass effect- brightness is less compared to the normal eye

* Crowding phenomenon- slipping of images

Treatment of choice:

* Occlusion of the normal eye (4 to 6 hours/day) using patches.

* Penalization: Blurring of vision using atropine.

Prism correction is not the right treatment as the child doesn't have strabismus.

Other options:

Option A: Brain lesion does not cause difference in visual acuity in both eyes.

Option B: Retinoblastoma can be identified by fundoscopy.

Option C: Congenital cataract presents with loss of red reflex immediately after birth.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents with chronic mucopurulent discharge from her left eye and swelling near the medial canthus. Which of the following is the treatment of choice in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dacryocystorhinostomy

The clinical vignette is suggestive of chronic dacryocystitis and the treatment of choice for chronic dacryocystitis is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) as it re-establishes the lacrimal drainage.

Dacryocystitis is the inflammation of the lacrimal sac. It generally affects infants and adults, most commonly females over 40 years of age. Congenital dacryocystitis is almost always chronic, while acquired dacryocystitis may be acute or chronic.

Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) surgery involves removal of the bone adjacent to the nasolacrimal sac and suturing the lacrimal sac with the lateral nasal mucosa. This allows tears to drain directly from the sac via a new low-resistance pathway into the middle meatus.

One of the sequelae of chronic dacryocystitis is mucocele formation, which when infected, leads to pyocele formation and finally lacrimal fibrosis. Treatment of lacrimal sac fibrosis is dacryocystectomy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 58-year-old man after his retirement party came with the complaint of sudden painless loss of vision in his left eye for the past 2 hours. Fundoscopic examination shows a similar picture given below. What is the most probable cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CRAO

The given fundoscopic image shows a cherry-red spot, which is a feature of CRAO.

Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO):

Risk factors include

* Heart disease

* Carotid artery disease

* Mucormycosis

* Varicella infection

* Radiation exposure

* Trauma

Etiology:

* Emboli - emboli having carotid artery or cardiac origin are the most common cause of CRAO. Other emboli are - cholesterol emboli, calcium emboli, and platelet fibrin emboli

* Atherosclerosis-related thrombosis

* Retinal arteritis with obliteration

* Angiospasm

* Raised intraocular pressure

* Thrombophilic disorders

Clinical features are

* Sudden painless loss of vision

* Severe oedema- the whole retina looks white in colour

* Cherry red spots

* Marked attenuation of arteries – thread-like arteries

* Interrupted blood flow in vein – cattle track appearance

Treatment is to dislodge the emboli by suddenly decreasing the IOP by I/V acetazolamide or ocular massage. Ocular massage is considered the most effective method. Other treatment options include IV mannitol, vasodilators (nitrates), fibrinolytic therapy, or laser photo disruption in some cases. In cases of giant cell arteritis, steroids are beneficial.

Pearl PF1384: Important causes of cherry-red spots

* Commotio retinae

* Central retinal and cilioretinal artery occlusion

* Metabolic storage diseases

* GM1 gangliosidosis

* Mucolipidosis type I (sialidosis)

* GM2 gangliosidosis (Tay-Sachs disease and Sandhoff disease)

* Farber disease

* Niemann–Pick disease

* Retinotoxicity due to specific agents, including quinine, dapsone, gentamicin, carbon monoxide, and methanol

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy presented with a white pupillary reflex for which enucleation was done. The histopathological examination of the specimen revealed Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. What could be the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinoblastoma

This child with a whitish pupillary reflex and Flexner-Winterstein rosettes on histopathological examination has retinoblastoma. Flexner Winterstein rosettes refer to an arrangement of columnar cells around a central lumen, which is highly characteristic of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma is a malignant proliferation of immature retinal neural cells and is the most common intraocular malignancy in children. It is associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14. It belongs to small round blue cell tumours because the immature retinal neural cells are seen as small round cells with large nuclei.

White pupillary reflex or leukocoria is the most common presenting feature, followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision. Image below showing leukocoria of left eye

Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features of a well-differentiated tumour include Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen.

The histopathological image of retinoblastoma is shown below.

Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy. The commonly used three-drug regimen is the CVE regimen consisting of Vincristine, Carboplatin, and Etoposide. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy.

Enucleation is done when

* The tumor involves more than half of the retina

* The optic nerve is involved

* Glaucoma is present and the anterior chamber is involved

Other options:

Option B - Medulloblastoma is a malignant embryonal tumor of childhood that occurs exclusively in the cerebellum. Patients usually present with headaches, ataxia, and signs of brainstem involvement.

Histologically, the tumor is very densely cellular. Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and elongated or crescent-shaped hyperchromatic nuclei. Tumor cells form Homer Wright rosettes. They express neuronal markers such as synaptophysin.

Option C - Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood. The child usually presents with rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis. There are 4 subtypes - embryonal, alveolar, botyroid, and pleomorphic. Cells show light microscopic features of striated muscle differentiation. Immunohistochemistry is positive for desmin.

Option D - Astrocytoma of the retina and optic nerve head is rare. It is usually asymptomatic and is most frequently seen in tuberous sclerosis. Fundus examination reveals a yellowish or white plaque, nodule, or mulberry-like lesion. These lesions are semitransparent peripherally and calcified centrally.

Image showing calcified astrocytoma:

Pearl PF1837: Histological Features of CNS Tumors

Pilocytic Astrocytomas:

* Biphasic architecture - loose microcystic component and dense fibrillary areas

* Bipolar cells (tumor cells): thin, long hairlike processes that are GFAP - positive.

* Rosenthal fibers: eosinophilic corkscrew - shaped inclusions

* Eosinophilic granular bodies: mulberry - like inclusions

Medulloblastoma:

* Very densely cellular, with sheets of small primitive appearing small blue cells

* Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei that are frequently elongated or crescent-shaped

* Tumor cells form Homer - Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes) with a central neuropil

Ependymoma:

* Ependymal rosettes: gland - like round or elongated structures that resemble the embryologic ependymal canal, with long, delicate processes extending into the lumen

* Perivascular pseudorosettes: perivascular nuclear - free zone consisting of thin ependymal processes radiating toward the central blood vessel

Oligodendroglioma:

* Fried - egg appearance: sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei containing finely granular chromatin (similar to normal oligodendrocytes) surrounded by a clear halo of vacuolated cytoplasm.

* Chicken - wire capillaries: a delicate network of anastomosing capillaries

Retinoblastoma:

* Composed of collections of small, round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei

* Flexner - Wintersteiner rosettes: arrangements of a single layer of tumor cells around an apparent lumen

* Homer - Wright rosettes: a ring of cells with an eosinophilic fibrillary center

* Fleurettes: retinoblastoma cells that have undergone greater photoreceptor differentiation and group together as a bouquet. Fleurettes lack mitosis or necrosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A contact lens user presents with the following clinical picture. He had watering, redness, and foreign body sensation in the eye for the past 2 months. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Giant papillary conjunctivitis

The clinical history of watering, redness, foreign body sensation in a contact lens user, along with the image showing giant papillae in the conjunctiva suggests a probable diagnosis of giant papillary conjunctivitis.

Giant papillary conjunctivitis is a severe form of mechanically induced papillary conjunctivitis. It is most commonly associated with contact lens wear. It can also be associated with ocular prostheses, exposed sutures, and scleral buckles.

The patients usually present with redness, foreign body sensation, increased mucus production, itching, blurring, and loss of contact lens tolerance. On examination, giant papillae are seen on the upper tarsal conjunctiva with hyperemia. Focal apical ulceration and whitish scarring may develop on larger papillae.

Papillae are reddish, flat-topped raised areas that give a red and velvety appearance to the tarsal conjunctiva These are the hyperplasia of the normal vascular system with glomerulus-like bunches of capillaries growing into the epithelium.

The image below shows papillae in the tarsal conjunctiva.

Treatment includes removing the offending cause. Mast cell stabilizers such as sodium cromoglycate, and drugs like azelastine and olopatadine which have combined antihistamine and mast cell stabilizing effects are effective. Steroids can be used for resistant cases.

Other options:

Option A - Trachoma is caused by chlamydia trachomatis. In acute trachoma, sago grain follicles are characteristically seen as shown below.

Option B - Follicular conjunctivitis has follicles which are greyish-white raised areas seen on fornices and palpebral conjunctiva. These are formed due to localized aggregations of lymphocytes in the sub-epithelial adenoid layer. It is most commonly caused by herpes and adenoviruses. The image is shown below.

Option D - In spring catarrh (vernal catarrh), cobblestone appearance is a papillary reaction in the palpebral conjunctiva, ropy discharge, and Maxwell–Lyon sign are present. Horner-Tranta’s spots which are discrete whitish raised dots along the limbus can also be seen. It is more common during summer.

Image showing Horner-Tranta’s spots.

Pearl PF1374: WHO Programme to Control Trachoma: SAFE Strategy

* S—Surgery: Trichiasis and entropion correction surgery → 3° prevention.

* A—Antibiotics: Oral azithromycin, topical 1% tetracycline, topical 1% azithromycin → 2° prevention

* F—Facial hygiene → 1° prevention.

* E—Environmental cleanliness → primordial prevention

Strategy depends on the prevalence of trachoma follicle in children (1–9 yrs)

* Prevalence >10% → SAFE

* 5 to 10% → FE

* < 5% → NO intervention

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with corneal scar has a visual acuity of 6/36, which improves to 6/18 with a pinhole. The most likely reason for this is ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Irregular astigmatism

The given findings suggest that the most likely reason is irregular astigmatism.

In refractive errors up to 3D, there is an improvement with pinhole to 6/6, if the macula is normal. Pinhole prevents the peripheral rays and also reduces the spherical aberration.

However, in this patient, it improved to only 6/18. A thing to note is that the corneal scar mentioned in the case would make the surface highly uneven, indicating irregular astigmatism. So, the best answer is irregular astigmatism.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A worried mother brought her son for vision examination when she noticed him reading a book too closely. She says he also narrows his eyes while watching television. Examination revealed myopia. Which of the following lens should be prescribed to correct this child's vision?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Concave

Concave lenses are used for correcting myopic errors.

Myopia, also known as 'short sight', is that dioptric condition of the eye in which, with the accommodation at rest, incident parallel rays come to a focus anterior to the light-sensitive layer of the retina.

Other options:

Convex lenses are used in the correction of hypermetropic eye and presbyopic eye.

Cylindrical lenses are used in the correction of astigmatism.

Pearl PF1369: Causes of Myopia

Myopia

Etiology

Axial myopia

(Most common)

Increase in the anteroposterior length of the eyeball.

Curvatural myopia

Increased curvature of the cornea, lens, or both

Positional myopia

Anterior placement of the crystalline lens in the eye

Index myopia

Increase in the refractive index of crystalline lens

Nocturnal myopia

Due to spherical aberration and accomodation

Pearl PF1370: Surgical correction of Myopia

Cornea-based procedures

Lens-based procedures

Laser-based:

Photorefractive keratectomy (PRK)

Laser in-situ keratomileusis (LASIK)(Most common)

1. Refractive lens exchange
2. Phakic intraocular lens
3. Clear lens extraction

Refractive lenticule extraction (ReLEx) (or)

Small incision lenticule extraction (SMILE)

Intracorneal ring segment (ICRS) implantation

Orthokeratology

Radial keratotomy (obsolete)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An 18-year-old boy presents with a history of injury to the eye caused while climbing a tree 5 days ago, resulting in pain, photophobia, and redness of the eye for 2 days. Slit-lamp examination reveals a lesion as shown below. Which among the following is a feature of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Satellite lesion

The given clinical vignette and the image suggest that it is a fungal corneal ulcer. Satellite lesions are a feature of fungal ulcers.

A fungal corneal ulcer is usually caused by trauma with vegetative or organic matter. Signs are more pronounced than symptoms. The corneal ulcer appears dry.

Causative organisms :

* Aspergillus

* Fusarium

* Candida albicans

Signs of a fungal ulcer:

* Irregular margins of the ulcer.

* Presence of satellite lesions surrounding the ulcer.

* An immune ring (Wesseley) may be seen around the ulcer due to the deposition of the immune complexes.

* Slough is usually dry, with feathery borders surrounded by a yellow line of demarcation.

* Hypopyon may be present or absent. If present, it is thick, immobile due to the direct invasion of the fungal hyphae into the anterior chamber.

Treatment:

* Topical drugs: These include topical natamycin, voriconazole or amphotericin B drops which are effective against Aspergillus and Fusarium. Nystatin is effective against Candida.

* Systemic drugs: Severe ulcers with hypopyon, perforation or suspected endophthalmitis might warrant the use of oral antifungal agents such as ketoconazole or voriconazole.

Other options :

Option A: Reverse hypopyon is the collection of emulsified silicone oil in the anterior chamber. This can lead to complications such as glaucoma.

Option B: Dendritic ulcer is seen in epithelial keratitis caused by herpes simplex virus. An image of a dendritic ulcer with fluorescein dye is as shown below

Option C: Ring abscess is seen in helminthic keratitis, especially by acanthamoeba. There is gradual enlargement and coalescence of infiltrates which forms an abcess.

Pearl PF1375: Clinical differential diagnosis of corneal ulcer

Bacterial
Fungal
Viral
Parasitic

Risk factors

Contact lens wear

Trauma

Chronic steroid use

Anesthetic cornea

Dry eyes

Exposure keratopathy

Trauma with vegetable matter

Low immunity

Recurrent attacks

Contact lens wear

Exposure to contaminated water (acanthamoeba)

Clinical features

Hypopyon is fluid and mobile

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is likely to have a rapid course, with deep corneal necrosis.

Less pain and watering compared to the extent of vision loss and signs.

Tend to be indolent but progressive

Hypopyon is thick, immobile.

Relatively more pain and watering compared to the extent of vision loss and signs.

Recurrences are characteristic.

Disproportionately severe pain is a characteristic feature.

Indolent course and in initial stages, often mistaken to be viral/ fungal infection, leading to a delay in diagnosis

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An industrial worker was admitted to the hospital after an eye injury sustained while cutting stone with a hammer and iron chisel. A foreign body was suspected to be impacted in his eye. Which of the following is the best investigation for foreign body localization?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CT

CT scan is the best method for intraocular foreign body (IOFB) localization.

The foreign bodies most likely to penetrate and be retained in the eye are minute chips of iron or steel. While chipping stone with an iron chisel, the chip of the iron chisel is more likely to enter the eye than the stone. A foreign body entering the eye may cause damage by:

* mechanical effects

* introduction of infection

* reacting with the intraocular tissues

Anteroposterior and lateral view X-rays are recommended for locating an IOFB as most foreign bodies are radio-opaque. Ultrasonographic localization can tell the position of even non-radiopaque foreign bodies. CT scan is the best method of IOFB localization.

MRI is contraindicated for metallic IOFB.MRI can be detrimental for a patient with a history of an intraocular foreign body (IOFB) after cutting stone with a hammer and chisel. It can cause further damage by producing movements of the foreign body if it is magnetic. The use of MRI is contraindicated for metallic (iron) foreign bodies and is not recommended as a screening procedure.

Management: A foreign body should always be removed unless:

* it is inert and probably sterile

* little damage has been done to vision

* the process of removal will destroy sight

Siderosis bulbi refers to the ocular degenerative changes produced by an iron foreign body. It usually occurs 2 months to 2 years after the injury. This condition is due to the electrolytic dissociation of the metal by an intrinsic resting current in the eye which disseminates the metal, combining it with cellular proteins and cause atrophy.

Clinical features:

* Iris: first stained greenish and later turns reddish-brown, causing heterochromia iridis.

* Pupil: iron deposition in sphincter leads to mydriasis.

* Lens: iron deposition in a radial fashion on the anterior capsule of the lens, leading to anterior capsular cataract.

* Retina: pigmentary retinopathy; followed by atrophy of the retina and retinal pigmentary epithelium.

* Secondary open-angle Glaucoma: due to damage to the trabecular meshwork.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the condition shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Entropion

The image shows the inward rolling of the eyelid margin which is called entropion.

Entropion refers to the inward rolling and rotation of the lid margin towards the globe. It is more common in the lower lid. In longstanding cases of entropion, pseudotrichiasis is seen, which may cause corneal irritation and erosions.

Causes include:

* Horizontal lid laxity

* Vertical lid instability

* Over-riding of the pretarsal by the preseptal orbicularis during lid closure

* Orbital septum laxity

Ectropion refers to the outward turning of the lid margin.

Trichiasis refers to the inward misdirection of cilia, which usually rub against the eyeball with the normal position of the lid margin.

Pearl PF1635: Surgical Modalities Used in Correcting Entropion

Cicatricial entropion

Senile entropion

Anterior lamellar resection

Transverse everting suture

Tarsal wedge resection

Weiss operation

Transposition of the tarsoconjunctival wedge. (Modified Ketssey’s operation)

Plication of lower lid retractors (Jones operation).

Posterior lamellar graft

Quickert procedure

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which is the most common cause of preventable childhood blindness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin A deficiency

The most common cause of preventable childhood blindness is vitamin A deficiency.

The most common cause of blindness (including adults), is however, cataract.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the best line of treatment in a 3-year-old child presenting with a recent onset of 15-degree accommodative esotropia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Refractive correction

The best line of treatment in accommodative esotropia is a refractive correction.

Esotropia for distance is corrected by the treatment of hypermetropia: convex glasses

Esotropia for near is corrected by +3DS lens.

Algorithm for the management of accommodative esotropia is as follows:

* R: Refractive correction: Glasses/Miotics

* O: Orthoptics/Occlusion: for amblyopia

* O: Operative correction: for non-accommodative component

* P: Prism correction: for remaining error

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following surgeries use this instrument?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dacryocystorhinostomy

The given image is that of a Bone punch and it is used in dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) operation.

Bone punch consists of a stout spring handle and two blades attached at a right angle. It is used to enlarge the bony opening during dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) operation by punching the bone from the margins of the opening.

The given set of instruments is used for Dacryocystorhinostomy.

Instrument 1 shows Muller's self-retaining lacrimal wound retractor. It is made up of two limbs with three curved pins on each for engaging the edges of the skin incision. The limbs are kept in a retracted position with the help of a fixing screw.

* Used to retract the skin during surgery on the lacrimal sac (e.g. DCT or DCR).

Instrument 2 shows Nettleship's lacrimal punctum dilator. lt has a cylindrical corrugated metal handle with a conical pointed tip.

* Used to dilate the punctum and canaliculus during syringing, probing, dacryocystography, DCT, and DCR procedures.

Instrument 3 shows Bowman's lacrimal probe. It has blunt ends with a central stable platform.

* Uses:

* To probe the lacrimal gland in the management of congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction

* To identify the lacrimal sac during DCR and DCT.

Instrument 4 shows Lacrimal cannula. It is a long curved hypodermic needle with a blunt tip.

* Uses:

* For syringing the lacrimal passages

* For injecting air, tryphan blue dye, pilocarpine, and balanced salt solution in the anterior chamber during intraocular surgery

Instrument 5 shows a Bone punch. It consists of a stout spring handle and two blades attached at a right angle. The upper blade has a small hole with a sharp cutting edge. The lower blade has a cup-like depression.

* Used to enlarge the bony opening during DCR operation by punching the bone from the margins of the opening.

Instrument 6 shows Chisel. It consists of a blade having a sharp-cutting straight edge with one surface beveled. It has a long and stout handle.

* Uses to cut the bone during DCR and orbitotomy operations.

Instrument 7 shows Hammer. It is a small steel hammer attached to a corrugated handle.

* Used to hammer the chisel during DCR and orbitotomy operations.

Instrument 8 shows Lacrimal sac dissector and curette. It is a cylindrical instrument, one end of which is a blunt-tipped dissector, and the other end is curetted.

* Used to curette the lacrimal sac in lacrimal sac surgery.

Instrument 9 shows Freer's periosteum elevator. It has a rounded handle with two slightly curved, tear-drop tips.

* Used for blunt debulking and lifting periosteum from bones in confined areas. It is used in endoscopic septoplasty and DCR.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: 3 months following cataract surgery, a patient comes with complaints of decreased visual acuity. On examination, posterior capsular opacification is seen. What type of laser can be used to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nd-Yag laser

The given history mentions decreased visual acuity 3 months post-cataract surgery and the presence of posterior capsular opacification is suggestive of after-cataract. A posterior capsulotomy (creating a hole in the posterior capsule) using an Nd: YAG laser is the mainstay of treatment.

Posterior capsular opacification, otherwise known as after cataract/secondary cataract, is the most common late complication of uncomplicated cataract surgery. It occurs due to the proliferation of lens epithelial cells that have been left out inside the capsular bag after cataract surgery. The rate of posterior capsule opacification following extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) and phacoemulsification varies with the age of the patient, the surgeon, the surgical technique, the type of intraocular lens used, and the duration after surgery.

Symptoms of after cataract include:

* Reduction of visual acuity

* Slowly worsening blurring

* Glare and occasionally monocular diplopia

They can present in different patterns such as:

* Elschnig's pearls: present as vacuolated (pearl-type) grape-like clusters of swollen cells

* Soemmering's ring: present as a white annular proliferation that is formed at the periphery of the capsular bag.

* Fibrosis type: present as fibroblastic metaplasia of the epithelial cells

Treatment:

* Nd-YAG laser capsulotomy: The laser used in posterior capsulotomy is Nd: YAG laser (1064 nm) whose principle is photodisruption. The plasma produced at the laser target expands and disrupts the tissues creating an opening.

* Surgical treatment: Posterior capsular opacification is managed by creating an opening on the posterior capsule along the visual axis, a procedure called a posterior capsulotomy.

Pearl PF1396: Complications of cataract surgery

Early postoperative complications

Occurs within the first few days to 4 weeks.

* Endophthalmitis

* Retained lens matter

* Corneal edema

* Wound leak and dehiscence

* Toxic anterior segment syndrome

Late postoperative complications

Occurs within months to years.

* Posterior capsule opacification (most common)

* Cystoid macular edema

* Secondary glaucoma

* Retinal detachment

* Intraocular lens malpositions:

* Windshield wiper syndrome— intraocular lens haptic rubs on the endothelium

* Sunset syndrome—inferior subluxation

* Sunrise syndrome—superior subluxation

* Complete dislocation of the intraocular lens.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy has been observed by his parents to be increasingly clumsy for the past 6 months. On physical examination, there is a cauliflower-like growth in the left eye along with leukocoria and an absent red reflex. The microscopic appearance of the specimen shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. Which is the causative gene in the given condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rb gene

The clinical history of a boy presenting with progressive clumsiness and eye findings such as leucocoria, absent red reflex, and cauliflower like growth along with the microscopic finding of Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes is highly suggestive of retinoblastoma, which occurs due to a mutation in the Rb gene located on chromosome 13q14.

Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children. White pupillary reflex or leukocoria is the most common presenting feature, followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision.

Clinical features of retinoblastoma:

* Present within the first two years of life

* Leukocoria

* Strabismus

* Painful red eye with secondary glaucoma

* Orbital inflammation mimicking orbital or pre-septal cellulitis.

* Orbital invasion or visible extraocular growth may occur in neglected cases.

* Metastatic disease involving regional lymph nodes and the brain before the detection of ocular involvement is rare.

Signs:

* An intraretinal tumor is a homogeneous, dome-shaped white lesion that becomes irregular, often with white flecks of calcification.

* An endophytic tumor projects into the vitreous as a white mass that may "seed" into the gel.

* An exophytic tumor forms multilobular subretinal white masses and causes an overlying retinal detachment.

Investigations:

* Red reflex testing with a direct ophthalmoscope is a simple screening test for leukocoria.

* Dilated fundus examination using indirect ophthalmoscope

* MRI of the orbit + brain is the investigation of choice.

The HPE image below shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, the clustering of small blue cuboidal or short columnar cells around a central lumen.

Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy. The commonly used three-drug regimen is the CVE regimen consisting of vincristine, carboplatin, and etoposide. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy. Enucleation is done when:

* Tumor involves more than half of the retina

* Optic nerve is involved

* Glaucoma is present and the anterior chamber is involved

In the stage of extraocular extension, the globe bursts through the sclera, usually near the limbus or the optic disc. This is followed by rapid fungation and involvement of extraocular tissues resulting in marked proptosis. Distant metastasis occurs through the lymphatic spread and the direct extension by continuity to the optic nerve and brain.

Other options:

Option B: COL5A1 mutation affects type 5 collagen. This mutation is seen in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Option C: Retinitis pigmentosa occurs due to inherited or acquired mutations in the rhodopsin gene.

Option D: NOTCH1 is the most commonly affected gene in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL).
