questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 68-year-old female patient has had a diabetic cataract for the past 3 months. Accumulation of which of the following substances is responsible for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sorbitol + fructose

A diabetic cataract occurs due to the accumulation of sorbitol and fructose within the lens.

In diabetic patients, increased levels of blood glucose lead to high levels of glucose in the aqueous humor. The excess glucose in the aqueous humor is metabolized into sorbitol through the polyol pathway by the enzyme aldose reductase. Sorbitol is then converted to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase but at a much slower rate. In addition, the polar nature of sorbitol prevents its intracellular removal through diffusion.

Sorbitol and fructose accumulate in the lens and the osmotic stress so produced results in overhydration, hydropic lens fibers, and apoptosis of the lens epithelial cells. Thus, the secondary osmotic overhydration is responsible for cortical opacities in a distinct pattern causing snowflake cataracts as shown below.

Pearl PF1394: Diseases and Associated Cataracts - Images

Wilson's Disease/Chalcosis: Sunflower Cataract

Diabetes mellitus:  Snowflake cataract

Blunt trauma: May present as rosette-shaped cataract

Myotonic dystrophy - Christmas tree cataract

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 70-year-old patient who was using presbyopic glasses for the past few years is now able to comfortably read the newspaper without the glasses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Index myopia

The clinical scenario of improvement in near vision of a presbyopic patient is termed the second sight phenomenon. This is seen due to index myopia caused by the formation of nuclear cataracts.

Presbyopia, also known as the eyesight of old age, is a condition of physiological insufficiency of accommodation leading to a progressive fall in near vision. The treatment of presbyopia is the prescription of appropriate convex glasses for near work.

In nuclear cataracts, nuclear sclerosis occurs leading to an increase in refractive index. This leads to progressive myopia known as index myopia. When a presbyopic patient develops a nuclear cataract, this increase in the refractive index of the lens compensates for the physiological insufficiency of accommodation that the patient has.

Thus, a patient with presbyopia may be able to read again, without the aid of spectacles due to this improvement in near vision, termed second sight. At the same time, this increased refractive index causes a deterioration in far vision.

Option B: Index hypermetropia occurs in cortical cataracts and sclerosis that lead to a decrease in the refractive index of the lens in old age. In such patients, there will be worsening of the near vision which does not align with the history of a presbyopic being able to read with his glasses.

Option C: Presbyopia occurs due to a decrease in the accommodative power of the crystalline lens with increasing age, and thus does not regress spontaneously. It can however be easily corrected with the prescription of appropriate convex glasses for near work.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A child has elevated liver enzyme levels. A ring-like structure is noted on ocular examination as shown in the image below. Which of the following is the cause for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Copper

This clinical scenario of elevated liver enzymes and Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring seen in the image is suggestive of Wilson's disease. KF ring is formed due to the deposition of copper in Descemet’s membrane of the cornea.

Wilsons disease:

The autosomal-recessive disease is caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, which encodes a membrane-bound, copper-transporting ATPase.

Clinical symptoms:

* Hepatitis and cirrhosis

* Behavioral disturbances

* Wing beating tremor

* Ophthalmic characteristics:

* Deposition of copper in the posterior capsule of the lens resulting in sunflower cataract

* KF ring

Kayser-Fleischer ring (KF) Ring:

* KF ring is a golden-brown ring formed due to the deposition of copper in Descemet’s membrane of the cornea

* Characteristically observed in Wilson's disease but is not pathognomonic

* Does not interfere with vision

* Present in almost all patients of Wilson's disease with neurological/psychiatric symptoms

* Present only in 30–50% of patients diagnosed in the hepatic or presymptomatic state, therefore the absence of KF rings does not exclude the diagnosis of Wilson's disease

The image below is that of a patient with a KF ring and a sunflower cataract:

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to you with pain and redness in the right eye following an injury during welding. On examination, the image as seen below is observed. Which of the following is the appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Removal by 26G needle

A history of injury to the eye while welding along with the the given image is suggestive of a superficial foreign body in the eye. Removal of the foreign body using a 26G needle is the next step in the management of this patient.

Foreign bodies, which are usually small particles of dust, iron, steel, etc., may impinge upon the conjunctiva or cornea and cause sudden discomfort and reflex blinking. The foreign body sticks to the palpebral conjunctiva and is liable to be dragged across the cornea, causing excoriation. Particles of steel and iron fly straight onto the cornea and penetrate the epithelium or substantia propria.

Fluorescein or oblique illumination of the anesthetized eye with a slit lamp can be used to determine the position of a foreign body. If not removed, they expose the cornea to organisms in the conjunctival sac causing ulceration and extrusion of the foreign body in the slough. The ulcer thus formed may heal, but if virulent organisms are present, a spreading ulcer, with or without hypopyon, may develop.

Foreign bodies are managed by removal as soon as possible.

* If the foreign body is found lying loose in either fornix, it can be removed with a clean swab after everting the eyelids.

* Double-eversion of the upper eyelid with a Desmarres retractor can be done if required.

* If embedded in the bulbar conjunctiva or cornea, it can be removed by a foreign body spud or fine forceps under topical anesthesia.

* A disposable hypodermic (26 or 27 gauge) needle can be used.

Following removal in all cases, an antibiotic ointment should be applied and the eye kept bandaged for a day. Foreign bodies in the eye are extremely common in industrial workers, especially in those working with grinding tools, lathe work, or hammering on a chisel, and thus eye must be protected by educative notices, lectures, and the provision of comfortable goggles.

Cases of ferruginous intraocular foreign bodies (IOFB) may give rise to anterior capsular cataracts and reddish-brown staining of the iris leading to heterochromia iridis. MRI is contraindicated here and instead, CT with axial and coronal cuts is used to localize a metallic IOFB. Magnetic removal is done for the removal of ferrous foreign bodies.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient who presents to the OPD has a visual field defect as shown below. What is the probable site of the lesion based on the image displayed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3

The visual field defect in the image is indicative of bitemporal hemianopia, so the probable site of the lesion is the optic chiasma marked as 3 in the image given.

Options marked in the image are:

1. Left optic nerve
3. Otic chiasma
4. Left optic tract
5. Left lateral geniculate nucleus

Hemianopia or hemianopsia refers to loss of sight in half the visual field. Bitemporal hemianopia refers to loss of sight in the temporal halves of the visual field, seen in lesions affecting the optic chiasma. The most common cause of this is pituitary gland tumours. Other causes include suprasellar aneurysms, chronic arachnoiditis, and suprasellar tumours like craniopharyngioma and suprasellar meningioma.

Damage to the middle part of the optic chiasm affects fibres crossing at the nasal retina of each eye, leaving the uncrossed fibres from the temporal retinas intact. The resulting loss of vision is confined to the temporal visual field of each eye and this is known as bitemporal hemianopia. It is also called heteronymous hemianopia to emphasize the fact that the parts of the visual field that are lost in each eye do not overlap.

Individuals with this condition are able to see in both left and right central visual fields, with both eyes open. However, all information from the most peripheral parts of visual fields (which are seen only by the nasal retinas) is lost.

Pearl PF1675: Lesions in the optic pathway

Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above.

* The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other.

* A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye.

* Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia.

* A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness).

* Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Fundoscopy findings are shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CRAO

The given fundus picture showing a cherry-red spot is suggestive of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO).

Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO):

Risk factors include:

* Heart disease

* Carotid artery disease

* Mucormycosis

* Varicella infection

* Radiation exposure

* Trauma

Etiology:

* Emboli - emboli having carotid artery or cardiac origin are the most common cause of CRAO. Other emboli are - cholesterol emboli, calcium emboli, and platelet fibrin emboli

* Atherosclerosis-related thrombosis

* Retinal arteritis with obliteration

* Angiospasm

* Raised intraocular pressure

* Thrombophilic disorders

Clinical features are:

* Sudden painless loss of vision

* Amaurosis fugax - transient monocular blindness that is due to ischemia. As seen in this patient.

* Direct pupillary reflex is absent

* Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is positive

Fundus examination shows:

* Marked attenuation of arteries – thread like arteries

* Interrupted blood flow in vein – cattle track appearance

* Cherry red spot

* Severe edema

* Retinal pallor

Treatment is to dislodge the emboli by suddenly decreasing the IOP by I/V acetazolamide or ocular massage. Ocular massage is considered the most effective method. Other treatment options include IV mannitol, vasodilators (nitrates), fibrinolytic therapy, or laser photo disruption in some cases. In cases of giant cell arteritis, steroids are beneficial.

Other options:

Option B: In CRVO, funduscopy shows engorged and tortuous retinal veins, massive retinal hemorrhages with splashed tomato appearance, and cotton wool spots.

Option C: Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy can have microaneurysms, intraretinal hemorrhage, and mild intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA). Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is characterized by neovascularization at the optic disc (NVD) or neovascularization elsewhere (NVE).

Option D: In cystoid macular edema, the fundus shows a dull foveal reflex/absent foveal reflex. The fluorescein angiography image shows a flower petal pattern.

Pearl PF1384: Important causes of cherry-red spots

* Commotio retinae

* Central retinal and cilioretinal artery occlusion

* Metabolic storage diseases

* GM1 gangliosidosis

* Mucolipidosis type I (sialidosis)

* GM2 gangliosidosis (Tay-Sachs disease and Sandhoff disease)

* Farber disease

* Niemann–Pick disease

* Retinotoxicity due to specific agents, including quinine, dapsone, gentamicin, carbon monoxide, and methanol

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In relation to which wall of the orbit is the canaliculi that opens into the lacrimal sac present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Medial wall

The canaliculi that open into the lacrimal sac are present in relation to the medial wall of the orbit.

Anatomy

The lacrimal drainage system consists of the following structures:

* The puncta are openings on the lid margin.

* Each canaliculus (superior and inferior) has two parts:

* Vertical (2 mm)

* Horizontal (8 mm)

* The superior and inferior canaliculi usually unite to form the common canaliculus, which opens into the lateral wall of the lacrimal sac.

* A small flap of mucosa (Rosenmüller valve) overhangs the junction of the common canaliculus and the lacrimal sac and prevents the reflux of tears into the canaliculi.

* The lacrimal sac is 10–12 mm long and lies in the lacrimal fossa. The lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla separate the lacrimal sac from the middle meatus of the nasal cavity.

* The nasolacrimal duct is 12–18 mm long and is directed downwards, backward, and laterally.

Image: Lacrimal apparatus

Pearl PF1078: Structures opening into meatuses of nose

* Inferior meatus: Nasolacrimal duct, guarded by the valve of Hasner

* Middle meatus: Frontal sinus, maxillary sinus, anterior ethmoidal sinus. All these together form the osteo-meatal complex or Picadle’s circle.

* Superior meatus: Posterior ethmoidal sinus

* Sphenoethmoidal recess: Sphenoid sinus

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The SAFE strategy given by WHO forms the mainstay of the management of trachoma. What does the S in this acronym represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Surgery

The S in the acronym stands for surgery.

Trachoma is treated according to the WHO classification using the SAFEstrategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial hygiene, and Environmental improvement). Azithromycin is the antibiotic of choice, and surgery involves the correction of trichiasis and entropion. In case of significant corneal scarring, penetrating keratoplasty is done.

Trachoma is a form of chronic infective conjunctivitis and is one of the leading causes of blindness. It is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, more specifically the TRIC (trachoma inclusion conjunctivitis) serovars A, B, Ba, C. It has an ‘active’ inflammatory stage and a ‘cicatricial’ chronic stage. The active inflammatory stage is more prevalent in children and presents with nonspecific symptoms of ocular irritation, foreign body sensation, and discharge (often mild symptoms). Examination findings at this stage show:

* Conjunctival follicles contain Leber cells (multinucleated lymphocytes)

* Corneal Herbert's follicles (similar to conjunctival follicles)

The cicatricial chronic stage is seen in middle age. The patient complains of pain, lacrimation, photophobia and later blurring, and finally loss of vision. Conjunctiva shows concretions (whitish deposits of inspissated mucus in depressions called glands of Henle). Corneal signs include:

* Herbert pits (pitted scars in the limbal which are remnants of healed Herbert follicles)

* Corneal opacity is seen in later stages.

The below image shows Herbert's pits.

There can be associated trichiasis ( when at least one eyelash rubs the eyeball) and entropion.

At present WHO grading with `FISTO’ is in use.

Pearl PF1843: WHO Programme to Control Trachoma: SAFE Strategy

* S—Surgery: Trichiasis and entropion correction surgery → 3° prevention.

* A—Antibiotics: Oral azithromycin, topical 1% tetracycline, topical 1% azithromycin → 2° prevention

* F—Facial hygiene → 1° prevention.

* E—Environmental cleanliness → primordial prevention

The strategy depends on the prevalence of trachoma follicle in children (aged 1–9 yrs)

* >10% → Mass antibiotic treatment at the community level and FE measures

* 5 to 10% → Targeted antibiotic treatment (affected families) and FE measures

* < 5% → FE measures

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the yoke muscle of the right lateral rectus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left medial rectus

The right lateral rectus and left medial rectus represent a pair of yoke muscles.

Yoke muscles are also known as contralateral synergists. They are pair of muscles, one from each eye, which contracts simultaneously during version movements. Version movements also known as conjugate movements are synchronous (simultaneous) symmetric movements of both eyes in the same direction.

Examples:

* Right MR and Left LR

* Right LR and Left MR

* Right SO and Left IR

* Right IO and Left SR

* Right SR and Left IO

* Right IR and Left SO

(MR: Medial rectus; LR: Lateral rectus; SO: Superior oblique; IO: Inferior oblique; SR: Superior rectus; IR: Inferior rectus.)

These pairs of contralateral synergists receive equal and simultaneous innervation during version movements according to Herring’s Law of Equal Innervation.

Pearl PF1399: Laws governing ocular movements

Sherrington’s Law of Reciprocal Innervation

During ocular motility, an increased flow of innervation to the contracting muscle is accompanied by the decreased flow of innervation to the relaxing antagonist muscle.

Example:

During dextroversion, an increased innervation flow to the right lateral rectus (LR) and left medial rectus (MR) is accompanied by decreased flow to the right MR and left LR.

Herring’s Law of Equal Innervation

According to this law, equal and simultaneous innervation flows from the brain to the contralateral synergists and contralateral antagonists.

Example:

* During convergence: Both medial recti get equal innervation

* During dextroversion: Right LR and left MR get equal innervation

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy presents to the outpatient department with complaints of itching and a foreign body sensation in his eye. Upon examination, a shield ulcer is observed. The condition commonly associated with these findings is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Spring catarrh

Considering the symptoms of itching and foreign body sensation in the eye, and the presence of a shield ulcer, the most likely condition in this context is Spring catarrh.

Spring catarrh, or vernal keratoconjunctivitis, is a chronic form of allergic conjunctivitis. It typically occurs seasonally, often in the spring and summer. It presents with symptoms such as itching, foreign body sensation, and mucous discharge. While shield ulcers are not the primary feature of spring catarrh, severe and chronic cases may lead to corneal complications, including ulcers.

Classical features of conjunctiva in VKC:

Palpebral VKC

* Cobblestone papillae: upper tarsal conjunctiva

* Associated with ropy discharge

* Maxwell–Lyon sign: pseudomembrane formation of the upper lid when everted and exposed to heat

* Limbal VKC: Horner–Trantas spots are white dots consisting of eosinophils and epithelial debris in the limbal area.

Corneal signs in VKC:

* Shield ulcers

* Vernal plaques

* Subepithelial scarring

* Pseudo-gerontoxon resembles arcus senilus; it has a cupid's bow outline

The condition presents in three types, which are :

* Palpebral, affecting the upper tarsal conjunctiva, characterised by hypertrophied 'cobblestone' papillae

* Bulbar-limbal, characterised by dusky red triangular congestion of the conjunctiva, gelatinous limbal papillae and Horner-Tranta's spots that are formed due to eosinophils and epithelial debris at the limbus

* Mixed

Treatment of VKC includes allergen avoidance, antihistaminics, steroids, and immunomodulators both topical and systemic depending on the severity of the disease.

The image below represents Horner-Trantas spots.

The above below depicts cobblestone appearance:

Other options:

Option A) Autoimmune conditions can affect the eyes, but a shield ulcer in a child would not be a common presentation for autoimmune diseases.

Option C) Trachoma is an eye infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. It can lead to chronic inflammation, scarring, and the development of a shield ulcer. However, trachoma is more commonly associated with chronic conjunctivitis and trichiasis (in-turned eyelashes) than with a shield ulcer.

Option D) Tuberculosis is not commonly associated with a shield ulcer in the eye. Ocular tuberculosis can manifest in various ways, but itching and a shield ulcer are not typical features.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 42-year-old female who is on antitubercular therapy (ATT) experiences red-green color discrimination issues. Which of the following ATT drugs is most likely responsible for this side effect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ethambutol

The most likely ATT drug responsible for the red-green color discrimination issue in this case is ethambutol. It is important to monitor patients on this drug for visual side effects and, if necessary, consider dosage adjustments or discontinuation under medical supervision.

Ethambutol inhibits arabinose transferase III, thereby decreasing arabinogalactan biosynthesis. This results in, disruption in mycobacterial cell wall synthesis. It is primarily excreted unchanged by kidneys and accumulation occurs in renal failure. Ethambutol does not undergo hepatic metabolism and can be safely prescribed for the treatment of TB in patients with hepatitis.

Optic neuritis resulting in decreased visual acuity and loss of ability to differentiate red from green is the most serious adverse effect of ethambutol. It is a dose-dependent adverse effect that can be unilateral or bilateral.

Tests of visual acuity and red-green discrimination before the start of therapy and periodically thereafter are recommended.

Other options:

Option A:Isoniazid is known for causing peripheral neuropathy and hepatotoxicity as potential side effects.

Option C: Pyrazinamide is more commonly associated with hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia.

Option D: Rifampicinis known for causing orange discoloration of body fluids.

Pearl PF0763: Key points on the first line drugs used in the treatment of TB

Drugs
Isoniazid
Rifamycins
Pyrazinamide
Ethambutol

Mechanism of action
Blocks mycolic acid synthesis.
Inhibition of RNA polymerase, leading to the inhibition of RNA synthesis.
Inhibition of fatty acid synthase-I, leading to the inhibition of the cell membrane.
Inhibition of arabinosyl transferase, leading to a reduction in arabinogalactan needed for the cell wall.

Unique side effects

Shoulder hand syndrome and CNS side effects.

Orange urine, sweat, and tears. Flu-like symptoms with intermittent dosing.

The most hepatotoxic drug. It also causes hyperuricemia.

Optic neuritis and hence, not preferred in children.

Mechanism of resistance

Kat G mutation- the most severe form of resistance.

Inh a gene overexpression-  confers cross-resistance with ethionamide.

Mutation in rpoB- the gene coding for the β subunit of RNA polymerase.

Mutation of the Pnca gene.

Mutations in the embB gene.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with complete anopia in the right eye. The lesion would be present in which specific anatomical structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right optic nerve

The most likely site of the lesion causing unilateral complete anopia in the right eye is (c) Right optic nerve. This suggests that there is a problem affecting the visual information from the right eye before the optic chiasma.

Unilateral complete anopia refers to complete blindness in one eye. To determine the location of the lesion, we need to understand the visual pathway:

Right optic radiation: The optic radiation transmits visual information from the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Lesions in the optic radiation typically lead to homonymous visual field defects (loss of vision on the same side in both eyes). Since the patient presents with unilateral anopia in the right eye, the optic radiation is less likely to be the site of the lesion.

Optic chiasma: The optic chiasma is where the optic nerves partially cross. Lesions at the optic chiasma often result in bitemporal hemianopia, affecting the temporal visual fields of both eyes. Given that the patient's symptoms are unilateral, the optic chiasma is less likely to be the site of the lesion.

Right optic nerve: The optic nerve carries visual information from the eye to the optic chiasma. A lesion in the right optic nerve would lead to unilateral blindness (anopia) in the right eye, making it a likely site of the lesion in this case.

Right optic tract: The optic tract carries visual information from the optic chiasma to the visual cortex. Lesions in the optic tract could lead to homonymous visual field defects. Since the patient's anopia is unilateral, the right optic tract is less likely to be the site of the lesion.

Pearl PF1675: Lesions in the optic pathway

Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above.

* The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other.

* A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye.

* Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia.

* A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness).

* Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with the complaint of blurring of vision. On examination, you note that there are aqueous flares with numerous keratic precipitates. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iridocyclitis

The features of aqueous flares and keratic precipitates indicate a diagnosis of Fuch's heterochromic iridocyclitis (FHI).

Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is a chronic, non-granulomatous anterior uveitis, that is usually unilateral. It is normally seen in middle-aged people who may complain of symptoms such as blurring of vision and persistent floaters.

Heterochromia iridis (the affected eye is hypochromic/hyperchromic) is noted in FHI. Rubeosis iridis and posterior subcapsular cataract are also fairly common findings.

On examination, stellate keratic precipitates known as endothelial dusting are seen. Tiny crystals (Russell bodies) and iris nodules (Koeppe nodules)  may also be found on the iris surface. Iris atrophy which appears as a smooth-looking iris can also be seen.

Long-term monitoring is indicated to detect glaucoma and other complications.

The below image shows an example of heterochromia iridis (the left eye is hypochromic when compared to the right eye).

Other options:

(a) Intermediate uveitis: Intermediate uveitis primarily involves inflammation in the vitreous humor, which is the jelly-like substance in the middle of the eye. It is less likely to present with aqueous flares and keratic precipitates, making it an incorrect option.

(c) Posterior uveitis: Posterior uveitis involves inflammation in the posterior segment of the eye, including the choroid and retina. Aqueous flares and keratic precipitates are less likely to be observed in posterior uveitis, making it an incorrect option.

(d) Toxoplasma uveitis: Toxoplasma uveitis is a specific type of uveitis caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii. While it may involve the anterior or posterior segment of the eye, the presence of aqueous flares and keratic precipitates is not specific to Toxoplasma uveitis alone.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient was diagnosed with glaucoma. What is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prostaglandin analogues

Prostaglandin analogues are the drug of choice for glaucoma.  This class of anti-glaucoma drugs acts by increasing the uveo-scleral outflow.

Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analog and a commonly used medication for glaucoma. Prostaglandin analogs are often preferred due to their effectiveness and once-daily dosing convenience.

Topical PGF2 alpha (prostaglandin) analogs are used as a first line in glaucoma. Latanoprost is the most commonly used anti-glaucoma medication. Other prostaglandin analogues are travoprost, bimatoprost, tafluprost, and unoprostone.

Mechanism of action: It reduces intraocular pressure by altering the ciliary muscle tension and improving the outflow of the aqueous humor.

Adverse effects:

* Blurring of vision

* Iris pigmentation

* Thickening and darkening of eyelashes

* Macular edema especially in aphakic patients.

* Orbital fat atrophy

Pearl PF1386: Antiglaucoma drugs: Mechanism of lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) at a glance

Drugs that increase trabecular outflow

* Miotics (e.g., pilocarpine)

* Epinephrine, dipivefrine

* Bimatoprost

Drugs that increase uveoscleral outflow

* Prostaglandins (latanoprost)

* Epinephrine, dipivefrine

* Brimonidine

* Apraclonidine

Drugs that decrease aqueous production

* Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide, dorzolamide)

* Alpha receptor stimulators in ciliary process (e.g., epinephrine, dipivefrine, clonidine, brimonidine, apraclonidine)

* Beta-blockers

Hyperosmotic agents - (e.g., glycerol, mannitol, urea)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An 18-month-old child visited the ophthalmologist exhibiting a white eye reflex, and ultrasonography revealed an intraocular mass with calcifications. The family history indicated that the child's father had a similar condition and underwent the removal of one eye (enucleation). What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinoblastoma

The clinical history of leukocoria, an intraocular mass with calcifications on ultrasound, and a positive family history, the most likely diagnosis is retinoblastoma (option b).

Retinoblastoma is a malignant tumor of the retina that predominantly affects children, and early detection and treatment are crucial for better outcomes. point toward a diagnosis of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in children associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14.

It most commonly presents with leukocoria followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision.

Signs:

* An intraretinal tumor is a homogeneous, dome-shaped white lesion that becomes irregular, often with white flecks of calcification.

* An endophytic tumor projects into the vitreous as a white mass that may "seed" into the gel.

* An exophytic tumor forms multilobular subretinal white masses and causes an overlying retinal detachment.

Investigations:

* Red reflex testing with a direct ophthalmoscope is a simple screening test for leukocoria.

* Dilated fundus examination using indirect ophthalmoscope

* MRI of the orbit + brain is the investigation of choice.

Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features of a well-differentiated tumor include Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen.

Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy.Vincristine, Carboplatin, Etoposide are the choice of drugs for chemotherapy. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy.

Enucleation is done when the tumor involves more than half of the retina, optic nerve involvement, glaucoma, and anterior chamber involvement.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An elderly diabetic patient presented with complaints of blurring of vision. He underwent a cataract surgery 1 month ago. The patient's fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) showed a flower-petal appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystoid macular edema

The given scenario of a diabetic patient with the blurring of vision and an FFA showing a flower petal pattern (petaloid appearance) is suggestive of cystoid macular edema (CME). It occurs due to the accumulation of dye in the macular region.

CME is defined as a collection of fluid between the outer plexiform (Henle's layer) and an inner nuclear layer of the retina. This results in the formation of cyst-like cavities around the foveola. It occurs due to a break in the inner and outer blood-retinal barrier.

Common causes of CME include uveitis, previous cataract surgery (Irvine-Gass syndrome), retinal vein occlusions, diabetic retinopathy, and retinitis pigmentosa.

Patients may complain of blurring, distortion, and micropsia. In clinically established cases, the macula will show a 'honeycomb' appearance on ophthalmoscopy due to multiple cystoid spaces. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) image shows intraretinal cystoid spaces and foveal depression. In advanced cases, a lamellar macular hole may develop.

Treatment includes topical anti-prostaglandins (ketorolac), steroids, systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (oral acetazolamide), and managing the causative factor.

Given below is the FFA image showing the classic flower-petal appearance, followed by an OCT image showing intraretinal cystoid spaces in CME:

Other options:

Option A: Central serous retinopathy is the spontaneous serous detachment of the macular region neurosensory retina with/without retinal pigment epithelium detachment. Patients complain of sudden onset painless loss of vision, micropsia, and metamorphopsia. FFA shows two patterns of leakage, ink-blot pattern and smoke-stick pattern. OCT image of central serous retinopathy is seen below which neurosensory retinal detachment and accompanying small detachments of the retinal pigment epithelium.

Option B: Macular hole is a partial or full-thickness hole in the neurosensory retina of the foveal region. Causes include trauma, CME, or idiopathic. There is a decrease in vision, typically around 6/60 for full-thickness holes. FFA shows early foveal hyperfluorescene without a leak.

OCT image of the macular hole is seen below which shows a full-thickness hole in the foveal retina.

Option D: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is bilateral disease affecting people who are above 50 years of age. It can be exudative or non-exudative types. There can be a gradual or sudden loss of vision depending on the type of AMD. Drusens (yellowish-white elevated spots caused by extracellular deposits in the macular region) of various types can be noted. FFA shows punctate hyperfluorescence due to the drusen.

OCT and FFA image of drusens is shown below:

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During a dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR), which of the following bones are typically removed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lacrimal

During a dacryocystorhinostomy, a portion of the lacrimal bone is typically removed to create a passage for tear drainage.

The lacrimal bone is indeed a key bone involved in dacryocystorhinostomy. In this procedure, a portion of the lacrimal bone is often removed to create a passage for tear drainage.

Other options:

Frontal (a): The frontal bone is not typically removed during a dacryocystorhinostomy. DCR primarily involves the lacrimal bone and sometimes parts of the nasal bone.

Ethmoidal (b): The ethmoidal bone is not typically removed during a standard DCR. The primary bone involved is the lacrimal bone.

Maxillary (c): The maxillary bone is not typically removed during a dacryocystorhinostomy. The main focus is on the lacrimal bone.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of childhood blindness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin A deficiency

The most common cause of preventable childhood blindness is vitamin A deficiency.

The most common cause of blindness in adults, is however, cataract.

Vitamin A deficiency is a major cause of childhood blindness, particularly in developing countries. Lack of sufficient vitamin A can lead to conditions like xerophthalmia, which includes night blindness and can progress to more severe forms, ultimately causing irreversible damage to the cornea and leading to blindness.

Other options:

(a) Refractive error: Refractive errors, such as myopia (nearsightedness), hyperopia (farsightedness), and astigmatism, can cause vision problems, but they are usually correctable with glasses or contact lenses. While refractive errors can affect children's vision, they are not typically a direct cause of childhood blindness.

(c) Retinopathy of prematurity: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is a condition that primarily affects premature infants and is related to abnormal blood vessel development in the retina. While it can lead to vision impairment or blindness in severe cases, it is not as prevalent as vitamin A deficiency, especially on a global scale.

(d) Injuries: While injuries can certainly lead to vision impairment or blindness in children, they are not as prevalent on a population level as vitamin A deficiency.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following instruments is shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lim’s forceps

The instrument shown in the image above is Lim's forceps.

Lim's forceps are a type of surgical instrument used in ophthalmic procedures. They are designed for delicate manipulations within the eye during surgery. These forceps typically have fine tips and a delicate grip, allowing surgeons to handle delicate tissues with precision.

Other options:

Option B: McPherson suture tying forceps are commonly used in ophthalmic surgery for grasping and tying sutures. They have a fine, curved tip which allows surgeons to manipulate sutures within the eye or in areas where precision is required, such as in delicate eye surgeries like cataract surgery.

Option C: Corneoscleral forceps are specialized instruments used in eye surgery for handling the cornea and sclera, the outer layers of the eye. These forceps have a unique design that allows surgeons to securely grasp and manipulate these tissues during various procedures, such as corneal transplantation or scleral flap surgery.

Option D: Lens holding forceps are surgical instruments used in ophthalmic procedures involving the removal or manipulation of the lens of the eye. They are designed to securely grasp the lens during procedures such as cataract surgery or intraocular lens implantation, allowing surgeons to manipulate the lens safely and precisely.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following types of cataract would be present in a patient after a blunt trauma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rosette cataract

A rosette cataract typically follows closed globe injuries (blunt trauma).

In blunt trauma, there may be minute ruptures in the lens capsule resulting in an influx of aqueous humor, leading to hydration and subsequent opacification of the lens. Commonly there is posterior subcapsular opacification in a flower shape along the posterior sutures. Hence it is called rosette cataract.

Iridodialysis occurs due to dehiscence of the iris from the ciliary body at its root. The pupil becomes D-shaped.

The following image shows a rosette cataract.

Apart from this, blunt trauma can cause a ring-shaped anterior subcapsular opacity underneath the Vossius ring.

Other options:

(a) Sunflower cataract: Sunflower cataract is associated with Wilson's disease, a genetic disorder that leads to copper accumulation in the body. It is not related to blunt trauma.

(c) Christmas tree cataract: Christmas tree cataract is often seen in cases of myotonic dystrophy, a genetic neuromuscular disorder. It is not related to blunt trauma.

(d) Sparkle cataract: It does not correspond to a well-defined category of cataract associated with blunt trauma or any other specific condition.

Pearl PF1394: Diseases and Associated Cataracts - Images

Wilson's Disease/Chalcosis: Sunflower Cataract

Diabetes mellitus:  Snowflake cataract

Blunt trauma: May present as rosette-shaped cataract

Myotonic dystrophy - Christmas tree cataract

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presents with epiphora and probing reveals a soft block at 7 mm. What is the best treatment option for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Conjunctival Dacryocystorhinostomy

A soft stop 5–8 mm from the punctum implies a canalicular obstruction. Conjunctival Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is the management of choice for proximal canalicular obstruction at 7mm. If present more than 8 mm from the punctum, the obstruction is probably at the common canaliculus.

The canalicular obstruction is divided as proximal (<8 mm from puncta) and distal (>8 mm from puncta).It can be congenital or acquired. Acquired causes are post-traumatic, repeated syringing or chronic inflammation/infection of the system. It may follow prolonged use of idoxuridine.

Conjunctival DCR (Jones procedure) creates a bypass between the conjunctival fornix and nasal cavity using a Pyrex or silicone tube. The procedure involves creating a fistula through the lacrimal bone, bypassing the blocked canalicular system entirely. The tube is placed from conjunctiva to nose, secured with sutures, and typically left in place for 3-6 months. It has a success rate of around 80% in properly selected cases.

The main advantage is its ability to create an alternative drainage pathway when the proximal lacrimal system is non-functional or absent.

This procedure is specifically indicated for:

* Canalicular obstruction

* Failed standard DCR

* Cases with extensive canalicular damage

* Congenital absence of canaliculi

The given set of instruments is used for dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR)

Other Options:

Option B: External DCR: An osteotomy is created between the lacrimal sac and nasal cavity through an external skin incision. While effective for nasolacrimal duct obstruction, it cannot address canalicular blocks at 7mm.

Option C: Endonasal DCR: Creates similar bypass as external DCR but through nasal approach. Not suitable for proximal canalicular system problems as it only addresses distal obstruction.

Option D: Dacryocystectomy: Complete removal of lacrimal sac. Too radical for this case and eliminates possibility of future reconstructive procedures. Only indicated in chronic dacryocystitis with mucocele or tumor.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 6-year-old girl came to your clinic with refractive power of +1D in right eye and -2D in left eye. Fundus examination reveals normal acuity and retinal findings. What is the correct diagnosis? D - dioptre
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anisometropia

The history of defective vision and 2 different refractive errors of the eyes suggests a diagnosis of anisometropia.

Anisometropia occurs when the total refraction of both eyes are unequal. A difference of 1D in the two eyes causes a 2% difference in the size of retinal images formed. A difference up to 2.5D is well-tolerated, but beyond 4D cannot be tolerated. Anisometropia can occur as a combination of emmetropia, myopia, hypermetropia, and astigmatism.

It is diagnosed after retinoscopic examination and autorefractometry.

Treatment includes the usage of spectacles (it can be tolerated up to a maximum difference of 4D), contact lenses, intraocular lenses (for uniocular aphakia), refractive corneal surgery, or refractive lens exchange methods (used in high degree anisometropia).

Other options:

Option B: Myopia (Short-sightedness): The parallel rays of light coming from infinity are focused in front of the retina when accommodation is at rest.

Option C: Hypermetropia(Long-sightedness): The parallel rays of light coming from infinity are focused behind the retina when accommodation is at rest.

Option D: Amblyopia or 'lazy eye' is a developmental defect of spatial visual processing that occurs in the central visual pathways of the eye.

Pearl PF1369: Causes of Myopia

Myopia

Etiology

Axial myopia

(Most common)

Increase in the anteroposterior length of the eyeball.

Curvatural myopia

Increased curvature of the cornea, lens, or both

Positional myopia

Anterior placement of the crystalline lens in the eye

Index myopia

Increase in the refractive index of crystalline lens

Nocturnal myopia

Due to spherical aberration and accomodation

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A child presents with eyelid crusting and a gritty sensation between the eyelashes. He also has difficulty in opening eyelids. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chronic Blepharitis

Based on the presenting symptoms - eyelid crusting, gritty sensation between eyelashes, and difficulty opening eyelids - the most likely diagnosis is chronic blepharitis.

Blepharitis is characterized by inflammation of the eyelid margins and typically presents with these exact symptoms, particularly the crusting and difficulty opening eyes in the morning due to accumulated debris.

Additional typical findings seen in Chronic Blepharitis are:

* Redness of lid margins

* Collarettes around eyelash bases

* Mild conjunctival injection

Types:

* Posterior blepharitis

* Inflammation of the inner portion of the eyelid (more common)

* Caused by meibomian gland dysfunction

* Associated with acne rosacea

* Anterior blepharitis

* Inflammation of the base of eyelashes

* Two types

* Seborrhoeic type which is associated with dermatitis. This is characterized by dandruff-like skin changes and greasy scales.

* Staphylococcal type is characterized by fibrinous scales and crust around the eyelashes caused by colonization of the eyelids by Staphylococcus aureus and CoNS

Parasitic causes of blepharitis

* Blepharitis acarica caused by Demodex folliculorum - A key clinical feature of this infestation is the presence of dandruff-like scaling at the base of eye-lashes.

* Phthiriasis palpebrarum caused by crab louse.

Other options:

Option A: Conjunctivitis primarily affects the conjunctiva with redness and discharge, it doesn't typically cause significant eyelid crusting between the lashes.

Option C: Dry eye syndrome mainly presents with burning, foreign body sensation, and tearing but lacks the characteristic eyelid margin involvement and crusting.

Option D: Meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD) can be associated with blepharitis but primarily presents with tear film instability and evaporative dry eye.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A newborn baby brought by the mother with complaints of the left upper eyelid moving up and down during breastfeeding or thumb sucking which disappears when the baby is not being fed. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Marcus–Gunn Jaw-Winking Syndrome

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon.

Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking syndrome:

* About 5% of all cases of congenital ptosis are associated with the Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon.

* The vast majority are unilateral.

* Etiology: a branch of the mandibular division of the fifth cranial nerve is misdirected to the levator muscle.

* Signs

* Retraction of the ptotic lid with stimulation of the ipsilateral pterygoid muscles by chewing, sucking, opening the mouth, or contralateral jaw movement.

* Less common stimuli to winking include jaw protrusion, smiling, swallowing, and clenching of teeth.

* Jaw-winking does not improve with age although patients may learn to mask it.

The following image shows a woman with Marcus–Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon. See how her right eyelid ptosis retracts with the opening of the mouth.

Other options:

Option A: In 3rd nerve palsy (oculomotor nerve) - Due to the involvement of the superior rectus and medial rectus, elevation and adduction will also be impaired, which is not the case here.

Option B: Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular junction (NMJ) disorder associated with a decrease in postsynaptic depolarization due to the blocking of acetylcholine receptors by autoantibodies. It is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles.

Option C: In lagophthalmos, there is incomplete closure of the palpable aperture when the patient attempts to close the eyes due to congenital deformity, paralysis of the orbicularis muscle, ectropion or contraction of the lid.  It may be due to a malfunction of the facial nerve. Treatment includes the management of exposure keratopathy with frequent instillation of lubricants.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient came to the hospital with complaints of breathlessness and is diagnosed with a Pancoast tumor. Which of the following findings is not typically associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Exophthalmus

Pancoast syndrome is associated with Horner's syndrome, resulting in ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis. It is not associated with exophthalmus.

Horner syndrome occurs when the sympathetic nerves serving the head, eye, or neck are damaged at any point along their pathway. It is also referred to as oculosympathetic paresis.

Clinical features include:

* Ptosis - usually due to weakness of Muller’s muscle (Option D).

* Miosis - due to unopposed action of sphincter pupillae leading to anisocoria (Option C).

* Anhidrosis - reduced ipsilateral sweating (Option B).

* Heterochromia iridis- seen in congenital and long-standing disease. The affected eye is lighter in color.

* Anisocoria that is accentuated in dim light

* Enophthalmus

Pancoast syndrome  is also called a superior sulcus tumor. It develops when a tumor located at the apex of the lung extends locally. Local extension involves the C8 - T2 nerve roots.

It presents with pain that radiates to the ulnar distribution of the arm, often with the destruction of the 1st and 2nd ribs. Patients with the central or endobronchial growth of the primary tumor may present with a cough, hemoptysis, wheeze, stridor, dyspnea, or post-obstructive pneumonitis.

Regional spread of the tumor can cause:

* Tracheal obstruction, esophageal compression with dysphagia

* Recurrent laryngeal paralysis with hoarseness

* Phrenic nerve palsy with the elevation of the hemidiaphragm and dyspnea

* Sympathetic nerve paralysis with Horner’s syndrome (enophthalmos, ptosis, miosis, and anhydrosis).

The below images show chest X-ray and management of the Pancoast tumor.

Pearl PF1717: Horner's syndrome

Horner's Syndrome:

Horner's syndrome occurring due to occulo-sympathetic paresis is characterized by the classic triad of:

* Mild ptosis (due to paralysis of Muller's muscle).

* Miosis (due to paralysis of dilator pupillae).

* Reduced ipsilateral sweating (anhydrosis).

Other features include:

* Mild enophthalmos,

* Loss of cilio-spinal reflex,

* Heterochromia, i.e., the ipsilateral iris is lighter in colour,

* Pupil is slow to dilate, and there occurs slight elevation of lower eyelid.

Cocaine test (2% to 4%): Small pupils fail to dilate in Horner's syndrome.

In congenital Horner's syndrome, the additional features seen are heterochromia iridis and unilateral straight hair.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient has a history of a flying foreign body injury to the eye. After 8 weeks, heterochromia iridis is noted. Which of the following substances is most likely involved in the deposition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iron

History of trauma from a flying object followed by subsequent heterochromia iridis is suggestive of siderosis bulbi which happens due to iron deposition.

The presence of iron deposits in the eye especially in industrial workers is called siderosis bulbi. It refers to the ocular degenerative changes produced by an iron foreign body. It usually occurs 2 months to 2 years after the injury. This condition is due to the electrolytic dissociation of the metal by an intrinsic resting current in the eye which disseminates the metal, combining it with cellular proteins and causing atrophy.

The earliest change is the deposition of iron in the anterior capsule of the lens where oval patches are arranged in a ring corresponding with the edge of the dilated pupil. This eventually leads to the formation of cataract.

Clinical features:

* Iris: first stained greenish and later turned reddish-brown, causing heterochromia iridis.

* Pupil: iron deposition in the sphincter leads to mydriasis.

* Lens: iron deposition in a radial fashion on the anterior capsule of the lens, leading to anterior capsular cataract.

* Retina: pigmentary retinopathy; followed by atrophy of the retina and retinal pigmentary epithelium.

* Secondary open-angle glaucoma: due to damage to the trabecular meshwork.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with non-pulsatile proptosis that increases when bending down. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Orbital varices

This patient with non-pulsatile propotosis that increases on bending down most likely has orbital varices.

Orbital varices:

* They are venous malformations of the orbit caused by vascular dysgenesis.

* Patients usually present with non-pulsatile, intermittent, and reducible proptosis.

* On activities such as forward bending or lowering of the head, turning the head forcefully, hyperextension of the neck, and coughing, the varices fill up, causing proptosis, and then, they regress on shifting to a non-dependent position.

Treatment:

* Small lesions generally do not require treatment

* Surgical excision is technically difficult and often incomplete because the lesions are friable and bleed easily; Specialized techniques such as embolization and carbon dioxide laser surgery may be helpful.

Other options:

Option A: Thyroid eye disease (TED) is the most common cause of both bilateral and unilateral proptosis in an adult in the euthyroid state. The main features of TED include lid retraction, proptosis, periorbital edema, chemosis, and restrictive myopathy.

Option C:  In cavernous sinus thrombosis, proptosis is initially unilateral but soon becomes bilateral due to the spread of infection to the contralateral sinus through the intercavernous communication. Also, cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with high-grade fever with chills, rigor, and headache.

Option D: Orbital cellulitis is the most common cause of unilateral proptosis in children. It refers to the acute infection of the contents of the orbit behind the orbital septum. Features include pain, lid edema, erythema, chemosis, and axial proptosis. Increased pain with movement of eyes and ophthalmoplegia (decreased ocular motility) is a classic symptom.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with right-sided visual field defects in both eyes while central vision remains unaffected. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

Visual field defect involving the right sides of each eye with central vision preserved is called bilateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. It occurs in lesions of the occipital lobe.

Homonymous hemianopia (HH) involves loss of vision on the same side of the visual field in both eyes. HH is characteristically seen in lesions involving the visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasma.

Lesions involving occipital lobe usually shows macular sparing because macular representation is seperate and quite large as compared to peripheral vision. Moreover, macular area in occipital lobe is supplied both by posterior and middle cerebral artery. In case of vascular lesions (eg stroke) affecting occipital lobe, it is less likely to involve both these arteries.

HH may be either complete or incomplete.

* A complete HH is characterised by loss of entire hemifield on the same side in both eyes.

* An incomplete HH is characterised by partial loss of visual field on the same side in both eyes. Incomplete HH is further classified as congruous or incongruous, depending on whether the extent of partial loss of visual field in both the eyes is same or different, respectively.

Other Options:

Option A: Optic Chiasm Lesion: Bitemporal hemianopia refers to loss of sight in the temporal halves of the visual field, seen in lesions affecting the optic chiasma.

Option B: Optic Tract Lesion : Lesions at the occipital lobe, optic tract and optic radiation would all cause homonymous hemianopia, but macular sparing will occur in the setting of optic lobe damage.

Option C: Damage to the middle part of the optic chiasm affects fibres crossing at the nasal retina of each eye, leaving the uncrossed fibres from the temporal retinas intact. The resulting loss of vision is confined to the temporal visual field of each eye and this is known as bitemporal hemianopia. It is also called heteronymous hemianopia.

Pearl PF1675: Lesions in the optic pathway

Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above.

* The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other.

* A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye.

* Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia.

* A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness).

* Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with vision problems and has a history of cataract surgery. OCT findings are given. What is the syndrome associated with these findings? OCT- Optical coherence tomography
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Irvine-Gass Syndrome

The given scenario of a patient with a history of cataract surgery and an OCT showing intraretinal cystoid spaces is suggestive of Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) in the setting of Irvine-Gass syndrome. It occurs due to the accumulation of dye in the macular region.

CME is defined as a collection of fluid between the outer plexiform (Henle's layer) and an inner nuclear layer of the retina. This results in the formation of cyst-like cavities around the foveola. It occurs due to a break in the inner and outer blood-retinal barrier.

Common causes of CME include uveitis, previous cataract surgery (Irvine-Gass syndrome), retinal vein occlusions, diabetic retinopathy, and retinitis pigmentosa.

Irvine-Gass syndrome is the late postoperative complications of cataract surgery. The characteristic flower-petal appearance is due to the accumulation of dye in the outer plexiform layer at the fovea. CME occurs due to a break in the inner and outer blood-retinal barrier.

Patients may complain of blurring, distortion, and micropsia. In clinically established cases, the macula will show a 'honeycomb' appearance on ophthalmoscopy due to multiple cystoid spaces. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) image shows intraretinal cystoid spaces and foveal depression. In advanced cases, a lamellar macular hole may develop.

Treatment includes topical anti-prostaglandins (ketorolac), steroids, systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (oral acetazolamide), and managing the causative factor.

Given below is the FFA image showing the classic flower-petal appearance, followed by an OCT image showing intraretinal cystoid spaces in CME:

A few other late postoperative complications of cataract surgery include,

* Delayed chronic postoperative endophthalmitis

* Pseudophakic bullous keratopathy

* Retinal detachment

* After cataract or secondary cataract

Other options:

Option A: Central serous retinopathy is the spontaneous serous detachment of the macular region neurosensory retina with/without retinal pigment epithelium detachment. Patients complain of sudden onset painless loss of vision, micropsia, and metamorphopsia. FFA shows two patterns of leakage, ink-blot pattern and smoke-stick pattern. OCT image of central serous retinopathy is seen below which neurosensory retinal detachment and accompanying small detachments of the retinal pigment epithelium.

Option B: Posner–Schlossman syndrome is characterized by recurrent unilateral acute raised intraocular pressure (IOP) (>40 mmHg) changes, with mild anterior uveitis. It is also known as glaucomatocyclitic crisis or hypertensive uveitis.

Option D: Elschnig’s pearls are where the subcapsular epithelial cells proliferate and develop into vacuolated soap bubble like clusters along the posterior capsule. It is a type of after-cataract/ secondary cataract or posterior capsular opacification, which is a late postoperative complication that follows extracapsular extraction of the lens.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient sustained blunt trauma to the eye 6 months ago and now presents with double vision. What is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Iriododialysis

The given image shows iridodialysis.

Iridodialysis refers to detachment of the iris root from the ciliary body and is associated with a D-shaped pupil. A black biconvex area is seen at the periphery at the site of detachment.

The given image depicts iridodialysis and a D-shaped pupil.

Other Options:

Option A: Cycloiriditis is inflammation involving both the ciliary body and iris, leading to pain, photophobia, and decreased vision. It's characterized by cells and flare in the anterior chamber, keratic precipitates, and possible synechiae formation.

Option B: Vossius ring is a circular ring of faint or stippled opacity, seen on the anterior surface of the lens due to brown amorphous granules of pigment lying on the capsule of the lens. It is usually seen after blunt trauma to the eye and orbit.

Option D: Coloboma is a congenital anomaly, that develops due to a defect in the closure of the embryonic cleft. It is characterized by poorly developed uveal tissue. These colobomas may involve the optic nerve, choroid, retina, and iris.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with a history of diabetes presents with cataract. Which of the following metabolic products is primarily responsible for cataract formation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sorbitol

A diabetic cataract occurs due to the accumulation of sorbitol within the lens.

In diabetic patients, increased levels of blood glucose lead to high levels of glucose in the aqueous humor. The excess glucose in the aqueous humor is metabolized into sorbitol through the polyol pathway by the enzyme aldose reductase. Sorbitol is then converted to fructose (option B) by sorbitol dehydrogenase but at a much slower rate. In addition, the polar nature of sorbitol prevents its intracellular removal through diffusion.

Sorbitol and fructose accumulate in the lens and the osmotic stress so produced results in overhydration, hydropic lens fibers, and apoptosis of the lens epithelial cells. Thus, the secondary osmotic overhydration is responsible for cortical opacities in a distinct pattern causing snowflake cataracts as shown below (Option B).

Other Options:

Option A: Mannitol is used to lower intracranial pressure. Features of raised of intracranial pressure are vomiting and papilledema.

Option C: In Classic Galactosemia, deficiency of galactose-1-uridyltransferase leads to the accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol (dulcitol).

Pearl PF1394: Diseases and Associated Cataracts - Images

Wilson's Disease/Chalcosis: Sunflower Cataract

Diabetes mellitus:  Snowflake cataract

Blunt trauma: May present as rosette-shaped cataract

Myotonic dystrophy - Christmas tree cataract

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The cover-uncover test is performed to diagnose various eye conditions. Which of the following is not detected by this test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Amblyopia

The cover-uncover test cannot detect Amblyopia.

This test consists of two parts:

* Cover test

* Uncover test

Cover Test: This is used to detect heterotropia (Manifest Squint) (Option B). Light is first shone and corneal reflections are observed. This is done to assess fixation in the deviating eye. The procedure for testing using an accommodative target and for distance is as follows.

* The patient is asked to fixate on a target straight ahead.

* The eye in which deviation is not suspected is covered first. For example, if a right eye deviation is suspected, the left eye is covered.

* Any movement of the right eye to take up fixation is noted.

* The following are the possible results:

Movement of the eye
Suspected defect

No movements
Orthotropia/ Heterotropia of the covered eye

Adduction
Exotropia

Abduction
Esotropia

Downward movement
Hypertropia

Upward movement
Hypotropia

The test is then repeated for the opposite eye.

Uncover test: This is used to detect heterophoria (latent squint)(Option A). The test is performed for both near and distant as follows.

* The patient fixates a distant target straight ahead.

* The examiner covers an eye for 2-3 seconds and the cover is then removed.

* If the covered eye had deviated, a re-fixation movement is observed on being uncovered.

* The following are the possible results based on the re-fixation movements of the eye.

Movement of the eye
Suspected defect

No movements
Orthophoria

Adduction (Nasal recovery)
Exophoria

Abduction
Esophoria

Downward/Upward movement
Vertical phoria

* The speed and smoothness of the recovery is noted as well as evidence of the strength of motor fusion.

* The test is then repeated for the opposite eye.

Other options:

Option C: Amblyopia is a developmental defect of spatial visual processing that occurs in the central visual pathways of the eye.  Generally, a difference of two lines or more on an eye chart test of visual acuity between the two eyes or a best-corrected vision of 20/30 or worse would be defined as amblyopia.

Treatment modalities include:

* Occlusion of the normal eye (4 to 6 hours/ day) using patches. It allows an amblyopic eye to be used.

* Penalization: Blurring of vision using atropine. Instilling atropine into the fixing eye, forces the squinting eye to be used for seeing near objects.

Pearl PF1402: Cover tests in ophthalmology

Cover–uncover test:

* To detect the presence of heterophoria: Latent squint

* One eye is covered with the occluder, and the other eye is made to fix an object.

* In the presence of heterophoria, the eye under the cover will deviate.

* When the cover is removed, the eye under the cover will return back to its normal.

* This movement is observed.

* The direction of movement determines the type of heterophoria.

Direct Cover test:

* Confirms the presence of manifest squint.

* Differentiates apparent squint from a manifest squint.

* The patient is asked to fixate on the point light.

* The normal-looking eye is covered.

* In manifest squint, the uncovered eye will move in the opposite direction to take fixation.

* In apparent squint, there will be no movement of the uncovered eye.

Alternate cover test:

* In the below image, the patient has right exotropia with left eye fixating.

* Both eyes move each time the cover alternates from one eye to the other.

* It reveals if the squint is unilateral or alternate.

* It differentiates between concomitant and paralytic squint.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the accommodative amplitude of a patient with a near point at 20 cm and a far point at infinity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 5 D

The amplitude of accommodation for the above patient would be 5 dioptres.

Near point of accommodation (NPA) is the closest distance at which the near object is clearly focussed without blur.

Amplitude of accommodation is the maximum power of the lens that permits clear near vision without blur. Its unit is dioptre (D). The amplitude of accommodation is the reciprocal of near point of accommodation (NPA) in meters.

20 cm is 1/5th of a metre. Therefore, the accommodative amplitude is its inverse, that is, 5D.

Note:

The NPA is measured clinically using a scale device such as the Prince, Berens, or Royal Air Force (RAF) ruler.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the recommended maximum time frame for cornea harvesting after death to ensure optimal transplant quality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 6 hours

Donor corneas are to be harvested within 6 hours of death.

Eye banks manage corneal and scleral tissue donation for transplantation. The process requires next-of-kin consent and involves screening donors for contraindications including infectious diseases, malignancies, and neurological conditions. Tissues must be harvested within 6-8 hours of death.

Two harvesting methods are used:

* Whole globe enucleation: Complete eyeball removal, stored in moist chamber bottles

* In situ corneoscleral rim excision: Direct corneal rim removal into storage medium

The process is regulated by the Transplantation of Organs and Tissues Act and coordinated by the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organization. Eye banks conduct public education and place counselors in hospitals to improve donation rates through the Hospital Cornea Retrieval Program.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding indirect ophthalmoscopy?
options: The image produced is erect and real
Condensor needs to be kept very close to the eye
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It provides 3-5x magnification

An indirect ophthalmoscope produces an inverted real image of 3 to 5 times magnification.

Advantages of the binocular indirect ophthalmoscope are:

* Visualization through hazy media is possible due to strong in built illumination system.

* Field of view is much larger than direct ophthalmoscopy.

* Examination of peripheral retina up to ora serrata is possible.

* Depth perception of the lesion is possible due to stereopsis with binocular indirect ophthalmoscope.

* Visualization of fundus in very high refractive error is also possible, where it may not be possible to focus the lesion with direct ophthalmoscope.

* A real, Inverted image is formed (Option A).

* There is an arms distance between the condensing lens and the patient's eye (Option C).

Other options:

Option D: 15 times magnification is seen with a direct ophthalmoscope.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient presents with complaints of long-standing dacrocystitis. What is the treatment of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dacrocystorhinostomy

The treatment of choice for long-standing chronic dacryocystitis is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) surgery. it involves removal of the bone adjacent to the nasolacrimal sac and suturing the lacrimal sac with the lateral nasal mucosa. This allows tears to drain directly from the sac via a new low-resistance pathway into the middle meatus.

Chronic dacryocystitis is a multifactorial disease affecting the lacrimal sac.

Clinical features can be divided into 4 stages.

* Stage of chronic catarrhal dacryocystitis: inflammation of lacrimal sac and blockage of nasolacrimal duct

* Stage of lacrimal mucocele: chronic stagnation and distension of the lacrimal sac forming a swelling

* Stage of chronic suppurative dacryocystitis: purulent discharge from punctum

* Stage of chronic fibrotic sac: thickening of mucosa to form a fibrous sac

Treatment

Dacrocystorhinostomy (DCR) is the treatment of choice once local infection if present is controlled with topical antibiotics. it re-establishes the drainage

Dacrocystecomy is considered if DCR is contraindicated like in advanced age, TB or syphilitic infection of the sac

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A child presented to the OPD with a characteristic type of cataract as seen in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Galactosemia

The image shown below shows an oil drop cataract seen in galactosemia. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency leads to classical galactosemia which is an autosomal recessive disorder.

Clinical features :

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver causes liver damage & leads to hepatomegaly, vomiting, convulsions.

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate depletes the liver of inorganic phosphate leading to diminished ATP synthesis which affects gluconeogenesis resulting in hypoglycemia.

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the nerves causes intellectual disability.

* Accumulation of galactitol in the lens causes oil-drop cataract.

* Patients with galactosemia are at an increased risk of developing Escherichia coli neonatal sepsis.

Urinary reducing sugar (Benedict's test) and the Mucic acid test is positive.

Treatment is a galactose-free diet.

Diabetes show snow flake cataract, Wilson’s disease shows sunflower cataract and myotonic dystrophy shows Christmas tree cataract.
