questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A hypertensive patient comes to the OPD with complaints of visual disturbances. On fundoscopy, multiple flame-shaped hemorrhages , cotton wool spots, and disc edema were found. What is the grade of hypertensive retinopathy in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Grade IV

Cotton wool spots and flame shaped hemorrage with disc edema is seen in grade IV of hypertensive retinopathy.

Grading of hypertensive retinopathy:

* Grade 1: Mild generalized retinal arteriolar narrowing

* Grade 2: Focal arteriolar narrowing and arteriovenous nipping.

* Grade 3: Grade 2 plus retinal hemorrhages (dot, blot, flame) or exudates (chronic retinal edema may result in the deposition of hard exudates around the fovea as a ‘macular star’ and cotton wool spots; may also be associated with banking of veins distal to arteriovenous crossings (Bonnet sign), tapering of veins on either side of the crossings (Gunn sign); copper-wire appearance; more prominent arteriovenous compression.

* Grade 4: Severe grade 3 plus optic disc swelling (a marker of malignant hypertension) and silver-wiring of arterioles.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A male patient complained of visual disturbances. On examination, the light reflex is absent but the accommodation reflex is present. what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neurosyphillis

The clinical picture where his pupils accommodate but do not react to light is called Argyll Robertson pupil. It is seen in neurosyphillis.

Features of Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP) are bilateral small pupils with the following characteristics:

* Accommodation Reflex Present (ARP): Reduce in size on a near object (i.e., they accommodate)

* Light Reflex absent: Do not constrict when exposed to bright light (i.e., they do not react to light).

* This is an example of light near dissociation.

* Seen in neurosyphilis, along with other features such as the following:

* Loss of reflexes in the legs; impaired position and vibratory sense; Romberg’s sign; and, in almost all cases, bilateral Argyll Robertson pupils, which fail to constrict to light but accommodate.

Other causes of light-near dissociation are:

In unilateral eye

* Adie pupil

* Herpes zoster ophthalmicus

* Aberrant regeneration of the third cranial nerve

In bilateral eyes

* Type 1 diabetes mellitus

* Myotonic dystrophy

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient complains of visual blurring which is relieved on its own. Fundus examination showed papilledema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amaurosis fugax

Visual blurring in papilledema is called amaurosis fugax

Amaurosis fugax is the transient loss of vision due to an interruption in the blood supply to the retina or brain by emboli or spasms. The onset is abrupt and may follow a falling curtain pattern. The symptoms are relieved upon removal of the insult or the emboli and they recover in the same pattern the vision loss occured.

In papilledema, amaurosis fugax lasts 30-60 seconds. It's usually bilateral but can be unilateral in asymmetric disc edema due to giant cell arteritis or raised intracranial pressure

Other systemic causes can present as amaurosis fugax. Notably, cardiovascular abnormalities like arrhythmias, mitral valve prolapse, venous stasis retinopathies, fibromuscular dysplasia, etc.

Treatment is based on the cause. It's often self-limiting in papilledema. Aspirine or persantine may be used in cases of platelet emboli-induced disease. Severe emboli may require dis-obliteration of the vessels.

Other options:

Option A: Retinal detachment is the separation of retinal epithelium. They may present as visual blurring but is not transient. Fundus examination will show a greyish or whitish tint to the detached portions with evident tears and holes in cases of larger detachments.

Option C: Blindness as per WHO is visual acuity less than 3/60 or corresponding visual field defects in the better eye with the best possible correction.

Option D: Angle-closure glaucoma presents with painful loss of vision with redness. Fundus examination may show hyperemic disc or maybe even normal disc.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to the OPD with complaints of vertical diplopia upon climbing downstairs. On examination, he tilts his head on his shoulder while going downstairs. Which is the cranial nerve involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cranial nerve 4

The patient is suffering from a weak superior oblique and the cranial nerve involved in CN 4.

Vertical diplopia upon moving downstairs points towards a weakness in muscles used to depress the eye. The muscles used in the depression of eye are inferior rectus and superior oblique. The correction effort by the patient will be in line with the direction of action of the weak muscle. A correction effort my tilting head is in line with the direction of action of superior oblique (SO) muscle and so the cranial nerve involved in CN 4 which supplies the SO

There are seven extraocular muscles present in the eye. They are:

* Levator palpebrae superioris - Which elevates the upper eyelids

* Four recti muscles - Superior, inferior, medial, and lateral recti

* Two obliques - Superior and inferior oblique

The muscles originate from the back of the orbit in a common tendinous ring called the annulus of Zinn and are inserted into the sclera.

All the extraocular muscles (including inferior oblique) are innervated by the oculomotor (III) nerve except:

* Lateral rectus which is supplied by abducens (VI) nerve

* Superior oblique which is supplied by trochlear (IV) nerve

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An industrial worker was admitted to the hospital with complaints of visual disturbances. On examination, there is iron deposits in his eye. What is the most likely diagnosis behind this occular finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Siderosis bulbi

The presence of iron deposits in the eye especially in industrial workers is called siderosis bulbi.

Siderosis bulbi refers to the ocular degenerative changes produced by an iron foreign body. It usually occurs 2 months to 2 years after the injury. This condition is due to the electrolytic dissociation of the metal by an intrinsic resting current in the eye which disseminates the metal, combining it with cellular proteins and causing atrophy.

Clinical features:

* Iris: First stained greenish and later turned reddish-brown, causing heterochromia iridis.

* Pupil: iron deposition in the sphincter leads to mydriasis.

* Lens: iron deposition in a radial fashion on the anterior capsule of the lens, leading to anterior capsular cataract.

* Retina: pigmentary retinopathy; followed by atrophy of the retina and retinal pigmentary epithelium.

* Secondary open-angle Glaucoma: due to damage to the trabecular meshwork.

Option B: Chalcosis refers to the electrolytic dissociation of copper particles and its deposition in the eye forming a brown coloured ring similar to the KF ring in Wilson's disease.

Option C: Kayser-Fleischer ring refers to the golden brown arc along the limbus seen at the level of descemets membrane in copper metabolism disorder Wilson

Option D: Retinitis pigmentosa refers to the degenrative disease of the retinal pigmental epithelium. It presents with scotomas and otherwise normal on general and slit lamb examination

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The fundoscopy findings of a known case of HIV with low CD4 counts in shown below. What is the treatment of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ganciclovir

The above image depicts "sauce and cheese" retinopathy, which is characteristic of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. Ganciclovir is the treatment of choice.

CMV retinitis is the most probable diagnosis as the patient is immunocompromised (transplant recipient) and the fundoscopy shows patchy areas of retinal necrosis with irregular borders and overlying retinal hemorrhages.

CMV retinitis is mainly of 2 types

Central CMV retinitis

* Dense, white areas of retinal necrosis

* Retinal hemorrhage in the areas of necrosis

* Pizza pie or sauce and cheese appearance

Peripheral CMV retinitis

* Less demarcated

* Infection spreads along the vascular arcades in a brush fire-like fashion.

The serological assay is not informative in the case of the immunocompromised patient and PCR assay is the gold standard for diagnosis.
CMV mostly causes infection in immunocompromised patients such as transplant recipients and AIDS. The most common infections are interstitial pneumonitis, gastroenteritis, esophagitis, and retinitis. Apart from ganciclovir, valganciclovir, foscarnet, and cidofovir are approved for treatment of CMV retinitis in patients with AIDS.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the dye used to stain the anterior capsule of the lens in cataract surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trypan blue

Trypan blue dye can be used to stain the lens capsule for better visibility. It is used in anterior capsulotomy like capsulorrhexis.

In capsulorrhexis, an opening is made in the anterior capsule of the lens. Continuous curvilinear capsulorrhexis (CCC) is considered to be superior to all the pre-existing methods because when done correctly, it does not leave any edges or tears.In ECCE, a portion of the anterior capsule of the lens is removed, allowing extraction of the lens nucleus and cortex. This leaves the remainder of the anterior capsule, the posterior capsule, and the zonular support intact. The intact lens nucleus is then removed from the eye through a limbal incision.

An anterior capsulotomy is followed by hydrodissection using a balanced salt solution. This helps to separate the corticonuclear mass from the capsule. Removal of lens nucleus and aspiration of the cortex is done using a two-way irrigation and aspiration cannula. An intraocular lens (IOL) is then implanted and the incision is then closed.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which among the following are the yoke muscles of levodepression?
options: Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior rectus (IR)
Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior oblique (IO)
Right medial rectus (MR) and left medial rectus (MR)
Right medial rectus (MR) and right lateral rectus (LR)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior rectus (IR)

Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior rectus (IR) are the yoke muscle pair for levodepression.

The term "yoke muscles" refers to contralateral synergists.

* Includes a pair of muscles, one from each eye, which contract simultaneously during version movements.

* Examples are

* Right MR and Left LR for levoversion

* Right LR and Left MR for dextroversion

In an outward deviated eye, the elevation and depression is by recti. So here, one of the muscles is left inferior rectus.

Easy method to determine other muscle yoke muscle pairs:

Just take the opposite of each word:

Left  → Right

Inferior → Superior

Rectus → Oblique

So right superior rectus is the pair.

Similarly, the following are yoke muscle pairs:

* Right IO and Left SR - Levoelevation

* Right SR and Left IO - Dextroelevation

* Right IR and Left SO - Dextrodepression

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which among the following is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Malignant melanoma

Malignant melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults

Intraocular tumours are tumors affecting the ocular tissue. They are often malignant. They are initially dormant but can cause secondary glaucoma based on the location. It can cause extraocular extension and finally metastasis if left untreated. Types of intraocular tumours:

* Malignant melanoma: Involves the choroid, ciliary body, or iris. Its start as lens-shaped masses and enlarges. Retinal melanoma can cause retinal detachment. Radiological investigations like CT, MRI, and radioactive tracers, fluorescein angiography are used for diagnosis. Treatment includes surgery, radiation therapy, and enucleation in severe cases

* Retinoblastoma: Is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children. It presents as a yellow pupillary reflex and cataract. Diagnosis is via demonstration of calcifications in radiographs and CT. Treatment involves brachytherapy and surgery.

* Reticulum cell sarcoma: It is a primary neoplasm of histiocyte similar to a microglioma in the CNS

* Secondaries: These mostly arise from the breast and alimentary canal.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which is the drug of choice for refractive testing in a child with squint?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1% atropine

1% atropine is the drug of choice in refractive testing in a child with a squint.

The most common cause of squint in children is due to ciliary spasm. Hence proper evaluation is required for refractive testing with cycloplegia as well. Atropine is used because of its high cycloplegic capacity and useful in children who inherently have high ciliary tone

Option B: Tropicamide is short-acting and the maximum effect lasts just 30 mins. Hence not preferred

Option C: Homatropine is less potent

Option D: Cyclopentolate has a shorter duration of action and has less cycloplegic effect. Hence not preferred

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following cataract surgery prefers suturing with nylon 10-0?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Extracapsular cataract extraction

Suturing with nylon 10-0 is preferred in extracapsular cataract extraction.

In ECCE, a portion of the anterior capsule of the lens is removed, allowing extraction of the lens nucleus and cortex. This leaves the remainder of the anterior capsule, the posterior capsule, and the zonular support intact. The intact lens nucleus is then removed from the eye through a limbal incision.

An anterior capsulotomy is followed by hydro dissection using a balanced salt solution. This helps to separate the corticonuclear mass from the capsule. Removal of lens nucleus and aspiration of the cortex is done using a two-way irrigation and aspiration cannula. An intraocular lens (IOL) is then implanted and the incision is then closed.

The newer techniques of cataract surgery like phacoemulsification, MICS and FLACS doesn't require a suturing either because they use self sealing incisions or doesn't require a long incision.,

Pearl PF1395: Different extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) techniques

Conventional ECCE

* Incision: 10 to 2 o'clock

* Anterior capsulotomy

* Can opener’s technique

* Envelope technique

* Continuous circular capsulorrhexis

Manual SICS

* Incision: 4-6 mm

* A self-sealing sclerocorneal tunnel incision is made.

Phacoemulsification

* Incision:1.5–2.4 mm

* Phacoprobe and foldable IOL is used

* Sutureless surgery is possible with self-sealing sclerocorneal tunnel or clear corneal incision.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 21-year-old female patient underwent surgery on her middle ear and a nerve was injured intraoperatively. She came a week later to OPD with difficulty in closing her eyes on the same side. Ocular examination reveals decreased corneal sensation and dryness of the cornea. Which of the following cranial nerves was most likely injured during the surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. VII

This patient with a past history of intra-op nerve injury during middle ear surgery presented with dry eye, decreased corneal sensation, and incomplete eyelid closure (lagophthalmos) due to injury to cranial nerve (CN)VII.

Lagophthalmos can be caused by conditions such as facial nerve injury, parkinsonism (reduced muscle tone), lid scarring, and proptosis. The facial nerve runs horizontally in the medial wall and vertically in the posterior wall of the middle ear. Hence, they can be injured due to surgery of the middle ear.  Clinical features include dry eyes, decreased corneal sensation which can eventually lead to  mild punctate epithelial changes and epithelial breakdown.

CN VII lies in proximity to the middle ear. Hence there are chances of nerve injury during middle ear surgery.
The given image shows the course of the facial nerve within the middle ear cavity.

Treatment depends on whether the exposure is reversible or permanent. Reversible exposure can be treated with artificial tears and eye ointments. The eyelid can be taped closed at night or external barriers like bandage silicone hydrogel or scleral contact lenses can be used. Permanent exposure requires permanent tarsorrhaphy.

Other options:

Option B - CN IV palsy leads to paralysis of superior oblique muscles.

Option C - CN VI palsy leads to lateral rectus palsy and lateral gaze palsy.

Option D - CN III injury leads to injury of levator palpebrae superioris and ptosis.

None of these nerves pass through the middle ear.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 61-year-old university professor presents with a loss of vision in his left eye. He describes the sensation as a curtain being drawn over his affected eye. The patient had a history of flashing lights and floaters 7 days back. He also gives a history of having cataract surgery in the same eye 3 weeks ago. What is the likely cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Retinal detachment

The patient with sudden painless loss of vision has been complaining of floaters and curtain falling sign with a recent history of cataract surgery suggests the diagnosis of retinal detachment.

Retinal detachment occurs due to the accumulation of fluid between the neurosensory retina(NSR) and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) due to a retinal tear.

Types of Retinal detachment:

A. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment- fluid accumulates after a break (tear) occurs in the retina.

Causes include High myopes, Retinoschisis-splitting of neurosensory retina plus vitreous degeneration (typical retinoschisis-split at the level of the outer plexiform layer, atypical retinoschisis-split at the level of the nerve fibre layer), trauma, pseudophakia, and aphakia.

The most dangerous type of retinal break is horseshoe tear and the most dangerous location of the retinal break is the superior-temporal retina.

Clinical features include photopsia, floaters, and visual field defects (a black curtain/veil in front of the eye).

Signs

* Hypotony- as the liquefied vitreous in the subretinal space is absorbed through the RPE.

* Shafer sign-pigments in the anterior vitreous (tobacco dusting) are a feature of fresh retinal detachment.

* The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is corrugated with undulations.

Treatment

* Prophylactic laser barrage

* Scleral buckling

* Pneumatic retinopexy

* Pars plana vitrectomy

B. Tractional retinal detachment: Fibro-vascular membranes in the vitreous due to long-standing retinal neovascularization exert traction on the retina.

Causes include proliferative diabetic retinopathy, central retinal venous occlusion, Eale's disease, retinopathy of Prematurity(ROP)

The detached retina is concave in configuration. No breaks are seen

Treatment

* Pars plana vitrectomy with endo photocoagulation.

C. Exudative retinal detachment: Exudative fluid from the choroid, collects in the subretinal space leading to retinal detachment.

Causes include inflammatory conditions like choroiditis, posterior scleritis choroidal tumours like melanoma, toxaemia of pregnancy, malignant hypertension, Coat's disease

Floaters due to vitreous but no photopsia and visual field defect is seen

The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is smooth. No break is seen. Shifting fluid is seen.

Treatment

* Systemic steroids

* Treatment of the cause

The image below shows a fundus which reveals retinal detachment inferiorly from 3-9 o'clock with a tear at 3:30

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 65-year-old female patient presented with sudden painless loss of vision. She has been a known diabetic for 12 years. Ophthalmoscopy shows evidence of loss of fundal features, floating debris and a dark red glow. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitreous haemorrhage

This patient with long-standing diabetes with sudden, painless vision loss, floating debris and a dark red glow on fundoscopic examination is most likely suffering from vitreous haemorrhage.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy, which can arise in people with long-term diabetes mellitus, is a common risk factor for vitreous haemorrhage caused by the breakage of the fragile blood vessels on the retina's surface. Intravitreal blood blocks light from reaching the retina, resulting in patients experiencing sudden onset cloudy vision, sometimes with a red tint, or vision loss.

Vitreous haemorrhage has a variable presentation depending on the severity of the haemorrhage. The mild haemorrhage causes sudden onset floaters and diffuse blurring of vision, but may not affect visual acuity, whilst a dense bleed may result in sudden painless loss of vision.

Causes: Acute posterior vitreous detachment is associated either with a retinal tear or avulsion of a peripheral vessel. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion and sickle cell disease.

The investigation of choice for vitreous haemorrhage is an ultrasound B-scan.

Treatment: Patients with vitreous haemorrhage can be adequately managed with bed rest to prevent additional bleeding and elevation of the head to promote blood settling away from the visual axis and correcting the underlying cause of the bleeding. (eg. photocoagulation for proliferative retinopathy). Vitreoretinal surgery with photocoagulation is indicated in patients with persistent vitreal haemorrhage.

Other options

Option A: Patients with retinal detachment can develop floaters and have acute vision loss. However, photopsia is common and fundoscopy reveals an elevated retina with folds or tears. An image showing retinal detachment at the fovea and the macula is shown below.

Option C:  Patients with macular degeneration typically have painless central blurring of vision which is progressive as opposed to vitreous hemorrhage which is acute in its presentation. An image depicting age-related macular degeneration with the presence of drusens is shown below.

Option D: Patients with central retinal vein occlusion can also present with sudden, painless loss of vision but would have scattered, diffuse hemorrhages, disc swelling and cotton wool spots. Image showing central retinal vein occlusion is as follows.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presented with complaints of headache and blurring of vision. On examination, there was a difference in visual acuity. In the right eye, it was (+5D) and in the left, it was (+1D). After the best possible correction for vision, visual acuity in the right eye is 6/18 and in the left is 6/24. On fundoscopy, no pathology could be appreciated. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anisometric Amblyopia

The presence of unequal refractive errors (+5D vs +1D), poor visual acuity even after correction, and a normal fundus examination strongly point towards Anisometropic Amblyopia.

A young child with a difference of vision in both eyes that is not improved after correction for refractive error supports the diagnosis. Due to the difference in refractive power, vision in one eye gets suppressed which is not apparent on examination.

Amblyopia is an uncorrectable decrease in vision in one or both eyes with no apparent structural abnormality seen to explain it. It is a diagnosis of exclusion. Generally, a difference of two lines or more on Snellen's visual acuity chart between the two eyes would be defined as unilateral amblyopia.

It may be of the following types:

* Strabismic - monocular suppression of the deviating eye in case of abnormal binocular interaction may develop in children with an accommodative squint. It is the most common type.

* Refractory- Anisometropic, Isoametropic, Meridional - due to a difference in refractive error between the two eyes

* Stimulus deprivation - in the case of vision deprivation

* Organic

* Reverse

* Idiopathic

Clinical features:

* Decreased contrast sensitivity

* Diminution of vision

* Sunglass effect- brightness is less compared to the normal eye

* Crowding phenomenon- slipping of images

Treatment of choice:

* Occlusion of the normal eye (4 to 6 hours/day) using patches.

* Penalization: Blurring of vision using atropine.

Other options:

Option A: Refractive error will be corrected after using visual corrections.

Option B: Astigmatism is a type of refractive error due to rotational asymmetry in the eye's refractive power. There is a difference in refractive power in the visual axis of the same eye.

Option C: It cannot be a case of malingering as the differences in vision and refractory error have been documented.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A construction site worker is brought to emergency with complaints of excessive redness and watering in the right eye. He gave a history of some chemical that had accidentally fallen into his eye few hours back. Which of the following treatment options is best suited for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Irrigation with normal saline

The initial step in the management of a patient presenting with chemical burns is immediate and thorough irrigation with normal saline or clean water delivered through an IV tubing. This is done to prevent further damage.

Along with irrigation, contaminant elimination through mechanical means should be done (e.g. using a swab stick to remove any visible particles)

After the initial steps, maintenance of favorable conditions for rapid and uncomplicated healing by following measures:

* Topical antibiotic drops, for example, moxifloxacin 4-6 times a day to prevent infection. Cycloplegics, such as atropine, might enhance comfort. (option B)

* Steroid eye drops to decrease inflammation, and neutrophil infiltration, and treat anterior uveitis. Caution is advised after 2 weeks, as steroids could disrupt collagen synthesis. (option C)

Grading of severity (Roper–Hall system) of chemical injuries is based on corneal clarity and severity of limbal ischemia:

* Grade 1  is characterized by a clear cornea (epithelial damage only) and no limbal ischemia (excellent prognosis).

* Grade 2 shows a hazy cornea but with visible iris detail and less than one-third of the limbus being ischemic (good prognosis).

* Grade 3 manifests as a total loss of the corneal epithelium, stromal haze obscuring iris detail, and between one-third and half of the limbus showing ischemia (guarded prognosis).

* Grade 4 manifests with an opaque cornea and more than 50% of the limbus showing ischemia (poor prognosis).

Temporal tarsorrhaphy is a surgical procedure in which the eyelids are stitched together. It is done for the protection of the cornea in cases of Bell's palsy or in cases of exposure keratopathy. (option D)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An exclusively breastfed 3-month-old baby was brought with complaints of lethargy, vomiting and diarrhoea. Further examination confirmed the presence of jaundice, hypotonia and hepatomegaly. Ocular examination revealed a bilateral cataract that resembled a drop of oil. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Galactosemia

The clinical scenario of an exclusively breastfed infant presenting with vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, hypotonia, hepatomegaly and bilateral oil drop cataract is suggestive of classical galactosemia.

Classical galactosemia is an autosomal recessive disorder. The enzyme deficient here is galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT). Normally, newborns receive up to 40% of their calorie intake as lactose (glucose + galactose). Without GALT, the infant cannot metabolize galactose 1-phosphate, which accumulates and causes injury to the kidney, liver, and brain.

Clinical features include vomiting, hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, jaundice, congenital cataracts, aminoaciduria, and failure to thrive. There is an increased incidence of Escherichia coli neonatal sepsis. Long-term complications include speech delays, learning impairment, motor dysfunction, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (in females).

Diagnosis: The presence of galactose in urine (positive Benedict's test), elevated blood galactose level, and elevated erythrocyte galactose-1-phosphate level help in confirming the diagnosis.

Treatment is a galactose-free diet. Supportive therapy and the prevention of complications are important.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the instrument.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wire speculum

The image shown is of a wire speculum.

Eye speculums are used to keep the lids apart during intraocular operations (e.g. cataract surgery, glaucoma surgery and keratoplasty), extraocular surgery (e.g. squint surgery, pterygium surgery), enucleation and evisceration operation, removal of conjunctival and corneal foreign bodies, cauterization of corneal ulcer, examination of the eye in a patient with blepharospasm.

Other options:

Option A: Evisceration spatula consists of a small but stout rectangular blade with a slightly convex surface and blunt edges attached to a handle. It is used to separate the uveal tissue from the sclera during evisceration operation.

Option C: Chalazion clamp consists of two limbs like forceps, which can be clamped with the help of a screw. The tip of one limb is flattened in the
form of a round disc while the tip of the other arm has a small circular ring. It is used to fix the chalazion and achieve hemostasis during the incision and curettage operation.

Option D: Bone punch consists of a stout spring handle and two blades attached at a right angle. It is used to enlarge the bony opening during
dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) operation by punching the bone from the margins of the opening.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The World health organisation(WHO) definition of blindness is ________.
options: Best corrected visual acuity of less than 1/60 in the better eye
Best corrected visual acuity of less than 3/60 in the better eye
Presenting visual acuity of worse than 3/60 in the better eye
Presenting visual acuity of worse than 6/60 in the better eye
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Presenting visual acuity of worse than 3/60 in the better eye

The World Health Organisation has adopted the International Classification of Diseases 11 (ICD 11) definition of visual impairment and blindness. As per the new definition, blindness is defined as presenting visual acuity of worse than 3/60 or a corresponding visual field loss to less than 10° in the better eye.

Note: Earlier, the WHO definition of blindness was: Best corrected visual acuity of less than 3/60 in the better eye ( Option B).

Refractive error is the main cause of visual impairment in individuals aged 0-49 years, followed by cataracts, amblyopia, and corneal opacity. However, in the age group >50 years, cataract is the major cause, followed by refractive errors and surgical complications of cataract.

Definitions of blindness and visual impairment as per WHO :

Blindness

Presenting visual acuity <3/60

Mild visual impairment

Presenting visual acuity <6/12 – 6/18

Moderate visual impairment (MVI)
Presenting visual acuity <6/18 – 6/60

Severe visual impairment (SVI)
Presenting visual acuity <6/60 – 3/60

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following anaesthetic agents is most suitable for cataract surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2 % lignocaine

2% Lignocaine (Lidocaine) is the infiltrative anaesthetic suitable for this patient due to its moderate duration of action, which lasts for 30–60 minutes.

Lidocaine is a local anaesthetic that can be used for peripheral nerve blockade, and topical, infiltrative, spinal, and epidural anaesthesia. The duration of infiltration anaesthesia can be prolonged by the addition of epinephrine to lidocaine (up to 120 minutes). It is also used for intravenous regional anaesthesia (IVRA) in short surgical procedures (<90 minutes) on the limbs.

It is metabolized by CYP enzymes in the liver. Large amounts of lidocaine can exacerbate symptoms of myasthenia gravis and cardiac toxicity, as well as transient neurological symptoms.

Bupivacaine, ropivacaine, and tetracaine are all long-acting drugs. (option B,C & D)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following features is associated with vitamin A deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bitot spots

Bitot spots are triangular, pearly-white or yellowish, and foamy spots on the bulbar conjunctiva on either side of the cornea are associated with Vitamin A deficiency.

Option A: Pinguecula is a degenerative condition of the conjunctiva, characterized by the formation of a yellowish-white patch on the bulbar conjunctiva near the limbus. It usually presents as a triangular patch on the nasal side, with the triangle's apex commonly pointed away from the cornea.

Option C: Pterygium is a degenerative condition of the sub-conjunctival tissue. It is a connective tissue disorder and is never inflammatory.  It is made up of three parts: a "cap" (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge), a head, and a body. It occurs due to exposure to radiation: UV-B. The most common site is nasal.

Option D: Stocker's line - deposition of iron on the advancing edge is seen in Pterygium.

Up to the level of Stage 2, the manifestations are reversible if treated with vitamin A supplements.

However, active conjunctival xerosis and Bitot’s spots begin to resolve within 2—5 days after supplementation. Most will disappear within 2 weeks, although a significant proportion of temporal lesions may persist in shrunken form and may therefore not be completely reversible.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 15-year-old patient presents with a history of severe itching and recurrent eye. On examination, a shield ulcer is present, which has developed as a sequela of the underlying disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vernal keratoconjunctivitis

A 15-year-old with a history of severe itching and recurrent eye redness with shield ulcer points is highly suggestive of a diagnosis of Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).

VKC, also known as spring catarrh or warm weather conjunctivitis, is a recurrent inflammation of the conjunctiva with seasonal incidence, commonly occurring in individuals with an atopic background and seasonal allergies due to Th2 lymphocyte alteration followed by IgE response. It is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction.

Classical features of conjunctiva in VKC:

Palpebral VKC

* Cobblestone papillae: upper tarsal conjunctiva

* Associated with ropy discharge

* Maxwell–Lyon sign: pseudomembrane formation of the upper lid when everted and exposed to heat

* Limbal VKC: Horner–Trantas spots are white dots consisting of eosinophils and epithelial debris in the limbal area.

Corneal signs in VKC:

* Shield ulcers

* Vernal plaques

* Subepithelial scarring

* Pseudo-Gerontoxon resembles arcus senilis; it has a cupid's bow outline

The condition presents in three types, which are :

* Palpebral, affecting the upper tarsal conjunctiva, characterised by hypertrophied 'cobblestone' papillae

* Bulbar-limbal, characterised by dusky red triangular congestion of the conjunctiva, gelatinous limbal papillae and Horner-Tranta's spots that are formed due to eosinophils and epithelial debris at the limbus

* Mixed

Treatment of VKC includes allergen avoidance, antihistaminics, steroids, and immunomodulators both topical and systemic depending on the severity of the disease.

The image below represents Horner-Trantas spots.

The above image shows cobblestone appearance.

Other options:

Option B: Phlyctenular conjunctivitis presents with small whitish nodules at the limbus due to hypersensitivity (usually to TB or staphylococcus) and does not lead to shield ulcer formation.

Option C: A bacterial ulcer typically presents with acute pain, redness, watering, purulent discharge, and a corneal infiltrate, often with hypopyon in severe cases and not shield ulcer. The ulcer, in this case, is oval with an associated hypopyon (shown below)

Option D: Herpes simplex keratitis, a form of viral keratitis, is characterized by pain, watering, and photophobia. A distinctive feature is a dendritic ulcer on the cornea, which, upon fluorescein staining, reveals terminal bulbs.The below image shows the characteristic dendritic ulcers of herpes simplex keratitis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 21-year-old student presents with ocular redness, foreign body sensation, and excessive tearing. History reveals she recently returned from a beach vacation, where she frequently wore contact lenses while swimming and admits to poor lens hygiene. What is the most probable causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acanthamoeba

The given clinical history is suggestive of amoebic keratitis caused by Acanthamoeba.

Acanthamoeba exists as an active trophozoite form and a resistant cystic form, both of which are infective. The large, 20–50 μm trophozoite form is distinguished by spine-like pseudopodia called acanthopodia. Human beings acquire infection by inhalation of cysts or trophozoites, ingestion of cysts or through traumatized skin or eyes.

Following inhalation, the trophozoites reach the lungs and invade the central nervous system through the bloodstream, producing granulomatous amebic encephalitis (GAE). It presents chiefly as two chronic conditions: (1) keratitis and (2) granulomatous amoebic encephalitis

Acanthamoeba keratitis is an infection of the eyes that typically develops from the entry of the amebic cyst through abrasions on the cornea. Most of the cases are associated with the use of contact lenses and individuals who swim or bathe in contaminated water.

Patients usually present with photophobia, excessive tearing, redness, and foreign body sensation, which can be bilateral in contact lens users. Pain is disproportionate to the degree of keratitis due to perineural invasion. It presents as a ring lesion or ring stromal infiltrate, as shown below.

Diagnosis of amoebic keratitis is made by the demonstration of the cyst in corneal scrapings by wet mount, histology, and culture. The cysts are smaller (12-25 micrometres) and polygonal or star-shaped.

Management:

* Debridement of the involved epithelium may facilitate eye drop penetration.

* Administer topical biguanides or chlorhexidine, with or without diamidine agents.

* Oral NSAIDs can be used for pain management

* In severe cases, penetrating keratoplasty can be done.

Polygonal cysts of Acanthamoeba in interface contrast microscopy:

Other options:

Option B: Aspergillus fumigatus is a common agent of mycotic corneal ulcers. The slough is usually dry on examination, with feathery borders surrounded by a yellow line of demarcation. Thick, immobile, hypopyon due to direct invasion of fungal hyphae into the anterior chamber can be seen. Satellite lesions may be present. Below is an image showing a fungal ulcer with a dry feathery border and hypopyon.

Option C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common gram-negative organism isolated from corneal ulcers and is a frequent cause of contact lens–associated keratitis. Other risk factors include chlorinated swimming pools, hot tubs, ventilators, nebulizer, and vaporizer solutions, and ophthalmic solution bottles. It has a rapid and fulminant course if left untreated and are associated with a worse visual prognosis than that caused by most other common bacterial pathogens. Pseudomonas spp. can cause corneal perforation in just 48 hours.

Option D:  Keratitis is the inflammation of the cornea characterized by corneal edema, cellular infiltration, and ciliary congestion. Herpes simplex causes epithelial keratitis and in severe forms, dendritic ulcers develop. Most of the patients present with redness, photophobia, watering, and blurred vision. On examination, visual acuity and corneal sensation are reduced. Follicular conjunctivitis and blepharitis may develop but are usually mild. Clinical reactivation occurs due to multiple stress factors and causes recurrent infections. The fluorescein-stained image under slit-lamp examination shows dendritic ulcers, a pathognomic feature of epithelial keratitis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presents with complaints of a painful lid swelling. Physical examination reveals a swollen and painful lid with a pus point on the lid margin. Which of the following glands is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zeis gland

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hordeolum externum, or stye, which is a staphylococcal infection of the Zeis glands.

Hordeolum externum or stye is a staphylococcal infection of the Zeis gland or Moll gland. It presents as a collection of pus usually pointing at the base of a single cilium. The entire lid may be edematous. Treatment is with antibiotics and a warm compress. The abscess may also be drained by pulling out the affected cilia. Incision and drainage may also be done.

Other options:

Option A: Acute dacryoadenitis, which is the inflammation of the lacrimal gland, is typically associated with painful swelling of the lateral part of the upper lid, leading to an S-shaped swelling. Painful proptosis may also be observed.

Option B: Hordeolum internum is the suppurative inflammation of the Meibomian gland and may occur as a primary infection or secondary to infected chalazion. There is a tender swelling with a pus point facing toward the tarsal conjunctiva. The image below shows an internal hordeolum.

Option D: The glands of Krause and Wolfring are accessory conjunctival glands.

Pearl PF1388: Layers of the Tear Film

Lipid layer

* Outermost layer

* Secreted by the meibomian, Zeis glands

* Prevents evaporation of tears

Aqueous layer

* Middle layer

* Secreted by the lacrimal and accessory lacrimal glands

* Provides lubrication

Mucin layer

* Innermost layer

* Secreted by the goblet cells of the conjunctiva

* Help in spreading the tear film over the ocular surface

The maximum density of the goblet cells is seen on the nasal bulbar conjunctiva.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old female came to the clinic with headache and visual field loss. A pituitary adenoma was found compressing the optic chiasma. What visual field defect will be seen in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bitemporal hemianopia

The pituitary tumour compressing the optic chiasma results in bitemporal hemianopia.

Pituitary macroadenoma can compress the optic chiasm, causing bitemporal hemianopia, which leads to the loss of vision in the temporal halves of the visual fields in both eyes. This occurs when damage to the middle part of the optic chiasm affects the crossing fibres from the nasal retina of each eye while the uncrossed fibres from the temporal retinas remain intact. As a result, individuals retain central vision but lose peripheral vision on the sides.

The most common cause of bitemporal hemianopia is a pituitary adenoma. Other common causes include:

* suprasellar aneurysms

* chronic arachnoiditis

* suprasellar tumours like craniopharyngioma and suprasellar meningioma

Other options:

Option B: Loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes (e.g., right half of both eyes causes right homonymous hemianopia), but here it's the temporal fields of both eyes.

Option C: Homonymous anopia, sometimes used loosely, but strictly means loss of the same entire visual field ('an-' = absence) in both eyes.

Option D: Inferior quadrantanopia is seen in the lesion of parietal lobe optic radiation → “pie on the floor” defect.

Pearl PF2187: Lesions in the optic pathway

Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above.

* The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other.

* A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye.

* Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia.

* A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness).

* Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with difficulty reacting to bright light. On examination, the pupillary reflex is absent, but the near reflex is preserved. Where is the lesion likely located?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pretectal area of the midbrain

This is a classic case of light–near dissociation, also known as argyll robertson pupil where the lesion lies in the pretectal region of the midbrain.

Argyll Robertson Pupil (ARP) is characterized by a light-near dissociation, meaning the pupils react to accommodation (near reflex) but not to light. This condition is linked to neurosyphilis, causing a dorsal midbrain lesion that affects the pupillary light pathway while sparing the more ventrally located pupillary near reflex pathway.

Key features of Argyll Robertson pupil include:

* Bilateral, small, and irregular pupils in dim light.

* Accommodation Reflex Present: The pupil constricts when focusing on a near target.

* Light Reflex Absent: The pupils do not constrict when exposed to bright light.

Cocaine Eye Drops Induced Mydriasis: Pupils will dilate in response to cocaine eye drops.

Other clinical features in neurosyphilis:

* Fleeting and repetitive lancinating pains, primarily in the legs

* acute abdominal pain with vomiting(visceral crisis)

* Tabes dorsalis with Ataxia and gait disturbances due to loss of position sense

* Loss of reflexes in the legs

* Paresthesias, bladder disturbances

Pupillary light reflex pathway:

* First neurons (sensory) connect each retina with both pretectal nuclei in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculi.

* Second neurons (internuncial) connect each pretectal nucleus to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei.

* Third neurons (preganglionic motor) connect the Edinger–Westphal nucleus to the ciliary ganglion.

* Fourth neurons (postganglionic motor) leave the ciliary ganglion and pass in the short ciliary nerves to innervate the sphincter pupillae.

Other options:

Option A: If the optic nerve were damaged, both the light reflex and the near reflex would be lost, because no visual impulses would reach the brain to trigger either reflex.

Option B: If the oculomotor nerve were damaged, the pupil would not constrict at all, so both the light reflex and the near reflex would be absent. Since the near reflex is still present in this patient, the lesion cannot be in the oculomotor nerve.

Option C: If the Edinger-Westphal nucleus were damaged, again, both the light reflex and the near reflex would be lost because this nucleus supplies the parasympathetic fibers responsible for pupil constriction.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man was prescribed +12D glasses. He has deep anterior chamber with a deep jet-black pupil and no lens was seen on the slit lamp examination. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aphakia

The need for +12 D glasses, a deep anterior chamber with jet-black pupil, and absence of lens on slit lamp are classical findings that together confirm aphakia.

Aphakia is the absence of the natural crystalline lens of the eye, usually caused by surgical removal, trauma, or congenital absence.

Signs of surgical aphakia include the following:

* Limbal scar

* Anterior chamber deeper than normal

* Iridodonesis (tremulousness of the iris)

* Jet black color of the pupil

* Only the first and second images (normally, four images are seen) seen on Purkinje’s image test

* Small disc seen on fundus examination

* High hypermetropia seen on retinoscopy

Aphakic eyes (eyes without a lens) only produce two Purkinje images, as the absence of the lens eliminates the reflections from the anterior and posterior lens surfaces. The test helps differentiate pseudophakia from aphakia and is useful for confirming the presence of an IOL.

Intraocular lens (IOL) implantation is done to correct aphakia following cataract surgeries. Singh and Worst’s lens is fixed on the iris by enclavating the mid-peripheral iris stroma into claw-shaped haptics, without sutures. Haptics refer to the supporting structures that hold the lens in place within the eye. They are associated with a high incidence of postoperative complications.

Posterior chamber lenses (PCIOLs) are placed entirely behind the iris. Anterior chamber IOLs are placed entirely in front of the iris. They are supported at the angle of the anterior chamber.

Other options:

Option B: Pseudophakia is wrong because in pseudophakia, the patient has an intraocular lens implant (IOL) after cataract surgery. On slit lamp examination, the IOL would be clearly visible within the pupillary area.

Option C: Hypermetropia has the lens present and usually needs only low-to-moderate (+1D to +6D) correction.

Option D: Myopia necessitates the use of minus (–) power lenses, not +12D. In this case, the patient requires strong positive correction due to an absent lens, thereby excluding a diagnosis of myopia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 65-year-old elderly diabetic female presents to the emergency department with complaints of a sudden onset of severe pain in one eye, marked redness, blurred vision, and headache. On examination, there is a hazy cornea with a mid-dilated and fixed pupil with a shallow anterior chamber. What is the likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute angle closure glaucoma

This is a case of acute angle-closure glaucoma, which typically presents with sudden onset of a painful red eye, corneal haze, a mid-dilated fixed pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber.

Angle-closure glaucoma involves a sudden increase in intraocular pressure due to blockage of the anterior chamber angle. It is characterized by severe eye pain, blurred vision, and a mid-dilated pupil, with diffuse redness rather than the circumcorneal congestion seen in uveitis. It has constantly raised IOP >21mmHg, optic disc cupping, and visual field defects.

The primary goal in managing Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (PACG) is to prevent optic nerve damage by reducing IOP. In acute attacks, treatment involves aggressively lowering IOP using intravenous mannitol and oral acetazolamide to quickly control symptoms. Topical medications such as pilocarpine, beta-blockers, cholinergic agents, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are also used to address the acute episode.

Once the immediate crisis is managed, YAG laser iridotomy (YAG PI) is performed to create an alternate drainage pathway for the aqueous humor, both in the affected eye and the fellow eye. For ongoing management, patients with PACG may require glaucoma medications to maintain target IOP. In cases where maximal medical therapy fails, surgical options such as trabeculectomy or glaucoma drainage devices may be necessary, particularly if there is progressive visual field loss or non-compliance with treatment. Cyclodestructive procedures may be considered for patients with a painful, blind eye or those with recurrent surgical failures.

Signs:

Corneal edema- coloured halos
Conjunctiva- congestion, chemosis
IOP- elevated 40–70 mm Hg
AC- very shallow
Pupil- vertically oval, mid-dilated
Angle- completely closed, Grade 0

Other options:

Option B: Retinal detachment presents with painless, sudden loss of vision, photopsia (flashes), floaters, curtain falling sensation. No corneal haze or painful red eye.

Option C: Open-angle glaucoma is chronic, asymptomatic until late. Gradual painless loss of peripheral vision (tunnel vision).No redness, no acute pain.

Option D: Acute uveitis presents with painful red eye but typically has constricted pupil (miosis), not mid-dilated fixed. Aqueous flare, keratic precipitates may be seen. No shallow anterior chamber.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A myopic patient presents with photopsia and floaters. On examination, pigmentation in the anterior vitreous is observed. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment

The given clinical scenario of a myopic patient presenting with photopsia, floaters and pigmentation in the anterior vitreous (Shafers' sign) is highly suggestive of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

Definition of retinal detachment: The separation of the neurosensory retina from the RPE.

Types of retinal detachment:

A. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment – It is due to the accumulation of fluid between the neurosensory retina (NSR) and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) due to a retinal tear.

* Causes:

* High myopes

* Retinoschisis – splitting of neurosensory retina plus vitreous degeneration

* Typical retinoschisis-split at the level of the outer plexiform layer

* Atypical retinoschisis-split at the level of the nerve fiber layer

* Trauma

* Pseudophakia

* Aphakia

* The most dangerous type of retinal break is a horseshoe tear.

* The most dangerous location of retinal break is the superotemporal retina.

* Clinical features

* Photopsia – flashes of light due to vitreoretinal traction at the site of the break

* Floaters

* Visual field defect – a black curtain/veil in front of the eye

* Signs

* Hypotony – as the liquefied vitreous in the subretinal space is absorbed through the RPE.

* Shafers' sign pigments in the anterior vitreous (tobacco dusting) are a feature of fresh retinal detachment.

* The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is corrugated with undulations.

* Treatment

* Prophylactic laser barrage

* Scleral buckling

* Pneumatic retinopexy

* Pars plana vitrectomy

B. Tractional retinal detachment: Fibro-vascular membranes in the vitreous due to long-standing retinal neovascularisation exert traction on the retina.

* Causes

* Proliferative diabetic retinopathy

* Central retinal venous occlusion

* Eales disease

* Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP)

* Signs

* The detached retina is concave in configuration. No breaks are seen

* Treatment

* Pars plana vitrectomy with endo photocoagulation.

C. Exudative retinal detachment: Exudative fluid from the choroid collects in the subretinal space, leading to retinal detachment.

* Causes

* Inflammatory conditions like choroiditis, posterior scleritis

* Choroidal tumours like melanoma

* Toxaemia of pregnancy

* Malignant hypertension

* Coats disease

* Clinical features

* Floaters due to vitritis but no photopsia

* Visual field defect

* Signs

* The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is smooth. No break is seen.

* Shifting fluid is seen.

* Treatment

* Systemic steroids

* Treatment of the cause

The image below shows a fundus which reveals retinal detachment inferiorly from 3-9 o'clock with a tear at 3:30

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presented to OPD with complaints of ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. A diagnosis of superior orbital fissure syndrome was confirmed after examination. Which nerves are compressed in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. III, IV, V(1), VI

In Superior Orbital Fissure Syndrome, Cranial nerves III (oculomotor), IV (Trochlear nerve), VI (Abducens nerve), and V1 (Ophthalmic division of the Trigeminal nerve) get compressed causing ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, and sensory loss in the V1 area.

The superior orbital fissure is an important anatomical opening in the skull that allows several critical structures to pass through. Among these structures, the frontal nerve and nasociliary nerve are branches of the ophthalmic nerve, the first division of the trigeminal nerve (V1), which is responsible for sensory innervation to parts of the face. The frontal nerve provides sensation to the forehead, the anterior scalp, and the dorsum of the nose, while the nasociliary nerve supplies sensation to parts of the nasal cavity.

Superior orbital fissure syndrome is characterized by the following:

* Pain, typically labeled as retro–orbital ache

* Sensory loss/disturbances in the distribution of the ophthalmic division of the 5th cranial nerve

* Ipsilateral ophthalmoplegia due to the involvement of the 3rd, 4th, and 6th cranial nerves involvement

* Ptosis, due to 3rd nerve paralysis

Trauma affecting the orbital region is the most common cause of superior orbital fissure syndrome. Other causes include infections such as herpes zoster ophthalmicus, inflammatory disorders, and tumors. Diagnosis is mainly clinical, supported by imaging modalities like CT or MRI to identify the underlying pathology. Management depends on the cause and may involve surgical decompression, corticosteroid therapy, or antiviral treatment.

Pearl PF0436: Superior orbital fissure

Structures passing through the Superior orbital fissure

Above the common tendinous ring: LFT (Superolateral compartment)

* Lacrimal nerve

* Frontal nerve

* Trochlear nerve

* Superior opthalmic vein

Within the common tendinous ring: BAN (Intermediate compartment)

* Both divisions of oculomotor nerve

* Abducens nerve

* Nasociliary nerve

Below the common tendinous ring (Inferomedial compartment)

* Inferior ophthalmic vein

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. The radiological image shows the following findings. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Orbital blowout fracture

The given CT image shows the characteristic "hanging drop sign" indicating a blowout fracture of the orbital wall.

Hanging drop/tear-drop sign is characteristic of an orbital "blow-out" fracture, which represents the orbital contents herniating through the floor of the orbit into the maxillary antrum.

Blow-out orbital fractures are caused by trauma to the orbit by a large, rounded object, e.g cricket ball, a human fist, etc. This force can cause the displacement of the eyeball backwards and an increase in intraorbital pressure. This leads to fracturing at the weakest point of the orbital wall (orbital floor and sometimes medial wall). Clinical signs are periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis and subconjunctival haemorrhage (later stages).

Definitive treatment is by surgical repair 10-14 days after injury with initial supportive management with analgesics and antibiotic

Indications for surgery in a "blow-out" fracture are as follows:

* Diplopia not resolving significantly in the early days after trauma

* A fracture with a large herniation of tissues into the antrum

* Incarceration of tissues in the fracture, resulting in globe retraction and increased applanation tension on attempted upward gaze

* Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm

The most useful projection for detecting an orbital floor fracture is the Water’s view.

Other options:

Option B: Zygomatic fracture Involves zygomatic bone (cheekbone), producing “flattened cheek” and step deformity at the infraorbital rim.

Option C:  Maxillary fracture Involves alveolar process / maxillary sinus walls. Here, the fracture is confined to the orbital floor.

Option D: Le-fort 1 fracture is a horizontal fracture of the maxilla, separating the upper alveolar part (upper teeth + palate) from the rest of the face.

Pearl PF1981: Le-Fort's classification of Maxillary Fracture

Le-Fort I is a transverse fracture of the maxilla

* Fracture line passes through the lower part of nasal septum, maxillary antra and the pterygoid plates

* It separates palate from the rest of the face leading to floating teeth or palate

* Also called Guerin’s fracture.

Le-Fort II is a pyramidal fracture

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, lacrimal bone, floor of the orbit, upper part of the maxillary sinus and pterygoid plates

* X-ray or CT appears like hanging maxilla

* It is associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

Le-Fort III is craniofacial dysjunction i.e., facial skeleton completely disconnected from its cranial attachment

* Fracture line passes through the root of the nose, ethmo-frontal junction, superior orbital fissure, lateral wall of the orbit, fronto-zygomatic and temporo-zygomatic sutures and the upper part of pterygoid plates

* It is also associated with CSF rhinorrhea.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a painless ulcer in the eye. On examination, a long branching ulcer with desquamated epithelium is seen on the cornea. What could be the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dendritic ulcer

A long branching corneal ulcer with desquamated epithelium is typical of a dendritic ulcer seen in herpes simplex keratitis. As shown in the image below:

Herpes viral keratitis, also known as herpetic keratoconjunctivitis, is a form of keratitis caused by recurrent herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection in the cornea. The virus, which lies dormant in the trigeminal ganglion after an initial infection, periodically reactivates and replicates. These reactivations result in unilateral symptoms of epithelial or stromal keratitis.

Patients with epithelial keratitis complain of foreign-body sensation, light sensitivity, redness, and blurred vision associated with focal or diffuse reduction in corneal sensation. Stromal keratitis manifests as a disc-shaped area of corneal edema. In patients who are immunocompromised due to pre-existing disease or using corticosteroids, the ulcer may become large; in such cases, the lesion is called a geographic ulcer.

Treatment:

Topical antivirals are the first-line treatment.

* Trifluorothymidine 1% drops four times a day for 5 days, acyclovir 3% ointment five times a day for 21 days, or 3% vidarabine ointment five times a day for 2 weeks

* Systemic antivirals in cases of increased severity or recurrence

* Topical antibiotics to prevent secondary bacterial infection

Other options:

Option A: Fungal ulcer is typically painful, with grayish-white infiltrates, feathery margins, hypopyon and satellite lesions.An immune ring, also known as a Wesseley ring, can form around the ulcer, caused by the deposition of immune complexes.

Option C: Acanthamoeba keratitis usually occurs in contact lens users or after exposure to contaminated water and is very painful, often out of proportion to the clinical signs due to perineural invasion with a characteristic ring-shaped stromal infiltrate.

Option D: A bacterial ulcer is typically painful, with redness, watering, and a localized corneal infiltrate that may lead to hypopyon in severe cases. It does not usually present as a long, branching, or dendritic pattern.
