questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient underwent an eye examination, and when light was shone into the right eye, the pupil of the left eye also constricted. What explains the constriction in the left eye?
options: Contraction of the ciliary muscle due to parasympathetic stimulation
Relaxation of the ciliary muscle due to sympathetic stimulation
Stimulation of the afferent pathway from the left eye
Stimulation of the efferent pathway with crossover at the Edinger-Westphal nucleus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stimulation of the efferent pathway with crossover at the Edinger-Westphal nucleus

The pupillary light reflex pathway involves several components, with the pretectal nucleus in the midbrain serving as the central integrative center for the reflex. When light is shone into one eye, it causes bilateral constriction of the pupils, a response known as the pupillary light reflex. This reflex has two components:

Direct light reflex: constriction of the pupil in the eye being illuminated.
Consensual light reflex: constriction of the pupil in the opposite eye.

Pathway for light reflex

* Afferent fibers travel from the retina to the optic nerve, optic chiasma, and terminate in the pretectal nucleus.

* Internuncial fibers connect the pretectal nucleus with Edinger Westphal nuclei of both sides.

* Parasympathetic fibers arise from the Edinger Westphal nuclei of both sides, travel along the oculomotor nerve, and relay in the ciliary ganglion.

* Postganglionic fibers travel along short ciliary nerves to innervate sphincter pupillae.

Clinical correlate- Since internuncial fibers connect the pretectal nucleus with Edinger Westphal nuclei of both sides, consensual light reflex is seen.

Other options:

Option A: The ciliary muscle controls accommodation, not the pupillary light reflex.

Option B: The sympathetic pathway mainly controls pupil dilation (by innervating the dilator pupillae muscle), not constriction.

Option C: If the light is given to the right eye, the afferent pathway from the left eye is not involved at all.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A posterior staphyloma was noted on indirect ophthalmoscopy. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pathological myopia

Posterior staphyloma is a hallmark of pathological myopia.

Pathological/degenerative myopia is characterized by progressive anteroposterior elongation of the scleral envelope associated with secondary ocular changes due to the mechanical stretching of the involved tissues. The following changes are seen:

* A pale tessellated (tigroid) appearance of the fundus is seen as the choroid becomes visible due to diffuse attenuation of the RPE

* Temporal myopic crescent

* Focal chorioretinal atrophy

* Anomalous optic nerve head with tilted conformation

* Acquired optic disc pit formation

* Lattice degeneration

* Cystoid degeneration

* Lacquer cracks are fine, irregular yellow lines crisscrossing at the posterior pole due to ruptures in the Bruch membrane.

* Subretinal coin hemorrhages develop from lacquer cracks.

* Fuchs spot: It is a raised, circular, pigmented scar at the macula that develops after absorption of subretinal hemorrhage.

* Posterior staphyloma occurs due to progressive thinning and outpouching of the posterior sclera, visible on indirect ophthalmoscopy.

Staphyloma is an abnormal protrusion of the uveal tissue through a weak and thin portion of the cornea or sclera. Posterior staphyloma presents as a scleral and choroidal bulge behind the equator. Ophthalmoscopy reveals an excavated area with dipping retinal vessels. It is lined internally by uveal tissue and externally by weak cornea or sclera.

Types of Staphyloma:

* Anterior staphyloma: It is characterized by ectasia of the pseudo-cornea, which occurs after the total sloughing of the cornea. It is lined internally by the iris and externally by the newly formed epithelium.

* Intercalary staphyloma: This is located at the limbus and is lined by the root of the iris and the anterior-most part of the ciliary body

* Ciliary staphyloma: It is characterized by ectasia of weak sclera lined by the ciliary body. This affects the ciliary zone, which includes the region up to 8 mm behind the limbus.

* Equatorial staphyloma: This occurs at the equatorial region up to 14 mm behind the limbus of the eye.

* Posterior staphyloma: This affects the posterior pole of the eye.

Note :
The most common cause of anterior staphyloma is a sloughing corneal ulcer.
The most common cause of posterior staphyloma is degenerative high axial myopia.

Other options:

Option B: Hypermetropia is a refractive error of the eye in which parallel rays of light from infinity focus behind the retina when accommodation is at rest. Fundoscopy findings in hypermetropia include shot silk appearance (retina may shine due to the greater brilliance of light reflections) and pseudopapillitis.

Option C: Scleritis refers to an inflammation of the sclera proper. It usually occurs in females more than males. It is frequently associated with an underlying systemic inflammatory condition. The patient presents with moderate to severe pain, redness, lacrimation, photophobia, and diminution of vision.

Option D: Corneal ulcer is an anterior segment lesion of the cornea, while posterior staphyloma is a fundus finding due to pathological myopia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Hirschberg's test is being performed in this patient with squint. Which of the following is correct about the case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 90 Prism dioptre exotropia

From the given image of a Hirschberg test, it can be inferred that the patient has 90 prism dioptres (PD) of exotropia.

In the Hirschberg test, if the light reflection is on the nasal limbus, it means 45 degrees exotropia. One degree is equal to 2 PD (prism dioptre). Therefore, 45 degrees exotropia would mean 90 PD exotropia in the right eye.The Hirschberg test is used to detect squint.

The Hirschberg test gives a rough objective estimate of the angle of manifest strabismus. A pen torch is shone into the eyes from arm’s length, and the patient is asked to fixate on the light. The corneal reflection of the light will be centered in the pupil of the fixating eye but will be decentred in a squinting eye, in the direction opposite to that of the deviation. The distance of the corneal light reflection from the center of the pupil is noted; each millimeter of the deviation is approximately equal to 7°.

Other options:

Option A: 90 degrees exotropia is incorrect because ocular deviations are measured in prism dioptres, not in degrees.

Option B: 90 Prism dioptre esotropia is incorrect as the deviation is outward (exotropia), not inward (esotropia).

Option D: 90 degrees esotropia is incorrect due to wrong unit (degrees instead of prism dioptres) and wrong direction (exotropia, not esotropia).

Pearl PF1401: Classification of Strabismus

* Pseudostrabismus—Apparent squint

* Pseudo esotropia

* Pseduo exotropia

* Heterophoria—Latent squint

* Esophoria: Convergent

* Exophoria: Divergent

* Hyperphoria: Deviation upwards

* Hypophoria: Deviation downwards

* Cyclophoria: Rotation around AP axis

* Heterotropia—Manifest squint

* Concomitant

* Amount of deviation remains constant in all directions of gaze.

* Esotropia: Convergent

* Infantile

* Accommodative

* Sensory

* Consecutive

* Exotropia: Divergent

* Congenital

* Primary

* Secondary: Sensory deprived

* Consecutive

* Hypertropia: Vertical squint

* Incomitant

* Amount of deviation varies in different directions of gaze

* Paralytic squint

* Restrictive squint

* A and V pattern heterotropia

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the defect shown in the image:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Herbert pits

The image shows tiny lesions at the limbus, indicating Herbert's pits. This finding is seen in trachoma, which is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, more specifically the trachoma inclusion conjunctivitis (TRIC) serovars A, B, Ba, and C.

Trachoma is a form of chronic infective conjunctivitis and is one of the leading causes of blindness. It has an ‘active’ inflammatory stage and a ‘cicatricial’ chronic stage.

The active inflammatory stage is more prevalent in children and presents with nonspecific symptoms of ocular irritation, foreign body sensation, and discharge (often mild symptoms). Examination findings at this stage show:

* Conjunctival follicles contain Leber cells (multinucleated lymphocytes)

* Limbal Herbert's follicles (similar to conjunctival follicles)

Cicatricial chronic stage is seen in middle age. And when the chronic infection with sequelae sets in, the patient complains of pain, lacrimation, photophobia, and later blurring, and finally loss of vision. The conjunctiva shows concretions (whitish deposits of inspissated mucus in depressions called glands of Henle). Corneal signs include:

* Herbert pits (pitted scars in the limbal, which are remnants of healed Herbert follicles)

* Corneal opacity is seen in later stages.

There can be associated trichiasis (when at least one eyelash rubs the eyeball) and entropion.

At present, WHO grading with 'FISTO' is in use.

Trachoma is treated according to the WHO classification using the SAFE strategy (Surgery, Antibiotics, Facial hygiene, and Environmental improvement). Azithromycin is the antibiotic of choice, and surgery involves the correction of trichiasis and entropion. In case of significant corneal scarring, penetrating keratoplasty is done.

Other options:

Option B: Horner–Trantas dots (image below) are distinct white, chalky, gelatinous nodules made up of eosinophils and epithelial debris that appear at the limbus, and they are characteristic of limbal vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).

Option C: In giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC), gelatinous papillae initially appear as small, elevated nodules on the conjunctiva. These papillae eventually grow larger, forming macropapillae and giant papillae, and may be accompanied by Trantas dots at the limbus.

The image below shows giant papillae in the conjunctiva:

Option D: Progressive pannus in trachoma involves the infiltration of the cornea with new blood vessels developing in the upper part, lying between the epithelium and Bowman's membrane. As the condition advances, these superficial vessels contribute to the destruction of Bowman's membrane, with corneal infiltration occurring before significant vascularization.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the refractive error in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Regular astigmatism

The given figure is a Sturm's conoid, which is characteristically seen in regular astigmatism.

When light passes through a regularly astigmatic surface (surface with toric curvature), vertical and horizontal rays converge at different points. The distance between the points of convergence (focus) of the vertical and horizontal rays is called the focal interval of Sturm (distance between points B and F). The circle of least confusion/circle of diffusion lies at the midpoint of this interval.

For the given Sturm's conoid,

* At point A, a horizontal oval is formed because vertical rays converge more rapidly than horizontal rays.

* At point B, vertical rays come to a focus, while horizontal rays are still converging, so it will be a horizontal straight line.

* At points C, D, and E, the vertical rays are diverging and horizontal rays are still converging.

* At point D, the vertical rays have diverged as much as the horizontal rays have converged, so we get a perfect circle called the circle of least confusion.

* At point E, a vertical oval is formed.

* At point F, a vertical straight line is formed

* At point G and beyond, both rays are diverging, and we always get a vertical oval/prolate ellipse.

Astigmatism is a type of refractive error in which the eye does not focus light evenly on the retina. This results in a distorted or blurred vision. Other symptoms include eyestrain or asthenopia with headaches.

Types:

* Regular astigmatism: In this, refractive power changes uniformly from one meridian to another, resulting in 2 principal meridians

* Irregular astigmatism: It is characterized by an irregular change of refractive power in different meridians, and hence it has multiple meridians.

Types of regular astigmatism:

* With the rule astigmatism: The vertical meridian is more curved than the horizontal meridian but they are placed at right angles to one another

* Against-the-rule astigmatism: Here the horizontal meridian is more curved than the vertical meridian

* Oblique astigmatism: Here, the two principal meridians are not the horizontal and vertical meridians, although they are at right angles to each other. It is a type of regular astigmatism. e.g., one may be at 45 degrees and the other at 135 degrees.

* Bioblique astigmatism: Here, the two principal meridians are not at right angles to each other; for example, one may be at 40 degrees and the other at 100 degrees. It is also a type of regular astigmatism.

Note: Refractive types of regular astigmatism:

* Simple astigmatism: rays are focused on the retina in one meridian: either in front (simple myopic, as shown in the above image) of the retina or behind the retina (simple hyperopic)

* Compound astigmatism: rays in both the meridians are focused in front or behind the retina

* Mixed astigmatism: Light rays in one meridian are focused in front of the retina and those in the other meridian are focused behind the retina

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 21-year-old man presented with the following lesion in his eye. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bitot's spots

The image depicts Bitot's spot, a pathognomonic feature of xerophthalmia.

Bitot's spot is a triangular, silvery-white, foamy patch on the bulbar conjunctiva which is usually bilateral. The most common site is temporal.

Ocular manifestations of vitamin A deficiency include loss of sensitivity to green light (earliest to appear), nyctalopia (night blindness), and xerophthalmia.

Xerophthalmia includes conjunctival xerosis (dryness) with Bitot’s spots (white patches of keratinized epithelium appearing on the sclera), corneal ulcers, and keratomalacia (softening of the cornea) that leads to corneal scarring and ultimately, blindness.

Pearl PF0046: WHO grading of Vitamin A deficiency

The term xerophthalmia is reserved to cover all the ocular manifestations of vitamin A deficiency.

Stage
Features
Pathophysiology

XN
Night blindness
Lack of rhodopsin

X1A
Conjunctival Xerosis
Conjunctival epithelial alteration, loss of goblet cells

X1B
Bitot’s spots
Conjunctival keratinization and plaque formation

X2
Corneal xerosis
Corneal epithelial alteration

X3A
Corneal ulceration/ Keratomalacia affecting <1/3rd of the corneal surface
Liquefaction of corneal stroma

X3B
Corneal ulceration/ Keratomalacia affecting >1/3rd of the corneal surface
-

XS
Corneal scar
-

XF
Xerophthalmic fundus
Degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium

The first symptom of xerophthalmia is nyctalopia.

The first sign of xerophthalmia is conjunctival xerosis.

The pathognomonic feature of xerophthalmia is the appearance of Bitot's spots.

Note:

Up to the level of Stage 2, the manifestations are reversible if treated with vitamin A supplements.

However, active conjunctival xerosis and Bitot’s spots begin to resolve within 2—5 days after supplementation. Most will disappear within 2 weeks, although a significant proportion of temporal lesions may persist in shrunken form and may therefore not be completely reversible.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 23-year-old man presents with a history of injury to the eye resulting in pain, photophobia, and redness of the eye for the past 2 days. He said he had brushed his eyes against some leaves and thorns when he was gardening.What would be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fungal keratitis

The given clinical situation suggests that it is a case of fungal keratitis as it is caused by trauma with vegetative matter like leaves and thorns.

Salient features of a fungal corneal ulcer:

* It is caused by trauma with vegetative or organic matter.

* Signs are more pronounced than symptoms.

* The corneal ulcer appears dry.

* Delicate feathery finger-like extensions are present.

* A sterile, immune ring (yellow line of demarcation) may be present

* Multiple, small satellite lesions may be present around the ulcer.

* Usually, a big hypopyon is present.

* Pigmented ulcer (brownish) may be caused by some dematiaceous species of fungi.

* Perforation in mycotic ulcers is rare but can occur..

Image: Fungal corneal ulcer, with the arrowhead indicating a satellite lesion

Steroids are contraindicated in a fungal corneal ulcer. Steroids make the fungi facultative pathogens which are otherwise symbiotic saprophytes.

Pearl PF1375: Clinical differential diagnosis of corneal ulcer

Bacterial
Fungal
Viral
Parasitic

Risk factors

Contact lens wear

Trauma

Chronic steroid use

Anesthetic cornea

Dry eyes

Exposure keratopathy

Trauma with vegetable matter

Low immunity

Recurrent attacks

Contact lens wear

Exposure to contaminated water (acanthamoeba)

Clinical features

Hypopyon is fluid and mobile

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is likely to have a rapid course, with deep corneal necrosis.

Less pain and watering compared to the extent of vision loss and signs.

Tend to be indolent but progressive

Hypopyon is thick, immobile.

Relatively more pain and watering compared to the extent of vision loss and signs.

Recurrences are characteristic.

Disproportionately severe pain is a characteristic feature.

Indolent course and in initial stages, often mistaken to be viral/ fungal infection, leading to a delay in diagnosis

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with a deformed eye. He was treated for a corneal ulcer 2 weeks back which took a long time to heal despite antibiotics treatment. His physical examination is remarkable for the findings shown in the image. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anterior staphyloma

The clinical vignette is suggestive of a diagnosis of anterior staphyloma.

Staphyloma (a bunch of grapes) is a clinical condition characterized by ectasia of the outer coats (cornea, or sclera or both) of the eye, with the involvement of the uveal tissue. The basic underlying pathology is the weakening of the eyewall, which can be caused by many inflammatory or degenerative diseases involving these structures.

Types of staphyloma

* Anterior staphyloma: an ectasia of the pseudocornea, which results from the total sloughing of the cornea. It is lined internally by the iris and externally, by the newly formed epithelium.

* Intercalary staphyloma: This is located at the limbus and is lined by the root of the iris.

* Ciliary staphyloma: Ectasia of weak sclera lined by the ciliary body. This affects the ciliary zone that includes the region up to 8 mm behind the limbus.

* Equatorial staphyloma: This occurs at the equatorial region up to 14 mm behind the limbus of the eye.

* Posterior staphyloma: This affects the posterior pole of the eye.

Note:

*  The most common cause for anterior staphyloma is sloughing corneal ulcer.

*  The most common cause for posterior staphyloma is degenerative high axial myopia.

Image showing the types of staphyloma.

Treatment: Local excision and repair with a corneal and scleral patch graft. Enucleation and replacement with an implant can be done for disfigured and blind eyes. Degenerative diseases responsible should be treated early to prevent secondary glaucoma and staphyloma formation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy was brought to the ophthalmology OPD with complaints of intense itching, photopobia and ropy discharge from his eyes. Moreover, on examination the following finding is present. What is the most probable diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vernal keratoconjunctivitis

The above image depicts cobblestone appearance, which is a papillary reaction in the palpebral conjunctiva, and also the presence of ropy discharge points towards the diagnosis of vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) or spring catarrh .

* It is also called as warm weather conjunctivitis

* It primarily affects boys, and the onset is generally from the age of 5 years.

* It is primarily a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction that is IgE mediated. It also involves type 4 hypersensitivity reaction.

Classical features of conjunctiva in VKC:

Palpebral VKC

* Cobblestone papillae: upper tarsal conjunctiva

* Associated with ropy discharge

* Maxwell–Lyon sign: pseudomembrane formation of the upper lid when everted and exposed to heat

Limbal VKC: Horner–Trantas spots are white dots consisting of eosinophils and epithelial debris in the limbal area.

Corneal signs in VKC:

* Shield ulcers

* Vernal plaques

* Subepithelial scarring

* Pseudo-gerontoxon resembles arcus senilus; it has a cupid's bow outline

Image: Horner Trantas spots

Below image- Bitot spots

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old diabetic male presents with a history of decreased vision. Fluorescein angiography showed the following image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Proliferative diabetic retinopathy

The given image of fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) depicts neovascularization, which is the hallmark of proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

The neovascularization arises from the optic nerve head; there is neovascularization of the disc (NVD) along the large vessels and neovascularization elsewhere (NVE).The treatment available for proliferative diabetic retinopathy is photocoagulation of the ischaemic areas to reduce the metabolic demand and decrease or prevent the release of vasoproliferative factors.

Stages and fundus picture in diabetic retinopathy:

Background Diabetic Retinopathy:

* Microaneurysms

* Dot and Blot hemorrhages

* Exudates

Preproliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (indicates progressive retinal ischemia):

* Intra-retinal microvascular abnormalities

* Venous changes (such as beading)

* Cotton wool spots

* Deep retinal hemorrhages

Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy:

* NeoVascularization of the optic Disc (NVD)

* NeoVascularization Elsewhere in the periphery of the fundus (NVE)

Advanced Diabetic Eye Disease:

* Tractional retinal detachment

* Vitreous hemorrhage

* Neovascular glaucoma

Diabetic Maculopathy is a separate entity that is applied to the changes that occur in the macula such as macular edema or ischemia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man was brought to the OPD by his daughter with complaints of drooping of his left eyelid and double vision. The pupils were dilated in the same eye and an examination of his eye movements is shown below. What is the likely injured nerve here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oculomotor

The image of the left eye being "down and out" along with ptosis, double vision and pupillary dilation is suggestive of oculomotor nerve palsy.

Isolated 3rd nerve palsy

Causes

* Microvascular disease associated with systemic risk factors such as hypertension and diabetes is the most common cause of third nerve palsy.

* Aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery at its junction with the internal carotid, both direct and secondary to subdural hematoma with uncal herniation.

* Episodic- migraine, compression, ischemia, and alterations in intracranial pressure

* Miscellaneous- tumour and inflammatory diseases such as syphilis, Lyme disease, and sarcoidosis; giant cell arteritis; and vasculitis associated with collagen vascular disorders.

Signs

* Profound ptosis due to the weakness of the levator muscle

* Abduction and depression in the primary position ("down and out")

* Normal abduction as the lateral rectus is intact

* Limited adduction due to medial rectus weakness

* Limited elevation due to the weakness of the superior rectus and inferior oblique

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A child is brought to the OPD with fever, severe pain, and swelling of the left eye. He was bitten by a dog over the eye a few days back. On examination, there is mild proptosis with restriction of ocular movements. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Orbital cellulitis

In the above clinical scenario of a patient with a history of a dog bite over the eye followed by severe swelling around the eye, proptosis, with restricted eye movement, it is suggestive of orbital cellulitis.

Orbital cellulitis is the acute inflammation of the soft tissues of the orbit behind the orbital septum. It can occur due to exogenous infection (penetrating injuries) or extension of an endogenous infection (dental infection). It presents with fever, severe pain, and eye swelling, which increases with movement, chemosis, axial proptosis, and restriction of ocular movements. Complications include subperiosteal abscess, orbital abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, and general septicemia.

It is the most frequent acute complication of ethmoid sinusitis. The lamina papyracea forms part of the medial wall of the orbit, is paper-thin, and perforated by numerous foramina for nerves and blood vessels. Hence, ethmoid sinusitis frequently leads to orbital cellulitis. It can vary in degree and severity and is typically graded with the Chandler classification.

Chandler stages

Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Stage 4
Stage 5

Preseptal cellulitis

Postseptal cellulitis or orbital cellulitis without abscess

Subperiosteal abscess

Orbital abscess

Cavernous sinus thrombosis/abscess

Inflammation does not extend beyond the orbital septum (where the medial orbital periosteal reflection attaches to the medial eyelid at the tarsal plate).

Inflammation extends into the tissues of the orbit.

There is abscess formation deep to the periosteum of the orbital bones, typically at the lamina papyracea from ethmoid sinusitis.

There is abscess formation within the orbit which has breached the periosteum.

The inflammatory process has extended into the cavernous sinus which thromboses and may progress to abscess formation.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) is advised as first-line imaging because of its superiority in demonstrating bony anatomy and pathology of the orbit and sinuses, with its speed and ease of examination. MRI provides outstanding soft tissue detail without radiation exposure.

Intravenous treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics is the first line of management

Other options:

Option B: Endophthalmitis is defined as the inflammation of the inner structures of the eyeball, i.e., uveal tissue and retina, associated with the pouring of exudates into the vitreous cavity, anterior chamber, and posterior chamber.

Option C: Panophthalmitis is an intense purulent inflammation of the whole eyeball, including Tenon’s capsule.

Option D: Preseptal cellulitis refers to infection of the subcutaneous tissues anterior to the orbital septum. In this condition, proptosis is absent and ocular movements are normal.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A man sufferred trauma to the eye from a punch while fighting with another person. What is the most common site of fracture in the orbit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Floor

The most common site of an orbital fracture due to blunt trauma is the floor of the orbit as it is relatively weak.

The floor consists of three bones: the zygomatic, maxillary, and palatine bones. The posteromedial portion of the maxillary bone is relatively weak and may be involved in a "blowout" fracture.

Isolated fracture of the orbital floor when a large blunt object strikes the globe is called blowout fracture. The orbital contents herniate through the antrum.

Clinical signs: periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis and subconjunctival hemorrhage (later stages).

Investigations:

* X-Ray (Water's view) shows a teardrop opacity

* CT scan is used for confirmation of the diagnosis

Treatment:

Initial treatment consists of observation, oral antibiotics, ice packs, and nasal decongestants. Subsequent treatment is aimed at the prevention of vertical diplopia and cosmetically unacceptable enophthalmos.

Indications of surgery:

* Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm

* Persistent and progressive diplopia in the primary position

* Entrapment of orbital contents

* Fractures involving more than half of the orbital floor with or without herniation will develop enophthalmos if not corrected

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A mother noticed a mucopurulent discharge from the right puncta of her 3-month-old child. There is a history of increased watering in his right eye. Which of the following is the appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sac massage with topical antibiotics

The above history of epiphora (increased watering) and mucopurulent discharge from the punctum is suggestive of congenital dacryocystitis.

Congenital dacrocystitis is the chronic inflammation of the lacrimal sac. It occurs due to the stasis of secretions which in turn is due to congenital blockage of the nasolacrimal duct.

Regurgitation test (applying pressure over the lacrimal sac causes regurgitation of mucopurulent discharge from the lower punctum) is usually positive.

More than 90% of patients with congenital nasolacrimal obstruction undergo spontaneous resolution by 1 year of age.

Treatment depends on the age of the child:

* Less than 9 months

* Massaging (Crigler’s massage, which increases the hydrostatic pressure)

* Antibiotics eye drops

* 9 months to 4 years

* Probing

* Older children (> 4 years):

* Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR)

* In DCR, an opening is made into the nasal cavity from the lacrimal sac.

* DCR gives the best result.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A neonate is brought with complaints of photophobia and watering. Clinical examination shows normal tear passages and clear but large cornea. The image of his eye is shown below which reveals Haab's striae. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Buphthalmos

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of buphthalmos. Haab’s striae are horizontal/circumferential breaks in Descemet’s membrane seen in buphthalmos.

Buphthalmos (Bull-like eyes) is an enlargement of the eyeball seen in true congenital and infantile glaucoma, usually when the disease onset is before 3 years.

The image given below shows Haab's striae and a child having buphthalmos in congenital glaucoma.

Vogt's striae are vertical, fine, whitish lines (folds/tears) in Descemet's membrane commonly found in patients with keratoconus.

Pearl PF1677: Vogt's striae

The above image shows “Vogt’s Striae” which are characteristically seen in Keratoconus.

* Vogt's striae are vertical (rarely horizontal) fine, whitish lines in the deep/posterior stroma and Descemet's membrane commonly found in patients with keratoconus.

* It may be asymmetric depending on the degree of keratoconus in each eye.

* It is considered that there is a positive correlation between the orientation of the lines with the steepest axis of the cornea and the mechanism is thought to be related to mechanical stress forces on collagen lamellae radiating from the cone apex.

* The striae can temporarily disappear with external pressure to the globe.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient chronically on corticosteroids was diagnosed with a complicated cataract and his slit lamp examination finding is shown below. What is this type of cataract called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior subcapsular cataract

The clinical scenario of chronic use of steroids along with slit lamp examination showing a granular appearance in the lens is suggestive of posterior subcapsular cataract.

Posterior subcapsular opacity lies in front of the posterior capsule and has a granular or plaque-like appearance on oblique slit lamp examination .On retro- illumination , black vacuoles are seen which are swollen migratory lens epithelial cells called as Wedl cells (or bladder cells). As it is in the centre of the eye it has a significant impact on vision. Symptoms like glare are often perceived and aggravated by miosis , near visual activity and in bright light.

The following conditions mainly present with a posterior subcapsular cataract and therefore have a similar clinical picture:

* Complicated cataract

* Steroid-induced cataract

* Radiation

These cataracts present with central opacities and has difficulty in seeing objects in bright light because:

* When a person is exposed to bright light, the pupil undergoes miosis (constriction).

* These central opacities come to lie directly in the path of axial rays, allowing no transmission of rays.

* Therefore, there is an inability to see objects in bright light.

* However, in dim light, when there is mydriasis (dilatation of pupil), some rays may pass around the opacity, leading to an improvement in dim-light vision.

Cortical cataract is further divided into the cuneiform and cupuliform types.

Cuneiform (70%)
Posterior subcapsular/Cupuliform (5%)

Radial spoke-like opacity starting in the periphery and extending centrally

Central saucer-shaped opacity in the posterior cortex just below the capsule

Late visual loss

Early loss of visual acuity

Most visually handicapping senile cataract

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient was diagnosed with stroke and his visual field testing revealed macula sparing homonymous hemianopia. Where is the likely site of lesion in optic pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Occipital lobe

The likely site of the lesion is occipital lobe as the patient presents with homonymous hemianopia along with macular sparing.

Homonymous hemianopia (HH) involves loss of vision on the same side of the visual field in both eyes. HH is characteristically seen in lesions involving the visual pathway posterior to the optic chiasma.

Lesions involving occipital lobe usually shows macular sparing because macular representation is seperate and quite large as compared to peripheral vision. Moreover, macular area in occipital lobe is supplied both by posterior and middle cerebral artery. In case of vascular lesions (eg stroke) affecting occipital lobe, it is less likely to involve both these arteries.

HH may be either complete or incomplete.

* A complete HH is characterised by loss of entire hemifield on the same side in both eyes.

* An incomplete HH is characterised by partial loss of visual field on the same side in both eyes. Incomplete HH is further classified as congruous or incongruous, depending on whether the extent of partial loss of visual field in both the eyes is same or different, respectively.

Pearl PF0246: Lesions in the optic pathway

Transection of the pathways at the locations indicated by the letters causes the visual field defects shown in the diagram above.

* The fibers from the nasal half of each retina decussate in the optic chiasm, so that the fibers in the optic tracts are those from the temporal half of one retina and the nasal half of the other.

* A lesion that interrupts the optic nerve causes blindness in that eye.

* Lesions affecting the optic chiasma destroy fibers from both nasal hemiretinas and produce a heteronymous (opposite sides of the visual fields) hemianopia.

* A lesion in one optic tract causes blindness in half of the visual field and is called homonymous (same side of both visual fields) hemianopia (half-blindness).

* Occipital lesions may spare the fibers from the macula because of the separation in the brain of these fibers from the other subserving vision.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A person has vision of < 3/60 but > 1/60 in his better eye. The limitation of field of vision is less than 10 degrees from the center of fixation. What type of blindness does he have?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Social Blindness

Since the patient has less than 3/60 in his better eye and the limitation of the field of vision to be less than 10 degrees from the center of fixation he is having social blindness.

Type of Blindness
Description

Social Blindness
Presenting distance visual acuity of less than 3/60 (20/400) in the better eye and limitation of the field of vision to be less than 10 degrees from the center of fixation

Economic blindness
The inability of a person to count fingers from a distance of 6 meters

Manifest blindness
Vision 1/60 to just perception of light

Absolute blindness
No perception of light

Curable blindness
That stage of blindness where the damage is reversible by prompt management, e.g., cataract

Preventable blindness
Loss of vision that could have been completely prevented by the institution of effective preventive or prophylactic measures e.g.,  xerophthalmia, trachoma, and glaucoma

Avoidable blindness
The sum total of preventable and curable blindness is often referred to as avoidable blindness.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Among the following options,which is the most common treatment for recurrent Pterygium of eye?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Conjunctival autograft

The most commonly used technique for recurrent pterygium among the following is conjuctival autograft.

A pterygium is a degenerative subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea. It is a connective tissue disorder and is never inflammatory. Histologically, it is made up of elastotic degenerative changes in vascularized subepithelial stromal collagen. It is most commonly seen on the nasal aspect of the eye. It is made up of three parts:

* cap (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge)

* head

* body

Patients may be asymptomatic or present with irritation, grittiness, or episodes of inflammation. As they enlarge, it may obstruct vision and lead to astigmatism.

Treatment:

* A pterygium is best left alone unless:

* It is progressing towards the pupillary area

* Causes excessive astigmatism

* Restricts ocular motility

* Causes disfigurement.

* Excision: Simple excision of the pterygium is associated with a high recurrence rate, and should be combined with:

* Mitomycin C drops- applied pre-operatively/ intra-operatively or post-operatively to prevent a recurrence. However, it may lead to complications like scleral necrosis, cataract, and iritis and should be used judiciously.

* Beta-radiation applied postoperatively to the pterygium base was popular for many years, but is associated with late scleral necrosis.

* Conjunctival autografting- limbal tissue from the same or other eye is grafted and secured with fibrin glue or sutures.

* Amniotic membrane graft

* Peripheral lamellar keratoplasty if the lesion is deep.

Currently, the most widely used techniques are conjunctival autografting, amniotic membrane transplantation, and mitomycin-C application either preoperatively or postoperatively (can be applied intraoperatively also) of which conjuctival autografting has less recurrence rates and is a simple and quick procedure which reduces the risk of granuloma formation, scleral thinning and necrosis.

Note:

A combination of conjuctival autografting with intraoperative mitomycin C is the most preferred as it has the least recurrence rates as per studies.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: For which of the following condition is the V-Y procedure used as a treatment modality ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ectropion

V-Y procedure is done for Cicatricial ectropion.

Ectropion is the eversion of the lid margin and eyelashes away from the globe.

Cicatricial ectropion is commonly the result of burns, trauma and chronic inflammations of the skin which shorten the anterior lamina of the eyelid which pull the eyelid away from the globe.

Treatment of cicatricial ectropion requires release and relaxation of the scarred tissues, and an elongation of the skin muscle lamina by some form of surgery called as blepharoplasty. However, localized areas of scarring can be released by Z or V–Y plasty.

A V incision is made just below the eyelid with the base of the triangle in line with the ectropion which is pulled up to repair the ectropion. The V incision is now in the shape of a Y which is closed and the normal structure is retained.

Types:

* Involutional/senile- affects the lower lid of elderly patients.

* Cicatricial- caused by the scarring or contracture of the skin and underlying tissues

* Paralytic- caused by ipsilateral facial nerve palsy

* Mechanical- caused by tumors on or near the lid margin that mechanically evert the lid

* Congenital

Pearl PF1603: Surgical Modalities Used in Correcting Ectropion

Ectropion

Procedure

Involutional ectropion

• Medial conjunctivoplasty
• Horizontal lid shortening
• Byron–Smith-modified Kuhnt–Szymanowski operation
• Lateral tarsal strip technique

Paralytic ectropion

• Horizontal lid tightening
• Palpebral sling operation

Cicatricial ectropion

• V-Y operation
• Z-plasty (Elschnig’s operation)
• Excision of scar tissue and full-thickness skin grafting

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the condition which presents as painless loss of vision.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO)

The image shows a splashed tomato appearance which is characteristic of central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO).

CRVO refers to sudden or acute occlusion of the central retinal vein. It presents with a sudden loss of vision. On examination, a relative afferent pupillary defect is present.

Funduscopy shows engorged and tortuous retinal veins, massive retinal hemorrhages with splashed tomato appearance, and cotton wool spots. The disc is edematous and hyperemic. Changes that occur later include neovascularization at the disc or periphery with pigmentary changes at the macula.

Complications:

* Rubeosis iridis or neovascularization of the iris

* Neovascular glaucoma (NVG) or 100 day glaucoma

* Vitreous hemorrhage

100-day glaucoma is a type of neovascular glaucoma (NVG) and is so-called because it typically develops 3 months after the episode of CRVO.

Treatment usually involves treating the underlying cause and complications.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In a patient showing salt and pepper appearance of the fundus, which of the following is not a differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tuberculosis

Salt and pepper fundus is not seen in tuberculosis.

Causes of pseudo-retinitis pigmentosa (salt and pepper fundus):

* Rubella

* Syphilis

* Refsum’s disease

* Carriers of albinism

* Leber’s congenital amaurosis

* Retinitis pigmentosa sine pigmentosa

Salt and Pepper Retinopathy seen in Congenital Rubella Syndrome is shown below:

The image given below shows the salt and pepper fundus.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The given sago-grain appearance of conjunctiva is caused by ________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chlamydia Trachomatis

The given sago-grain appearance of conjunctiva is seen in trachoma caused by Chlamydia trachomatis.

Conjunctival appearance:

1. In trachoma

* Sago-grain appearance

* A follicular reaction

2. In vernal keratoconjunctivitis

* Cobblestone appearance

* A papillary reaction

* Seen in palpebral conjunctiva

3. Phlyctenular conjunctivitis

* White-pinkish nodule in bulbar conjunctiva

4. Xerophthalmia

* Epithelial xerosis

* Bitots spot in bulbar conjunctiva

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the refractive error seen in the condition shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myopia and astigmatism

The image shown is of Keratoconus , in which there is steepening of the cornea associated with irregular stromal thinning, resulting in a cone-like bulge (protrusion) and significant loss of vision.The refractive error seen in this condition is myopia and irregular astigmatism.

Keratoconus is a progressive bilateral corneal ectatic disorder.  It manifests as characteristic cone-like steepening of the cornea associated with irregular stromal thinning, resulting in a cone-like bulge (protrusion) and significant loss of vision.

Important associations:

* rigid contact lens wear

* chronic eye rubbing

* Marfans, Down’s, EDS syndrome

* Osteogenesis imperfecta, MVP

* RP, Leber congenital amurosis

* VKC, aniridia, ectopia lentis

Investigations:

* Corneal topography

* Pachymetry

* Keratometry:

* Steep cornea

* Bow tie pattern

* Paracentral thinning of the cornea (thinnest point)

Treatment:

* Spectacle correction

* Rigid gas-permeable Contact lens

* Corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL) - instillation of riboflavin drops to photosensitize the eye followed by exposure to ultraviolet-A

light

* Intra-corneal ring segments (INTACS)- small curved PMMA ring or set of rings that are implanted in the cornea to help flatten corneal curvature in an effort to improve vision

* Corneal transplantation- Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) and penetrating keratoplasty (PKP)

Pearl PF1604: Clinical findings in keratoconus

External signs:

* Munson’s sign- V-shaped conformation of the lower lid produced by the ectatic cornea in downgaze

* Rizzuti’s sign- sharply focused conical beam of light near the nasal limbus, produced by lateral illumination of the cornea from the temporal side

Slit-lamp signs:

* Vogt’s striae- fine vertical stress lines in the deep stroma, parallel to the steep axis of the cone. May disappear with external pressure on the globe.

* Fleischer ring- deposition of iron in the epithelium in a ring shape at the base of the conical protrusion.

* Corneal thinning- predominantly in the inferotemporal area.

* Hydrops- an acute rupture in Descemet’s membrane causing imbibition of aqueous into the corneal stroma. It is a complication of long-standing keratoconus.

* Prominent corneal nerves- increased visibility of the corneal nerve fibres.

* Rupture in Bowman’s layer- irregular superficial opacities that develop due to breaks in Bowman’s layer.

Retroillumination signs:

* Scissoring reflex- during retinoscopy, two bands of the light beam reflexed from the retina, moves like the blades of the pair of scissors, towards and away from each other. This sign is diagnostic of keratoconus.

* Oil droplet sign (“Charleaux” sign)- dark reflex in the area of the cone on observation of cornea in dilated pupil by distant direct ophthalmoscopy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the gold standard for measuring intraocular pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Goldmann applanation tonometer

Goldmann applanation tonometer is used to measure intraocular pressure (IOP).

The concept behind the procedure was introduced by Goldmann. It is based on Imbert-Fick law, which states that the pressure inside a sphere(P) is equal to the force (W) required to flatten its surface divided by the area of flattening (A).

P = W/A

The different types are Goldmann tonometer, Perkin’s tonometer, pneumatic tonometer, pulse air tonometer, tono-pen.

The image of a Goldmann applanation tonometer is given below:

Other options:

Gonioscope is used to visualize the angle of the anterior chamber (gonioscopy).

Hertel's exophthalmometer measures protrusion of the apex of the cornea from the outer orbital margin (with the eyes looking straight ahead).

Tonopen is a hand-held electronic contact tonometer which is used for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP) in a scarred cornea.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 21-year-old student presents with ocular redness, foreign body sensation, and excessive tearing following the use of a contact lens. An interface contrast microscopy from his corneal scraping is shown below. What would be the most probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acanthamoeba

The given clinical history and the demonstration of polygonal cysts in interface contrast microscopy are suggestive of amoebic keratitis caused by acanthamoeba.

Acanthamoeba culbertsoni is an opportunistic protozoan pathogen. It exists as trophozoite form and resistant cystic form. Both these forms are infective. The trophozoite is large and characterized by spine-like pseudopodia (acanthopodia).

Human beings acquire the infection by inhalation of cysts or trophozoites, directly through traumatized skin or eyes, or ingestion of cysts.

It chiefly presents as two chronic conditions:

* Acanthamoeba keratitis

* Granulomatous amoebic encephalitis

Acanthamoeba keratitis is an infection of the eyes that typically develops from the entry of the amebic cyst through abrasions on the cornea. Most of the cases are associated with the use of contact lenses.

Patients usually present with photophobia, excessive tearing, redness, and foreign body sensation and it can be bilateral in contact lens users.

Diagnosis of amoebic keratitis is made by the demonstration of the cyst in corneal scrapings by wet mount, histology, and culture. The cysts are smaller (12-25 μm) and polygonal or star-shaped.

Topical administration of biguanides or chlorhexidine with or without diamidine agents can be used for the management of acanthamoeba keratitis. In severe cases penetrating keratoplasty can be done.

The below image shows the ring lesion seen in acanthamoeba keratitis.

The below image shows cysts of acanthamoeba in lactophenol cotton blue staining.

Other options:

Option B- Naegleria fowleri causes a brain infection, primary amebic meningoencephalitis that leads to brain tissue destruction. Their cysts are spherical and have a smooth double wall.

Option C- Entamoeba histolytica causes intestinal and extraintestinal amebiasis. Their cysts are spherical in shape. A mature quadrinucleate cyst is the infective form.  An amebic ulcer is a typical lesion seen in intestinal amebiasis which is a flask-shaped ulcer in cross-section. Amebic liver abscess is extraintestinal amebiasis which has a center of abscess that contains thick colored brown pus termed anchovy sauce pus.

Option D- Balamuthia mandrillaris is a free-living ameba that causes granulomatous amebic encephalitis. Their cyst is usually spherical and surrounded by a three-layered cyst wall.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 27-year-old male patient suffers trauma to his eye with vegetative matter. He now presents with a corneal ulcer, alongside hypopyon and satellite lesions. He reports mild pain with photophobia and redness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fungal keratitis

The given clinical scenario most likely describes fungal keratitis with ulceration.

A fungal corneal ulcer is usually caused by trauma with vegetative or organic matter. Signs are more pronounced than symptoms. The corneal ulcer appears dry.

Causative organisms:

* Aspergillus

* Fusarium

* Candida albicans

Signs of a fungal ulcer:

* Irregular margins of the ulcer.

* Presence of satellite lesions surrounding the ulcer.

* An immune ring (Wesseley) may be seen around the ulcer due to the deposition of the immune complexes.

* Slough is usually dry, with feathery borders surrounded by a yellow line of demarcation.

* Hypopyon may be present or absent. If present, it is thick, and immobile due to the direct invasion of the fungal hyphae into the anterior chamber.

Treatment:

* Topical drugs: These include topical natamycin, voriconazole or amphotericin B drops which are effective against Aspergillus and Fusarium. Nystatin is effective against Candida.

* Systemic drugs: Severe ulcers with hypopyon, perforation or suspected endophthalmitis might warrant the use of oral antifungal agents such as ketoconazole or voriconazole.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy has been observed by his parents to be increasingly clumsy for the past 6 months. On physical examination, there is a cauliflower-like growth in the left eye alongside leukocoria and an absent red reflex. A diagnosis was made and enucleation was done. The microscopic appearance of the specimen shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinoblastoma

The histology, clinical history and gross specimen point towards a diagnosis of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma is due to mutation in the Rb gene located on chromosome 13q14.

Retinoblastoma was the first cancer known to be directly associated with a genetic abnormality.

Clinical features of retinoblastoma:

* Present within the first two years of life

* Leukocoria

* Strabismus

* Painful red eye with secondary glaucoma

* Orbital inflammation mimicking orbital or pre-septal cellulitis.

* Orbital invasion or visible extraocular growth may occur in neglected cases.

* Metastatic disease involving regional lymph nodes and the brain before the detection of ocular involvement is rare.

Signs:

* An intraretinal tumour is a homogeneous, dome-shaped white lesion that becomes irregular, often with white flecks of calcification.

* An endophytic tumour projects into the vitreous as a white mass that may "seed" into the gel.

* An exophytic tumour forms multilobular subretinal white masses and causes an overlying retinal detachment.

Investigations:

* Red reflex testing with a direct ophthalmoscope is a simple screening test for leukocoria.

* Dilated fundus examination using indirect ophthalmoscope

* MRI of the orbit + brain is the investigation of choice.

The HPE image below shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, the clustering of small blue cuboidal or short columnar cells around a central lumen.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the casualty with a sudden loss of vision and painful ocular movements. On examination of the affected eye, a relative afferent pupillary defect with a normal optic disc is seen. Visual field testing was done which revealed central scotoma in the same eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Optic neuritis

The given clinical scenario of a sudden painful loss of vision in the absence of fundoscopic changes, RAPD and central scotoma is suggestive of optic neuritis, specifically retrobulbar neuritis.

There are 3 types of optic neuritis: papillitis, neuroretinitis, and retrobulbar neuritis. The common causes of retrobulbar neuritis include demyelinating disorders such as multiple sclerosis (MS) and neuromyelitis optica (NMO or Devic's disease).

Clinically, optic neuritis is characterized by sudden, progressive visual loss.  Ocular movements are painful in retrobulbar neuritis and painless in papillitis and neuroretinitis. Glowing sensations known as phosphenes may be induced with sound or movement. Color vision may also be impaired.

On examination, Marcus Gunn pupil or relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is usually noted due to asymmetric involvement. The most common visual field defect is a central or centrocecal scotoma.

Type
Retrobulbar neuritis
Papillitis
Neuroretinitis

Pathology
Inflammation of the optic nerve behind the disc
Inflammation of the optic nerve head
Inflammation of the optic nerve head and the macula

Fundus appearance
Optic disc appears normal

Hyperemia and oedema of the optic disc with or without peri-papillary flame-shaped hemorrhages

Macular star (due to exudates that form around macula)

Prevalence
Most common in adults

Most common in children

Least common type

Associated conditions
Strong association with demyelinating disorders like MS, NMO

Weak association with demyelinating disorders

Cat-scratch disease, Lyme disease, Syphilis etc.

The image below shows papillitis.

The image below shows macular star appearance in neuroretinitis.

Causes of RAPD:

* Severe retinal disease (e.g., central retinal artery occlusion, extensive retinal detachment)

* Maculopathy (macular degeneration )

* Optic nerve lesions (e.g., optic neuritis, retrobulbar neuritis in multiple sclerosis , anterior ischemic optic neuropathy , glaucoma)

* Optic tract lesions (e.g., infarction)

Causes of central/centrocaecal scotoma

* Optic neuritis

* Compressive lesion eg. Pituitary adenoma

* Optic neuropathy due to

* Poor nutrition

* Tobacco

* Alcohol

* Drug- induced optic neuropathy

*

* Toxin- induced optic neuropathy

* Hereditary optic atrophy

* Sarcoidosis

* Leukemia

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy was brought to the ophthalmology OPD with complaints of intense itching, photophobia, and ropy discharge from his eyes. Moreover, on examination the following finding is present. What is the most probable diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vernal keratoconjunctivitis

The above image depicts a cobblestone appearance, and also the presence of ropy discharge points towards the diagnosis of vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) or spring catarrh.

VKC is bilateral allergic conjunctivitis that is common in children above the age of 5 years and in warm dry climates such as the Mediterranean, sub-Saharan Africa, and the Middle East.

It is IgE and cell-mediated inflammation of the conjunctiva. It results in the following findings:

Palpebral disease

* Cobblestone papillae: Macropapillae (<1 mm) have a flat-topped polygonal appearance reminiscent of cobblestones

* Associated with ropy discharge

* Maxwell–Lyon sign: pseudomembrane formation of the upper lid when everted and exposed to heat

Limbal disease

* Horner-Trantas dots which are limbal conjunctival papillae

Keratopathy

* Superior punctate epithelial erosions

* Shield ulcers, which may develop when the exposed Bowman membrane becomes coated with mucus and calcium phosphate, leading to inadequate wetting and delayed re-epithelialization.

* Pseudogerentexon resembling arcus senilus. It has a cupid's bow outline

Treatment of VKC includes allergen avoidance, antihistaminics, steroids, and immunomodulators both topical and systemic depending on the severity of the disease.

Other options:

* Trachoma is a form of chronic infective conjunctivitis and is one of the leading causes of blindness. It has an ‘active’ inflammatory stage and a ‘cicatricial’ chronic stage. The active inflammatory stage is more prevalent in children and presents with nonspecific symptoms of ocular irritation, foreign body sensation, and discharge (often mild symptoms).

* Phlyctenular conjunctivitis is a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction due to endogenous allergens like Staphylococcus aureus (most common) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

* Xerophthalmia is a term used to cover all ocular manifestations of vitamin A deficiency.

Image: Horner Trantas spots

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 61-year-old university professor presents with a loss of vision in his left eye. He describes the sensation as a curtain being drawn over his affected eye. In addition, 7 days ago the patient noticed what he described as flashing lights and floaters. He gives a history of having cataract surgery in the same eye 3 weeks ago. A B-scan image of his left eye is shown below. What could be his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Retinal detachment

The given clinical scenario and the B-scan suggest a diagnosis of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. It is due to the accumulation of fluid between neurosensory retina(NSR) and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) due to a retinal tear.

Definition of retinal detachment: The separation of the neurosensory retina from the RPE.

Types of Retinal detachment:

A. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment- fluid accumulates after a break (tear) occurs in the retina.

* Causes:

* High myopes

* Retinoschisis-splitting of neurosensory retina plus vitreous degeneration

* Typical retinoschisis-split at the level of the outer plexiform layer

* Atypical retinoschisis-split at the level of the nerve fiber layer

* Trauma

* Pseudophakia

* Aphakia

* The most dangerous type of retinal break is horseshoe tear.

* The most dangerous location of retinal break is the supero-temporal retina.

* Clinical features

* Photopsia-flashes of light due to vitreoretinal traction at the site of the break

* Floaters

* Visual field defect- a black curtain/veil in front of the eye

* Signs

* Hypotony- as the liquefied vitreous in the subretinal space is absorbed through the RPE.

* Shafers sign-pigments in the anterior vitreous (tobacco dusting) are a feature of fresh retinal detachment.

* The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is corrugated with undulations.

* Treatment

* Prophylactic laser barrage

* Scleral buckling

* Pneumatic retinopexy

* Pars plana vitrectomy

B. Tractional retinal detachment: Fibro-vascular membranes in the vitreous due to long-standing retinal neovascularization exert traction on the retina.

* Causes

* Proliferative diabetic retinopathy

* Central retinal venous occlusion

* Eales disease

* Retinopathy of Prematurity(ROP)

* Signs

* The detached retina is concave in configuration. No breaks are seen

* Treatment

* Pars plana vitrectomy with endo photocoagulation.

C. Exudative retinal detachment: Exudative fluid from the choroid, collects in the subretinal space leading to retinal detachment.

* Causes

* Inflammatory conditions like choroiditis, posterior scleritis

* Choroidal tumours like melanoma

* Toxaemia of pregnancy

* Malignant hypertension

* Coats disease

* Clinical features

* Floaters due to vitritis but no photopsia

* Visual field defect

* Signs

* The detached retina is convex in configuration. The surface is smooth. No break is seen.

* Shifting fluid is seen.

* Treatment

* Systemic steroids

* Treatment of the cause

The image below shows a fundus which reveals retinal detachment inferiorly from 3-9 o'clock with a tear at 3:30

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A middle-aged woman presents with a pterygium that has been steadily progressing towards the pupillary area. What is the best means of management in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Excision with conjunctival autograft

The best mode of management in the given options for progressive pterygium is excision with conjunctival autograft.

A pterygium is a degenerative subconjunctival fibrovascular tissue encroaching the cornea. It is a connective tissue disorder and is never inflammatory. Histologically, it comprises elastotic degenerative changes in vascularised subepithelial stromal collagen. It is most commonly seen on the nasal aspect of the eye. It is made up of three parts:

* cap (an avascular halo-like zone at the advancing edge)

* head

* body

Patients may be asymptomatic or present with irritation, grittiness, or episodes of inflammation. As they enlarge, it may obstruct vision and lead to astigmatism.

Treatment:

* A pterygium is best left alone unless:

* It is progressing towards the pupillary area

* Causes excessive astigmatism

* Restricts ocular motility

* Causes disfigurement.

* Excision: A simple pterygium excision often leads to a high chance of recurrence. Measures to prevent recurrence are:

* Mitomycin C drops- applied pre-operatively/ intra-operatively or post-operatively. However, it may lead to complications like scleral necrosis, cataract, and iritis and should be used judiciously.

* Beta-radiation applied postoperatively to the pterygium base was popular for many years, but is associated with late scleral necrosis.

* Conjunctival autografting- limbal tissue from the same or other eye is grafted and secured with fibrin glue or sutures.

* Amniotic membrane graft

* Peripheral lamellar keratoplasty if the lesion is deep.

Currently, the most widely used techniques are conjunctival autografting, amniotic membrane transplantation, and mitomycin-C application either preoperatively or postoperatively (can be applied intraoperatively also), of which conjunctival autografting has fewer recurrence rates and is a simple and quick procedure that reduces the risk of granuloma formation, scleral thinning, and necrosis.

Note:

A combination of conjunctival autografting with intraoperative mitomycin C is the most preferred as it has the least recurrence rates as per studies.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient has significant distress on reading text off paper or screen. On examination of his eyes, all domains including visual acuity are essentially normal except for Schirmer's test which reads 5mm. What is the best way to treat this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lubricants

The given clinical scenario is most likely to be one of dry eye or keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS). The best initial management would be to lubricate the eye.

Treatment of dry eye includes medical treatment (lubricating eyedrops, most commonly methylcellulose derivatives) or surgical treatment (lacrimal punctum occlusion using silicone plugs).

The tests used to diagnose dry eye (KCS) are:

1. Schirmer test

Inference

* 15 mm: Normal

* 5-10 mm: Moderate keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS)

* < 5 mm: Severe KCS

2. Tear film break-up test (TBUT)

Inference

* 15-35 seconds: Normal

* < 10 seconds: Unstable tear film

3. Rose Bengal staining

Inference

* A pattern: Confluent staining → Severe KCS

* B pattern: Extensive staining → Moderate KCS

* C pattern: Fine punctate stains → Mild KCS

4. Tear osmolarity test

Abnormal osmolarity is defined by

* An elevated reading, >300 mOsm/L, indicating loss of homeostasis, or

* When the inter-eye difference is >8 mOsm/L, indicating instability of the tear film.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a hard painless nodule on the upper eyelid. It was observed to be growing outwards, away from the lid margin. What could be the most probable diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chalazion

The given clinical picture is suggestive of a chalazion (tarsal cyst/meibomian cyst). It has the malignant potential to become an adenocarcinoma of the meibomian gland.

It is the chronic lipogranulomatous inflammation of the meibomian gland. It presents as painless swelling of the eyelid. It is more common in adults than children. Treatment includes incision and curettage and intralesional injection of triamcinolone acetate.

Other options:

* Hordeolum externum or stye is the suppurative inflammation of the gland of Zeis. It is hard and painful, and there is a visible pus point on the lid margin.

* Entropion refers to the inward rolling and rotation of the lid margin towards the globe. It is more common in the lower lid

* Loss of eyelashes is seen in chronic blepharitis.

*

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with sarcoidosis shows Koeppe's nodules on ophthalmologic examination. Where are these seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Iris

Koeppe's nodules and Bussaca's nodules develop on the iris in granulomatous uveitis.

Koeppe's nodules are seen at the pupillary margin. Bussaca's nodules are seen on the peripheral part of the anterior surface of iris.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A young boy suffers trauma to his right eye and develops monocular diplopia. What is the most likely cause for his symptom?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Iridodialysis

The most likely cause for the boy's symptom is iridodialysis.

Iridodialysis refers to the detachment of the iris root from the ciliary body and is associated with a D-shaped pupil. A black biconvex area is seen at the periphery at the site of detachment.

Causes of Uniocular Diplopia:

* Refractive errors

* Dry eye syndrome

* Corneal abnormalities

* Cataracts

* Retinal disorders

Causes of Binocular Diplopia:

* Strabismus

* Cranial nerve palsy

* Graves' disease

* Trauma or injury

* Multiple sclerosis

* Myasthenia gravis

Other options:

* Festooned pupil - It is seen in posterior synechiae with the adhesion of the pupillary margin to the lens capsule.

* Iris bombe refers to the forward bowing of the iris seen in closed-angle glaucoma with irido-lenticular contact and in seclusio pupillae with 360-degree posterior synechiae. Drainage of aqueous is blocked due to the irido-lenticular apposition and pressure of the accumulated aqueous causes the iris to bow forward.

* Iridodonesis refers to a tremulous iris caused by a lack of support. It is seen in pseudophakia after cataract surgery and in lens dislocation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the lesion in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Viral keratitis

The above image shows a dendritic ulcer caused by herpes simplex virus.

Herpes simplex causes epithelial keratitis and in severe forms, dendritic ulcers develop. Most of the patients present with redness, photophobia, watering, and blurred vision. On examination, visual acuity and corneal sensation are reduced. Follicular conjunctivitis and blepharitis may develop but are usually mild. Clinical reactivation occurs due to multiple stress factors and causes recurrent infections.

The fluorescein-stained image under slit-lamp examination shows dendritic ulcers, a pathognomic feature of epithelial keratitis. They are mostly treated with acyclovir 3% ointment or ganciclovir 0.15% gel.

Pearl PF1376: Ocular lesions of Herpes Simplex

Primary herpes:

* Cornea

* Fine epithelial punctate keratitis

* Coarse epithelial punctate keratitis

* Dendritic ulcer

* Conjunctiva: acute follicular conjunctivitis

* Skin lesions

Recurrent herpes:

* Active epithelial keratitis

* Punctate epithelial keratitis

* Dendritic ulcer

* Geographical ulcer

* Stromal keratitis

* Disciform keratitis

* Diffuse stromal necrotic keratitis

* Trophic keratitis (meta-herpetic)

* Herpetic iridocyclitis

Pearl PF1375: Clinical differential diagnosis of corneal ulcer

Bacterial
Fungal
Viral
Parasitic

Risk factors

Contact lens wear

Trauma

Chronic steroid use

Anesthetic cornea

Dry eyes

Exposure keratopathy

Trauma with vegetable matter

Low immunity

Recurrent attacks

Contact lens wear

Exposure to contaminated water (acanthamoeba)

Clinical features

Hypopyon is fluid and mobile

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is likely to have a rapid course, with deep corneal necrosis.

Less pain and watering compared to the extent of vision loss and signs.

Tend to be indolent but progressive

Hypopyon is thick, immobile.

Relatively more pain and watering compared to the extent of vision loss and signs.

Recurrences are characteristic.

Disproportionately severe pain is a characteristic feature.

Indolent course and in initial stages, often mistaken to be viral/ fungal infection, leading to a delay in diagnosis

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following combination of cylindrical lenses can be used to treat with-the-rule astigmatism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. - 3.00 DC x 180, +1.00 DC x 90

- 3.00 DC x 180, + 1.00 DC x 90 can be used to correct with-the-rule astigmatism.

In with-the-rule astigmatism, the vertical meridian is steeper than the horizontal meridian. Hence, to make up for this, we need a combination of cylindrical lenses with relatively greater power in the horizontal meridian than the vertical meridian.

Before considering the options, also remember that a cylinder aligned along the horizontal meridian (180 axis) has action in the vertical meridian and vice versa.

In option A, the cylinder acting along the horizontal meridian (- 3.00 DC x 90) has lesser power than the one acting along the vertical meridian (+ 5.00 DC x 180). This is also the case with options B and C.

Only option D has a cylinder with greater power along the horizontal meridian ( +1.00 DC x 90) compared to the vertical meridian (- 3.00 DC x 180). Hence, option D is the answer.

Alternative method:

This method involves the use of the optical cross technique

STEP 1:

* Frame the optical cross with the given powers in their respective meridians.

* While framing the optical cross, the power which is given in 180 needs to marked in 90 and vice versa.

For example, option A has + 5.00 DC x 180, - 3.00 DC x 90 which means the eye gets a correction of + 5.00 in vertical meridian (i.e in 90 degree) and correction of - 3.00 in horizontal meridian (i.e in 180 degree). Keeping this in mind, if one frames the optical crosses for the given options, the end image would be as given below

STEP 2:

Now we need to interpret the optical crosses to find which meridian is steeper with certain hints.

* If the power in one axis is ‘+’ and the power in other axis is ‘-’, then the axis with ‘-’ power is steeper.

* If powers in both the axis are ‘-’, then the higher number of the two will be steeper.

* If powers in both the axis are ‘+’, then the lower number of the two will be steeper.

STEP 3:

Applying these hints to the options will give option D as with-the-rule astigmatism.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following factors should be kept in mind while choosing the power of an intraocular lens (IOL) in a child 1 year of age?
options: Growth of the lens capsule with age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myopic shift

A myopic shift is a common occurrence post IOL implantation is children <1 year of age. The rate of shift occurs most rapidly during the first one and one-half years of life. In general, earlier the surgery and IOL implantation, larger is the myopic shift.

Other options:

* Hyperopic shifts occur when either the effective axial eye length is decreased (i.e. retrobulbar tumors, choroidal tumors, central serous chorioretinopathy) or when the refractive power of the eye is reduced (i.e. corneal flattening, decreased refractive power of the lens (cataractous changes, posterior displacement

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with a gradual decrease in vision and elevated IOP in the right eye. The left eye is completely normal. Gonioscopy is as shown. The patient recalls being hit in the eye with a cricket ball ten years ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Angle recession glaucoma

Angle recession glaucoma is a form of secondary open-angle glaucoma that develops months to years after blunt ocular trauma due to a tear between the longitudinal and circular fibers of the ciliary muscle, causing damage to the trabecular meshwork.

The gonioscopy image shows a markedly widened ciliary body band, the hallmark of angle recession.

• Cause: Blunt ocular trauma → tear of the ciliary muscle → angle recession → trabecular dysfunction.
• Diagnosis: Gonioscopy is essential in every patient with a history of blunt ocular trauma.
• Treatment: Similar to primary open-angle glaucoma (topical IOP-lowering drugs); filtration surgery may be required if medical therapy fails.

Differentiate from Other Secondary Glaucomas

• A. Pigmentary glaucoma: Bilateral, young myopic males; Krukenberg spindle, dense trabecular pigmentation.
• B. Pseudoexfoliative glaucoma: Elderly; dandruff-like pseudoexfoliative material on lens and pupillary margin.
• D. Neovascular glaucoma: Iris neovascularization (rubeosis iridis) due to diabetes or CRVO.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe unilateral eye pain, headache, and blurred vision after watching a movie in a dark theatre. On examination, the eye is red, cornea is hazy, and pupil is mid-dilated and non-reactive. What is the first line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mannitol + Pilocarpine

Sudden eye pain and decreased vision after being in a dark environment (movie theater) suggests acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG).

• Darkness → pupillary dilation (mid-dilated pupil)
• Leads to pupillary block → iris bows forward → angle closure
• Rapid rise in IOP

First-line management:

• Mannitol (IV): Rapidly lowers IOP by osmotic dehydration
• Pilocarpine: Causes miosis → opens angle by pulling iris away from trabecular meshwork

Why not others:

• Moxifloxacin: Antibiotic, no role
• Atropine: Causes mydriasis → worsens angle closure
• Lubricants: No role in IOP reduction

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old female comes with a sudden onset of pain in the right eye. It is associated with colored halos, decreased visual acuity and a steamy cornea is seen, the pupil is mid-dilated and fixed. IOP is 60 mmHg. What is the diagnosis?
options: Secondary angle closure glaucoma by uveitis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute angle closure glaucoma

Acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) is an ophthalmic emergency caused by sudden closure of the anterior chamber angle, leading to a rapid rise in intraocular pressure.

Classical clinical features:

• Sudden severe eye pain
• Colored halos around lights (corneal edema)
• Decreased vision
• Steamy/hazy cornea
• Mid-dilated, fixed pupil
• Markedly raised IOP (often >50–60 mmHg)

Pupillary block → iris bows forward → trabecular meshwork obstruction → acute rise in IOP

Why not others:

• A. Neovascular glaucoma:

• Gradual onset, associated with diabetes/CRVO
• Iris neovascularization, not acute mid-dilated pupil

• C. Secondary angle closure glaucoma (uveitis):

• Associated with inflammation signs (cells, flare, posterior synechiae)
• Usually not such abrupt presentation with classic halos

• D. Phacomorphic glaucoma:

• Lens-induced angle closure (intumescent cataract)
• Typically with visible lens swelling and shallow anterior chamber, less classic mid-dilated fixed pupil picture

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 80 year old male presented with diminution of vision since 2 years. The right eye was red and painful. On examination, the IOP was 50 mmHg in left eye and 16 mmHg in right eye. The right eye had deep anterior chamber with some cells and flare. What could be the possibility?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phacolytic glaucoma

Phacolytic glaucoma is a lens-induced secondary open-angle glaucoma seen in elderly patients with long-standing hypermature cataract.

• Elderly patient with gradual visual loss (cataract history)
• Painful red eye
• Very high IOP (e.g., \~50 mmHg)
• Deep anterior chamber (open angle)
• Cells and flare in anterior chamber due to inflammatory response

Pathophysiology:

• Leakage of lens proteins from hypermature cataract
• Macrophages ingest proteins → block trabecular meshwork
• Leads to acute rise in IOP

Why not others:

• Phacomorphic glaucoma:

• Due to intumescent lens → shallow anterior chamber (angle closure)

• Malignant glaucoma:

• Shallow/flat anterior chamber, usually post-surgery

• Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis:

• Chronic, mild uveitis with low-grade inflammation, not markedly raised IOP

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with vision problem in his right eye. On examination IOP of his right eye is 50 mmHg and left eye is 16 mm Hg. Slit lamp examination shows presence of flare cells in anterior chamber and cataractous lens in the right eye. What is the diagnosis of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phacolytic glaucoma
