• A lesion involving the optic nerve (pre-chiasmatic lesion) results in complete loss of vision in the affected eye (ipsilateral monocular blindness) because all visual information from that eye is interrupted before any fibers cross at the optic chiasm.
• The optic nerve contains fibers from both the nasal and temporal retina of the same eye. Damage to the nerve therefore abolishes all visual input from that eye, while vision in the opposite eye remains normal.

Why not the other options?

• B. Bitemporal hemianopia: Results from a lesion of the optic chiasm, where crossing nasal retinal fibers are compressed (classically by a pituitary adenoma).
• C. Contralateral homonymous hemianopia: Occurs due to lesions posterior to the optic chiasm (optic tract, lateral geniculate body, optic radiations, or occipital cortex).
• D. Contralateral superior quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky"): Caused by a lesion of the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) affecting the inferior retinal fibers that carry the superior visual field.

High-yield visual pathway lesions

| Site of lesion | Visual field defect

| -------------- | -------------------

| Optic nerve | Ipsilateral monocular blindness

| Optic chiasm | Bitemporal hemianopia

| Optic tract / Occipital cortex | Contralateral homonymous hemianopia

| Temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) | Contralateral superior quadrantanopia ("Pie in the sky")

| Parietal lobe (Superior optic radiations) | Contralateral inferior quadrantanopia ("Pie on the floor")

Exam pearl:

• Before the chiasm → One eye affected.
• At the chiasm → Temporal visual fields lost.
• After the chiasm → Homonymous visual field defects.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A middle-aged female patient presents with pain on eye movement. Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is present, and fundus examination shows a normal optic disc. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retrobulbar optic neuritis

Retrobulbar optic neuritis is an inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the optic nerve posterior to the optic disc, classically presenting with acute unilateral vision loss, pain on eye movements, and a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). Because the inflammation is behind the optic disc, the fundus initially appears normal, giving rise to the saying: “The patient sees nothing, and the doctor sees nothing.”

• The combination of:

• Pain on eye movement
• RAPD
• Normal optic disc

is classic for retrobulbar optic neuritis.

Why not the other options?

• B. CRAO (Central Retinal Artery Occlusion): Presents with sudden, painless vision loss and a cherry-red spot on fundus examination.
• C. Papilledema: Characterized by bilateral optic disc swelling due to raised intracranial pressure; visual acuity is often preserved initially.
• D. Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AION): Presents with sudden painless vision loss and a swollen, pale optic disc, not a normal disc.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient has Bilateral right sided loss of vision. What is the most likely site of lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left optic tract

Bilateral right-sided loss of vision = Right homonymous hemianopia, which indicates a lesion posterior to the optic chiasma on the left side.

Localization logic:

• Right visual field (both eyes) is processed by the left visual pathway
• Lesions after the chiasma cause homonymous hemianopia

Most likely site: Left optic tract

Why not others:

• Right optic tract: Causes left homonymous hemianopia
• Optic chiasma: Causes bitemporal hemianopia
• Optic radiation: Can cause homonymous hemianopia but often with quadrantic defects depending on location

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with a pupil that does not react to light but constricts with a near stimulus. Where is the lesion most likely located?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pretectal area of Midbrain

Light–near dissociation (pupil does not react to light but constricts to accommodation) indicates a lesion in the pretectal area of the midbrain.

Pathophysiology:

• Light reflex pathway is interrupted at the pretectal nucleus
• Near reflex pathway bypasses pretectal area, so it remains intact

Clinical associations:

• Seen in Argyll Robertson pupil (neurosyphilis)
• Also in dorsal midbrain lesions

Why not others:

• Optic nerve → both light and near affected
• Edinger–Westphal nucleus → both reflexes lost
• Oculomotor nerve → no constriction at all

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with difficulty in left gaze; right gaze is normal, but on attempting left gaze, the right eye shows limited movement while the left eye exhibits nystagmus. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Right Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia

Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO) results from a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), which coordinates conjugate horizontal eye movements between the two eyes.

• On gaze toward the side opposite the lesion:

• Ipsilateral eye (to lesion) → impaired adduction
• Contralateral eye → abducting nystagmus

• Convergence is typically preserved (helps differentiate from 3rd nerve palsy)

In this question:

• Difficulty in left gaze
• Right eye fails to adduct + left eye shows nystagmus

→ Indicates right-sided MLF lesion → Right INO

Why not others:

• Thyroid eye disease: Restrictive myopathy, not abducting nystagmus pattern
• 3rd nerve palsy: Affects multiple movements + ptosis, pupil involvement
• Esotropia: Static deviation, not gaze-specific internuclear defect

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with the eyeball positioned down and out. Which cranial nerve palsy is most likely present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Third nerve palsy

Third nerve (oculomotor nerve) palsy results in a characteristic “down and out” eye position due to unopposed action of:

• Lateral rectus (CN VI) → abducts eye
• Superior oblique (CN IV) → depresses and intorts

Key features:

• Eye deviated down and out
• Ptosis (levator palpebrae paralysis)
• Dilated pupil (parasympathetic involvement)
• Loss of adduction, elevation, and depression

Why not others:

• Sixth nerve → only abduction defect
• Fourth nerve → vertical diplopia, head tilt
• Seventh nerve → facial muscle involvement

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with a pituitary macroadenoma causing compression of the optic chiasm now develops a characteristic pattern of visual disturbance. What type of visual field defect is expected in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bitemporal Hemianopia

Compression of the optic chiasm (classically by a pituitary macroadenoma) leads to bitemporal hemianopia due to involvement of decussating nasal retinal fibers.

• Nasal retinal fibers carry temporal visual field information
• These fibers cross at the optic chiasm
• Chiasmal compression → loss of both temporal fields

Clinical features:

• “Tunnel vision” (loss of peripheral vision)
• Difficulty with side vision (e.g., bumping into objects)

Visual pathway correlation:

• Optic nerve → monocular loss
• Optic chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia
• Optic tract → homonymous hemianopia

Why not others:

• A. Homonymous hemianopia → post-chiasmal lesion (optic tract/radiations)
• B. Superior quadrantanopia → temporal lobe (Meyer’s loop) lesion
• D. Macular sparing hemianopia → occipital cortex lesion

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A person is kept in a dark room for a prolonged period. Which of the following is correct regarding the physiology of dark adaptation (night vision)? 1. Conversion of retinal pigment to vitamin A 2. Increase in pupillary size 3. Increased sensitivity to light 4. Conversion of retinal and opsin to photosensitive pigment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2, 3 and 4

Dark adaptation is the process by which the eye becomes progressively more sensitive to low levels of illumination after entering a dark environment. It is primarily mediated by rod photoreceptors through regeneration of rhodopsin (visual purple).

During dark adaptation:

• Pupillary dilatation (mydriasis) increases the amount of light entering the eye.
• Regeneration of rhodopsin occurs by recombination of 11-cis retinal with opsin, increasing rod sensitivity.
• Sensitivity to light progressively increases, allowing vision in dim light.

Why is A correct?

• 2. Increase in pupillary size
• 3. Increased sensitivity to light
• 4. Conversion of retinal and opsin to photosensitive pigment (rhodopsin)

Why is 1 incorrect?

• Retinal is derived from vitamin A (retinol), not converted into vitamin A. During dark adaptation, vitamin A is converted to 11-cis retinal, which combines with opsin to regenerate rhodopsin.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Contralateral homonymous upper quadrantanopia is the type of visual loss seen when the lesion is located at which one of the following anatomical locations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Temporal lobe

A lesion involving the temporal lobe, specifically the Meyer’s loop (inferior optic radiations), produces a contralateral homonymous superior (upper) quadrantanopia, classically described as “pie in the sky” visual field defect.

The inferior retinal fibers, which carry information from the superior visual field, pass anteriorly through the temporal lobe (Meyer’s loop) before reaching the occipital cortex. Damage to these fibers results in loss of the contralateral upper visual field in both eyes.

Why not the other options?

• A. Frontal lobe: Does not contain the visual pathway responsible for quadrantanopia.
• C. Parietal lobe: Contains the superior optic radiations, and lesions produce contralateral homonymous lower quadrantanopia (“pie on the floor”).
• D. Occipital lobe: Lesions usually cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing if due to posterior cerebral artery infarction.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which cranial nerve provides sensory innervation to the orbit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trigeminal nerve

The sensory innervation of the orbit is provided by the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve (CN V).

• Trigeminal nerve (CN V) → main sensory nerve of the face

• Ophthalmic division (V1) supplies:

• Cornea (highly sensitive)
• Conjunctiva
• Eyelids
• Lacrimal gland
• Orbit and surrounding structures

Important branches of V1:

• Nasociliary nerve → corneal sensation (afferent limb of corneal reflex)
• Frontal nerve
• Lacrimal nerve

Why not others:

• Vagus nerve (CN X): Visceral functions, no orbital sensory role
• Oculomotor nerve (CN III): Motor to extraocular muscles + parasympathetic to pupil
• Facial nerve (CN VII): Motor to facial muscles; lacrimation (parasympathetic), but no sensory supply to orbit

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which defect is shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Homonymous hemianopia

Homonymous hemianopia is a visual field defect involving loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes (e.g., right half in both eyes).

• Occurs due to lesions posterior to the optic chiasm:

• Optic tract
• Lateral geniculate body
• Optic radiations
• Occipital cortex

Clinical interpretation:

• Right homonymous hemianopia → lesion in left visual pathway
• Left homonymous hemianopia → lesion in right visual pathway

Why not others:

• Bitemporal hemianopia: Chiasmal lesion (e.g., pituitary tumor)
• Binasal hemianopia: Rare, due to bilateral lateral retinal/optic nerve lesions
• Altitudinal defect: Seen in ischemic optic neuropathy

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which is not a feature of 3rd nerve palsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Abduction limitation

Oculomotor nerve (3rd nerve) palsy affects most extraocular muscles except lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV).

Typical features of 3rd nerve palsy:

• Ptosis → paralysis of levator palpebrae superioris
• Pupil dilatation (mydriasis) → loss of parasympathetic supply
• “Down and out” eye → unopposed action of lateral rectus and superior oblique
• Loss of adduction, elevation, and depression

Why D is correct (NOT a feature):

• Abduction is preserved because it is controlled by the lateral rectus (CN VI)
• Hence, no abduction limitation in isolated 3rd nerve palsy

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is/are true about optic neuritis? I. Proportionate loss of colour vision and contrast to visual acuity II. 70% cases of multiple sclerosis are affected III. Treatment is done by oral steroids IV. Optic neuritis presents with normal fundus or disc edema
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Only IV

I. Proportionate loss of colour vision and contrast to visual acuity : FALSE

• In optic neuritis, colour vision loss is disproportionately severe compared to visual acuity
• Especially red desaturation

II. 70% cases of multiple sclerosis are affected :FALSE

• Optic neuritis is common in MS, but:

• \~20-25% present with optic neuritis as first manifestation
• \~50% of MS patients develop optic neuritis during lifetime

III. Treatment is done by oral steroids :FALSE

• Based on Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT):

• IV methylprednisolone → speeds recovery
• Oral steroids alone are contraindicated (↑ recurrence risk)

IV. Optic neuritis presents with normal fundus or disc edema : TRUE

• Two forms:

• Retrobulbar neuritis → fundus normal (“patient sees nothing, doctor sees nothing”)
• Papillitis → disc edema present

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following patterns of visual field loss is seen in right optic tract lesion?
options: Right temporal and Left nasal vision loss
Right nasal and Left temporal vision loss
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right nasal and Left temporal vision loss

A lesion of the right optic tract (as shown) causes left homonymous hemianopia, i.e., loss of the left visual field of both eyes.

• Right eye: Loss of the nasal visual field
• Left eye: Loss of the temporal visual field

Hence, the visual field defect is right nasal + left temporal vision loss.

Why not the other options?

• A. Right temporal and Left nasal vision loss: Represents right homonymous hemianopia.
• C. Bilateral temporal vision loss: Bitemporal hemianopia, caused by optic chiasm lesions (e.g., pituitary adenoma).
• D. Bilateral nasal vision loss: Binasal hemianopia, rare; due to bilateral lateral optic chiasm compression.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following sensory receptors undergoes hyperpolarization rather than depolarization during sensory transduction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Photoreceptors of the retina

Photoreceptors are unique because exposure to light causes hyperpolarization. Light activates rhodopsin → transducin → phosphodiesterase, reducing intracellular cGMP. Closure of cGMP-gated Na⁺ channels decreases inward current, resulting in hyperpolarization and reduced glutamate release.

Other options:

• B. Cochlear hair cells: Depolarize when mechanically gated K⁺ channels open.
• C. Taste receptor cells: Most taste modalities produce depolarization.
• D. Olfactory receptor neurons: Odorants cause depolarization via cAMP-mediated Na⁺/Ca²⁺ influx.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which visual field defect is shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Enlarged blind spots

Enlarged blind spot-on visual field testing indicates pathology involving the optic nerve head or peripapillary retina.

• Enlargement of the normal physiological blind spot
• Seen temporal to fixation in visual field charts
• Often bilateral if due to raised intracranial pressure

Common causes:

• Papilledema (most important cause)
• Optic disc edema
• Optic neuritis (early)
• Peripapillary lesions

Why not others:

• Altitudinal defect: Seen in ischemic optic neuropathy
• Arcuate scotoma: Seen in glaucoma (follows nerve fiber layer)
• Nasal step (Roenne’s): Early glaucomatous defect

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: 22-year-old patient with high myopia presents with floaters in his eyes. What is the cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinal detachment

High myopia predisposes to retinal thinning and peripheral degenerations (e.g., lattice degeneration), increasing the risk of retinal tears and retinal detachment.

• Floaters (± flashes) in a young myopic patient → think retinal tear/detachment
• Caused by vitreoretinal traction leading to retinal break and separation

Pathophysiology:

• Elongated eyeball in myopia → stretched retina
• Degenerative changes → weak areas
• Vitreous traction → retinal tear → fluid accumulation → detachment

Why not others:

• Subarachnoid hemorrhage: Neurological symptoms, not isolated floaters
• Vitreous hemorrhage: Can cause floaters, but typically associated with diabetes/trauma
• Branch retinal artery occlusion: Causes sudden visual field defect, not floaters

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 1-year-old child who was born premature at 34 weeks POG weighing 1400 gms presents with leukocoria. On CT, intraocular calcification is seen. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Retinoblastoma

Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) + intraocular calcification on CT is highly suggestive of retinoblastoma, the most common intraocular malignancy in children.

• Intraocular calcification → hallmark of retinoblastoma
• Best detected on CT scan

Clinical features of retinoblastoma:

• Leukocoria (most common presenting sign)
• Strabismus
• Decreased vision
• May be unilateral or bilateral (bilateral often hereditary)

Why not others:

• ROP (Retinopathy of Prematurity):

• Occurs in premature infants but shows fibrovascular proliferation/retinal detachment, no calcification

• Congenital cataract:

• Leukocoria present, but no calcification

• Coats disease:

• Retinal telangiectasia with exudation
• Can mimic leukocoria but no calcification

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy presents with mental retardation and an inability to walk. The fundoscopy image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tay-Sachs disease

Tay–Sachs disease is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by hexosaminidase A deficiency, leading to accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neurons.

• Developmental delay / regression
• Hypotonia → inability to walk
• Exaggerated startle response
• Progressive neurodegeneration

Fundoscopy finding:

• Cherry red spot at macula with surrounding retinal pallor (due to ganglion cell accumulation)

Important distinction:

• Tay–Sachs → no hepatosplenomegaly
• Gaucher / Niemann–Pick → organomegaly present

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 60-year-old patient presents with sudden onset flashes of light and floaters. Fundus examination is as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment

Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) is the most common type of retinal detachment and occurs due to a full-thickness retinal break (tear or hole) that allows liquefied vitreous to enter the subretinal space, separating the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium.

The image shows a horseshoe (U-shaped) retinal tear with an elevated, corrugated retina, which is characteristic of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

• Sudden flashes of light (photopsia)
• Floaters
• Curtain or shadow descending over the visual field
• Painless, progressive loss of vision
• Risk factors: Posterior vitreous detachment, high myopia, trauma, previous cataract surgery, lattice degeneration
• Treatment: Urgent retinal repair with laser photocoagulation/cryopexy, pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckle, or pars plana vitrectomy, depending on the case.

Differentiating the Types of Retinal Detachment

• Rhegmatogenous: Retinal tear present; flashes and floaters are common.
• Tractional: Due to fibrovascular membranes (e.g., proliferative diabetic retinopathy); no retinal tear.
• Exudative (serous): Fluid accumulates without a tear or traction (e.g., tumors, inflammation, VKH).
• CRVO: “Blood-and-thunder” fundus with widespread retinal hemorrhages, not retinal elevation or

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 65 year old male patient presented with sudden, painful diminution of vision, difficulty in vision in light, and circumferential congestion with hypopyon as shown. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute Anterior Uveitis

Acute anterior uveitis (iritis) presents with painful red eye, photophobia, decreased vision, and circumcorneal (ciliary) congestion, often with cells, flare, and hypopyon in the anterior chamber.

• Circumcorneal congestion (ciliary flush)
• Photophobia (difficulty in light)
• Pain + decreased vision
• Small, irregular pupil (due to sphincter spasm/posterior synechiae)
• Hypopyon (in severe inflammation)

Pathophysiology:

• Inflammation of iris and ciliary body
• Breakdown of blood-aqueous barrier → cells & protein (flare) in AC

Why not others:

• Acute glaucoma: Mid-dilated pupil, steamy cornea, very high IOP
• Conjunctivitis: Diffuse redness, discharge, no photophobia or hypopyon
• Episcleritis: Mild discomfort, localized redness, no AC reaction

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 70-year-old patient presents with distant visual acuity of 6/18, which improved on pin-hole testing. On ocular examination findings as shown in image were seen. Patient has which of the following refractory error.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Index Myopia

Index myopia is caused by an increase in the refractive index of the lens, most commonly due to nuclear sclerosis (early cataract).

• Elderly patient with decreased distance vision (6/18)
• Improves with pinhole → refractive error
• Improved near vision (“second sight”) → hallmark of nuclear cataract
• Slit lamp: nuclear sclerosis

Pathophysiology:

• Increased lens density → ↑ refractive index
• Light bends more → image shifts in front of retina → myopia

Why not others:

• Axial myopia: Due to increased eyeball length
• Curvatural myopia: Due to increased curvature (cornea/lens)
• Positional myopia: Due to forward displacement of lens

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A child presented with hydrocephalus, intracranial calcification, and bilateral chorioretinitis. What can be the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Congenital Toxoplasmosis

Congenital toxoplasmosis classically presents with the triad of:

• Hydrocephalus
• Intracranial calcifications (diffuse)
• Chorioretinitis

Etiology: Caused by transplacental infection with Toxoplasma gondii (often from undercooked meat or cat feces exposure in mother)

• Diffuse intracranial calcifications (vs periventricular in CMV)
• Severe ocular involvement → chorioretinitis
• May also have seizures, developmental delay

Why not others:

• Congenital rubella: Cataract, PDA, deafness
• Congenital syphilis: Hutchinson teeth, saddle nose, interstitial keratitis
• Gonorrhea: Neonatal conjunctivitis, not CNS involvement

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A child presented with leukocoria and an intraocular mass. On microscopic examination, following appearance was seen. The mass was also positive for synaptophysin. The diagnosis can be:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Retinoblastoma

Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy of childhood, classically presenting with leukocoria.

• Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes on histology

• Tumor cells arranged around a central lumen
• Indicative of photoreceptor differentiation

• Scant cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei
• Immunopositivity for synaptophysin → confirms neuroectodermal origin

Clinical clues:

• Leukocoria
• Strabismus
• Intraocular mass ± calcification (on imaging)

Why not others:

• Medulloblastoma / Pinealoblastoma: CNS tumors (may show rosettes but not intraocular mass)
• Retinal detachment: No tumor cells or rosettes

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A diabetic patient presented to you with visual acuity of 6/9 in one eye. Further investigations revealed pre-retinal hemorrhages with neovascularization at the optic disc. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pan-retinal photocoagulation

Neovascularization at the disc (NVD) with preretinal hemorrhage = Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), which requires urgent treatment.

Management of choice: Pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP)

• Causes regression of neovascularization
• Reduces risk of vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment

Pathophysiology:

• Retinal ischemia → ↑ VEGF → abnormal fragile new vessels
• These vessels bleed → preretinal/vitreous hemorrhage

Why not others:

• Focal laser: For macular edema
• Grid laser: For diffuse macular edema
• Scleral buckling: For rhegmatogenous retinal detachment

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient develops bilateral ocular inflammation following a penetrating injury to one eye. Examination shows granulomatous keratic precipitates and vitritis. Which type of uveitis is most characteristic?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Panuveitis

Sympathetic ophthalmia is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis that occurs after penetrating ocular injury or surgery to one eye, leading to an autoimmune reaction against uveal antigens.

• Bilateral involvement (injured eye + sympathizing eye)
• Granulomatous inflammation (mutton-fat keratic precipitates)
• Panuveitis → involvement of anterior chamber, vitreous, and choroid
• Dalen–Fuchs nodules (yellow-white lesions at RPE)

Pathophysiology:

• Exposure of uveal antigens after trauma → T-cell mediated autoimmune response

Why not others:

• Anterior uveitis (acute/chronic): Only anterior segment involved.
• Pars planitis: Intermediate uveitis (vitreous + pars plana).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient is prescribed a corrective lens with the following prescription: -1D spherical, -2D cylinder at 180 degrees. What type of refractive error is being corrected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. With the rule astigmatism

A prescription of −1 D sphere with −2 D cylinder at axis 180° indicates compound myopic astigmatism with a with-the-rule (WTR) axis.

Concept of axis:

• Cylinder axis at 180° (±20°) → with-the-rule astigmatism
• Steepest meridian is vertical (90°)
• Horizontal meridian is flatter

Interpretation of this prescription:

• Both meridians are myopic (because sphere and cylinder are negative)
• Difference in power between meridians → astigmatism
• Axis 180° → with-the-rule

Why not others:

• Against-the-rule: Axis around 90°
• Simple astigmatism: Only one meridian affected (not here)
• Mixed astigmatism: One meridian myopic, other hypermetropic

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient of rheumatic heart disease who is noncompliant with treatment presents with complaints of superior field vision loss for the past 1 week. What is the probable cause of the given condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Branched retinal artery occlusion

A patient with rheumatic heart disease (RHD) presenting with a superior visual field defect of one-week duration is most consistent with branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO).

Retinal arterial occlusions are typically caused by embolic events, where emboli travel from the cardiac or proximal arterial circulation to the ophthalmic artery and its branches. In RHD, the source is often cardiac thrombus, producing platelet–fibrin emboli.

Why other options are unlikely

• Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO): Causes sudden, profound, painless loss of vision, not a localized field defect. Vision is typically markedly reduced (counting fingers or worse).
• Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO): Presents with diffuse retinal involvement, “blood and thunder” appearance, and global visual blurring, not sectoral field loss.
• Branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO): Causes sectoral hemorrhages and edema, but is usually associated with venous risk factors (HTN, atherosclerosis) and produces less sharply demarcated field defects compared to arterial occlusion.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with bilateral sudden onset painless vision loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diabetic retinopathy

Sudden, painless, bilateral vision loss is most commonly due to vitreous hemorrhage secondary to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR).

• Chronic hyperglycemia → retinal ischemia
• ↑ VEGF → neovascularization
• Fragile new vessels rupture → vitreous hemorrhage → sudden vision loss

Painless + sudden + bilateral → think vascular cause, especially diabetes

Why not others:

• Iridocyclitis (anterior uveitis): Painful, photophobia, redness
• Acute congestive glaucoma: Severe pain, halos, red eye, high IOP
• Keratoconus: Gradual, progressive visual decline (not sudden)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with gradual loss of night vision and peripheral vision. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for these symptoms according to the given fundoscopic image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinitis Pigmentosa

Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a progressive rod–cone dystrophy presenting with:

• Early night blindness (nyctalopia) due to primary degeneration of rod photoreceptors
• Progressive peripheral visual field loss → tunnel vision due to later involvement of cones

Fundoscopic features (classic triad):

• Bone spicule pigmentation in mid-periphery
• Attenuated (narrow) retinal vessels
• Waxy pallor of optic disc

Why not others:

• Fundus flavimaculatus (Stargardt): Yellow pisciform flecks, central vision loss
• Retinal hemorrhage: Acute condition, not progressive night blindness
• Fundus albipunctatus: White dots but stationary night blindness, not progressive

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with ocular pain, redness, and blurred vision. On slit-lamp examination, the pupil is shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Posterior synechiae due to anterior uveitis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Posterior synechiae due to anterior uveitis

Posterior synechiae are adhesions between the posterior surface of the iris and the anterior lens capsule, most commonly resulting from anterior uveitis (iritis/iridocyclitis). These adhesions produce an irregular, distorted ("festooned") pupil that responds poorly to light and dilating agents. If circumferential (360°), they may cause seclusio pupillae, leading to iris bombe and secondary angle-closure glaucoma.

Why not the other options?

• B. Acute angle-closure glaucoma – Typically presents with a mid-dilated, vertically oval, fixed pupil, not an irregular pupil due to iris–lens adhesions.
• C. Adie’s tonic pupil – Characterized by a large, regular pupil with poor light reaction but preserved slow constriction during near response (light-near dissociation). There are no synechiae.
• D. Oculomotor nerve palsy – Causes a dilated, fixed pupil associated with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia, but the pupil remains round, not irregular.

High-yield pearl

• Irregular pupil → Think posterior synechiae (anterior uveitis).

Differentiate common pupillary abnormalities:

| Condition | Characteristic pupil

| --------- | --------------------

| Anterior uveitis | Irregular, constricted pupil due to posterior synechiae

| Acute angle-closure glaucoma | Mid-dilated, fixed, often vertically oval pupil

| Adie’s tonic pupil | Large, regular pupil with light-near dissociation

| Oculomotor nerve palsy | Dilated, fixed, round pupil with ptosis and "down-and-out" eye

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with the ocular deviation as shown in the image. What is the degree of deviation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 90 PD Exotropia

Ocular deviation is quantified in prism diopters (PD), not degrees.

• Exotropia = outward deviation of the eye
• Esotropia = inward deviation

A deviation of 90 PD exotropia represents a large-angle outward squint, commonly seen in conditions like long-standing sensory strabismus or third nerve palsy.

Key concept:

• 1 PD = deviation of 1 cm at 1 meter
• Clinical measurement of strabismus is always expressed in prism diopters, not degrees

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with an acute subarachnoid hemorrhage is found to have associated vitreous/intraocular hemorrhage on ophthalmological examination. What is this association known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Terson syndrome

Terson syndrome refers to intraocular hemorrhage associated with acute intracranial hemorrhage, classically subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).

The ocular hemorrhage may occur at different levels, including:

• Vitreous hemorrhage
• Subhyaloid/preretinal hemorrhage
• Intraretinal hemorrhage

It is classically described following aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, although it may also occur with other causes of sudden severe intracranial hemorrhage or raised intracranial pressure.

Why not the other options?

• B. Duane syndrome: Congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder characterized by limitation of horizontal eye movements with globe retraction and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on adduction.
• C. Brown syndrome: Characterized by restriction of elevation of the eye in adduction due to dysfunction of the superior oblique tendon–trochlea complex.
• D. Tolosa–Hunt syndrome: Causes painful ophthalmoplegia due to granulomatous inflammation involving the cavernous sinus, superior orbital fissure, or orbital apex.

Educational Objective:

• Remember the classic association:

• Subarachnoid hemorrhage + intraocular/vitreous hemorrhage → Terson syndrome

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with known myopia presents with complaints of floaters and flashes of light. On examination, the anterior chamber appears deep. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment

Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) occurs due to a retinal break/tear, allowing vitreous fluid to accumulate under the retina.

• Flashes (photopsia) + floaters
• Sudden, painless vision loss
• Common in myopia (predisposition to retinal thinning/tears)
• Deep anterior chamber (seen in high myopes)

Pathophysiology:

• Vitreous traction → retinal tear → fluid enters subretinal space → detachment

Why not others:

• Exudative RD → no flashes/floaters (no tear)
• Tractional RD → seen in diabetes, gradual
• CSR → central vision distortion, no flashes

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All of the following are causes of acute red eye, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Retinitis

Retinitis is primarily a disease of the retina and does not typically present as an acute red eye.

The other conditions commonly cause acute ocular redness:

• (a) Keratitis — Correct association: Corneal inflammation causes pain, photophobia, redness and reduced vision.
• (b) Retinitis — Incorrect association → Answer: Usually presents with visual disturbances, floaters or loss of vision rather than a red eye.
• (c) Episcleritis — Correct association: Produces localized sectoral redness, usually with mild discomfort.
• (d) Uveitis — Correct association: Anterior uveitis commonly causes pain, photophobia, blurred vision and ciliary congestion.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Arrange the following layers of the retina in the correct order from the outermost to the innermost layer.
options: 1 – Retinal Pigment Epithelium, 2 – Outer Nuclear Layer, 3 – Inner Plexiform Layer, 4 – Ganglion Cell Layer
1 – Outer Nuclear Layer, 2 – Retinal Pigment Epithelium, 3 – Ganglion Cell Layer, 4 – Inner Plexiform Layer
1 – Ganglion Cell Layer, 2 – Inner Plexiform Layer, 3 – Retinal Pigment Epithelium, 4 – Outer Nuclear Layer
1 – Retinal Pigment Epithelium, 2 – Inner Plexiform Layer, 3 – Outer Nuclear Layer, 4 – Ganglion Cell Layer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 – Retinal Pigment Epithelium, 2 – Outer Nuclear Layer, 3 – Inner Plexiform Layer, 4 – Ganglion Cell Layer

The retina is organized from outer (choroid side) to inner (vitreous side) in a highly structured manner that reflects the flow of visual information.

Correct order (outer → inner):

1. Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE)
2. Outer Nuclear Layer (photoreceptor cell bodies)
3. Inner Plexiform Layer (synapses between bipolar & ganglion cells)
4. Ganglion Cell Layer

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: As per the National Blindness and Visual Impairment Survey India (2015–2019), which one of the following is the most common cause of blindness in India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cataract (untreated)

According to the National Blindness and Visual Impairment Survey India (2015–2019), untreated cataract was the most common cause of blindness in India.

Why not the other options?

• (a) Glaucoma: An important cause of irreversible blindness, but less common than untreated cataract.
• (b) Diabetic retinopathy: An important cause of visual impairment, particularly with increasing diabetes prevalence, but not the leading cause of blindness in this survey.
• (c) Untreated refractive error: A major cause of visual impairment, but not the most common cause of blindness.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Consider the following causes of visual loss: 1. Obstruction of the central retinal artery 2. Vitreous and retinal haemorrhage 3. Cataract 4. Retinal detachment Which of the above causes are associated with acute visual loss in a patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

Acute visual loss is an ophthalmic emergency that requires prompt evaluation to prevent permanent blindness. Common causes include vascular occlusion, vitreous hemorrhage, and retinal detachment, whereas cataract typically causes gradual, progressive visual impairment.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Obstruction of the central retinal artery ✅

• Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) presents with sudden, painless, severe monocular vision loss and a characteristic cherry-red spot on fundus examination.

• 2. Vitreous and retinal haemorrhage ✅

• Sudden bleeding into the vitreous or retina causes acute painless visual loss or the sudden appearance of floaters and a curtain-like visual defect.

• 3. Cataract ❌

• Cataract causes gradual, painless, progressive diminution of vision, not acute visual loss.

• 4. Retinal detachment ✅

• Presents with sudden onset of flashes, floaters, and a curtain descending over the visual field, leading to acute painless visual loss.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During retinoscopy, the reflex is neutralized as shown in the image. What is the value of the cylindrical correction required to correct this patient’s astigmatism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. +2 cylindrical correction

In retinoscopy for astigmatism, the cylindrical power required equals the difference between the neutralizing powers of the two principal meridians.

• One principal meridian neutralizes at +2 D
• The other neutralizes at +4 D
• Cylindrical power = 4 D − 2 D = +2 D

Therefore, the required cylindrical correction is +2 D (axis determined by the meridian requiring the least plus power).

High-Yield Points

• Cylinder power = Difference between the refractive powers of the two principal meridians.
• Sphere = Power of the least ametropic meridian (after adjusting for working distance).
• Axis = Along the meridian with the least refractive power (least plus/most minus).
• Always subtract the working distance lens (commonly 1.5 D for 67 cm or 2.0 D for 50 cm) from the final retinoscopy result before prescribing.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Given below are some tests for visual acuity. Which of these is used for a pre-verbal child? 1. ETDRS chart 2. Optokinetic nystagmus 3. Teller’s visual acuity chart 4. Landolt’s C chart
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2 and 3

Assessment of visual acuity in pre-verbal children relies on objective or preferential looking methods, since they cannot recognize letters or communicate responses.\

Correct tests:

• Optokinetic nystagmus (OKN):

• Based on reflex eye movements elicited by moving striped patterns
• Presence of nystagmus indicates that the child can perceive the stimulus

• Teller’s visual acuity cards:

• Use preferential looking principle (child looks toward striped pattern vs blank field)
• Allows estimation of visual acuity without verbal response

Why others are incorrect:

• ETDRS chart:

• Standardized letter chart → requires reading ability
• Used in cooperative older children/adults

• Landolt’s C chart:

• Requires identifying the gap direction → needs cognitive/verbal response
• Not suitable for preverbal children

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In evaluating a patient with nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), which of the following findings would be atypical for a classification of 'very severe’?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neovascularization of disc

Very severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) is defined by the “4-2-1 rule”:

• 4 quadrants of severe retinal hemorrhages/microaneurysms
• 2 quadrants of venous beading
• 1 quadrant of IRMA (intraretinal microvascular abnormalities)

These findings indicate severe ischemia but WITHOUT neovascularization.

| NPDR Severity Level | Findings on Dilated Eye Exam

| ------------------- | ----------------------------

| Mild NPDR | Microaneurysms only

| Moderate NPDR | Microaneurysms with additional findings (dot & blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots), but less than severe NPDR

| Severe NPDR | Any one of the following (4-2-1 rule) and no signs of proliferative DR:• ≥20 intraretinal hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants• Venous beading in ≥2 quadrants• IRMA in ≥1 quadrant

| Very Severe NPDR | Any two of the 4-2-1 rule features

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In fluorescein angiography, how do microaneurysms typically appear?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hyperfluorescent dots

In fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA), microaneurysms—the earliest clinically visible lesions in diabetic retinopathy—appear as multiple small hyperfluorescent dots.

Why they appear hyperfluorescent:

• Microaneurysms are outpouchings of capillary walls
• They fill with fluorescein dye → appear as bright pinpoint spots in early phases

Important distinction:

• Microaneurysms:

• Early hyperfluorescence (dots)
• May show late leakage

• Leakage (e.g., macular edema, neovascularization):

• Progressive increase in size and intensity over time

• Hypofluorescence (dark areas):

• Due to blockage (hemorrhage) or capillary non-perfusion

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Match the lens with their respective correction factor:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-c, 2-a, 3-b, 4-d

Indirect ophthalmoscopy lenses differ in their magnification and field of view. Since these lenses alter the apparent size of retinal lesions, correction factors are used to estimate the true retinal dimensions during fundus examination and laser treatment.

Correct Match:

• 1. Volk 60 D → c. 1.15×
• 2. Volk 90 D → a. 0.76×
• 3. Volk 78 D → b. 0.93×
• 4. Goldmann 3-mirror → d. 0.9–1.1×

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Patient can see 3 green dots on the Worth’s 4 dots test. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. RE suppression

Worth’s 4-dot test assesses binocular single vision, suppression, and diplopia using red–green goggles. Interpretation principle:

• Red glass (right eye) → sees red dots
• Green glass (left eye) → sees green dots

In this case: Patient sees 3 green dots only

→ Only left eye (green filter) is functioning

→ Right eye image is suppressed

Key interpretations:

• 4 dots (2 green + 1 red + 1 yellow) → Normal fusion
• 3 green dots → Right eye suppression
• 2 red dots → Left eye suppression
• 5 dots → Diplopia

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Retinal ischaemia, flame-shaped haemorrhages and cotton-wool exudates are fundoscopy findings in which of the following grades of hypertensive retinopathy? 1. Grade 1 2. Grade 2 3. Grade 3 4. Grade 4 Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3 and 4 only

Using the Keith–Wagener–Barker classification of hypertensive retinopathy:

• Grade 1: Mild generalized arteriolar narrowing
• Grade 2: Grade 1 + arteriovenous (AV) crossing changes
• Grade 3: Grade 2 + retinal hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and retinal exudates
• Grade 4: Grade 3 + papilledema

Therefore, retinal ischemia, flame-shaped hemorrhages, and cotton-wool exudates are features of Grade 3 and Grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the approximate amplitude of accommodation in a 7-year-old child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 14 D

Amplitude of accommodation is the maximum increase in the refractive power of the eye that allows focusing on near objects. It is highest in childhood and progressively declines with age due to reduced elasticity of the crystalline lens (presbyopia). A 7-year-old child has an approximate amplitude of accommodation of 14 diopters (D).

Why not the other options?

• A. 7 D: Typical of middle age (around 45 years), not childhood.
• B. 12 D: Lower than the expected value for a 7-year-old.
• D. 10 D: Seen in older children or young adults, not at 7 years.

| Age | Amplitude of Accommodation

| --- | --------------------------

| 7 years | ≈14 D

| 10 years | ≈13 D

| 20 years | ≈10 D

| 40 years | ≈5 D

| 50 years | ≈2 D

| 60 years | ≈1 D

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the definition of blindness as per NPCB, India?
options: Vision less than 6/60 in better eye after best possible correction
Presenting vision less than 3/60 in better eye
Best corrected vision less than 3/60 in better eye
Vision less than 6/60 in better eye after correction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Presenting vision less than 3/60 in better eye

As per the National Programme for Control of Blindness (NPCB), India, blindness is defined as:

• Presenting visual acuity < 3/60 in the better eye

Important concepts:

• Presenting vision = vision with available correction (current glasses if any), not best possible correction
• NPCB uses this definition for public health screening and program implementation

Contrast with WHO definition:

• WHO defines blindness as best corrected visual acuity < 3/60 in the better eye
• NPCB uses a more practical, field-based definition (presenting vision)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the minutes of arc subtended by a standard letter of the chart shown in the image with 20/20 visual acuity line?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5 minutes

A standard Snellen chart letter (optotype) on the 20/20 (6/6) line subtends an angle of 5 minutes of arc, while each individual stroke (thickness of the letter) subtends 1 minute of arc at the testing distance. Visual acuity depends on the ability to resolve the 1-minute arc detail.

High-Yield Facts

• 20/20 (6/6): Letter subtends 5 minutes of arc.
• Minimum angle of resolution (MAR): 1 minute of arc.
• Visual acuity = 1/MAR

• 6/6 → MAR = 1
• 6/12 → MAR = 2
• 6/60 → MAR = 10

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the normal arteriovenous ratio at the optic disc?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2:3

The normal arteriovenous (A:V) ratio at the optic disc is 2:3, meaning:

• Retinal arteries are narrower
• Retinal veins are wider

Clinical significance:

• This ratio is an important indicator of retinal vascular health

• Arteriolar narrowing (↓ A:V ratio) is seen in:

• Hypertensive retinopathy
• Chronic vascular diseases

• Associated signs:

• AV nicking
• Copper/silver wiring of arteries

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which investigation is best used to visualize the inner layers of the retina in vivo?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Optical Coherence Tomography

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is the best non-invasive imaging modality to visualize the retinal microstructure in vivo, providing high-resolution cross-sectional images of the individual retinal layers.

• Uses low-coherence interferometry (light waves)
• Produces micron-level resolution images (like “optical biopsy”)

OCT shows Individual retinal layers (RNFL, photoreceptors, RPE)

Why not others:

• Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA):

• Evaluates retinal vasculature and leakage, not layers

• USG B-scan:

• Useful when media is opaque (e.g., vitreous hemorrhage, RD)
• Poor resolution for retinal layers

• Ophthalmoscope:

• Surface visualization only
• Cannot provide cross-sectional layer detail

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which is the investigation of choice for Best disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Electrooculogram (EOG)

Best disease (Vitelliform macular dystrophy) is characterized by dysfunction of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and the investigation of choice is Electrooculogram (EOG).

• Measures RPE function
• Shows reduced Arden ratio (↓ light peak to dark trough ratio)
• Abnormal even in early disease, before fundus changes are obvious

Why not others:

• ERG (Electroretinogram):

• Assesses photoreceptor function
• Usually normal in Best disease

• VEP (Visual Evoked Potential):

• Evaluates visual pathway beyond retina
• Not specific for macular dystrophies

• Multifocal ERG:

• Can detect macular dysfunction but not the primary diagnostic test

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following correctly describes the primary position of the right eye in right 3rd cranial nerve palsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Downwards and outwards

In oculomotor (3rd cranial nerve) palsy, the lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) muscles remain unopposed because they are not supplied by the oculomotor nerve. As a result, the affected eye assumes a “down and out” position due to the combined actions of:

• Lateral rectus → abducts the eye (outwards)
• Superior oblique → depresses the eye, especially in the adducted position (downwards)

Associated features of complete 3rd nerve palsy include:

• Ptosis due to paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris.
• Diplopia (double vision).
• Mydriasis and loss of accommodation if parasympathetic fibers are involved (pupil-involving 3rd nerve palsy).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in an inner segment of the photoreceptor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Disc

Disc membranes are specifically located in the outer segment of the photoreceptor, not the inner segment.

The inner segment contains most cellular organelles, including:

• Mitochondria
• Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
• Golgi apparatus
• Nucleus

The outer segment is characterized by the presence of disc membranes, which are crucial for phototransduction.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is not the treatment of amblyopia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Strabismus Surgery

Amblyopia (“lazy eye”) is a developmental decrease in visual acuity due to abnormal visual experience during the critical period, and treatment aims to improve visual input and force use of the amblyopic eye.

• Amblyopia treatment aims to improve visual acuity by stimulating the weaker eye, not just correcting alignment.

Actual treatments of amblyopia:

• Occlusion therapy (patching) → gold standard
• Refractive error correction → spectacles/contact lenses
• Penalization (e.g., atropine)
• Video games / perceptual learning → newer adjunct (especially dichoptic therapy)

WhyStrabismus surgeryis NOT a treatment:

• It corrects ocular alignment (cosmesis + binocular function)
• Does NOT directly improve amblyopia
• Amblyopia must be treated before or along with surgery, not by surgery itself

First vision is fixed amblyopia), then alignment (strabismus)”.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is typically seen in diabetic retinopathy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tractional retinal detachment

Diabetic retinopathy, especially in its advanced stage (proliferative diabetic retinopathy, PDR), is characterized by neovascularization and fibrovascular proliferation, which can lead to tractional retinal detachment (TRD).

• Chronic hyperglycemia → retinal ischemia
• ↑ VEGF → new fragile vessels form
• Associated fibrous tissue contracts → pulls retina away → TRD

Why not others:

• Myopic refractive error: Related to axial elongation, not diabetes
• Posterior staphyloma: Seen in pathological myopia
• Retinoschisis: Splitting of retinal layers, unrelated to diabetic changes

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following refractory condition is depicted in the figure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Astigmatism

Astigmatism is a refractive error caused by unequal curvature of the cornea or lens, leading to different refractive powers in different meridians.

• Light rays do not converge to a single focal point
• Instead, they form two focal lines (line foci) at different planes ; This results in a blurred or distorted image

Types:

• Regular astigmatism: Principal meridians perpendicular
• Irregular astigmatism: Non-orthogonal meridians (e.g., keratoconus)

Correction:

• Cylindrical lenses (spectacles/contact lenses)
• Refractive surgery (LASIK, etc.)

Why not others:

• Myopia: Image forms in front of retina
• Hypermetropia: Image forms behind retina
• Presbyopia: Loss of accommodation with age

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following stages of binocular vision does this image represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fusion

Binocular single vision (BSV) is achieved through three sequential components:

1. Simultaneous Macular Perception :

• Ability to perceive two different images from both eyes at the same time
• Example: each eye sees a different part of an image

2. Fusion:

• Brain combines the two images into one single image
• Requires proper ocular alignment

3. Stereopsis:

• Highest level → depth perception (3D vision)
• Based on slight disparity between images from two eyes

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statement is incorrect about Retinitis Pigmentosa?
options: It primarily affects rod photoreceptors in early stages
Peripheral field loss typically precedes central vision loss
Electroretinography shows reduced a- and b-wave amplitudes
Nyctalopia is a late manifestation of the disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Nyctalopia is a late manifestation of the disease

Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) is a progressive rod–cone dystrophy in which rod photoreceptors are affected first, followed later by cones.

• Early feature:

• Night blindness (nyctalopia) due to rod dysfunction

• Progression:

• Peripheral visual field loss → “tunnel vision”

• Late stage:

• Central vision loss (cone involvement)

Investigations:

• ERG: Shows reduced or extinguished a- and b-wave amplitudes (early diagnostic test)

Why option D is incorrect:

• Night blindness is NOT a late feature
• It is the earliest and most characteristic symptom

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which type of complication is most commonly associated with advanced diabetic retinopathy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tractional retinal detachment

In advanced diabetic retinopathy (proliferative diabetic retinopathy, PDR), the most common complication is tractional retinal detachment (TRD).

• Chronic retinal ischemia → VEGF release
• Formation of neovascularization (on disc and elsewhere)
• These vessels are associated with fibrovascular proliferation
• Contraction of these membranes → pulls the retina → tractional detachment

Why not others:

• Rhegmatogenous RD:

• Caused by retinal tear + vitreous fluid entry
• Not the primary mechanism in diabetic retinopathy

• Exudative RD:

• Due to fluid accumulation without traction/tear (e.g., tumors, inflammation)
• Not typical of diabetes

• No retinal detachment:

• Incorrect, as TRD is a well-known late complication
